May there be prosperity.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇapati.
The Nāṭyaśāstra,
Chapter Nineteen.
(The Definition of the Junctures):
The plot is proclaimed to be the body of drama;
its division is conceived through five junctures. (1)
Abhinavabhāratī, Chapter Nineteen:
That which is the establishment [of the Self] within the entire body, together with its joints and limbs, which effects the function of touch;
I bow to that Great Lord, the Maheśa, whose body consists of the sense-faculties and who is composed of internal touch.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "the arrangement of its body" (18.127), the *śarīra*— which consists of the plot (*itivṛtta*)—
and its *vidhāna*, which consists of the modes of that arrangement, as well as the *sandhis*, such as the *mukha* and others, and the *vidhis*,
which are the *sandhyaṅgas* by nature, are proposed as the subjects to be defined; among these, the *śarīra* comes first.
He shows that it is to be characterized by the words "but the plot" (*itivṛttaṃ tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction:

for poetry in general that is not intended for performance, the body is merely the plot; however, for that which is to be performed, whose form is to be enacted, it is the plot embellished in such a manner. Therefore—
That substance which is denoted by the term *itivṛtta* is the body, whereas the *rasas* are the soul;
thus, the wise man should conceive of *itivṛtta* as being twofold. (p. 2)
One [chapter] would be primary (ādhikārika), and another would be incidental (prāsaṅgika). || 2 ||

Words, which are of the nature of speech, manifest the body [of the object]; for this very reason, because they bring about the object, because of their identity with the object, because of the superimposition of the form of the object, because they are established within a single cognition with the object, because they color the object, or because they are the cause of the object, words share the same acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) as the object through their connection with the narrative content.

With that intention, it was stated previously: "That which must reside in speech is known as the body of drama" (Nāṭyaśāstra 14.2); here, however, it is shown that the *vṛtta* (plot) is the body, so there is no contradiction. But how is that [so]?
Anticipating the objection that there is a lack of variety in types, he says, "by means of five junctures" (*pañcabhiḥ sandhibhiḥ*). This is what is meant:

the junctures consist merely of the conceptualization of a variety of types. In that regard, the number five is established through a traditional succession; therefore, even though there may be fewer junctures, there is no contradiction here.

Others, however, maintain that there are only five types of junctures (*sandhi*) everywhere; yet, because a particular juncture lacks its full constituent parts, it is termed a "deficient juncture" (*hīnasandhi*). We shall elaborate on this in its proper place.
Thus, considering that the meaning of the portion of the word *itivṛtta* is not well-known, [the author] proceeds with the second half [of the verse].

This has been explained by the passage beginning with "by five," but this is not a definitive determination of the *sandhi* (junctures), because its varieties are manifold. Having thus described the body, [the author now discusses] its diversity of modes, which was indicated by the term "arrangement" (*vidhāna*).

"He shows that the plot is indeed twofold. The wise, discerning poet should conceive the established plot in exactly two ways; by the word "and" (ca), he implies that one should also conceive the plot in a *prakaraṇa* and other such forms.
And that is twofold. By the terms "one" and "the other," he says this: nothing is inherently either a primary plot (*ādhikārika*) or otherwise.
That which has been composed as the primary subject matter (*adhikārika*) by the poet's intention possesses a secondary, incidental character (*prāsaṅgikatā*);
this is indicated by the word "twofold" (*dvidhā*), and that very point is now demonstrated. Furthermore, [this is supported] by the rule *adhikaraṇavicāle ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.43).
(Page 3)

That action which is inferred by its capacity to bring about a specific result is to be known as *adhikārika* (pertaining to the primary purpose); others know that which is different from this to be *prāsaṅgika* (incidental).
Due to the connection with the result of the cause, there would be an "adhikārika" (pertaining to a specific office or topic) narrative;
this refers to the suffix *dhā*. For example, as in the command "divide one heap into two," by that [act], the very same single event becomes two-branched, so to speak.

He shows those two types in sequence with the words "that which is the effect" (*yatkāryaṃ hi*). An undertaking characterized by knowledge, desire, effort, and action, directed toward a fruit to be accomplished as the primary goal, is what will be called "the effect"—namely, that which is the subject matter of the qualification (*yadādhikārikaṃ vastu*, 19.26). Such an undertaking [is fulfilled] through the attainment of the principal fruit.

That is conceptualized as the *ādhikārika* (principal) plot; for it must be understood exactly in that way. By etymology (*nirukta*), *adhikāra* means "pervasive presence everywhere" or "presence in the heart," and this constitutes its purpose.
For even in the incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) plot, that [purpose] is indeed contained within it. As in the case of the *ādhikārika*.

Just as when the desire to communicate is accomplished by means of the desire to speak, there is no operation of another power (*śakti*) for the completion of the desire to convey the fruit [of the action], so too in every incidental case (*prāsaṅgika*),
there is likewise an absence of the operation of another power. This is because even if another power were to be operated separately, [it would be redundant].
Even that [the slaying of Rāvaṇa] would merely be a subordinate purpose (*adhikārika*). For even the fulfillment of the initial vow,

the removal of Rāvaṇa who was a thorn to the world, and the protection of Vibhīṣaṇa who had sought refuge— these too are not intended as the primary fruit, since the intended primary fruit is characterized by the recovery of Sītā.

However, even that which is to be accomplished through the operation of another power is brought about as an invariable concomitant of the performance of the four means— conciliation and the rest— which are useful for it, along with their various combinations of two, three, and so forth;
this is the case when the restoration of the kingdom is the primary fruit in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*.

In cases such as the union with Vāsavadattā and the attainment of Padmāvatī, it must be understood that there is no utility for any other action. For if the marriage to Padmāvatī were not stated to be the means for his attainment of Vāsavadattā, the King of Vatsa would not proceed toward it; and if he did not so proceed, how could the primary fruit be realized?

Everything incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) is of one and the same nature. For "incidental" (*prasaṅga*) means that which is attached (*prasakti*); that which comes from that is "incidental" (*prāsaṅgika*). Alternatively, it is called "incidental" because it is attached for the sake of accomplishing the primary result; thus, it is that which comes from such attachment. Therefore, the incidental is of many kinds according to whether it is associated with another capacity or not.

The commentators have stated that their teachers do not agree with that; for this very reason, he says, "from the cause, there is the connection with the fruit. This is the meaning: [it refers to] that which pertains to the office (ādhikārika). (p.
However, that which is mentioned as incidental is indeed for the sake of its equipment.
Through the poet’s effort, the guidance of skilled directors, and recourse to the rules, let it be called *itivṛtta* (the plot),

since it brings about the connection with the fruit; for that [plot], having been brought up by the poet as a means of description, is employed through the performance of actions conducive to its realization.
Anticipating the prima facie objection that "another [account] might likewise be an *itivṛtta*," he states the answer to that in the intermediate verse:

"But for the sake of its equipment (*tasyopakaraṇārtham tu*). The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because" and is placed out of its natural order; it means that even the incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) is being proclaimed.
Now, one might object: "The qualification (*adhikārika*) possesses a purpose by virtue of the purpose characterized as the attainment of the fruit."

If it is argued that the nature of being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) and the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*) exist even in the incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), and that this [attainment] is incidental—then this would be the case only if the distinction between the incidental and the primary (*adhikārika*) were already established. But since that very distinction is what must be proven, there is the fault of circular reasoning (*cakraka*) and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, the attainment of the fruit itself is specifically [the defining characteristic].
With the intention that this must be stated, he says: "By the effort of the poet, through the [proper] application of the leading characters.
Relying upon their excellence—that is, their preeminence—the attainment of the fruit is postulated;
the meaning is that the attainment of the principal fruit constitutes the *ādhikārika* (the primary purpose).

If it is objected that the fruit cannot be primary because it is something to be accomplished by the qualified person (*adhikārin*), then that very same fault remains; anticipating this, he says: "by the effort of the poet. That fruit which the poet intends to represent with excellence is the primary fruit. If it is then asked, "But what if human desire is unrestrained?"—then that same question arises once again.

Thus he says: among the leaders—those who are disciplined and classified as *dhīrodātta* (noble), *dhīroddhata* (haughty), and so forth—whoever is the leader appropriate and suitable for a particular context, the "fruit of the poet" is the primary goal because of the effort directed toward that basis, which is the object to be accomplished through his prescribed conduct (*vidhi*). And in that conduct...

Even in the absence of the intention—"This leader is appropriate and suitable for him; therefore, this must be done by me"—the result [of the action] occurs in his presence even without the status of being a leader, as in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, where the restoration of the kingdom to Vatsarāja is [effected] despite the minister not having intended it as his duty; for this very reason.
For he is the leader of this [kingdom] and the drawer forth of its fruit,
even of that which has been acquired through a succession of supreme means and intentions accomplished by his ministers.
For the attainment of the fruit is indeed postulated from the excellence of that fruit. || 5 ||
The worldly states known as pleasure and pain arise from the emergence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
the tenfold state of love (*manmatha*) is considered to be established in three ways. (6)

One might object: "Even so, in cases such as Rāma’s recovery of his own wife, the removal of thorns (the suppression of enemies), and the granting of fearlessness to those who are afraid, there is everywhere a propriety of duty;
nevertheless, the definition remains unsettled. To this, he says: "And of the fruit... and so forth.

By the use of the word *ca* (and), the repetition of the phrase "due to eminence" (*samutkarṣāt*) is indicated. By this, the following meaning is conveyed: whatever fruit possesses a degree of eminence in a particular respect, it is in that very respect that its propriety must be conceived by the poet.
For instance, from the destruction of Rāvaṇa until the recovery of Sītā, only the latter constitutes the most eminent [fruit].

The activity of others is directed solely toward the accomplishment of that very end; since the success of the King of Vatsa depends upon his ministers, the effort exerted by the group of ministers beginning with Yaugandharāyaṇa is precisely that great.
Therefore, the excellence in this context belongs only to the attainment of the kingdom as intended by those ministers and others. For he thinks thus:
"The anxiety regarding the burden of the kingdom that was felt by them has been taken up by me alone"—

when such a result, which revolves increasingly within the heart of the hero and is appropriate, is intended by the poet's effort to be accomplished as the primary outcome, then it constitutes the principal fruit, as seen in works such as the *Rāmābhyudaya*.

For, as in the case of the recovery of Sītā and so forth, there is no intention on the part of the poet to represent the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other such acts as being appropriate for the hero;
yet, even so, the poet’s intention alone remains the primary factor there, and the previously stated reason for the restriction [of the *dhvani*] is absent.
To this, he replies: "Because of reliance on the rule" (*vidhyapāśrayāt*). A "rule" (*vidhi*) is that which is prescribed; it is because of reliance upon that.
What is meant is this: when a poet proceeds by adopting a hero appropriate to the kind of human goal for which proficiency must be cultivated, he does not act according to his own whim.

By the word *hi*, which expresses conjunction, this is indicated: the meaning is that the attainment of the fruit is conceived as being based on excellence, arising from the poet’s effort toward the excellence of that fruit which belongs to those guides who are appropriate for reliance upon the injunctions.
When the connection with the fruit is to be accomplished, the five stages of the causal operation should be understood by practitioners in their proper sequence. (7)
The undertaking, the effort, the possibility of attainment, the certainty of obtaining the fruit, and fifthly, the union with the fruit. || 8 ||
When the bond of the seed consisting merely of eagerness is established for the sake of a great attainment of fruit, that is considered the commencement of the fruit. (9)
Now, regarding the activity (*vyāpāra*)— which is the effort (*parispanda*) consisting of speech and mind— that is to be accomplished through the exertion of the poet,

its various states (*avasthā*), namely its sequence (*ānupūrvī*), must be understood by poets as the things to be composed by practitioners according to the order of enumeration; these he points out with the words "the commencement" (*prārambhaśca*) and so forth, using the conjunctions (*cakāra*) and the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
Nor is a necessary sequence of these [stages] asserted;
for it is not fitting for a person acting with foresight to begin an undertaking when there is no contemplation of subsequent stages.
If such an undertaking were begun, it would necessarily proceed through each successive stage. By the word "fifth," the sequence is indicated.

He shows that this is what is intended to be expressed: "But [the state] whose bond is mere longing," and so forth. Regarding the great, primary fruit that is to be attained—which is appropriate for each respective hero—the "seed" is the excellence of the means; the "mere longing" for that [fruit] is...

The "bond" (*bandha*) is the firm rooting in the heart of the thought that "this [object] can be achieved by this means," corresponding to the longing to remember that object; it is the commencement [of the plot], and it belongs to the hero, the minister, the heroine, the rival hero, or destiny. For its determination is made precisely through such inference.

Furthermore, even that which is to be accomplished by fate—such as the attainment of what is desired by Samudradatta and so forth—is acquired through merit for the sake of achieving success through great effort; thus, it serves to demonstrate the assistance of fate in human exertion (puruṣakāra).
That activity directed toward a result by one who does not perceive the attainment of that result, and which involves a further state of intense longing, is proclaimed as "effort" (prayatna). 10.
When some slight attainment of the fruit is conceived, those who know the rules call that "the possibility of attainment" by virtue of its mere existence. (11)
But when one perceives with one's inner being that the attainment of the fruit is certain, they declare that certain attainment of the fruit to be "with qualities" (saguṇa). || 12 ||

And the state of being directed toward the fruit is demonstrated for the sake of attaining proficiency in that [means]. Thus, for one who does not see—meaning, for one who does not see the attainment of the fruit apart from its means—the vision of the fruit is impossible;
therefore, for one who discerns this, the activity directed toward the fruit [proceeds].

The characteristic of [this effort] is the attainment of supreme eagerness regarding the object that is the means; without that, this fruit does not come to be. Therefore, that very means must be sought. Thus, that effort has the nature of a continuous stream of memory and desire directed toward the object that is the means. Regarding the phrase "slight attainment" and so forth: it is called *bhāva* (the state) because it comes into being from this; it is the means (*upāya*). Of that—
The addition of other auxiliary causes (*sahakāryantarayoga*) and the removal of obstacles (*pratibandhakavāraṇa*) are excluded by the word "mere" (*mātra*).

This is the meaning: when, by means of a mere means that has been obtained, the attainment of a specific result is somehow conceivable or established through mere possibility, yet not ascertained—such is the case regarding attainment.

Possibility (*sambhava*) is the state of being fit for expectation, namely the third stage of the agent, characterized by the absence of impossibility. As for the phrase "when there is the certain attainment of the fruit": it is from this [stage] that the excellence of the fruit's attainment arises, which is the collection of auxiliary factors (*sahakārivarga*).

And the state of being accompanied by the destruction of obstacles constitutes the "totality" (*sāmagrī*). When one perceives that totality as being determined and constrained by that [particular] disposition through the primary means previously acquired—thereby making it non-deviant from its fruit—that is the stage called "the attainment of the certain fruit. Now, one might object:
Anticipating the objection that [this] refers to the agent, he says "saguṇām" (endowed with qualities): this state of his is figurative (gauṇī), i.e., metaphorical (upacaritā).
Because it concerns an agent who performs actions with restricted results, the term "attainment of restricted results" [refers to] the object.
When the desired, complete, and appropriate fruit of an action occurs within the narrative, that is proclaimed as the "connection with the fruit" (phalayoga). || 13 ||

For indeed, in the case of every effect that has been commenced by those seeking its fruit, [the term "vision"] is used—meaning it is stated—by means of a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the subject and the object. For this very reason, by the word "sees" (*paśyati*), it is shown that vision itself is the state. Alternatively, it exists together with the quality of vision.
The meaning is that the "state" (avasthā) is the vision of the attainment of a certain fruit.
However, those who explain it by eliding the vowel *a*—reading it as "by non-existence" (*abhāvena*)—and thus [interpreting it as] "certainly consisting of doubt," should be asked:
"If the attainment of the fruit is certain yet doubtful, how can these two contradictory things be reconciled?"

"And the intended [result] is complete. This means that in whatever narrative, within the state of the agent who is the protagonist (*nāyaka*), the intended result is not only appropriate—not unsuitable—but rather fitting and proper;

because it is possible, it is the full fruit of the action, having an immediate result (*samanantaphala*), and unlike the fruit of a ritual injunction such as heaven, it does not depend on another time.

That state of the protagonist, known as the "conjunction with the fruit" (*phalayoga*) or the "arising of the fruit" (*phalotpatti*), is now described. In that regard, since the state of even ministers, counselors, and others ultimately pertains to the protagonist alone, not all such states need necessarily be depicted directly as belonging to the protagonist in plays; rather—
By this it is shown that the intended meaning is that even though the attainment of the fruit occurs through the mediation of ministers and others, it belongs directly to [the hero] himself.

Although other stages may reside in ministers and others, they ultimately culminate in the hero alone; this very point was expressed by the great poet at the beginning of the *Ratnāvalī* in the verse: "In this [work], which is the cause of the master’s success... (1.7).
Having explained each step, our intended meaning has been clearly demonstrated.
Now, one might object: "Surely these states belong to the hero or his associates in human affairs;
would they not likewise occur in the case of the antagonist? In that regard, it is with respect to the supreme and excellent means [of attainment]. But where—
In that context, how could the fruit [of action] not be described as dependent on destiny (daiva),

especially for the sake of instilling a high regard for destiny in those who have adopted the views of the Cārvākas and others— who disregard destiny and pride themselves solely on human effort (puruṣakāra)?

It must be demonstrated that human effort may be fruitless, while even its absence may be fruitful; for this very reason, there are plays such as *Daridracārudatta* which deal with this subject. Therefore, since everything depends on destiny, how can these five stages [of life] be avoided? To answer this, he says: "For indeed, of everyone... and so forth.
The meaning is: "even though they come about by chance. For even in that case, these five stages indeed occur in a specific sequence. (14) p. 9)
The arrangement of these [energies], which are distinct by nature, through their mutual union in a state of oneness, is proclaimed as the cause of the fruit. || 15 ||

The agent does not exert effort (or rather, does not act) [in that way]; nevertheless, wherever a result occurs, there must necessarily be states such as the initial stage (*avasthā*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is he alone who at that time becomes the seeker of the result—that purpose with reference to which he acts—for they state that this is the definition of a motive (*prayojana*). To illustrate:
One whose heart is solely intent on producing bliss without undertaking any other means whatsoever— such as service and the like—

would not accept the fruit even if it were obtained from another source; for even if one does not accept it, it is precisely because of this desire for the fruit that there is satisfaction in another, superior fruit.
It has rightly been stated by the Sage that "all [states] indeed have five stages," because of the intention to include other fruits such as worldly renown (*prasiddhi*).
Now, one might ask: what is the difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the difference in their time (*kāla*), given that they are distinct in time?

And since there is no simultaneity [of cause and effect], how can it be said—as was stated [in verse 19.8]—that "the operation of the cause exists when the connection with the fruit is yet to be accomplished"? Furthermore, if the connection with the fruit is that which is to be accomplished, one might wonder what the state of the cause is at that time.
Anticipating the objection that this fifth state is merely the connection with the fruit and nothing else, he says: "Of these... (*āsām*).
Regarding the phrase "of those whose natures are distinct": by means of the difference in nature, a difference in time is also implied;
for when there is a difference in nature, even things separated by space and time—such as a staff, a wheel, and so forth—accomplish a single result.
Therefore, even for these things separated by time, through their mutual conjunction (*saṃgati*) with one another, they are invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatvena*).

The sense is this: relying upon that arrival, there is a specific arrangement which is the cause of the fruit; from that [arrangement], there is the removal of the beginning and the end, because even for the causes of causes of the determined successive effects, their status as causes does not fail.
As for what was asked—how there can be another connection with the fruit when there is already a connection with the fruit—he says in response: "by means of a single state" (*ekabhāvena*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause of the fruit": the relation is one of identity (*ekabhāva*). Therefore, this state of being is as follows: the first is the state of the arising of the fruit, which is connected with the protagonist; the second is that which was previously indicated in the passage "the connection with the fruit in what is to be accomplished," wherein the fruit is seen to arise appropriately through its conjunction with the three intermediate states.
(10) Thus has the narrative been fully explained, pertaining specifically to the individual soul (pratyagātman).
Its commencement and so forth should be performed until its conclusion, just as it truly occurs. || 16 ||
A full treaty should be concluded, or alternatively, even an inferior one;
by rule there should be a full treaty, but an inferior treaty may occur for a specific reason.

The meaning is that this refers to the fifth stage (*pañcamy-avasthā*). Having thus demonstrated the five stages, he says, "the plot (*itivṛtta*) has been fully described," in order to establish that the plot follows those stages and is therefore characterized by its authoritative purpose (*adhikārikatva*), beginning from the undertaking of the subject matter up to its fruition. This is because that which is to be done—the action—is the substance [of the work] from its commencement to its result.
And because it follows that state, it is called "pertaining to the office" (*adhikārika*) due to its being authorized;

and as for the word *ca*, in the sense of the word *vastu* (matter), it has already been correctly explained previously through the determination of the meaning of the word *iti*, so that it may become what is expressed by the word *itivṛtta* (historical narrative) by means of the five junctures (*sandhi*).
By the word "division" (*vibhāga*), this is stated once again for the purpose of introducing other matters to be discussed regarding that [topic].

Now, one might ask: "Are there only five junctures (*sandhi*) everywhere? To this he says, "and the complete juncture. Someone may suspect that there is an option (*vikalpa*) in all cases; addressing him, he says, "by way of a restriction. Some say, "by way of a general rule" (*utsargeṇa*).

But the teachers say: "In all cases, there is a traditional narrative consisting of five stages, just like the five junctures of the day; for no undertaking whatsoever can reach completion without these five states beginning with the initial commencement, nor can it be kept secret. And it has been said:
"For indeed, for every effect that has been commenced by those seeking its fruit,
these five stages occur in their proper sequence. (19.14) Thus,
everything must necessarily be accompanied by a fivefold juncture (*sandhi*) corresponding to the five stages.

By rule, there are five junctures (*sandhi*); however, the state of having "deficient junctures" is spoken of therein because of the cause characterized by the incompleteness of its limbs. For this very reason, it is also designated as "having complete junctures"—this is what is indicated by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase, "or again, even though it has deficient junctures."
When one [of the four] is omitted, the fourth is lost; when two are omitted, the third and fourth are lost;
when three are omitted—the second, third, and fourth—their omission is prescribed. (18)
In the case of incidental [verses], because they are for the sake of another, this restriction would not apply;
whatever meter is possible there should be employed, provided it is not contradictory. (19)
It will be stated that the *ḍima* and the *samavakāra* possess four junctures (*saṃdhi*), in which case there is an omission of the *avamarśa*.
Furthermore, the *vyāyoga* and the *īhāmṛga* must always have three junctures; here, there is an omission of both the *garbha* and the *avamarśa*.
However, the *prahasana*, the *vīthī*, the *aṅka*, and the *bhāṇa* have only two junctures. Regarding these:
By the word "three" (in the phrase "of the second, third, and fourth"), the third [member] is indicated through the omission of the *pratimukha*, *garbha*, and *avamarśa* [sandhis].
Among these, the *upakrama* (opening) and *upasaṃhāra* (conclusion) are necessarily present everywhere.
However, regarding those who act with foresight and undertake an extensive task that yields great fruit, [the following applies]:

There are exactly five junctures (*sandhi*). By means of the endurance of suffering, when a suspected contrary conviction is dispelled— according to the maxim that "two negations strengthen the affirmation"— the connection with the fruit of these [perfections] becomes very firm.
The protagonists of the *ḍima* and similar genres do not excessively fear downfall because they are characterized by extreme exuberance.
The protagonists of the *vyāyoga* and similar genres also do not take such precautions, as their connection with the fruit [of action] is subordinate to varying degrees.
However, the protagonists of the *prahasana* and similar genres, due to the predominance of unrighteousness (*adharma*) in their respective plots, [do not fear it].
Because their bodies have been chewed up, [the functions] such as *avamarśa* (reflection) rest merely in the beginning and the conclusion; thus they are incomplete.
In this way, by means of the five [functions], that which was explained by the word *iti-vṛtta* (narrative sequence) through the word *yasya hi* (for of whom) is [now] explained by this.
He shows that the meaning of the word "iti" in the *prāsaṅgika* (incidental) section is as follows:
the rule previously stated—that "from such a restriction, the *sandhi* would be complete," and so forth—would not apply there.
If, regarding the matter of Vibhīṣaṇa’s installation, Rāma’s eagerness, his binding [of the vow], and so forth were to be joined [in that context], then that alone [would suffice].

It would have to be accomplished with effort. Regarding what he refers to as "the plot" (*vṛtta*), that which is consistent with the primary subject matter (*adhikārika*) and possible within this incidental context (*prāsaṅgika*), as well as any one of the [five] beginnings (*ārambha*), is precisely what is fit to be joined with the incidental plot.

Now, it was indeed stated [in the passage beginning] "But the seed's bondage consists merely in longing" (19.9), and therein [it was shown that] there is an obstruction to the means and its auxiliary factors (p.
In the *itivṛtta* (historical narrative), five elements beginning with the "undertaking" (*ārambha*) are prescribed according to their respective states;
likewise, there are five "plot-essences" (*arthaprakṛti*), beginning with the "seed" (*bīja*). (20)

The seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the small banner (prakarī), and the purpose (kārya)—these five elements of the plot (arthaprakṛti) should be employed according to rule once they have been understood. || 21 ||

And although its destruction has been introduced there, its specific nature was not known; therefore, in order to show the nature of the collection of means, he says: "in the plot, according to the state [of affairs]" (*itivṛtte yathāvasthā*).
This means that regarding the subject matter of the plot (*itivṛtta*), in whatever manner—that is, by way of the characteristic of the disruption of the protagonist—[the action proceeds].

Five stages have been described; in that same manner, the five natures of the subject matter (*arthaprakṛti*) are also recited. If those were not mentioned, because the essential nature of the means (*upāya*) and so forth would not be fully understood, and because the stages such as the commencement (*prārambha*) would not be realized in their ultimate sense, the status of being "subject-matter" (*ādhikārikatva*) would remain unknown. In this context, the "subject matter" (*artha*) is the fruit (*phala*).

The *prakṛtis* are the means; the meaning is that they are the causes of the fruit. In that regard, there is a twofold division based on being insentient (*jaḍa*) or sentient (*cetana*). The insentient is the primary cause, either more hidden or as the first seed; the second is the effect, which is to be produced or employed. The sentient is also twofold: the primary and that which serves as an instrument (*upakaraṇa*).

The final [means] is also twofold: that which is conjoined with the accomplishment of one's own purpose along with the accomplishment of the purpose of others, and that which is pure. Among these, the first is the *bindu*, the second is the *patākā*, and the third is the *prakarī*. By means of these five methods, the full fruit is brought to completion. Therefore, it is said: "Having understood [them], they should be applied according to the rule."
The meaning is that there is a fixed order of arrangement for these [figures], similar to the manner of stating a general indication (*auddeśika*). Others, however, say:

"The *arthaprakṛtis* are the bases (*prakṛti*)—that is, the constituent parts of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*)—of the entire object expressed by the metaphor; this interpretation, however, does not particularly support the present context."

In this interpretation, even the *saṃdhis* and so forth would have the status of being "plot-elements" (*arthaprakṛti*). Furthermore, the *itivṛtta* (the narrative) alone would constitute the collective form. If one were to say that the "plot" (*artha*) consists of the *itivṛtta* and the "elements" (*prakṛtis*), the inclusion of the term "plot" (*artha*) would be redundant.
Moreover, the description of their similarity to the "states" (*avasthās*) would be a mere description; so what is the point of this?
That which, when sown even in a very small measure, spreads forth in many ways and culminates in fruit— that indeed is proclaimed as a seed. (22)
That which is the cause for the non-interruption of purposes when they are otherwise subject to interruption—
this pentad he defines, in the order of their enumeration, as "just a little" (*svalpamātram*). This refers to that object— namely,
[the sight of Sāgarikā] while she was residing in the inner apartments during the time of the Spring Festival (*vasantotsava*).

Because there is an absence of realization regarding its profound purpose, it is possible that what is merely trifling and almost ineffective might be discarded or interpolated through agreement; yet, since that which necessarily reaches its final fruit spreads in many ways and extends in every respect, even if one were to obstruct both the accomplishment and its fruit, [it would still prevail].

It proceeds toward its fruit by the very first casting [of the seed], like the seed of that [tree]; it is the seed which, depending upon the efficacy of place and time, and depending upon the task itself, is placed upon a succession of manifold means according to the principle of the waterwheel (ārghaṭṭa-parivartanī).

Because it is celebrated—that is, well-known—everywhere and on all sides; and because in some places it consists of the means alone, in some the result alone, in some both the result and the means, in some the material cause, in some the turning away from what is to be abandoned, and in some both; and even therein, in some cases by way of the protagonist.

It is divided in many ways through various distinctions, such as being based on a rival protagonist (*pratināyaka*) and so forth. Among these, in the *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, the attainment of a son by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) occurs through the benedictions of sages; this is the very nature of the fruit [of the plot].

Furthermore, even a future fruit is called a "seed" because it is inseparable from its means; in this same manner, other cases should also be illustrated as appropriate. Due to their infinite number and for fear of making the text overly cumbersome, they have not been written out individually.
Now, he defines *bindu* as "the non-interruption of purposes. Those means and performances by which a result is pursued—
when there occurs an interruption even of these due to the force of past events, such as through unavoidable duties and the like—
the *bindu* is that knowledge of the plot's substance (*sandhi-dravya-jñāna*) residing in the principal hero, which consists of a continuous connection (*anusandhāna*).

The investigation of knowledge is the means for attaining the fruit; as long as it is not carried out through uninterrupted retrospective reflection (*praty-anusandhāna*), not even the slightest task will be accomplished. (p.
That which lasts until the completion of the binding is proclaimed as the *bindu*. || 23 ||

Now, one might ask: "The seed indeed remains until the end of the fruit; but how can there be a persistence of the *bindu*? To this he says: "until completion. This means: as long as there is the complete attainment of its own fruit which is being bound. What is meant is this:
for the continuous connection (*anusandhāna*) exists for the sake of maintaining vigilance regarding all the means, as long as [the process] lasts for the primary protagonist.

As long as there is no retrospective connection (*pratyanusandhāna*), every element of the means (*upāya*), whether insentient or sentient in nature, remains essentially devoid of a means (*anupāyakalpa*). For instance, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*,
the retrospective connection with Vāsavadattā’s love is demonstrated by the King in each act:
"The day was spent gazing at the moon of her face, and so too was the evening"—thus it is said up until the sixth act:
"My ministers sustained my life-breaths, lured by the hope of attaining you; considering that, there is no lack of affection on my part as I cast off this body."
"The time for following you has arrived; why then is there this distress?
For at that cruel moment, my heart did not break into a hundred pieces.

(6.3) In this regard, there is the accomplishment of the primary goal, the accomplishment of the dependent goal, and the accomplishment of both; this *bindu* pertains to the accomplishment of the primary goal.

However, when success is dependent [on another], characterized by the attainment of sovereignty, the "link" (*bindu*) is the coordination (*anusandhāna*) performed solely by the group of ministers regarding that [sovereignty].

But when success belongs to both, it is performed by both; whichever of the two intends with predominance, that one alone coordinates it. Thus is the operation of the conscious activity of the primary coordinator.

The *bindu* favors the cause and is itself of the nature of the supreme cause; it is also called a "drop" (*bindu*) because it pervades everything like a drop of oil. Furthermore, the *bīja* unfolds its own self starting from the *mukhasandhi* (the opening juncture), whereas the *bindu* does so immediately thereafter—this is the distinction between the two; yet both are...
That which occurs throughout the entire narrative, being for the sake of others and serving as an aid to the primary plot, is [the secondary plot]. (p. 15)
And it should be conceived as being like the primary [element]; that is proclaimed as the "banner" (patākā). || 24 ||
That [plot] for which a fruit is devised solely for the sake of another, and which lacks a further connection (anubandha), one should designate as a *prakarī*. (25)
When a subject pertaining to a specific office is properly undertaken by the wise, that purposeful undertaking is proclaimed as "action" (kārya). || 26 ||

"Regarding the phrase 'that which is a conduct for the sake of another': that conduct—meaning the conscious deliberation—belonging to someone, even when it exists for the accomplishment of another's purpose, also accomplishes one's own purpose. For this very reason, he says:
'And like the primary [cause], the accomplishment of the banner [of success] is brought about through the deliberation of a sentient being.'"

It is beneficial to the principal element. In this way, even Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others, being assisted by Rāma and the rest, contribute to the benefit of Rāma and themselves, thereby accomplishing renown and excellence. Thus, by means of this [treatment], which is useful for the knowledge of propriety and impropriety, here—

The ancients call this the *patākā* (banner) because it serves as a banner; for it is from this that the fruit is projected. Furthermore, because one performs everything solely for the sake of another, it is the *prakarī* (subplot). As in the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa* and the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, [the role of] the Kulapati...

The Blessed One is Vāsudeva. He acts pre-eminently (*prakṛṣṭena*) without regard for his own self-interest. [The suffix] *ik* is added after all verbal roots; and because it denotes a feminine noun through its dependence on the act of consciousness (*saṃvit*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārād aktyarthāt*. "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to the accomplishment of what is to be done (*kartavya*), as it is that which bears fruit (*phalati*).

That which is called "pertaining to the main plot" (*yad-ādhikārika*) is the matter in the form of the fruit that is employed by the wise through the conscious characters— the principal hero, the banner-hero (*patākā-nāyaka*), and the secondary hero (*prakaraṇī-nāyaka*).
