16) Among these, whichever is required by whom, and from which a specific quality is desired—that should be made the primary factor; the others are secondary. || 27 ||

Whether a juncture (saṃdhi) be single or multiple, that which occurs within the *patākā* (the secondary plot) is proclaimed as an *anusandhi* (connecting juncture), because it follows the primary objective. || 28 ||

That which is accomplished— that is, that which is pursued as something to be accomplished for the sake of its fruit— is every object such as substance, action, quality, and so forth, which is denoted by the term "commencement" (*ārambha*), because it initiates the fruit of the primary means called the "seed" (*bīja*) previously grasped, which brings about completion. (Of which...)

If it is argued that "cooperation" (*sahakārī*) is called "action" (*kārya*) based on the etymological derivation that "the fruit is brought about by conscious beings," [we reply: "properly" (*samyak*) means by those endowed with the three powers of the sovereign—the power of counsel, the power of energy, and the power of majesty. By this, all such things as the variety of activities concerning the territory, the treasury, and the fortifications, as well as the group of means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), are included.
It is included within the task (*kārya*). In that regard, the supreme means (*abhyupāya*), which was first grasped and constitutes the primary factor, has been described as the seed (*bīja*).
Now, one might ask: as in the case of the "beginning" (*prārambha*) and so forth, do all these fundamental natures (*prakṛti*) apply everywhere? Or [do they not]?

To dispel three doubts—namely, whether "origination" (*sambhava*) corresponds respectively with "the nature of objects" (*arthaprakṛti*) and "the state of union" (*sandhivasthā*); whether there is a restriction [of correspondence] in that manner; and whether these [states] constitute the sequence of agents within their own self—he says "of these" (*eteṣām*), referring to the three groups of five by retaining only one from each group.

This is the meaning: not in every case are all the *arthaprakṛtis* (plot elements) present, as they are in the *ārambha* (commencement) and so forth. Rather, for whichever hero the attainment of the purpose is primarily accomplished through a particular *arthaprakṛti*, that alone is the principal; the others, even if present, are subordinate and as good as non-existent, just as in the following example.
For those possessed of great pride in their own prowess, the excellence of the *patākā* and *prakarī* is not even intended to be mentioned;

however, the *bīja*, *bindu*, and *kārya* are present everywhere without exception. Even therein, there is a relationship of primary and secondary importance: thus, among the junctures (*sandhi*), the states (*avasthā*), the purposes (*artha*), and the characters (*prakṛti*), that which has a connection appropriate to another is the primary one.

The view that it is a work such as a drama (*nāṭaka*) and so forth is also refuted by the second [point]. Since a quality (*guṇa*) is an assistance that is expressed immediately, that which constitutes the nature of the subject matter (*arthaprakṛti*)—one of the five types—must be composed as the primary element in abundance; the other is related to it as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*), and thus that [primary element] is the principal one.
When the establishment of the primary [factor] and the establishment dependent upon it are being set forth (p.
whichever factor is more contributory to a particular part must be made primary in that context.
For instance, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja* upon the attainment of Vāsavadattā, the *bindu* is primary;

however, in the attainment of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, both the *prakarī* and the *patākā* are primary. Some say that in the minister’s accomplishment of the kingdom, his own personal interest constitutes the *patākā*. Likewise, Susaṅgatā and Sāṃkṛtyāyanī [are examples].

This should be stated regarding the seed-plot (*bījadharmādi*) and so forth. Others, however, maintain that since the hero possesses such a nature from the very beginning, his status as a hero is not a separate *pramāṇa* (measure/standard); rather, Sugrīva and the others are indeed distinct individuals who are merely relied upon for the immediate task—thus, it is only a *pramāṇa*.
The nature of the banner (*patākā*) and so forth [is as follows]: in their view, in both the *Tāpasavatsarāja* and other works, the *bindu* alone is predominant;

furthermore, among the five types of plot-elements (*arthaprakṛti*), predominance belongs to one, two, three, four, or all of them, and this must be distributed according to the specific requirements of each case.

Since the *patākā* (sub-plot) is extended by analogy as being like the *pradhāna* (main plot), these [five] junctures (*sandhi*) should be counted separately. Let it be so, because it exists solely for the sake of another. And for this very reason, from where would a juncture be indicated, inferred, or composed? As in the *Māyāpuṣpaka*.
Just as Vālin of renowned power was slain,
as Laṅkā was forcibly burnt by the lone monkey,
and as the ocean was crossed by means of a bridge of mountains; so too [was this accomplished].
I consider such to be the playful sport of the fickle Creator.
For if there were a full description of a *patākā*, another *patākā* would arise, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, it was rightly said that because it is connected [to the main plot], it is not counted separately.
Likewise, Lollaṭa and others, however, maintain that when something is to be accomplished for the sake of another...
The *anusandhayaḥ* (connections) are the portions of the narrative belonging to the hero of the *patākā* (sub-plot). As in the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*:
"Blessed are those virtuous ones, and praiseworthy is the life of their birth, by whom their own interests are abandoned so that the interests of others may be accomplished."

Thus is the transition (*anusandhi*) of the *mukha* (opening). "Just as Vālī... is the transition of the *pratimukha* (development). Following the slaying of Lakṣmaṇa by Śakti, there is the transition of the *garbha* (embryo) in the bringing of the medicinal herb and in Aṅgada’s mission as an envoy. Following Mandodarī’s reproach, there is the transition of the *avamarśa* (crisis) in the passage beginning with "O powerless one, O ignoble one! Stay, stay! You are a great chariot-warrior (*atiratha*), she is not [such]," which constitutes the transition of the *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion). This, moreover, occurs as follows:
For it has been stated that all things indeed possess five states; however, we do not perceive any purpose in designating this [state] as "non-connection" (ausandhi). (p.
The *patākā* (subsidiary plot) ceases either at the *garbha* (embryo) or at the *vimarśa* (deliberation);
for what reason? Because its composition is proclaimed to be for the sake of another [the main plot]. (29)
When one meaning has been intended, another word with a different mark (liṅga) is employed;

for one striving to achieve his own result, there is necessarily a suspicion of a separate calculation in each such case. Therefore, the purpose [of our position] is to pacify that [suspicion]. But in which primary connection (sandhi), then, does this apply in our view?

To demonstrate its state of being a follower, he says: "From the *garbha* [act] or up to the *vimarśa* [act]. Whether in the *pratimukha*, the *garbha*, or otherwise, wherever the *patākā* (subsidiary plot) ceases after pervading a certain matter, the accomplishment of the fruit for the *patākā-nāyaka* (subsidiary hero) must be presented right there; however, once his fruit is accomplished, he becomes part of the primary fruit itself.
Even while engaged in activity, though seated, he is designated by the term "banner" (*patākā*) according to his former state, not in a primary sense.

Here [the author] asks: "Why? because it was stated: "Why should his intention be conceived as being like that of the Pradhāna? Furthermore, regarding what results from this accomplishment, the answer here is: "Because... (yasmāt).

If its fruit were produced at the very end of the *nirvahaṇa*, there would be no assistance to the primary element because of the absence of a causal relationship characterized by simultaneous conjunction; therefore, it would not benefit the principal.
The prefix *āṅ* here signifies "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). Those, however, who explain it as signifying "limitation" (*maryādā*) have not understood correctly.
In the juncture of the primary deliberation (*pradhāna-vimarśa-sandhi*), the secondary plot (*patākā*) serves a specific purpose through the remedies for misfortune (*vinipāta-pratīkāra*).
That wherein ingratitude is observed is not discussed here; rather, one who is grateful, having attained his fruit, should indeed counteract misfortunes.
In that regard, the hero of the secondary plot (*patākā-nāyaka*) acts for his own sake and accomplishes the welfare of others.
The condition of a servant or another [dependent], or even of one who is dull-witted, results in the welfare of others even when their own interest is at stake.

That is the "Station of the Banner" (*patākāsthānaka*), which is similar to a banner; for in that regard, while a dull-witted person lacks intention (*abhisandhāna*) in acting for the sake of both self and others, one such as Sugrīva possesses such intention.

The distinction from the *patākānāyaka* (subsidiary hero) is as follows: although even a non-insentient entity possesses intentionality (*abhisandhāna*) with respect to its own purpose, it lacks it with respect to the purpose of another; this is the specific difference. Furthermore, it might be argued that [the *patākānāyaka*] could be conceived like the *pradhāna* (primary hero). This is because the definition of the *patākā* states that the hero’s pervasiveness extends over a very extensive plot (*itivṛtta*), whereas for this [type of hero], the pervasiveness is limited to a restricted plot.
This is the distinction. Since that *patākāsthānaka* possesses various divisions which will be described later, he first states its general definition:
"When another matter (*artha*) is being considered... Here, *artha* means both purpose and means.
When another means or purpose is considered through the analysis of the performance of an action, that is a *patākāsthānaka* (flag-station) due to its adventitious nature. (30)
The sudden attainment of a virtuous object through a beneficial means is proclaimed as this first *patākāsthāna*. 31.
Another [type] is that where something else—characterized by a different means (*upāya*) or a different purpose (*prayojana*)—is joined or connected in an eminent manner;
this is the *patākāsthānaka*. Because it serves as the support for the banner (*patākā*), the plot (*itivṛtta*) is also metaphorically called *patākāsthānaka*.
However, the teachers say: "The *patākāsthāna* is the state of being the plot, and the meaning resides therein."

Even while being performed, it transitions to the preceding matter, as in the phrase "he stands with his neck unbent like Rājavāhana"; thus, by that [phrase], the *sthānaka* (station) of the banner is described as the very *itivṛtta* (past event). Therein, however, that which is being described consists of both the insentient and the sentient forms.

It is implied by the sense that it is "similar to a banner" (*patākā*). Furthermore, that other meaning is so called because, possessing its characteristic mark (*liṅga*), it "marks" (*liṅgayati*)—that is, embellishes—that primary meaning. Now, one might ask: what is the similarity to a banner in this case? To this he says: "by means of an adventitious state" (*āgantukena bhāvena*). A state (*bhāva*) is that which brings about (*bhāvanam*).
That causality is twofold: intrinsic and produced by auxiliaries.

That which is produced by auxiliaries is called adventitious. Therefore, because of the commonality of being an auxiliary—characterized by performing what is effective—it is said to have a resemblance to a banner.
If the establishment of one thing results from the intention directed toward another, even though it constitutes an ornament [of the argument], some have nevertheless taken it to be a fault;

by them, the word *artha* has been relied upon as signifying "means" (*upāya*). In the expression "having that as its mark" (*talliṅga*), the "means" is the basis for the application of the term, characterized by the absence of the property of being a cause. An example:

We shall demonstrate in that very place how the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) can be applied to the explanation of the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). He defines its divisions in sequence, beginning with "the sudden attainment of the object" (*sahasaivārthasaṃpattiḥ*).
This refers to where, depending on what is beneficial, there is a possession of qualities, excellence, and the fruit of the object.
Success that occurs suddenly and unexpectedly is called the "First" (Prathama);

because it is joined with the fruit of the objective, it is the primary *patākāsthāna*. For example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, when Sāgarikā has set out to hang herself, [the King], thinking she is Vāsavadattā—
When the king releases the noose, Sāgarikā recognizes his voice and exclaims, "Alas!

How is it my beloved Sāgarikā? Enough, enough of this excessive [fear]," and so forth. Here, one purpose was intended, yet another purpose, which produces a striking variety of effect, has come to pass; and in that regard, there is the intervention of fate.
The Leader, whose nature is such, is his own self appearing as if differentiated through the power of another's intention,
just like Sāgarikā (p. 20).
Speech that is highly refined, full of double meanings, and based upon poetic composition—this is proclaimed as the second *patākāsthāna*. (32)
Where the presentation of the meaning is subtle yet refined, and is accompanied by a clever retort, this is considered the third [type]. (33)

When one speaks with the underlying intention that death alone is appropriate, it partakes of the nature of a "patākā" (banner) hero. This occurs when, while one means has been considered, another means suddenly presents itself— as in the *Nāgānanda*, where Jīmūtavāhana, whose death-warrant had not yet been obtained from Śaṅkhacūḍa, [is saved] by the chamberlain.
The offering of a pair of garments.

Others, however, considering "the supreme four banners" to refer to the four future junctures (*saṃdhi*), explain the words "first," "second," and so forth as intending the application to the junctures such as the *mukha* (opening) and others.

In this regard, neither a logical justification is perceived nor does it possess aesthetic charm; thus, it is indeed non-existent. Let this position rest as an object of derision, for by those ancient authorities who, on the grounds of parity with this, would even include the five banners (patākās) alongside the elements and the senses in their enumeration, it has already been made a target of ridicule.

Regarding the phrase "the speech is *sātiśaya* (exceedingly) *śliṣṭa* (coherent/ambiguous)": the composition (*bandha*) of the subject matter (*prakṛta*) of the poem—that is, its arrangement through such means as poetic exaggeration (*atiśayokti*)—is the cause by virtue of which a certain speech becomes *sātiśaya-śliṣṭa*, meaning it becomes appropriately applicable to the non-subject matter (*aprakṛta*). That speech, or its meaning, or the speaker thereof [is what is intended].
Or, [the second *patākāsthāna*] occurs when something incidental proceeds to serve as an auxiliary to the subject at hand,
with reference to an intended connection; as, for example, in the third act of the *Rāmābhyudaya*,
Sugrīva’s message to Sītā:
What need is there for much speaking here? O Goddess, Rāghava will soon bring you back, even though you are situated on the far shore of the ocean.

In this context, even when a statement is uttered with another purpose and with an intention of excessive power—such as "even on the other side" and so forth—it constitutes a *patākāsthānaka* (the station of the banner) because of its superior utility for the subject at hand.
This is where there is a "suggestion of meaning" (*arthopakṣepaṇa*). That is to say, a collection of meanings that is "hidden" (*līna*), meaning its form is indistinct, is being suggested.

That third *patākāsthāna* occurs where one is endowed with a reply that is clever (*śliṣṭa*), suitable for connection, and though prompted by another intention, is accompanied by politeness and specifically characterized by the attainment of a particular certainty through the eyes.
(21) A composition of words that possesses a double meaning, is well-knit, employed poetically, and is excellently suited to the context— this is declared to be the fourth [type]. || 34 ||

[The *Nāṭyadarpaṇa*: As in the *Mudrārākṣasa*, Cāṇakya says: "I wonder if the evil-minded Rākṣasa might be captured. When such an indistinct matter has been introduced, Siddhārthaka enters and says, "Noble sir, he has been captured.
This reply, though employed with the intention of a mere message, brings about a specific determination through its propriety.

And so again Cāṇakya says (joyfully, to himself): "Ah! The wicked Rākṣasa has been captured. And this [episode], because it serves as a subordinate element useful for the primary goal to be accomplished, stands in the position of a *patākā* (subsidiary plot);
thus, its distinction from the *gaṇḍa* (a limb of the *vīthī*) is that [in the latter], on the contrary, both thighs are broken.

Since Duryodhana has been destroyed, his evil intention is also gone; what use would there be for it? Let it follow the course of the Pāṇḍavas. This is a *patākāsthānaka* (a secondary plot); although its subject matter is distinct, this form does not cause any deficiency.

A "twofold-meaning arrangement of words" refers to an arrangement of words—whether in the form of poetry (*kāvya*) or in the form of a narrative (*kathā*)—which, by virtue of its successful attainment of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), is beautiful and possessed of clarity; and which, through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), is "twofold-meaning," that is, endowed with multiple meanings. Being such, it is excellent when employed in the introduction for the purpose of suggesting another matter (*vastvantara*).

That which is appropriate constitutes the fourth [type]. For example, in the passage from the *Ratnāvalī* (Act 1, verse 23): "Just as one gazes upon the rising moon because of the excellence of its beauty," here the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is employed with the intention of giving the work the form of poetry, while there is another primary subject matter.

She lifts up the letter addressed to Sāgarikā: "This is that King Udayana to whom I was given by my father"—"This is that King Udayana to whom I was given by my father" (Ratnāvalī 1)—[thus she reads] with unrestrained longing.
(Where there is a highly distinguished statement that serves as an introduction to the subject matter, and which is seen to perish at the end, that indeed constitutes the *patākārdha*. || 35 ||
In drama, that which possesses four banners is considered supreme;
it should be composed with five junctures (sandhis), and I shall describe them hereafter. (36)

However, this is not an illustration [of that], for even though the double meaning (*dvyarthatā*) is understood here, the function of being a cooperative factor (*sahakāritā*) with the literal sense has never been observed in this context. Therefore, it is appropriate to regard this as an illustration of *vyāhāra* (speech) alone, which is a constituent element (*vīthyaṅga*) of the dramatic path.
To demonstrate the excellence of these [elements], he says: "the supreme among the four banners" (*catuṣpatākāparamam*). By the word "banner" (*patākā*),...

Immediately after, the *patākāsthānaka* (the episode of the banner) has been described; when those four are performed, it is intended that the most excellent and supreme work in the field of drama (*nāṭya*) should be accomplished. Therefore, the meaning is that one should act accordingly.
For that which must be performed even in part by the *patākānāyaka* (or *patākāsthānaka*) is accomplished by a single one of them.
Or [it may be] by means of four. Some say that there are four secondary heroes (*patākānāyaka*) at the four junctures (*sandhi*);

their indicators are the *patākāsthāna*s respectively, from the first in the *mukha*-juncture up to the fourth in the *avamarśa*-juncture. But that is incorrect, because [the *patākāsthāna*s] are like the secondary hero (*patākā*).
At that time, other indicators for the *prakara*, *kārya*, *bindu*, and *bīja* would also have to be stated;

furthermore, there would necessarily be four *patakās* and *nāyakas*. Moreover, according to the view that [the *prastāvanā*] extends up to the *garbha*, the statement "the supreme [drama] has four *patakās*" would be inconsistent. And if the *mukhya-nāyaka* were not an indicator of the plot (*itivṛtta*), [the definition would fail].

If the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) were stated first and then it were said that [the *patākānāyaka*] is described [later], it would result in a contradiction of the sequence; nor does the order— beginning with the first [element] in the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture), the second in the *pratimukhasandhi* (development juncture), and so forth— logically imply such a definition, nor is there any evidence in the actual dramatic works (*lakṣya*) to support it.
Enough of this.
Thus has the plot (itivṛtta) been explained, and its two varieties have been defined;
furthermore, as a secondary point for establishing the nature of the "dominant" (ādhikārika), the five stages constituting the points of continuity have been shown.

The *arthaprakṛtis* (essential plot elements) and the *patākāsthānas* (situations of the secondary plot) follow as a matter of course from that very context. Now, however, regarding the meaning of the word "iti" [at the end of the definition], it is said to be "joined with five junctures" (*sandhis*). In that regard, he makes a formal promise:
"I shall explain them. Now...
The Mukha (opening), Pratimukha (development), Garbha (embryo), Vimarśa (dissolution), and likewise Nirvahaṇa (conclusion)— these are the five junctures (*sandhi*) in a drama. (37)
The primary junctures are proclaimed as being endowed with five [types];
the remaining ones are the subordinate junctures that support the primary junctures. (38)
That in which the production of seeds occurs, giving rise to various meanings and sentiments, and which follows the body of the poem—that is proclaimed as the *mukha* (opening). 39.

Desiring to determine the [structure of the] *uddeśa* (brief statement), he first says: "The *mukha* (opening) and the *pratimukha* (development)," and so forth. By means of the conjunctive particles (*samuccaya*), it is indicated that all five [sandhis] necessarily occur everywhere. By means of the restrictive terms (*niyamavācin*), the sequence is fixed. "In a *nāṭaka*" means in a dramatic work (*abhineyarūpaka*) consisting of a great sentence-meaning (*mahāvākyārtha*).

The five stages of the dramatic purpose (*rūpakārtha*) are conceived according to their different states. Among them, that first stage of "commencement" (*ārambhāvasthā*), which was explained as belonging to the independent *mukhya* (hero), who possesses the entire objective within the plot, and who is therefore the protagonist (*nāyaka*), is applicable [to other cases] either through his own agency or by means of another.
Whatever mass of meaning there is constitutes the juncture (*sandhi*).

The intermediate portions of that mass of meaning are the constituent parts of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*), such as the *upakṣepa* (introduction) and so forth. The same should be stated for the other junctures. Thus, the components of the meaning, being joined together with one another and with the constituent parts, [form the whole].
The designation *sandhi* has thus been etymologically explained. This is their general definition.
Now, he states their specific definitions in sequence, beginning with "where there is the production of the seed.
Because it occurs prior to the commencement [of the action], it is like a "face" (*mukha*); that is, as long as there is a mass of objective parts possessing activity.

The perfect arising of the seed, which is the primary means (*mukhopāya*), is accompanied by the body in its nature as an undertaking; it is the production of aesthetic flavor (*rasasaṃbhava*) that arises incidentally from various objects according to their requirements. This is what is meant: whatever mass of objects is useful for the undertaking.
Through a series of related digressions, a manifold aesthetic relish has arisen;
such is the unfolding of the seed, which in some places appears as if seen and then vanished.

The *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) and its expressive components (*rūpaka*) are parts of the [drama]. For example, in the first act of the *Ratnāvalī*: since there is heroism (*vīra*) on the part of the minister, and heroism (*śṛṅgāra*) and wonder (*adbhuta*) on the part of the King of Vatsa, followed by love (*śṛṅgāra*), this much [is established] regarding Sāgarikā.
When the minister is introduced during the audience with the king, the "heap of wealth" becomes relevant; this is the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture).

In the same way, the *pratisandhi* (re-opening juncture) should be explained as that wherein there is the disclosure of the seed (*bīja*). Some say it is that which was seen as an effect and has now vanished as a cause.

Some say that what is seen in the conduct of the hero (*nāyaka*) is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), while what is seen in the conduct of the antagonist (*pratināyaka*) is "lost" (*naṣṭa*). Others maintain that what is seen in the conduct of the hero is "seen," while what is seen in the conduct of the antagonist is "lost. However, this is not correct, because a connection (*sandhāna*) is impossible without a single common subject; furthermore, even the "loss" regarding subjects such as what is to be abandoned (*heya*) must be understood as "seen" precisely by virtue of its commencement.

Because of the perfection of the means of unification (*saṃgraha*). Therefore, this is the meaning here: the "unfolding of the seed" (*bījodghāṭana*) is a particular stage of development corresponding to the fruit; although it is visible, due to the proximity of opposing factors, it is as if destroyed—like the state of sprouting of a seed covered by dust—as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.

The Chamberlain’s words: "O Sage, this Bhīṣma— who was the conqueror of you whose axe remained unblunted until the seizing of weapons— has been laid low by the arrows of the sons of Pāṇḍu, for his destruction."

"And [this is] for the sake of the joy [felt] by the lone youth Abhimanyu, who was exhausted from his victory over many mature archers, yet whose bow was severed by the enemy, following the slaying of Bhīṣma. (A 2-2). Here, there is the unfolding of the protagonist's rise—which was introduced in the opening—following the slaying of Bhīṣma.
Some say that it should be understood as "seen" because of Abhimanyu’s death and "lost" because of his subsequent disappearance; however, in that case, the meaning would not be fully integrated.

Others maintain that "being seen" is useful for the *pratimukha* (the second juncture), while "being lost" pertains only to the *avamarśa* (the third juncture); they thus describe "seen-ness" and "lost-ness" as a progressive gradation of unfolding intensity. For the prior state is...

Even though it has been seen, it is considered "lost" in view of the subsequent expansion of the vision; likewise, they consider the expansion of the simile to be relative to what follows. In this case as well, the sense of the particle *iva* ("as if") does not at all fit.
Therefore, the meaning here is this: having treated what was seen as if it were lost, it is then placed upon the face.
Like a seed in the earth, Sāgarikā’s conduct was concealed—and as it were lost—by the minister through the Vasantotsava festival, the worship of Kāmadeva, and other such activities.
That which is placed upon the face everywhere is indeed known as *pratimukha*.
The manifestation of that seed, whether it be its attainment or even its non-attainment, and where there is further investigation—this is designated as the "embryo" (garbha). || 41 ||
For the conduct of Sāgarikā is like the soil that, while appearing to be a cover for the seed,
actually serves to awaken its power to produce the effect; having rendered it as if seen and yet lost,
another [action] follows, which is therefore like the opening of that saffron seed.

Where there is an unfolding (*udghāṭana*) throughout the entire collection of narrative portions, that is the *pratimukha* [sandhi]. It is called "counter-face" (*prati-mukha*) because it faces toward the primary [face], for its operation here occurs by way of being directed toward the primary [face] (*mukhasya abhimukhyena*). For turning away (*parāṅmukhatā*) is an illustration of the conceptualization of what was seen and then lost. As in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Even though I am defiled by dependence on others... (*parappesattaṇadūsidaṃ vi me...*)
"By the sight of him today, my body— though defiled by being another's property— has become highly esteemed," and so forth, from the speech of Sāgarikā in the *Anaṅgāṅka* (the first act).

The poetic composition from the second act up to the reunion with Susaṅgatā and Aracita constitutes the *pratimukha-sandhi* (the secondary juncture). One should understand that what has been cited by Śaṅkuka and others as merely a small portion of the seed (*bīja*) being opened up is actually a definition of only one part of it.

Regarding the term "unfolding" (*udbheda*): the "embryo" (*garbha*) is that state where there is the unfolding of the seed—which is characterized by both the stage of arising and the stage of revelation—and which consists in its being oriented toward the production of the plot. He explains this unfolding with the words beginning "attainment," and so forth.
Attainment refers to the hero (*nāyaka*), while non-attainment refers to the conduct of the antagonist (*pratināyaka*).

Furthermore, "searching" (*anveṣaṇa*) is common to both [the hero and the villain]. However, others have said this because such a meaning exists only in the context of the *vīra* (heroic) and *raudra* (furious) rasas, and thus it is not all-pervasive: one who is joined by these states of being—attainment, non-attainment, and searching—which occur again and again.

The *garbhasandhi* (the juncture of the embryo) consists in being joined with the stage known as *prāptisambhava* (the possibility of attainment), because the fruit is contained within it. For instance, in the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*, Susaṅgatā says: "Now you are indeed ungracious, you who do not release your anger even though you have been taken by the hand by the Lord. (adakṣiṇā idānīm...)

"Since you do not relinquish your anger even though you have been thus grasped by the hand by your husband"— in such instances, there is *prāpti* (attainment). Furthermore, in the third act, upon the entrance of Vāsavadattā, there is *aprāpti* (non-attainment), as Vasantaka has gone out in search of her whereabouts and delays his return.
(26) That which arises from the meaning of a seed [plot] being split open within the womb, or one produced by seduction,
or even one born from the calamity of anger, is known as *vimarśa* (the juncture of deliberation). || 42 ||

Thus ends the search (*anveṣaṇa*). Vidūṣaka: "Hī hī! Oh, even by attaining the sovereignty of Kosambī, there will not be such satisfaction for this dear horse as that which will come from hearing about my dear friend," and so forth;
here we have attainment (*prāpti*). Furthermore, [Mādhava says], "That too exists here upon Bimbā’s lip," to which the Vidūṣaka replies: "O friend, what..."

In this context, "inferior" (avaram) refers to the non-attainment [of the goal] due to the recognition of Vāsavadattā; then there is the search following Sāgarikā’s arrival at the place of appointment; and finally, attainment occurs upon the construction of the noose of creepers—such is the "embryo" (garbha). Furthermore, the element of non-attainment is necessarily present here, for otherwise, it would merely consist of a mere possibility.

How could the occurrence of attainment (*prāpti*) be certain? For in the case of *avamarśa* (reflective awareness), there is a predominance of non-attainment itself, while the aspect of attainment is subordinate; this is the distinction. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the seed bursting forth from within," some read it as *vimarśa*, while others read it as *avamarśa*. In that regard:

Vimarśa (deliberation) consists of doubt. Now, it might be argued that this is not appropriate, since first there is a cognition of possibility and from that arises doubt; for logicians declare that *tarka* (reasoning) exists in the interval between doubt and certainty. Furthermore, the juncture of deliberation is pervaded by the state of attaining a certain result, and that state of necessity—

"And doubt"—what does this mean? On this point, they say: after *tarka*, when the possibility of it being a *bādha* (contradiction) or a *chala* (quibble) has been eliminated by means of another reason (*hetvantara*), why would doubt not arise? (p. 27)

And here too, when a result that has been rendered possible by the force of a sign is obstructed by something more powerful, and the causal factors themselves are powerful, then— given the equality of strength between the producer and the destroyer— how can there not be doubt?

Furthermore, when one observes that the expansive fruit is being joined together by shaking off the deficiency produced by opposing injunctions of equal strength, human effort (*puruṣakāra*) stands forth with its neck held high; thus, after deliberation (*tarka*), there arises doubt here, and from that, a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*)—this alone is most appropriate. For instance, it is only for those endowed with human effort...

They are praised as truly wonderful, for by him the self was rescued even from the risk of death; where there is no possibility [of success], yet from that very source— whether through the efforts of others or through adverse efforts— the man who exerts human effort (*puruṣakāra*) also applies himself with great exertion, characterized by a desire for victory.

The attainment of the fruit is said to be certain through that intention. Seeing that "prosperities have many obstacles," one who possesses self-confidence thinks, "In this matter, I must remove the obstacles," and thus multiplies his own thread of exertion a thousandfold; for it is so even in the *Sāgarikā-bandhana*.
First, the conduct of the Aindrālika as employed by the Great Minister has been very skillfully composed.

Others, however, understand *avamarsa* (the "crisis") to be an obstacle. By the word *bīja* (seed), the fruit of the seed is meant; by the word *artha*, the completion [of the purpose] is expressed. Therefore, that which is the purpose of the fruit of the seed—whose face has been revealed through the unfolding of the *garbha* (embryo)—is what is intended.

"Reversal," moreover, refers to the accomplishment of that very [state]—[meaning the production of the fruit through the state of being a life-force free from obstacles]. By the word "that" (*sa*), the phrase "wherein" (*yatra*) is implied. And that reversal may be caused by anger, or by greed, or by addiction, or by a curse and so forth; the word "even" (*api*) implies other causes of obstacles.
This is a summary of matters that are impossible to describe step by step; it begins from the time Queen Vāsavadattā cast Sāgarikā into prison, up until this speech of the King in the fourth act:
"Having obtained an embrace of her neck, [this garland] has slipped away from her..."
This body of mine, being in the same state, is comforted like a friend.
In this case, the obstacle is caused by Vāsavadattā’s anger. However, greed is also a cause of obstacles, as in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*:

"My ministers have sustained my life, enticed by the prospect of attaining you" (6.3). Others do not accept this, arguing that here the greed for obtaining Vāsavadattā is not an obstacle to the primary goal (*prakṛta-phala*).

The word "kārī" refers to this example: in that very context, even though Padmāvatī had been married to him, the king—failing to obtain Vāsavadattā—resolved upon death; thus, for one desiring to die, it is due to the non-attainment of her.
In the case of ministers, the cause for the acquisition of sovereignty is primarily long-standing greed;
however, in the *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, it is shown that the calamity of a curse is caused by indignation (*amarṣa*).
Other instances should be inferred in this manner. For example, in the case of an insult (*avamarsa*), the power of a rival wife's knowledge (*vidyā*) serves as the cause.

In some cases it is fate (*daiva*), and in others it is the occasion (*samaya*)—as, for example, in the *Vikramorvaśī*, when Urvashi resolves to return to heaven because she has beheld the face of her son.
Others, however, imagining the word "vimarśa" (deliberation) to mean "return," explain it thus: [the hero] having emerged from the womb...

In that constituent of the narrative which consists of deliberation (*vimarśa*), the fruit of the seed-meaning exists because it serves as the cause for [subsequent] deliberation and so forth; thus, it is called "deliberation. In this interpretation, the primary nature of this juncture (*sandhi*)—namely, its character as a convergence of obstacles—would remain entirely untouched.

Others, however, maintain that the state of destruction (*nāśāvasthā*) and the state of seeking (*anveṣaṇāvasthā*)—which consist in the fitness for attainment (*lābhayogyatva*)—may be included within the *garbha* (intermediate stage) according to one's preference.

In that regard, when the state of attainment (*prāpti*), which is of the nature of acquisition (*lābhātmikā*), is composed by means of the *pratimukha* [sandhi], then the other two states are included within the *garbha*. When the state of destruction is included within the *avamarsa* [sandhi], then...

When one searches for [the object] within the womb [of the mind], and when there is no longer a search for its destruction within that same womb, then one should apply deliberation (*avamarśa*) and inquiry:
"How is it that I have lost what was almost attained? Was a flawed means (*viguṇopāya*) practiced by me here, or is it simply that this is not something capable of being attained?"

As Udbhaṭa said: "That which is the ground of investigation is *vimarśa*, [meaning] deliberation. However, this explanation contradicts the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) and is logically untenable, because it conflicts with the previously stated demonstration of the fixed sequence of the five stages beginning with *ārambha*.
Let it be that [the action] is contradictory.

That wherein the agent reflects, "I have been incited by this person to engage in a fruitless activity," is [the cause] produced by seduction. As for anger, addiction, and so forth, however, it is that which has as its object the failure of the result when [the intended] result is being frustrated.
That deliberation of the author is "vimarśa" (reflection) born from the vice of anger; thus, *vimarśa* is essentially of the nature of reflection.

As for the failure of the plot (*kāryavinipāta*), it serves to nourish the sentiment of wonder (*adbhutarasaparipoṣakatva*) by being bound together with the subsequent *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture).

"It is bound," says the venerable Śaṅkuka. In his view, since deliberation (*vicāra*) is not a means for any of the junctures (*sandhi*), it would have to be designated by the distinct term "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*).
Some maintain that deliberation has "disaster" (*vyāpatti*) as its object; furthermore, its very path is such that it cannot be [fully] explained through commentary.

This has been demonstrated in due order. However, as for the example provided under "enticement" (*vilobhana*), it does not fall within the scope of the *vyāpatti-vimarśa* (the deliberation on failure); thus, everything [else] is inconsistent and merely imagined according to one's own whim—enough of this.
The *nirvahana* (conclusion) is that which consists of the bringing together of the plot elements introduced at the beginning along with their seeds, culminating in various states of being. (43)

Regarding "the bringing together": the meanings of the four junctures beginning with the *mukha*, starting with the *ārambha* (commencement) and so forth— those which exist in conjunction with the *bījas* (seeds) and the transformations of the *bījas*, occurring respectively through the four stages characterized by *utpatti* (origination), *udghāṭana* (unveiling), *udbheda* (emergence), and *garbhanirbheda* (the bursting open of the womb).

It is that collection of objects in which various states consisting of pleasure and pain— such as delight, laughter, sorrow, anger, and so forth— are brought together, whereby those [states] that have attained excellence by becoming the locus of wonder in the subsequent [moments] are unified.

They are employed for the accomplishment of the fruit; that fulfillment (nirvahaṇa) is pervaded by the state of non-connection with the fruit. Regarding this, some do not desire that all these junctures (saṃdhi) be employed separately in the fulfillment of the fivefold states.

Others, however, although they maintain that within each junction (*sandhi*) there is an entry into subsequent junctions, do not see a reason for the prior state to consist of a transformation into states increasing by one; rather, [they hold that those states] become effects.
Thus, relying on the shadow of the Sāṃkhya system, [they argue] from a single state...

They consider it entirely appropriate that the connection with the fruit occurs through various intermediate states which, by attaining the status of being auxiliary to the relationship of the connection with the fruit, possess a single unified nature. Others, however, [hold that] those primary matters which are supported as the initial elements within the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture)...

They explain that these means (*upāya*) of great power are the achievers of the perfection of the fruit; their "conjunction" (*samānayana*) consists in the attainment of those fruits. According to the reading "of those of great power and those conjoined with the fruit"—when there is the state of possessing a fruit through the attainment of pleasure, then there is an abundance of *rati*, *hāsa*, and so forth.
Since the elimination of suffering is the fruit of [dramatic] undertakings and so forth,

one should observe that there is an abundance of mental states consisting of sufferings such as anger and grief, accompanied by their appropriate transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). An example follows:
In the *Ratnāvalī*, from the entrance of the magician until the conclusion,

it has already been stated that there is no rule requiring that these stages— such as the junctures (*sandhi*) and so forth— be presented through the mouth of the hero alone; rather, they may also be employed through the mouths of his minister, his retinue, the heroine, and others.
(30) These junctures (sandhis), however, are to be understood by the performers of a drama;
likewise for the *prakaraṇa*, and learn now those of the remaining [genres]. (44)
The *ḍima* and the *samavakāra* are proclaimed to have four junctures (*saṃdhi*);
however, poets should never include the *avamarśa* (the juncture of conflict) in these two.
One should always have the Vyāyoga and the Īhāmṛga performed with three junctures;
in these two, there should be no *garbha* or *avamarśa* junctures, and their style (*vṛtti*) should be *kaiśikī*.

The *prahasana* (farce), however, has two junctures (*sandhi*), as do the *vīthī*, the *aṅka*, and the *bhāṇa*; in these, the *mukha* (opening) and *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion) junctures must always be employed by poets. (47)
For the *vīthī*, the *bhāṇa*, and likewise the *prahasana*—these works should always be composed by poets as being devoid of the *kaiśikī* style. || 48 ||

He analyzes their application with the passage beginning "But these... and ending with "...should always be employed by poets when the *mukha* and *nirvahaṇa* [junctures] are to be performed. This matter was already determined previously during the commentary on the verse beginning "When one is omitted, the fourth [is used]," and so forth (19.18).

Why are those two (the *ḍima* and the *samavakāra*) said to have four junctures? He explains this with the words "not of those two," and so forth. The particle *tu* indicates the reason (*hetu*), because it is impossible to compose an *avamārsha* for them. The same applies to what follows. This constitutes a separate section on the reasons.
Thus indeed should the junctures (sandhis) be composed by practitioners in the *Daśarūpa*.
Now, learn the arrangement of the constituent parts (aṅgas) of these junctures. (49)

One should understand that those sections which describe the occurrences in the various regions in their proper sequence, being endowed with the qualities of its own excellence, constitute the constituent parts (aṅgas). 50.

This [rule] is not to be applied here, for it was already stated previously—under the rule *ekalope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), etc.—that there is no elision by virtue of its being a substitute (*lopasthānitva*).
Now, one might ask: since the body of the narrative consists of the fivefold *saṃdhi*, how can there be divisions such as the *daśarūpaka* and so forth at the beginning?

Anticipating this objection, he says, "For thus" (*evaṃ hi*). [Some] explain, raising an objection: "Since the junctures (*saṃdhi*) occur by means of the method of application (*viniyoga*) as stated above, there is consequently a division of the ten forms (*daśarūpa*). But that is incorrect, because the division of the ten dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*) has already been demonstrated precisely through the difference in their definitions (*lakṣya*). And this must necessarily be so; otherwise—

Since the *ḍima* and *samavakāra* are indistinguishable in having four junctures (*saṃdhi*), how could there be a difference between them—or for that matter, between the *nāṭaka* and others? Therefore, this is a concluding passage [introduced by] "for" (*hi*). By means of the "rule" (*kalpa*)—that is, the manner of arrangement—of the constituent parts (*aṅga*), other matters as well that are useful for the plot (*itivṛtta*) are generally established.

In order to demonstrate the general nature of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) by way of their purpose, he speaks a set of six verses— beginning with "The meters (*vṛtta*) related to the junctures (*sandhi*)" and ending with "it attains beauty, there is no doubt"— illuminating both [the nature and the purpose] through one verse for the former and two for the latter.
It has been stated that "junction" (*saṃdhi*) refers to a group of thematic portions;

therein, the "sections of the plot" (*vṛttāni saṃvidhānakhaṇḍāni*) are those elements to be connected within the junctions. "In due order" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*) means according to the sequence necessitated by the accomplishment of the primary purpose, and not according to an order artificially constructed for the sake of defining technical characteristics.

He asks, "Why are they called 'limbs' (aṅga) because they exist in the parts—the beginning, middle, and end? He replies: "Because they are joined to—that is, appropriate for—the excellence and accomplishment of the connection of their own possessor (the whole);
since they bring about that connection, they are called 'limbs' (aṅga). This is the meaning.
The composition of the desired subject matter, the non-omission of the narrative,
the attainment of passion, and the concealment of secrets in the performance [of the drama]. (51)
The marvelous nature of the designation, and the illumination of those things to be illuminated—this sixfold purpose of the constituent parts is indeed observed in the scripture. (52)
Just as a man deprived of a limb is not capable of undertaking any task, so too a poem lacking its essential parts is not fit for performance. 53.

Others, however, say: "The excellences (*guṇas*)—such as the seeds, the production, and the unfolding of one's own perfection (*svasaṃpat*)—and the varieties of word and meaning, or the excellences of those very perfections, are what the compositions are endowed with.
By the words "of the desired," etc., he states the purpose (*prayojana*). It is the composition that brings about the tasting of *rasa*, which is the desired purpose.

Expansion (*vistāraṇā*): the non-depletion of the narrative through its gradual clarification, such that it does not become like a mere collection of iron rods; this is the common purpose for all [the dramatic elements].
*Rañjanā* (pleasingness) is the attainment of passion, both by the characters themselves and toward one another, within the performance of the plot, resulting in their fitness for being pleasing.

Alternatively, because there is no basis for its derivation, or because it appears redundant and so forth, those meanings which are secret and ought to be concealed are here concealed. Knowledge is inference because it consists of certainty, being distinct from the form of reasoning (*yukti*) which is difficult to grasp. As [it is said]:

34. *Ākṣipti*: "The disclosure of the *garbha* (the central plot-seed) is *ākṣipti*. That which remains within the heart, even though it has been re-established, its disclosure due to some cause is an undeniable [element].

The manifestation of clarity is *ākṣipti* (suggestion), for in that context, *ākṣepa* means the drawing forth of the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*). This occurs, for example, in the case of Vāsavadattā—who has been taken by both the King and the Vidūṣaka as being Sāgarikā—within her own utterances such as: "O Sāgarikā, the moon is your face, your eyes are lotuses... When two parties are engaged in mutual deception, whichever one relies more heavily upon [resources such as] assistants and intelligence is alone capable of deceiving or outmaneuvering the other.

This is *adhibala* (superior force). (Vāsavadattā, aside: Noble husband, I am indeed ashamed of this cruelty; therefore, remove her bonds.

Just as one does not remember kinsmen [due to such absorption].

"O sister, let this be appropriate for me.

62. *Bhāṣaṇa*—Speech endowed with conciliation, gifts, and other [stratagems]. Even though it occurs within the *garbha* [act],...

This limb has been called "the means of attraction" (*saṃgraha*); nevertheless, it is mentioned again here by another term in order to demonstrate that it must necessarily be employed in this context. As Vasubhūti says: "O Queen, you bear the title 'Queen' most appropriately."
The preceding section, however, should be understood as demonstrating the meaning as it has been stated. The attainment of the granting of the boon is intended as the conclusion of the poem. (103)
