In this context, the mere restatement of the means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and others mentioned in the *garbha* juncture (*sandhi*) by way of a clear path is not what constitutes impropriety; rather, that which primarily consists of stating, "Thus has this been obtained," is the element known as *bhāṣaṇa* (discourse).

63. *Pūrvavākya* (Prior Statement)—the *pūrvavākya* is the illumination of the matter as previously stated. For example, Bābhravya says: "Now I have become one whose exertion has borne fruit. 64. *Kāvyasaṃhāra* (Conclusion of the Poem)—the attainment of the granting of a boon is called *kāvyasaṃhāra*. For example:
Yaugandharāyaṇa: "Your Majesty, let it be said: 'What further favor may I offer you? and so forth, up to 'Vikramabāhu has attained equality with himself,' and so forth.
The pacification of the king's command is called *praśasti* (the benediction).
These constituent parts (*aṅgas*) of the drama should be performed according to their respective junctures (*saṃdhi*). || 104 ||
However, poets skilled in composition, taking into account the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and emotions (*bhāva*), [employ] the *praśasti*.
Regarding the term *praśasti*: it refers to both the praise of a king and the peace of his realm. (As in the *Ratnāvalī*):
"May Indra, shedding his desired rain, cause the earth to produce abundant crops."
"May the foremost of Brahmins duly provide satisfaction to the inhabitants of the three worlds through their desired offerings;

and may the ointment of the *vajra*—the avoidance of the words of the malicious—ensure that the assembly of the virtuous, accumulated through successive rites, remains united without any occasion for separation until the end of the kalpa. (4/22) Thus it is said.

"According to the juncture" (yathāsandhi) means that whatever [verse] has fitness for a particular juncture; and the poet alone knows this fitness, not merely a composer of detached verses (*muktaka*), but one capable of arranging a continuous composition (*prabandha*). Thus he says, "by poets," and so forth. Now, one might ask: what kind of skill does a poet possess in the construction of such a composition? To this he replies: "having regard for rasa and bhāva."

And skill (*kauśala*) consists in having regard for that [the audience]. For it has been stated that the science consisting of drama (*nāṭya-śāstra*) provides proficiency through aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone, which is [ultimately] delight. Consequently, just as whatever is useful to someone is made palatable by being combined with other flavors—such as curd, sugar, milk, and so forth—that are pleasing to them—
Just as that [medicine], having entered within by means of that [door], effects nourishment and the cessation of disease,

so too the means to human goals, being unable to enter the heart directly, attains entry through the affection for the most beautiful and appropriate aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); thus it serves as a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*) for the attainment of the objectives of those to be trained.
It is appropriate. And it has been stated in the sixth [chapter] that the transference of rasa occurs only through the form of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, and not otherwise.
"These" refers to these [following]. (p. 62)
Sometimes, however, they may be mixed together by means of two or three combinations. || 105 ||

Those [parts] which are written down become endowed with the fulfillment of the intended rasa, bhāva, and so forth; whereas those [parts] where the minds of those intent on a single rasa follow the bed of composition in a state of mutual rivalry and without regard for anything else, through a fitting disposition— even when there is an interruption in the plot— it serves to nourish the rasa itself, otherwise, in the event of an interruption...

Since the permanent emotions (*sthāyins*) and so forth have been shown to be fragmented, where is there any talk of rasa? Therefore, this entire array of limbs—consisting of the excitants (*vibhāvas*) and so on—is actually the equipment of rasa itself. For instance, in the verse beginning "In the fire of the lac-house," the introductory phrase fulfills the portion of the excitant for both the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) rasas; and the phrase "the enmity which had grown" fulfills the excitant for anger within the heroic rasa.

In the *raudra* (furious) rasa, where the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) serves to reawaken the nature of the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), the *parikara* (poetic elaboration) and the *parinyāsa* (concluding resolution), such as "with arms quivering" (*cañcadbhuja*), nourish the aspect of the *anubhāva* (consequent action). For example: "May the deities favor this resolve" (*aṇugeṇhaṃtu edaṃ vavasidaṃ devadā-o*;
Draupadī—may the deities favor this resolve; *Veṇīsaṃhāra* 1.21–22), and so forth.
Enticement (*vilobhana*) consists of being the primary vehicle for the conjunction of transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as mental satisfaction, longing, joy, intelligence, and memory;
other [types of *vilobhana*] should be applied in the same manner.
Objection: Should not the *saṃdhis* (junctures) be dependent upon the *aṅgas* (limbs)? From what source, then, does their dependence on *rasa* (flavor) arise?
It is said in reply: for the *saṃdhis* are dependent upon the [dramatic] states (*avasthā*).
As it has been stated: "The *mukhasaṃdhi* (opening juncture) is a segment of the narrative employed for a specific stage of the plot designated as 'commencement'."

The same applies elsewhere; even the *avasthās* (states) are described as specific modifications of other [elements]. To the question, "What follows from this? What happens because of this? he says: "But with respect to *rasa* and *bhāva*, the effect (*kārya*) is established; having understood its persistence in relation to that, the effect also has fulfilled its purpose by reaching the point of generating the flow of *rasa*."
The meaning is that it "is accomplished.

"Mixed" (saṃmiśrāṇi) means that what was stated in one juncture (*sandhyantara*) is also [applicable] in another juncture. Just as a formal device (*yukti*) may be mentioned in the introduction (*mukha*) and also composed within the development (*garbha*).
In the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, as previously cited (3.27), it occurs by way of nourishing the portions of deliberation (*vitarka*) and deviation (*vyabhicārin*):
"The spirited one [bearing] the burden of grief for his kinsmen slain by the enemy," and so forth. The phrase "two or three" means by way of their occurrence twice or thrice.
Therefore, even a single element of juncture (*sandhyaṅga*) should be employed twice or thrice within that same juncture. For example:

In the *Ratnāvalī*, the *vilāsa* (amorous playfulness) repeatedly depicted in the presence of Queen Sāgarikā intensifies the primary erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). In the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, the *saṃpheṭa* (mutual confrontation) and *vidrava* (flight) [are likewise employed].
Having understood the purpose and the state [of the work], one should arrange the constituent parts at their joints;
and these very parts should be connected with logical consistency of meaning. (106)
The intermediate forms of the strategic means (sandhi) are twenty-one specific varieties:
conciliation (sāma), sowing dissension (bheda), force (daṇḍa), bribery (pradāna), and execution (vadha). || 107 ||
Present-mindedness, stumbling over one's lineage, recklessness, fear, shamelessness, deceit, and anger; || 108 ||

Furthermore, the excitants (*uddīpana*) of the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments are demonstrated again. However, because excessive repetition would lead to distaste, the mention of "two or three" is made. Likewise, regarding the combination of two:

if that which is to be accomplished by two factors can be achieved by one alone, then what is the use of the other? The same applies to the combination of three. An example of the combination of two is as follows:
In the *Pratimāniruddha*, composed by Vasunāga, the son of Bhīma—immediately after the *upakṣepa* (introduction), there is no *parikara* (development);

rather, the *parinyāsa* (conclusion) is seen through the first [element] alone. Thus is the threefold combination (*triyoga*), as for example in the *Rāsakāṅka* of the *Rādhāvipralambha* composed by Bhejjala, where by the *upakṣepa* alone—namely, "li-alīssā" and so forth—[the structure is established].
When the task of deploying the retinue has become weighty and is being maintained, there is the examination of seduction with a single objective.
Thus, the peace treaty (*sandhi*) consists of four components until it is fully established.
Now, in order to show the other types of peace treaties, he says: "Of these very components," and so forth. In that regard:

Some say that *antara* means an interval, a gap, or a junction (*sandhi*). That is merely a limb; and because it exists therein, it stands in its place. Thus, because they reside in the gaps between the limbs of the junction, they are the "intervals of the junction" (*sandhyantara*). For this very reason, they are connected to the limbs. Now, is it by mere physical adhesion? No, he says: rather, it is by way of the meaning (*artha*).
"One should strive for this through yoga; therefore, these are the specific [applications] of the *saṃdhy-aṅgas*.
For that which is connected to the specific purpose of that [main action] becomes its subsidiary (*aṅga*).
Others think: "These are the specific forms of those very [elements], such as the *upakṣepa* and so forth, which were mentioned in general terms."

The intermediate subdivisions are as follows: (p. 64) indeed, the introduction (*upakṣepa*), vigor (*ojas*), concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*), error (*bhrānti*), and likewise the determination of the cause (*hetvavadhāraṇa*).
A messenger, a letter, a dream, and a painting—these are known as the "intoxicants" (mada). || 109 ||
The viṣkambha, the cūlikā, the praveśaka, the aṅkāvatāra, and the aṅkamukha—these are the five types of arthopakṣepa. || 110 ||

It is distinguished by specific types such as *sāma* (conciliation) and so forth; for instance, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, there is an introduction (*upakṣepa*) consisting of anger in the passage "the fire of the lacquer house" (*lākṣāgṛhānala*); in the *Rāmābhyudaya*, there is an introduction consisting of fear; in the *Pratimāniruddha*, it takes the form of a dream; and in the *Udāttarāghava*, it consists of the determination of a cause. In this manner, other examples should be followed accordingly.

And these are precisely of the nature of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*); there is nothing else in the world apart from these in dramatic performance (*prayoga*). The term "performance" (*prayoga*) is used for the sake of clarity. It has been stated that there are twenty-one [transitory states] by way of illustration for the purpose of utility therein, in order to demonstrate the path of the poet.

In that regard, conciliation (*sāma*) and the like are the causes of brilliance in the Heroic (*vīra*); slaughter is [the cause] in the Furious (*raudra*); presence of mind (*pratyutpannamati*), which is a transitory state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) characterized by intelligence, is [the cause] everywhere; the mention of lineage (*gotraskhalana*) is [the cause] in the Erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*); rashness (*sāhasa*) is [the cause] in the Heroic (*vīra*) and so forth; and fickleness (*cāpalya*) is [the cause] in the Comic (*hāsya*) and so forth. It is the same elsewhere. "Vigor" (*ojas*) means energy (*tejas*).

In the chapter on General Gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*), [the following] will be defined: concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*) is dissimulation (*avahittha*); wonder (*vismaya*) is astonishment (*citram*); and *śilpaviśeṣa* is a particular skill. All of these are easily found in every type of dramatic composition, such as the *nāṭaka*, and are themselves easy to recognize; therefore, by means of their illustration and application—[as seen in the passage] beginning with "insult, contempt, and so forth" (22.41)—[they are established].
The text has not been expanded;
65) it is intended for an audience of intermediate capacity, covering only the movement from the opening to the *mukha-sandhi* of the drama.
The Viṣkambhaka, however, should be performed by the domestic priest, the minister, and the chamberlain. || 111 ||
The Viṣkambhaka is to be known as being of two kinds: pure (śuddha) or mixed (saṃkīrṇa).
It is pure when performed by middle-ranking characters, and mixed when performed by low and middle-ranking characters. || 112 ||
When the suggestion of a plot element is made in various ways by the *sūta* and others stationed behind the inner curtain (*antaryavanikā*), that indeed is called a *cūlikā*. (113)

Following the sequence of other acts and concerning the summarized meaning of the *bindus*, that which is known as the *praveśaka* (interlude) should be understood as belonging to the context of the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*. || 114 ||
That which is not practiced by superior or middling persons, nor composed in refined speech, but follows the conventions of the common vernacular language, is to be known as the *praveśaka*. 114a.

When one act follows immediately after another act, having reached its performance and being joined with the application of the seed-meaning (bīja-artha), that should be known as an *aṅkāvatāra* (transition between acts). || 115 ||
That which is first introduced by a woman or a man with their faces separated from the stage is called the *aṅkamukha* (the opening of the act). (116)

Thus, as being inseparable from the determination of the plot (itivṭtta), the junctures (sandhi), the constituent parts of the junctures (sandhyaṅga), and the intermediate junctures (sandhyantara)— though they serve the rasa that constitutes their own essence— are primarily directed toward the bodily component consisting of the plot; for this very reason, they have been demonstrated as common to all four dramatic styles (vṛtti).

Now, however, by whose grace drama— which had become neck-deep submerged within the Śāstras, Itihāsas, and so forth— was rescued and established as an object of enjoyment for all people; and with reference to whom it was stated in the first chapter that "employ even the Kaiśikī [Vṛtti]," and "whatever substance is appropriate for her," and many other such things were said.

Therefore, even the constituent elements of *lāsya* (dance), which bring about its manifestation and possess an intense attachment to the portions of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional state (*bhāva*) that constitute its very soul, must be employed by poets and performers within the scope of the poetry to be enacted.
Other varieties of *lāsya* that are useful for drama have emerged from this [work], but they are to be performed by a single actor, as in the *bhāṇa*. || 117 ||

The *lāsya* should be understood as being like the *bhāṇa* and *kṛti*, performed by a single actor, or it may be inferred to be like a *prakaraṇa*; it should be composed with praise for the cloth (*kāryasaṃstava*) and various emotional states (*vividhabhāva*). (118) 5a The *geyapada*, *sthitapāṭhya*, *āsīna*, and *puṣpagaṇḍikā*.
The *pracchedaka* has three delusions, while that called *saindhava* has two delusions. || 119 ||
To show that [these elements] are to be applied in every respect, he says: "Other limbs as well in the performance of *lāsya*, etc.

By "drama" (*nāṭaka*) is meant merely that which is to be enacted. From here until the end of the chapter, those limbs which will be described as distinct from those already mentioned and pertaining to the performance of *lāsya* are also useful for drama.

[The author] dispels the doubt—namely, "In that case, since there is no difference between the constituent parts (*aṅga*), what is the difference between the whole (*aṅgin*), Lāsya, and Nāṭaka?"—with the words "(from this)": "From this Nāṭaka, characterized by imitation and representation, [the elements] have emerged and exist externally, to be carried by a single actor. By the word "as" (*iva*) in the phrase "as in the Bhāṇa," he refers to the Nāṭaka within the context of the Bhāṇa.
The nature of drama (*nāṭyarūpatā*) exists [in *lāsya*], yet it does not exist in *lāsya* in any way whatsoever, because of its distinct difference from the form of drama;
this has been established in detail in the fourth chapter.
Now, one might ask: "Which are the components of *lāsya* that will be taught in the context of drama? To this he says: "the tenfold [set] beginning with *geyapada*," and so forth.

This concludes the section ending with the definition of the limbs (*aṅga-nirdeśa*). Regarding this enumeration of limbs (*aṅga-uddeśa*), its tenfold specific characteristics will be explained in the chapter on *tāla* (chapter 31) during the discussion of *lāsya*, and he will likewise conclude by stating: "The characteristic of these [limbs] is to be understood in the rules for *lāsya*" (A-).
19) For it is precisely there that the complete limbs, as well as the most excellent of the excellent, are presented in this manner of question and answer.
For this tenfold characteristic of the description of the limbs belongs to the Lāsya dance. || 120 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "by those seated on seats," which describes that [performance] augmented by stringed instruments (*tantrībhāṇḍa*), the purpose here is to demonstrate its utility for drama (*nāṭya*). Therefore, the intended meaning is as follows: those constituent parts of the *lāsya* dance...

Some portion of variety not seen in the world shall be described; even if it is not observed in common life, it should be composed by poets for inclusion in drama for the sake of the variety of aesthetic delight (*rañjanā*).
Others, however, explain that here only such an application of the limbs of *lāsya* is performed; for instance, in the case of the sung verse (*geyapada*).
They show an illustration: then Malayavatī and a maidservant enter, playing the lute;
Malayavatī sings, "O you with hair like the filaments of a full-blown lotus," and so forth (*Nāgānanda* 1.13). But this is incorrect;
for here, the propitiation of the deity through an action other than [the primary one] is equal to a thousand recitations of a mantra, provided there is some singing.

By the force of such Puranic statements as "the recitation mixed with that [mantra] is the means for attaining ten million-fold fruit," it is intended as something to be performed by Malayavatī. And since she is the one who performs it, there is nothing here for the purpose of *lāsya* (dance), nor even any status as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of *lāsya*. Even where [it occurs], such as in the passage: "Then enter two maidservants singing... and so forth—[this refers to the entry of the characters].

(Ratnāvalī 1.13), and so forth. Even there, worldly conduct—such as wandering about and the like—is performed on occasions of joy and prosperity, such as the spring festival (*vasantotsava*). If it is performed for a specific purpose, even though it belongs to the character being imitated (*anukārya*), it would nonetheless result in its not being taught separately as a constituent element of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*), just as [in the following example].

For when an imitation of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha is to be performed, knowledge of the sacrificial components is required; thus, the components of sacrifice ought to be taught. Indeed, there is no such thing whatsoever that is not useful in drama. Therefore, those components which exist in lāsya—
Therefore, in this context, the sage intends to refer only to that worldly portion of the *upajīvyas* which is useful for pleasing [the audience] as a constituent of *lāsya*.

Otherwise, what would be the point of stating here, "By those seated on their seats," and so forth? Furthermore, it would be inconsistent that he did not state right here, "I shall explain the definition of these. Consequently:

Regarding "the *paridhānaka*," etc. (31–350): that which was described as the definition of the *lāsya-aṅgas* in the rule for the *pūrvaraṅga* (A-31) should also be employed here in the dramatic portion (*abhineyabhāga*).
Therefore, he says, "that which [is performed] by those seated on their seats," in order to show whatever portion is applicable to the drama (*nāṭya*).
The word *yat* is a particle used in the sense of "in which";
that which is sung by singers in a dry (meaningless) manner is called a *geyapada*. (121)
When a woman dances while seated, accompanied by song endowed with beloved qualities according to the rules for the primary and secondary limbs [of performance], that is called *geyapada*. (122)
When one recites in the Prākṛta language while remaining composed and filled with intense emotion,
with limbs scorched by the fire of love, that is called *sthitapāṭhya*.

Therefore, in whatever poem or performance [it occurs], the term *śuṣka* (dry) implies that it is to be imitated as something empty by singers— not by actors— and that they sing while seated in their places— not from behind the scenes (*nepathya*), as one might say "the song is sung from the wings"— thus singing while manifesting a particular state of absorption (*āveśa*) that has entered into the poet’s composition.

"Equipped with stringed instruments" means accompanied by all musical instruments, and not devoid of them like the *bhāvyāsīna* or *pāṭhya* [recitations]; it is called "the place of song" (*geyapada*) because it is the locus (*sthāna*) for singing. Therefore, that is where the fivefold *dhruvā* songs—devoid of intermediate interludes (*antarālāpa*) and specific notes (*svara*)—become fit for performance.

It is said that the application of poetry (*kāvyaprayoga*) constitutes the "sung verse" (*geyapada*). For in whatever performance this is firmly established, it becomes a delighter of the audience; thus, whatever portion of this [performance] has been utilized here from among the elements of *lāsya* and so forth—whether it be sung by singers or actors in a dry manner (meaning, based on clever wit), or even if it is merely chanted without musical accompaniment—this constitutes the sung verse.
The explanation that "geyapada" refers to those sung words where the singing is performed in such a manner as being triangular or square— that is entirely rejected.
Now, he says "Prākṛtam" (the Prakrit) in order to rely upon that which will be a constituent part of Lāsya, namely the *sthitaprāpi*.
Regarding the phrase "but that which is devoid of": even in *lāsya*, there is recitative (*pāṭhya*) material primarily intended to delight the gods and kings.

For the capture of their hearts is achieved therein through the recitative as well, introduced for variety in the middle; and while remaining standing or seated, one recites—this marvelous quality belonging to the recitative is an extraordinary element of delight.

Therefore, it is derived from that [specific] limb. For instance, even when one is distressed and deprived [of the proper conditions], one should recite that which is endowed with the characteristics of the Prakrit language, likewise possessing the *uttarasami*, suitable for the *rasa*, and preceded by the grasping of the essential notes (*sthāyisvara*). This is the extraordinary [element].

The *sthitapāṭhya* (fixed recitation) is that which is drawn from the limbs of the *sallāsyā*; this is an indicator of possession (*āveśa*). Therefore, it should also be understood that even one possessed by anger may recite in Sanskrit (*saṃskṛta*), and so forth.

Staged recitation (*sthitapāṭhya*) is prescribed as being joined with the *bahucārī* [footwork], accompanied by the five types of hand-gestures (*pañcapāṇikalā*), or alternatively, combined with the *cañcatpuṭa* [hand-gesture]. || 124 ||
Where he sits seated, devoid of all musical instruments, with his limbs not stretched out, and filled with anxiety and grief. (125)
Various meters (vṛttas) may occur, and it is based on singing;
where there is a basis for men's movements through gestures, that is the Puṣpagaṇḍikā.

Others, however, define *sthitapāṭhya* as that which is accompanied by the *bahucārī*, the *cañcatpuṭa*, and the *uttara*; they cite as an example the passage from the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*: "uddāmotkalikām... and so forth.
This has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, there is no occasion for *pāṭhya* here, nor is there any *tryaśra* or *caturaśra* rhythm (*tāla*).

However, as for its role as a constituent of *lāsya*, we shall explain all of that in the chapter on *tāla* itself. Now, he states the portion to be derived from the *āsīna-pāṭhya* (seated recitation): "That wherein one sits while seated" (*āsīnam āsyate yatra*). That portion is where one remains seated due to being devoid of gestures and the like, owing to an intense onset of grief.

The coloring quality (*uparañjakaguṇa*) is devoid of the four types of musical instruments; it consists primarily of the very delicate, low-pitched singing (*kākalī*) of women. That which remains here and captivates the mind is the worldly (*laukika*). Even compared to the worldly, for there, the state of that [singing] is perceived as having the mere purpose of similarity, and its status is that of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) called "the seated" (*tadāsīna*).

By subsisting on what is studied while seated, by sharing a portion of one's seat, and through the practice of yoga, that which is useful for winning over others in all matters, such as compassion and the like, is achieved. Thus it is said: "accompanied by anxiety and grief.
It is joined with the consequents (anubhāvas) such as lying on the ground, meditating, or looking downward. "In all [matters]"—so it is said.

The sense is that it is "soundless" (*niḥśabdam*), meaning that because sounds such as lamentations arising from meditation or the experience of grief and sorrow are not employed therein, it is said to be devoid of them. Following that, "with limbs unextended" (*aprasāritagātram*) means being devoid of physical gestures (*abhinaya*).
Others read "with limbs well-extended" (*suprasāritagātram*); in that case as well—
(Without the effort of separately demonstrating the excellence of the limbs,) there is a mere emptiness of expression due to the drooping of the body.
He states the portion derived from the *lāsya-aṅga* known as *puṣpagaṇḍikā*: "the *vṛttas*" (in the phrase) "in singing," [which refers to] the *tata* [instrumental music].
In the center, with a hollow space, and in the middle, bound together—
(where a woman in male attire recites charmingly in Sanskrit).
That [composition] should be known as a *puṣpagaṇḍikā*, intended for the amusement of her female companions. || 127 ||
Where there is various dancing accompanied by song and instrumental music,
and where women act like men, that should be known as *puṣpagaṇḍikā*.
That should be known as the "severer" [season], wherein women, struck by the moonlight, become attached even to those who do them harm, as if they were their beloveds. 129.

The variegated nature produced by the blending [of elements] in the roles is a delicate application that is indeed captivating even in performance, despite its being supermundane in its diversity. Because of their resemblance to a garland, these are called *puṣpagaṇḍikā* (flower-clusters), owing to their connection with the variety found in singing, dancing, and song; and because of the intention to use the feminine gender, they refer to female roles.

[The phrase] "stated in the *Puṣpagaṇḍikā* for men" should be applied alternately with the terms "gestures" (*ceṣṭā*) and "basis" (*āśraya*). Now, in order to apply the variety produced by the members of the *pracchedaka*, he says: "[Regarding] the *pracchedaka* in the rules for *lāsya*..."

It will be said: "Having seen the reflection of her beloved in moonlight, in wine, in water, or even in a mirror, she rejoices, thinking him thus adorned" (31.349). This describes the *pracchedaka* (the act of concealment/covering). In that context, there is water-play (*jalakrīḍā*), adornment in water, [reflection] in a mirror, and drinking in a drinking party (*pānagoṣṭhī*).

When the various forms [of her reflection] are seen slightly reflected, there is great joy for the beloved; thus, "reflection" (*pratiphalana*) is synonymous with "triple division" (*triccheda*). Consequently, in poetic works, poets have described how women—through the joy born from seeing their own reflections—possess the power to appease the lover’s feigned anger (*praṇayakopa*). As, for example: [Example omitted per instructions]
Bow down to Rudra, who delights in the reflections of his own feet upon the ten mirrors of his nails— reflections that cling to the feet of the Gaurī who was momentarily angered by his prostration.

Then she pressed her trembling body against his chest, which was marked by the reflection of her quivering breasts and where the tips of her nails had caused a thrill; thus she restrained (or tormented) him alone.
"Free from harshness, with smooth words, adorned with even meters, rich in masculine sentiments, and containing the three 'fools'—this is known as *trimūḍhaka*.
(130) And so forth. In that case, although there are three types [of drama], only moonlight (*jyotsnā*) is useful... [as is] the play of drinking (*pānalīlā*).

By means of perceiving a specific kind of enjoyment appropriate for one whose husband is under her own control. This is what is meant: in worldly life, a full moonrise does not always occur; however, in dramatic performance (*prayoga*), such a specific time must be adopted as it is conducive to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by virtue of its being imbued with the quality of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). And so it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:

"The rising of the moon has been described for the most part as 'now this [moon], which steals the luster of the lotus' (1.23), 'hidden behind the edge of the eastern mountain' (1.24), and 'while your face-moon exists, this other cool-rayed moon has risen' (3.13). Thus, there is the apprehension of specific non-worldly times suitable for aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
This is derived from Pracchedaka. As the venerable Upādhyāya said:
"A poet should not describe that which does not exist in a thing;
rather, he should describe that which is impossible [in it], for such a description bestows delight."
"Could there not be, at some time or in some place, a country separated by mountains, or the sky adorned with a lightning-bowl, or the river Kṛṣṇā? And so forth.
Now, in order to define the portion that is useful for the definition of the "three-fold delusion" (*trimūḍha*), he says:

"Words that are neither harsh nor overly smooth," and so forth. In the *trimūḍhaka* (the "three fools") section of the *lāsya*, there is the delusion (*moha*) of three characters: first, the hero's delusion caused by the offense of a single woman whom he dislikes; second, the delusion of a new woman due to her initial shyness born of affection;
and third, [the delusion of] the others. In that context, the words of the hero must necessarily be gentle, as in the case of Udayana.
There are indeed words. Therefore, in this context of words, that portion consisting of *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras* which is conducive to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) must be accepted.

For in the world, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from the collection of *guṇas* such as sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and so forth; indeed, whatever anyone says when permeated by these would itself be poetry. Even in its mere shadow, it exists partially.

Thus, because it is incomplete, it is indeed useless. Therefore, this extraordinary variety in the enjoyment of rasa is entirely produced by the collection of its qualities (*guṇas*). By the phrase "with even meters" (*samavṛttaiḥ*), the variety produced by the meter is indicated; by the phrase "rich with human emotions" (*puruṣabhāvāḍhyam*), that produced by the characters (*pātras*) is also indicated, such as the states of *helā* (sportiveness) and so forth. In this way, [the variety] is produced by specific factors.
By demonstrating that beauty exists in that drama where there is variety, he shows the influence of the *guṇas* themselves through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

The wise know that which possesses a vessel with lost conventions, yet is endowed with clearly manifest instruments and joined with vernacular speech, as *saindhavaka*. (131) [It is] joined with gestures, musical instruments, and so forth, and is devoid of recited speech (*pāṭhya*). (131a)
Indeed, that should be known as the Saindhava dance by those skilled in dramatic performance. || 132 ||

Now, in order to appropriate the portion of livelihood from Saindhavaka, he says: "The vessel whose conventional signs have fallen away"—the speech resorted to by those of Sindh should be known as Saindhava by the wise;
it is accompanied by instrumental music and the like.
And this will be stated in the section on the rules for the components of *lāsya* (31–359). In that context,
when the dialects such as Saindhavī are not employed merely as instrumental means for other common (*prākṛta*) languages,
but rather as coloring (*rañjana*) and so forth that serve the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), then this extraordinary meaning, which serves the purpose of coloring, arises from the *lāsya* component.
It is accepted as such; for indeed, since the Prākṛta language is exceedingly useful for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*),
Rājaśekhara composed his *saṭṭaka* titled *Karpūramañjarī* almost entirely in that language,
while Bhejjala composed his *rāsakāṅka* titled *Rādhāvipralambha* with a predominance of the Saindhava dialect, and Candraka [did likewise].

One's own dramatic roles (*rūpaka*), which are particularly suited for the *vīra* (heroic) and *raudra* (furious) sentiments, are expressed solely in the Sanskrit language. For this very reason, the predominance of one or another [language] in this context is determined by the varying degree of suitability for the respective aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
This is what he expresses with the words beginning "the character" (*pātra*) and so forth; the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*). Therefore, where there are characters...

[The performance] is joined with vernacular speech; for that very reason, the specific convention appropriate to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which was previously explained in the chapter on intonation (*kāku*), has here become corrupted—that is, the convention has been led to ruin where the manifestation of the *rasa* would otherwise be perfect. Therefore, the actor (*pātra*) is accompanied by instrumental actions such as playing the lute (*vīṇā*).
The term *saindhavaka* is used here through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the object and its possessor. Thus,

that variety of the ten dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*) based on language which was described by Kohala and others has indeed been accepted by the Sage (Bharata) in his definition of the *saindhava-aṅga*.
(73) Endowed with the *mukha* and *pratimukha* [junctures], with a four-square progression of steps,
and possessed of the aesthetic moods (*bhāva*) and sentiments (*rasa*) joined together, it is for the sake of variety in the *dvimūḍhaka*.

The reading "karuṇānvitam" is a corruption. Similarly, regarding the example "saindhavakam" (the Saindhava dance) being devoid of the prescribed [textual] recitation—as when the Vidūṣaka dances in the *Ratnāvalī*—the definition and illustration were provided simply by disregarding the opinion of the Sage [Bharata], considering it a deviation from the beloved [standard] due to the use of Prakrit; it was not stated [as a fault] on logical grounds.
The phrase "something" (*kiṃcit*) refers to that which is indeed non-existent [in itself].
Through the sequence beginning with "the face and the reflection," it adopts a portion of variety from the *dvimūḍhaka* (the two-stupid) form.
This occurs in that poetry which relies upon dance and song, and wherein there are either two characters—a hero and a heroine—or indeed two heroines.
Delusion is described there as being like the *trigūḍhaka* [meter]; for, in the definition of the *tāla*, it will be stated that a single *tāla*, being joined with four feet, revolves.
It is likewise endowed with the *mukha* and *pratimukha* [sections] and rests upon the *ācapuṭa* [rhythm].

"Just as it is with syllables and their combinations, so too it is endowed with twelve [elements]. (31.360/361) Therefore, in the sequential progression of the limbs and sub-limbs, that very following of the *tāla* and the completion of the movement (*gati*) in the four faces—
though not observed in the world in such movements and the like— is [the case here].
Because it brings about the proximity of the actors and the audience, and because the element of similarity— being of the nature of bliss—

is more intensely subservient to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) than other parts, that [element] is accepted. For the *mukha* (opening) is that which leads the audience forward, and from there, the *pratimukha* (development) leads them toward the other directions of the *lāsya* limbs.

Having made the *mukha* and *pratimukha* four-square as parts of the song, it is that in which there is a progression by means of steps that traverse the four quarters. He asks: what happens when this is so? He says: "for the sake of variety";
variety is the purpose here. If one asks what follows from that, he says: "by means of a connected state" (*śliṣṭabhāvena*).
That by which clarity has been attained—that is, reached—by means of the convergence of mental fluctuations characterized by total equanimity, [and] by means of the *rasas*.

One should know that the *uttamottamaka* (the highest of the high) is based on many sentiments (*rasa*), characterized by various poetic compositions in verse (*śloka-bandha*), and embellished with playful gestures and expressions (*helā-hāva*). 134.

Śrī Śaṅkuka and others maintain that [the drama] is endowed with the limbs of song (gītaka), the two introductory sections (mukha and pratimukha), excellence of structure, aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotions (bhāvas), and the portrayal of two heroines; however, this has already been examined previously.
The view that the *mukha* and *pratimukha* are the two junctures (*sandhi*) is also not correct,
because such a meaning is of no utility; therefore, one should accept the previously explained doctrine of the Teacher (*upādhyāya*), which is indeed faultless.

Now, in order to employ the *uttamottamaka* as a constituent element (*aṅga*) of drama (*nāṭya*), he says: "One should know the *uttamottamaka* as that which rests upon many sentiments," and so forth. By the passage beginning with "In the *uttamottamaka*, one should first employ the *narkuṭa*" and ending with "adorned with *helā* and *bhāva*," the *lāsyāṅga* will be defined (39–362–364).

And therein, that development of mental states which exists by way of the ornaments of gestures such as *helā* (sportiveness) and *hāva* (coquetry) is employed here as something transcendent (*alaukika*). For it is not the case that the noble wife of Rāma— an incarnation of the Blessed One— should be neglected, nor that an insult and humiliation should be endured by one who is a Kṣatriya.
Regarding the statement that "the thorns of the world must be uprooted," this refers to the preservation of the purpose of the scriptures;

however, setting aside such appropriate motives as the retrieval of Sītā abducted by Rāvaṇa, it is described as if it were not the ultimate truth, but rather something repeatedly assumed according to its outward appearance, and so forth. Such is his [position].

If it is argued that such a description is possible for Rāma as he descended in his third incarnation, and that it was likewise described by the Sage in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, then what of it? For even in the Veda, let it be described in that same way; we do not fear this.
Indeed, it has been stated more than once that that portion which overflows with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is poetry, and that is what is to be described.

Furthermore, this element of variety that accords with the hearts of disciples through the commencement of pleasing one side or another is found in drama precisely through the grace of the *lāsyāṅgas* (limbs of dance).
Among these, the *lāsyāṅgas* are indeed excellent, and even among them, this [drama] is the most excellent, for everything is a synonym for aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
This was shown previously. Thence, the suffix *kan* is applied to *saṃjñā*.

Because there is a resorting (*saṃśraya*) to many uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) within this [work], the variety of its composition (*ghaṭanāvicitratva*) is stated due to the multiplicity and novelty of the permanent moods (*sthāyin*). And in the verse (*śloka*), it is "bound" (*badhyate*), thus it is a "verse-composition" (*ślokabandha*).

By means of those various (and diverse) modes of bondage—which, though appearing manifold, are in reality the ultimate truth—there occurs, at certain times and in certain places, a mere manifestation.
Arising from anger or favor, based on words of reproach, consisting of speech and response, and thus joined with the meaning of a variegated song—such would be [the dialogue]. (135)

It is consistent with what has been described by her, as in the *Vikramorvaśī*: "O evil-minded Rākṣasa, where indeed are you going, having taken my beloved? (Reflecting: "This fresh rain-cloud is ready... and so forth; since even these words of Purūravas are explained by passion alone, what need is there for further elaboration?
It is adorned by the manifestation of playful gestures (*helā*) and calls (*hāva*), which take the form of an intensification [of emotion];
thus, the entire category of *sāttvika* and other *anubhāvas* is characterized by this intensity.
In that regard, it is rich with movements of the eyes and eyebrows, and endowed with the physical expression of erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
"With the neck slightly bent" (*sagrīvārecaka*) is to be known as that which arises from a state of feeling (*bhāva*);
that very same [state] is *hāva*, while *helā* consists of graceful acting (*lalitābhinaya*). (Compare 22.10, 11).
Thus ends the definition of *helā* and *hāva*.
Now, he speaks the final limb [of the definition] in order to make it applicable to drama, beginning with the words "produced by anger and favor" (*kopaprasādajanitam*).

By the first half-verse, the future characteristic is restated by way of a single part; by the second half, the portion concerning its variety (*vaicitrya*), drawn from that [definition], is stated as being applicable to drama. This is the meaning:

That which was stated—consisting of forms such as "arising from anger or favor" and "based on words of reproach," and so forth—has been answered; likewise, it will be said in the *Nāṭya* [chapter] (A-31) that "it is thus.
Immediately following this, he says "variegated" (*citram*) regarding the path that will be described: "Variegated" refers to that song which is the poetic composition for the *dhruvā* singing.
The connection with its object is that wherein, having seen a pleasing form, one delights the mind. (p. 76)
Her limbs scorched by the fire of passion—that is called the "Variegated Foot" (citrapada). || 136 ||
In that portion of the drama where the *uktapratyukta* (question and answer) occurs, its variety is indeed adopted from the *lāsyāṅga*.

For instance, in passages such as "O child, O Lord, release me, O proud one, [of this] form," there is a coordination of various distinct fragments of the expressed meaning (*vācyakhaṇḍalaka*) solely through the power of the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasāveśa*), and not otherwise.

The six means of valid cognition, such as direct audition (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), find no scope here; for what place is there for the hare-marked moon [the impossible] and what place for its lineage? Such is the very nature of this matter. Likewise: "She whose body was released, unable to bear the lotus petals... oh, she who was bound by an intense passion for that [unattainable] one! (Nalinīdalanissahamuktadehā | Ai dullāhapḍibaṃdhāṇurāiā |)
[She who possesses] an affection for obstacles that is exceedingly difficult to find.

In the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the meaning of a song such as *ityāder dvipadikā*, and of the meaning of a poetic passage such as *a a samāssasa* (*Śākuntala*), the immersion into the meaning through the performance (*sāveśakṛta*)— which is not observed in ordinary worldly experience— is exceedingly useful for the purpose of aesthetic coloring (*uparañjana*).

Although it will be stated in the analysis of drama (*nāṭya*)— in the section on the limbs of dance (*lāsyāṅga*) consisting of questions and answers arising from the grace of being overwhelmed by the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasāveśavaivaśya*)— "Whatever acting (*abhinaya*) is performed upon the *dhruvā* verses in their proper place" (22.49)—
nevertheless, the poet should compose such poetry and the performer should likewise sing such songs.

This is mentioned here as a constituent of dramatic representation (*rūpaka*) for the purpose of instruction that "this must be performed," and to dispel the doubt as to from where this limb has been derived; however, its definition as something to be enacted will occur in the context of general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*),
specifically in the passage beginning with "the bodily [acting] consists of six types" (22.43).

By the phrase "being produced by anger and favor," it is stated that the locus of the immersion of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) is the domain for the placement of this limb (*aṅga*). For, by the power of the definitions provided through statement and response,
one who accepts even the supramundane form consisting of celestial speech (*ākāśabhāṣita*) [is thereby characterized].

This is characterized by [terms such as] *sahacara*, *svagata*, *janāntika*, *apavārita*, and so forth; yet, because these do not occur anywhere in the world, they are not possible at all in drama (*nāṭya*) either.
When one who is tormented by the fire of passion sees a beloved in a dream and manifests various emotional states, that indeed is called *bhāvika*.
When a song is being sung, by the force of chance (*kākatālīya*), there occurs a correspondence with the meaning [of the words] through the mental activity of various listeners.
For example, in the *Harṣacarita*, as the goddess Sarasvatī heard the *aparavaktra* verse beginning, "You make my eyes tremble,
full of longing," all that occurred exactly as it did in the world.
If it were merely like direct perception (*pratyakṣakalpa*), how could there be such a cognition [of the unreal] that the very nature of drama (*nāṭyarūpatā*) would not collapse?
Others, however, state that there are two additional components, namely *citrapada* (variegated words) and *bhāvika* (the suggestive), and they recite:
"Where, having seen the form of a beloved, one delights the mind."
Her body heated by the fire of passion—that is called the "Variegated Foot" (citra-pada).

"Where one who is tormented by the fire of passion, having seen a beloved in a dream, manifests various emotional states— that indeed is called *bhāvika*. However, this [definition] is incorrect, because according to the text at [Nāṭyaśāstra 19.120], "Lāsya is of ten kinds," Lāsya possesses ten constituent parts (*daśāṅga*).

Furthermore, because this would contradict what will be taught in the chapter on *tāla* (chapter 31), it serves no purpose whatsoever. For instance, regarding the aesthetic element (*rasa*) that pertains to the extraordinary *Kaiśikī* style, whatever variety is entirely beneficial is expressed through the limbs of *lāsya*; and all of that is indeed subsumed within these ten [limbs].

For instance—variety may reside either in the primary element, which is the aspect of mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), or in the excitants and so forth (*vibhāvādi*), or in the quality of coloring (*uparañjakabhāva*). Among these, variety in the aspect of mental modification arises from the *uttamottama-kāku* (the highest of the high);

whereas variety pertaining to the aspect of the excitants arises from the *saindhava-kāku*, and that residing in the aspect of intonation (*kāku*) and so forth arises from *sthita-pāṭhya* (steady recitation).

In the portion concerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth, it is derived from the *trimūḍhaka*; in the portion concerning the meter (*vṛtta*), from the *puṣpagaṇḍika*; in the artificial (*āhārya*)—namely, the application of embellishing songs and musical instruments—and in the sattvic (*sāttvika*) state, even from the *āsīnapāṭhya*; furthermore, in the case of an embellishing emotion (*uparañjakabhāva*), from the word (*śabda*); in the portion of the *dhruvā* song, and in the employment of all musical instruments, from the *geyapada*, by the actors (*pātra*) [conveying] the meaning of the song.

In the dramatic representation of the meaning of a poem, the verbal aspect (*vācika*) arises from the dialogue of question and answer; the physical aspect (*aṅgika*) likewise arises from the two types of *mūḍhaka* (the *dvimūḍhaka*), which follows the modulation of voice and rhythm (*svaratāla*). As for the element of transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*), its variety arises only from the *uttamottama* (the highest of the high) style.
The characteristics of these [elements] in the performance of *lāsya* should be understood by those skilled in their application.
Beyond these, there is no further part; thus, there are exactly ten limbs (*aṅgas*).
The verbal portion is a subtle coloring factor (*uparañjaka*), for it is within the essence of the tone itself that it provides such variety. On the contrary—

The phrase "the supreme enjoyment of rasa" is an imitation of the Sage [Bharata] in terms of terminology; furthermore, it is understood that what is intended is that "drama has rasa as its soul," for rasa is indeed the essence of extraordinary wonder. And so it was said by Bhaṭṭatōṭa:

Characteristics, ornaments, qualities, defects, the modes of word-usage, the meters, the elements of dramatic junctures, the emotional intensity, and whatever collection of resources a poet may possess—
when these arise together, acting in mutual harmony, [they constitute the poetic work].
Wherein the aesthetic flavors (rasas) are manifested instantaneously through delightful qualities (guṇas).
That which is composed in simple meters, with affectionate *cūrṇa* words, featuring effortless and charming construction, and expressed in a well-known vernacular;
Whatever consists of such poetry alone, which evokes aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*),
is declared to be "generalized acting" (*sāmānyābhinaya*), known by the name "acting on the literal meaning" (*vācyābhinaya*).
Whatever object of this kind [exists] in any way whatsoever— (A-22)
The flavor that emerges from the transformation of a causal complex that is neither deficient nor excessive.
For the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) born therein,
this is the moon for the bold creative intuition (*pratibhā*) in the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of drama itself.

Thus, for that which is indeed the vital breath of poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*)—namely, that which is conceived as supreme in the world—is in reality the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The meaning here is this: the poet’s speech, being endowed with a collection [of qualities] that is transcendent by its very nature, immediately becomes permeated with aesthetic flavor (*rasamayī*), because its life-breath consists in its extraordinary character (*asādhāraṇatā*).

Now, one might object: "He who subsists on a portion derived from the elements of *lāsya* has indeed been mentioned here; however, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of those elements themselves must be stated.
Anticipating this, he says: "Of these, in the rule for *lāsya*" (p. 79). This refers to the definition of the ten types of dramatic representation (*daśarūpaka*).
However, that which has not been stated right here is for the purpose of terminating the incidental discussion. || 138 ||
It possesses five joints, four modes of occurrence, and is endowed with sixty-four limbs;
it is equipped with thirty-six characteristics and adorned with qualities and ornaments. (139)
It possesses great flavor and great enjoyment, is endowed with noble speech, is frequented by great men, and is dear to people of virtuous conduct. (140)
A poet should compose a drama with well-knit joints and connections, employing excellent technique, providing a source of pleasure, and characterized by the use of soft-sounding words. (141)
That state of the world which arises from pleasure and pain, and involves the movement of various persons, is represented here in this drama. (142)
In order to make it easy for poets to grasp and to collect [the requirements], he says "having five junctures" (*pañcasandhi*) and so forth.

By "drama" (*nāṭaka*), he means any poetic work intended for performance. In that context, the phrase "having five junctures" and so on should be understood as referring to the mere possibility [of these features]. "Great sentiments" (*mahānto rasāḥ*) are those conducive to the human goals (*puruṣārtha*); where there is great enjoyment (*mahān bhogaḥ*).

Others maintain that *ābhoga* is a sentiment (*rasa*) in which passion (*rañjanā*) predominates. By the phrase "endowed with expressions of loftiness" (*udāttavacanānvita*), it incorporates the poetic qualities (*guṇa*) such as *śleṣa*, *prasāda*, and so forth. By "well-knit through the conjunction of euphonic combinations" (*suśliṣṭasandhisaṃyoga*), it refers to the various types of junctions (*sandhi*);

by "possessing excellent application" (*suprayoga*), it refers to the constituent parts of the *lāsya* dance; and by "having a pleasant basis" (*sukhāśraya*), it refers to the variety of metrical forms (*chandas*).

The description of the intended meaning through soft sounds indicates the excellence of the qualities of sweetness (*mādhurya*), clarity (*prasāda*), and lucidity of sense (*arthavyakti*). One should compose a drama in this manner; and he who composes a drama is indeed a poet.
p. 80) There is no such knowledge, no such craft, no such science, no such art, no such action, nor indeed any yoga, that is not seen in this drama. (143)
This very nature of the world, consisting of various internal states, when joined with the representation of limbs and other gestures, is designated as "drama" (nāṭya). || 144 ||
That which consists of the past deeds and adventures of deities, sages, and kings of superior intellect shall be known as a *nāṭaka*. (145)
Because it is employed and understood by setting aside one's own nature through the sequences of the primary and secondary limbs, it is therefore remembered as *nāṭaka* (drama). || 146 ||
A drama is composed with all states of being, all sentiments, and the engagement in all types of actions, encompassing various internal conditions. (147)

To the question "What of that?", he says: "That state which... This means that state in which there is a transition through various persons, yet a single entry into the being [of the emotion] by way of the essence of rasa (*rasātman*), because such a state is prescribed—that is, accomplished and brought to the form of rasa—in the drama.
And this has been explained at length.

Now, having raised the doubt as to what states are present here in their entirety, he recites the very two verses stated in the first chapter: "That is not knowledge" (1.116) and "This which is the nature of the world" (1.199).
Since this has already been explained in that very place, what is the use of repeating it? How [is] the account of previous events to be understood?

He states that this is the meaning of the word *nāṭaka*: "because [the actor] abandons his own nature. Regarding the root *naṭ*, in the sense of "bending" (*natī*), bending is characterized by bowing down through the abandonment of one's own nature. As for others who read the root as *nṛt* ("dancing"), even in their view, the word *naṭa* here signifies "bending," according to the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.29] concerning the suffix *janidācyu*.
(Various kinds of crafts and manifold types of activities— those performers must execute all those forms without exception. || 148 ||
Having thoroughly observed the nature of the world, the strength and weakness of men,
as well as their enjoyment and the proper method, one should then compose a drama.
In the future age, for the most part, men will be ignorant; and even those who do exist will possess understanding only through effort and study. (150)
When the world perishes, all these—occupations, crafts, scriptures, and the powers of discernment—all perish. 151.
Thus, having carefully examined the strengths and weaknesses of worldly languages, a poet should compose a drama using soft-sounding words for the sake of pleasure. (152)

Those poetic compositions which exist through sounds such as *cekrīḍita* and others do not shine when held by twice-born men carrying water-pots, just as courtesans do not shine when accompanied by those who carry water-pots. (153)

He shows that [the term] is to be understood as derived [from the *uṇādi* suffix -aka, according to *uṇādi* 4.115]. Those *padakrama* recitations, together with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), are the various modes of movement. And it is known by the actors that all this is employed as an illustration of the constituent parts of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*); thus, because of that, the bowing of both [the actors and the audience] is mentioned.

(82) O best of the twice-born, I have thus declared the prescription of the ten dramatic forms (daśarūpa). Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the names of the styles of composition (vṛtti). || 154 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Junctures," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Appropriateness is established by the expectation [of the audience]. Regarding what was stated as "with soft words," he states its purpose:
it will serve for the sake of happiness in the Dvāpara or Kali ages, in comparison with the Tretā age; thus, the clarity of meaning is accepted for the sake of ease.

Concluding this and introducing another topic, he connects the present chapter with the next by stating, "And the prescription of the ten forms," etc. May there be auspiciousness! This is the composition of the true meaning of the Sandhyādhyāya as elucidated by the most excellent of the twice-born.
Composed by Abhinavagupta, who is like a bee at the lotus feet of Śiva.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter on the junctures (*sandhi*) in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭya-veda* composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara teacher Abhinavagupta.
May there be prosperity!
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇapati.

The Twentieth Chapter of the Abhinavabhāratī:

The *utthāpaka*, the *parivartaka*, the *sallāpaka*, and the *saṃghātya*—
in those dramatic sections or poetic fragments where there is speech intended to arouse or sustain the *sattva* (the inner essence), that [speech],
being joined with vocal and physical gestures (*vāgaṅgābhinaya*), comes under the heading of the *sāttvikābhinaya* (expression of the inner essence).

The connection is that the Sāttvatī vṛtti becomes endowed with an intensifying action (ādhikyakriyā). For, although the mind is immersed in the object in the case of the erotic (śṛṅgāra), despondent in the pathetic (karuṇa), and bewildered in the sentiment of disillusionment (nirveda),
its operation, even while occurring, does not shine forth with such excellence as it does in the cases of anger, wonder, and energy.

He shows [this] through the heroic, marvelous, and furious sentiments (*rasa*). "Insult" (*ādharṣaṇa*) is humiliation by means of speech. That mental impulse which causes one to rise up is the "instigator" (*utthāpaka*); the sequence of actions that indicates it is called the "action" (*upacāra*).
Thus, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Bhīma says: "Ho there! Listen, sirs!"
He by whom the hair of the beasts was grasped, by whom even the lower garment of the daughter of the Pāñcāla king was snatched away in the presence of the Kuru kings,
and for whose sake I vowed to drink the wine of blood from his chest.
"Thus, he has fallen into the cage of my arms; let him be protected, O Kauravas! (3.47).
As for the *parivartaka* (exchange): in that same place, Bhīma says— "Sahadeva, go and attend upon our elder.
I, too, shall enter the armory and become your companion with weapons."
Sahadeva: Noble brother, this is not the armory; this is the four-winged palace of the Princess of Pañcāla.
Bhīma: What indeed is this? (and so forth, until) Or rather, I must certainly consult with the Princess of Pañcāla.
p. 98) Its four varieties are to be understood by those who know the true principles of drama. || 44 ||
"I too shall rise; you, meanwhile, display your own power"—this [challenge] arising from rivalry is to be known by the experts as the *utthāpaka* (the inciter). (45)
He who, having abandoned undertakings already commenced, pursues other matters due to the influence of some gain, he too should be known as a "shifter" (parivartaka). || 46 ||

(One should know that the *parivartaka* [interlude] has three types: it concerns a matter already mentioned, is bound by elaboration (*prapañca*), is joined with laughter, and is produced by a particular kind of rivalry. || 47 ||
Whether born of pride or even devoid of pride, when it is joined with words of passion and accompanied by reproachful speech,
that too should be known as "sallāpaka" (flirtatious conversation).

The mental operation that effects another task—namely, the sight of Pāñcālī—by abandoning the entry into the arsenal, "transforms" the action; thus, the term *parivartaka* (transformer) is employed here by way of metaphorical extension (*upacāra*). The same applies in subsequent instances as well.
That speech which is accompanied by provocation is *sādharṣa* (provocative); that which is devoid of it is *nirādharṣa* (non-provocative).

Indeed, whether from words intended to humiliate or from any other source, that subsequent speech consisting of reproach or that overpowering mental action is designated by the term *saṃlāpaka*. For example:

"Aśvatthāman is slain," having spoken thus clearly by the son of Pṛthā, he then said at his ease in the remainder, "It is an elephant," indeed, by that speaker of truth. (Veṇīsaṃhāra 3.11). Here, the term "speaker of truth" (*satyavāc*) is used.
(That speech which arises from dharma and adharma, is joined with passion and hatred, and is accompanied by reproach, should be known as "sāṃlāpaka"). || 49 ||

Whether by the power of the meaning of a mantra or a sentence, by the force of fate, or through the influence of one's own defects, he who causes division within a community is known as a "sunderer" (saṃghātyaka) and should not be trusted by those who know the truth. (50)
A "kūṭasaṃghātya" is to be understood as a collection of fraudulent acts, which rely upon many deceptions and are employed with the intention of harming others. || 51 ||
Thus, this Sāttvatī style, which has four varieties, has been described by me;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Kaiśikī.

Regarding the phrase "producing the breaking up of a coalition" (*saṅghātabhedajanana*): that which produces the division of a coalition in battle is *saṅghātyaka*. Alternatively, it is *saṅghātyaka* because it is that by which the enemy host is to be properly struck down (*samyak-ghātya*), or because it pertains to the domain of a coalition. Furthermore, the breaking up of a coalition may be effected by another through the power of means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth; for example, as Bhīma did.
He has been won over by Yudhiṣṭhira through conciliation; therefore, one must fight him while placing Śikhaṇḍin at the forefront.

This will happen by fate, just as Droṇa declared that he would lay down his weapons once his son was slain. Or else, it may result from our own fault, characterized by the state of our own camp, as when Aśvatthāman quarreled with Karṇa.

"He is laying down his weapons. And here, it is the excess of passion (*sattva*) that commits the offense, thinking, "How is it that I have become such as this? (from the third act of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*).
The word *atha* means "immediately after. The phrase *ataḥparam* means "distinct from these aforementioned characteristics."

"Smooth" means delicate; it is so called because it clings to the heart. "Variegated by special attire" refers to garments, garlands, and so forth; it is that in which there is manifold and extensive singing and dancing, [and] the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
That which is variegated by the excellence of fine and delicate attire, accompanied by women, abounding in dance and song,
and characterized by the refinement arising from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
They cite that as the Kaiśikī style. || 53 ||

Accompanied by many musical instruments, dance, and song; adorned with the graceful representation of erotic sentiment and exquisite costumes; endowed with garlands and ornaments; possessing a praiseworthy appearance and being lovely. (54)

The Kaiśikī vṛtti is to be understood as that which is adorned with the composition of variegated words and sentences, characterized by laughter, weeping, anger, and the like, and associated with the passions of women and men. (55)
Narma, narmasphuñja, narmasphoṭa, and narmagarbha—these four varieties of Kaiśikī have indeed been fully described. || 56 ||

It is that in which the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) has been established, the instruments of expression are pure, and the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) has ceased; it is so called because its practice (*vyavahāra*), or conventional usage, abounds in that *śṛṅgāra* which has *rati* as its source.
