One should know that *narma* (jesting), which establishes the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), is primarily characterized by laughter; it consists largely of humorous speech and is of three kinds. || 57 ||
Humor (narma) is known as that which consists primarily of envy and anger, is permeated by reproachful speech, involves self-deprecation, and includes deception. 58.

The *narmasphuñja* is to be known as the enjoyment arising from a new union, joined with dress and speech appropriate for the occasion of amorous pleasure, and characterized by fear at its conclusion. (59)

"And that bending" (*natā ca tadā*) is the general definition. In this context, it is threefold: to indicate dejection or envy, to reproach another, or to direct one's own mind toward the heart of another. Regarding "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*): the directing of one's own or another's mind (*cittasya upakṣepaḥ*) means bringing it near to oneself. An example is Vāsavadattā.
(Pointing to the picture-board, with a laugh) This other woman who was painted near him is also there; this too is a work of the noble Vasantasena’s hand.

An example of the second [type] is as follows: when Vāsavadattā, having heard the verse beginning with *śītāṃśurmukha* (Ratnāvalī 3.11), is addressed by the King with the words "Dear Vāsavadattā," she replies with a smile, rebuking his speech, saying: "Noble Lord, do not speak thus," and so forth.

Susaṅgatā (smiling): Since Kāmadeva has been depicted by him in such a manner, I too have depicted Rati in a corresponding way. Therefore, please tell the story, for it is truly extraordinary. Having thus described the threefold *narma* (jesting), she speaks to reveal the *narmasphuñja* (the climax of the jest).

"Navasaṅgama" refers to that in which enjoyment (*sambhoga*) occurs at the very moment of a new union. To explain how such a union constitutes "enjoyment," he says "ratisamudaya": it is where there is a connection with a dress or speech characterized by the emergence—that is, the manifestation—of *rati*, which consists of the mutual bond of affection. And at the conclusion...
Fear caused by a former mistress; for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, the meaning is that the sudden appearance of Sāgarikā is an obstacle to the jesting of Udayana.

The *narmasphoṭa* should be understood as that which is adorned with various fragments of diverse sentiments through many specific qualities, wherein the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not fully developed nor abruptly interrupted. (60)
In this [drama], the hero conducts himself in disguise for the sake of his mission, possessing qualities such as wisdom, beauty, and nobility, yet containing within him an element of humor. (51)

(One should know that in dramatic performances, when the hero perishes while remaining in his former position and another remains there, that too is to be understood as containing *narma* [jesting] within it. || 62 ||
Thus, this Kaiśikī style, consisting of four varieties, has been described by me.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the Ārabhaṭī style, which possesses exalted sentiments.

Since various states such as fear, laughter, joy, terror, and anger exist only in fleeting fragments (*lava*), they cannot attain the status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) due to their partial nature; consequently, it is impossible for them to become aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) such as the terrible, the comic, or the furious. As for the erotic flavor (*śṛṅgāra*), however, it is already established [in the previous discussion].
When Susaṅgatā says, "Why do you remain right here?", there is a fragment of laughter (*hāsalava*), not the aesthetic sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*).
When Sāgarikā says, "Friend, for whose sake have I come here?", there is a fragment of fury (*raudralava*), but not the sentiment of fury (*raudra-rasa*).

The same applies elsewhere. By the word "jest" (*narmaṇaḥ*), there is the "bursting forth" (*sphoṭa*)—that is, the marvelousness (*vaicitrya*)—of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) characterized by that [jest].
"Wherein there is clarity produced by the manifestation of wonder"—this refers to *narmagarbha*.

It is that wherein the hero remains concealed by means of knowledge and other arts conducive to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), for the sake of achieving a new union; it is *narmagarbha* because it contains playful jesting (*narman*). [The phrase] "knowledge and so forth conducive to jesting" refers to those skills useful for such amusement.
The phrase "as if contained within" refers to the state of being concealed, just as a hero whose identity is hidden goes to a place of rendezvous.
That which consists primarily of boisterous gestures, is likewise endowed with much deceit and trickery, and contains hypocrisy and false speech, should be known as the style named Ārabhaṭī. (64)
Where there are constant feats of hurling, striking down, leaping, and jumping; cuttings out, illusions, sorcery, and various battles.
They call such a style Ārabhaṭī. || 65 ||

The *ārabhaṭī* style of performance is to be understood as that which is undertaken with the six dramatic qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), characterized by forcefulness, deception, and agitation, and produced for the sake of gain or loss. (66)
The *saṃkṣiptaka*, the *avapāta*, the *vastūtthāpana*, and also the *saṃpheṭa*—these indeed are its varieties; I shall now declare their definitions. (67)
It is endowed with appropriate craftsmanship, possesses many elaborate displays, and features variegated costumes.
(Regarding "udghata"): the "exalted" (*udghata*) refers to the intense sentiments (*rasas*), such as the Furious (*raudra*) and others. (Regarding "ārabhaṭā"):
it is that in which the qualities of the *ārabhaṭī* style—such as wrath, impetuosity, and so forth—are generally present in great abundance through many stratagems.

It is endowed with that which constitutes deception. Furthermore, the three types of deceit (*kapaṭa*) have been explained in the definition of the *samavakāra* (18.71). Precisely because there is an application of deceit in this [drama], there is a predominance of hypocrisy and the possibility of untruthful speech. It is designated by the name *saṃkṣiptaka*.
"Saṃkṣiptaka" (abbreviated) refers to that whose object consists of abbreviated items; he demonstrates those items [with the words] "anvartha" (corresponding to the meaning).
"Anvartha" means that in which the objects are followed by a purpose (*artha*), joined with craft, and fashioned by skilled artisans.
He indicates the direction for this very point [with the words] "bahupusta" (many volumes): the arising or manifestation of many, that is, extensive, volumes.
That which has a concise subject matter as its object should be known as "concise" (saṃkṣiptaka). || 68 ||

One should recognize this as the "falling" (avapāta) [of the body], which arises from fear or joy, involves rushing about, stumbling, and agitated movement, and consists of rapid entry and exit. || 69 ||

That drama which is composed by condensing all aesthetic flavors (rasas), whether based on the presence or absence of movement, should be known as the "Establishment of the Subject Matter" (vastūtthāpana).
And "varied costume" (*vicitraṃ nepathyaṃ*) refers to that in which there is the employment of a book [to represent the object], such as the sword, shield, armor, and so forth; for example,
the varied costume in the *Rāmābhyudaya* during the scene of the illusory head-deployment (*māyāśironikṣepe*), or as in the case of Aśvatthāman in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.

*Avapāta* is that [drama] in which there is the rapid entry and exit of characters due to extreme fear or extreme joy, as well as a sudden collapse (*vinipāta*) or assault (*avaskanda*) caused by speech and the like;
it is characterized by agitated conduct (*sambhramācaraṇa*), an action dominated by excitement (*āvega*), for one falls down (*avapatanti*) therein.
"Vessels" refers to the passage beginning from the entry of the man with a sword in hand and striking blows in the sixth act of the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*, continuing until he exits.
("The presentation of the matter" means the bringing forward of many matters [or points].")
That which is connected to a topic that has arisen incidentally is described as "prasaṅgāgatanibandhana. To the question "What are the entities? he says:

"consisting of all rasas" (*sarvarasa*). By the word *rasa*, both the stable (*sthāyin*) and the transitory (*vyabhicārin*) emotions are meant; where their composition is performed in brief, along with the "disturbances" (*vidrava*), such as the afflictions caused by fire and so forth, and [where it is] devoid of those—as in that very same case.
(In the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*): Mandodarī’s fear as she is being attacked by Aṅgada;

Aṅgada’s valor; Rāvaṇa’s laughter upon seeing him, saying such things as "Indeed, even by this boy the gods have been conquered"; and Rāvaṇa’s extreme rage, [expressed] by saying that he has seized him like a child and thrown him into his armpit.

While Aṅgada speaks, Rāvaṇa’s grief manifests as the dramatic representation of the sentiments of disgust, laughter, and wonder— this is the "arousing of the matter" (*vastūtthāpana*) based on flight (*vidrava*). Conversely, the opposite occurs in that same work (*Kṛtyārāvaṇa*), from the second act onwards, beginning with the tumultuous noise (*kalakala*) offstage.
The speech of Rāvaṇa as he pursues Sītā begins with "O guardians of the world, you cry out," and so forth.
He is possessed by fury and is skilled in many forms of combat, wrestling, and the detection of deception.
That which abounds in blows from weapons is to be known as "conflict" (sampheṭa). || 71 ||
In this way, these modes (vṛtti) based on drama are to be understood by the wise; now learn of their application to the aesthetic sentiments (rasa) as it is being described. 72.
The Kaiśikī style is described as abounding in the sentiments of humor and erotic love;
the Sāttvatī style, moreover, should be understood as resting upon the sentiments of heroism, wonder, and tranquility.
This is also stated thus because it brings about the manifestation of a future event. And so, in that very same place (*Kṛtyārāvaṇa*, second act), there is this speech of the sages:
"O evil-souled one, this Sītā is not being carried away by you for your own destruction; she is a *kṛtyā* [a magical weapon] being taken."
An example of *sampheṭa* (conflict) is the entire sequence beginning with the battle of Jaṭāyu [in the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*].

Now, he states the essential nature of these *vṛttis* (styles) in brief: "The *Kaiśikī* is known to abound in the *Hāsya* (comic) and *Śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiments, while the *Sāttvatī* should be understood as having its basis in the *Vīra* (heroic), *Adbhuta* (wonderful), and *Śama* (tranquility). Here, the word *śama* [refers to the sentiment of tranquility].
Those who advocate that [sentiment] maintain that it is possessed by the sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*). Others read "having a common basis" (*samāśrayā*).
The *ārabhaṭī* [vṛtti] should be known by the wise as existing in both the furious (*raudra*) and the fearful (*bhayānaka*) sentiments. (p. 106)
In the loathsome and the pathetic [rasas], the Bhāratī style is proclaimed. || 74 ||

For in practice, there is no poetic composition whatsoever that arises from a single flavor alone—whether it be a mental state (*bhāva*), a sentiment (*rasa*), an activity (*pravṛtti*), or even a dramatic style (*vṛtti*). (75)
Among all those combined together, that whose form is most predominant should be considered the stable emotion (sthāyībhāva); the rest are known as transitory emotions (sañcāribhāvas). || 76 ||
This enactment, which arises from speech, body, and spirit, has been correctly described by me at the conclusion of the section.
By establishing that it constitutes the remainder of this chapter, he concludes the subject matter of the chapter.

And at the end of the commentary (*vṛtti*), he indicates the meaning that is yet to come with the words "this is the end. *Vṛtti* refers to the subject matter of the dramatic performance (*abhinaya*), which consists of the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*).

The word "end" (*anta*) means that among the modes of performance (*vṛttis*), the *āhārya* (external) is the final portion or a specific part; the sense is that it is external, being distinct from the body. For the actor, the verbal performance (*vāgabhinaya*), which is essentially composed of *sattva* (inner being), is indeed that which must be articulated.

Because it is produced by direct effort, the word *tu* (but/however) specifically distinguishes this from that [other type] as being merely *āhārya* (assumed). I shall explain later that what is produced by costume (*nepathya*) is also *āhārya*. Thus, having been further elaborated, all is well.
I shall describe the artificial (āhārya) representation in its application; furthermore, I shall speak again regarding that which is produced by costume (nepathya). || 66 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Classification of Styles," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Thus has the nature of the mental mode (*vṛtti*) been made manifest here by the ascetic Nṛsiṃhagupta,
whose inner self’s nature as a mental mode was made manifest by the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva).

Thus ends the twentieth chapter on dramatic styles (*vṛtti*) in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the Indian science of dramaturgy (*nāṭyaveda*), composed by the illustrious Great Śaiva teacher, Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter Twenty-One.

(The Representation by Means of Accessories): O Brahmins, I shall explain the representation by means of accessories (*āhāryābhinaya*) in its proper sequence, for this entire performance is established upon the representation by means of accessories. || 1 ||
Various dispositions, previously established through costume, manifest effortlessly through the limbs and other expressive means. (2)
Abhinavabhāratī, Chapter Twenty-one: Costume Representation (Āhāryābhinaya).
That by whose mere volition the entire universe is wondrously manifested as a costume (āhārya).
I bow to that great form of Mānasa, and also to the Daughter of the Mountain.

Some maintain that the mention of the *āhārya* (artificial) [expression] last of all is due to its being external (*bahiraṅga*) compared to vocal expression and the other forms of dramatic representation; thus they claim this is the proper sequence. However, that is incorrect, as has been explained previously.

Rather, it is precisely because of the primacy of the *āhārya* that its capacity to support all [other modes of expression] is established here, in order to demonstrate its status as the foundation upon which everything depends.
The subsequent mention [of the sequence] is expressed by the phrase "that very [sequence] in due order. And so he says:
"Because this entire application consists of speech, gesture, and the inner being (sattva).
He states the justification for this very point with the words "various states" and so forth; that is, the various states such as pleasure, sorrow, and the like.
(109) That which is known as the "assumed representation" (āhāryābhinaya) is the procedure arising from costume (nepathya).
One who desires the welfare of the drama must apply diligent effort toward it. (3)
"Effort must be exerted toward that [costume] by one who desires success in the performance;
for it is proclaimed here that the costume is the ornament of drama. (4)
Costume (nepathya), however, is of four kinds: the puppet (pusta), ornament (alaṅkāra), the arrangement of limbs (aṅgaracanā), and that which is endowed with life (sajjīva). || 5 ||
Manuscripts, moreover, should be known to be of three types according to their various forms and dimensions;
they are proclaimed as being stitched (sandhima), sewn (vyājima), and wrapped (veṣṭima). || 6 ||
Furthermore, those various innate dispositions (*prakṛti*)— such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) and others,
or the superior and inferior types— which were previously established and manifested through effort by means of costume (*naipathya*),
are subsequently differentiated by means of the [dramatic] limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth, as well as the differentiation of the objects of the emotional states (*anubhāva*).
By presenting the names of the characters, their origins, and the divisions of place, time, and so forth, these [costumes] bring about the greatest clarity.
Therefore, the *āhārya* (external) is like the foundation for the variegated application of all acting (*abhinaya*).
Thus, even when all acting has ceased, a distinction is certainly perceived through the observation of the specific details of the costume (*naipathya*).
However, because that which is to be assumed (*āhārya*)— like another gesture (*abhinaya*)— does not change when joined with a different state, rather,

through the intensity of recollecting the "sutra of the stable emotion" (*sthāyibhāva*) that "this state has been reached by one who was previously such," it brings forth the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Thus, it is made known that the external [element] serves as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*); for instance, this sorrow has come upon Aśvatthāman, who was endowed with the fullness of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) in battle. Likewise, if one were to abandon the adoption of the brilliant virtues appropriate for war—and so forth—enough with this prolixity!

It should be known in the world as the rule for the costume (*naipathya*), which is the ornament; this is the "external representation" (*āhāryābhinaya*) here, while in drama it is established as "auspicious. (*Sandhimaḥ*): *sandhāna* is *sandhā*; that which is produced from it, having the form of a bowstring and so forth, is called *sandhima*. *Vyāja* consists of the pulling of a thread and so forth.
That which is produced by means of that [weaving] is called *vyājima*.
110) That form which is fashioned by the wise out of reeds, skins, cloth, and so forth, is [known as *vyājima*].
That which relies on drama is to be known as *sandhi*, which is full [of meaning]. || 7 ||
That which is produced by means of a mechanical device (yantra) should be known as *vyājima*;
and that form which is wrapped around is designated as *veṣṭima*. || 8 ||
Mountains, vehicles, celestial chariots, shields, armor, banners, and trees—whatever is fashioned for the purpose of drama is designated as *pusta* (modeling). || 9 ||

Ornamentation (alaṅkāra), moreover, should be understood as the manifold arrangement of garlands, jewelry, and garments; it is also traditionally defined as the method for arranging the primary and secondary limbs of the body. || 10 ||
Wreaths are traditionally said to be of five kinds: the wrapped (veṣṭima), the spread (vitata), the joined (saṃghātya), the knotted (granthima), and likewise the hanging (prālambita).

*Veṣṭima* means that which is produced by wrapping with lac, wax, or similar substances; they record the suffix *imapa* in the sense of "produced from" (*nirvṛtta*) when it follows a word ending in an abstract suffix (Pāṇini 4.3.10). *Kiliñja* refers to birch bark, bamboo leaves, and so forth. It is brought to a state of form (*rūpatām*), meaning it is made into a shape. By means of a mold (*yantra*).

Regarding the types such as *sandhi* and so forth through the application of *sūtra* and other methods, he explains where they are employed with the verse beginning "on the stone" (*śaila*) and so on.

"Combination" (*samāyoga*) refers to the joining together; this is constructed upon the primary limbs (*aṅga*), such as the head and hands, and the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*), such as the forehead and fingers. "Twisted work" (*veṣṭima*) is that which is constructed by twisting grass.
Or it is made by many layers of wrapping.

"Spread out" (vitata) means consisting of a mass of garlands that are wrapped around and mutually joined, or perhaps puffed up for fear of crushing the garments. Or it is a patchwork (saṅghātya) or circular (vṛtta).
A *prālambita* [garland] is one whose thread is passed through the interior of the mouth [of the flower], or one adorned with many clusters of flowers;
it is "knotted" (*granthima*) when it is bound with knots; it is "suspended" (*prālambita*) when it extends as far as the lattice-work (*jāla*) and so forth. (p.
Indeed, ornaments in drama should be understood by the wise as being of four kinds:
those to be pierced, those to be bound, those to be cast on, and those to be placed upon. (12)
Whatever here may be worn as earrings and such ornaments for the ears, as well as golden threads and various necklaces resting upon them, [should be offered]. (13)
On the waist-thread and armlets, pearl ornaments should always be fastened;
one should know that anklets should be worn, as well as garments and jewelry.
I shall indeed describe the various types of ornaments for men and women, which arise from different regions and castes. (15)
The crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) together with the crown is known as the ornament of the head;
the earring (kuṇḍala), the pendant (mocaka), and the pin (kīlā) are intended as ornaments for the ears.

The pearl necklace (muktāvalī), the joy-bringer (harṣaka), the thread (sūtraka), and the neck-ornament (kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa); the wristlet (vetikā) and the finger-ring (aṅgulimudrā) shall be the ornaments for the fingers. || 17 ||

He explains the *dhyā* and other terms himself with the passage beginning "to be pierced as earrings, etc. The phrase "having various bases" means that they possess many varieties due to differences such as creepers (*latā*) and numbers. A *cūḍāmaṇi* is [worn] in the middle of the head;
a *makuṭa* is above the forehead; an *earring* (*kuṇḍala*) is on the lower rim [of the ear]; and a *mocaka* is on the auditory canal.

A *kīla* (peg) is made for the central hole; an *uttarakarṇikā* (upper ear-ring) is well-known for the upper hole; a *harṣaka* is a small box (*samudgaka*) well-known for its form resembling a serpent and so forth; a *sūtraka* is well-known as a cluster, a neck-thread, and so on; and a *vetikā* is a finger-ring in the form of a fine bracelet, endowed with the shape of a bird or a lotus.
A hand-bracelet (*hastalī*) and an arm-staff ornament (*bāhunālī-vibhūṣaṇa*),
as well as a torque (*rucaka*) and a crest-ornament (*cūlikā*), should be fashioned as decorations for the wrist-joint (*maṇibandha*). || 18 ||
Keyūras and aṅgadas are ornaments for above the elbows;
likewise, the trisara and the hāra are ornaments for the chest.
A long pearl necklace and a garland are ornaments for the limbs;
likewise, a *talaka* and a *sūtraka* should serve as ornaments for the waist. (20)
This application of the *uruṣa* [measurement] should be performed for ornaments pertaining to gods and kings; furthermore, I shall describe that which pertains to women. (21)
The *rucaka* is stretched across the hollow of the wrist; above that is what is known as the *cūlikā*;
the *nikuñcaka* is located at the position of the forearms. This is the ornament for the wrists (*maṇibandha*).
The *keyūra* is above the elbow (*kūrpara*); above those two are the *aṅgada*s. The *trisara* consists of three strings of pearls. The *talaka*—
Below the navel, and even below that, is the cord (*sūtraka*). This is the "application of the person" (*puruṣaniryoga*), which is its propriety.
"The locus of ornaments" means the rule for ornaments.
Anticipating the objection that "every person is adorned by this," he says: "of the gods and of kings."
And so on. The *śikhāvyāla* is a serpent bound by knots in the center, serving as the position for the pericarp (*karṇikā*);

its circular petals, which are variegated designs formed by the joining of petals, are the *piṇḍīpatras*. The *cūḍāmaṇi* is a crocodile-shaped leaf (*makarapatra*) in the middle of the head, followed by a lattice of pearls extending to the forehead.
A *toraṇa* is well known in the form of a lattice-work and so forth; or else, it consists of a single golden pearl-jewel upon the head of a serpent itself. (p. 113)
The lock of hair, the serpent upon the crest, the cluster of leaves, likewise the crest-jewel, the makaraka ornament, and the lattice-windows of pearl-strings. || 22 ||
An ornament for the head, a variegated turban, a crest, a peacock-feather tuft, and a braid with its tail-end tied with a cord. || 23 ||
There was a forehead mark (tilaka) fashioned from various artistic crafts,
as well as a cluster [of ornaments] above the cluster of eyebrows, resembling flowers.
The *karṇikā*, the *karṇavalaya*, as well as the *patrakarṇikā*, the *kuṇḍala*, the *karṇamudrā*, and the *karṇotkīlaka*. (25)
Indeed, ivory leaf-ornaments variegated with various jewels serve as an adornment for the ears, as does the ear-pendant (karṇapūra). || 26 ||

It is variegated. From the head, there is a crest (*jolaka*) consisting mostly of a swinging ornament (*khelā* or *ḍolā*), and an ear-ornament (*karṇāvataṃsaka*) shaped like a peacock feather, made of multicolored gems.
Regarding the phrase "ear-ornament" (*karṇikā*) and so forth, some say that these ear-ornaments are optional, yet they should be combined because they are distinct ornaments for different locations.
Tilakas and patralekhas shall be the ornaments for the cheeks;
and the trivani is to be known as the ornament for the chest. (27)
One should know the application of collyrium to the eyes and the coloring of the lips;
likewise, there is the various staining of the teeth and the whiteness of the four [teeth]. (28)
Furthermore, with the internal variation of passion, they become even more brilliant through their beauty;
for the charming and lovely women, they possess a splendor illuminated by pearls. (29)
Or else, her teeth may be deep red, colored like the petals of a lotus;
her lower lip, radiant with the glow of a ruby, shall possess the luster of a young sprout.
And their graceful charm consists of glances accompanied by playful movements;
[their ornaments are] strings of pearls, rows of snakes, clusters of blossoms, and garlands of jewels. (31)
The *ratnāvalī* and the *sūtraka* are to be known as ornaments for the neck;
likewise, there are those with two strands, three strands, and four strands.
Likewise, there should be a chain as an ornament for the neck;
and armlets and bracelets are ornaments for the base of the arms. (33)
And there are various ornaments made by craftsmen, such as necklaces and breast-jewels; this is *vilāsa*.
By this, the meaning is as follows: when there is such a variety of coloring on the teeth and lips, it is accompanied by a wandering [glance]—(p.
And her breast-ornament should be encrusted with a network of jewels. || 34 ||
The *kharjūraka*, the *socchitika*, the arm-staff ornament (*bāhunālī-vibhūṣaṇa*), the *kalāpī*, the bracelet (*kaṭaka*), the conch (*śaṅkha*), the hand-leaf (*hastapatra*), and the *sapūraka*. (35)
A seal-ring and finger-ornaments for the fingers, a palm adorned with a network of pearls, as well as a girdle or a golden waist-band. (36)
The *raśanā* and the *kalāpa* serve as ornaments for the hips;
the *kāñcī* consists of a single cord, while the *mekhalā* consists of eight cords.
The girdle consists of two times eight strings; the bundle [of hair] consists of twenty-five;
and likewise, there are thirty-two, sixty-four, and one hundred and eight [beads]. || 38 ||
These become pearl necklaces for the women of gods and kings, as well as anklets, small bells, tinkling ornaments, and lattices of jewels. (39)
That smile which was observed would be exceedingly charming; thus, the graceful charm (*vilāsa*) is produced.
*Talaka* refers to that which is joined with two panels.
*Yaṣṭi* means a creeper. *Nūpura* is [an ornament] below the knee. *Kiṅkaṇīkā* refers to small bells attached to the ankles.
On the *saghoṣa* and the *kaṭaka*, there should be an ornament for above the ankles;
on the two shanks, a leaf-pattern for the feet; and on the toes, finger-rings. (40)
There were also thumb-marks of vermilion and ornaments on the feet, as well as the red dye of lac applied in various decorative patterns.
The shade of the Ashoka sprouts is indeed natural;
this is the ornament of a woman from her hair down even to her nails. (42)
O best of the twice-born, it should be understood according to its actual state, essence, and condition;
likewise, there is the scripture, the means of valid cognition, and the description of its form.
Even by those of great intelligence who employ their skill, a task cannot be accomplished merely through thought;
for it is not possible [to create such a work] even with gold, pearls, and gems. (44)
An ornament should be applied according to one's own preference as something within one's control;
when applied according to its proper division, it brings beauty to the limb. (45)

*Ratnajālaka* means that which covers the forepart of the foot (*prapada*). *Saghoṣe saśabde kaṭake* refers to the bracelets that produce sound. *Aṅguṣṭhatilakāḥ* refers to those made with various artistic designs. *Ākeśāt* means starting from the mass of hair on the crest (*śikhāpāśa*), that is, beginning from the crest-ornament (*śikhāvyāla*). *Ānakhāt* means up to the point of the red lac-dye (*alaktakarāga*). *Āgama*.
This means "the material cause. "Measure" refers to being commensurate with the dimensions of the fingers and so forth.

"Description of form" refers to the production of white and other colors according to their respective natures. The meaning is that the effect is exactly as described and ordained by Viśvakarman. [This should be understood] well.
The meaning is that it is well-known in the world;
for example, like an ornament located elsewhere that is joined with jewels.
However, in the performance of a drama, heavy ornaments must not be worn.
For that indeed produces exhaustion due to strenuous exertion; and for one who is dejected by the weight [of the body], perspiration and fainting arise. (47)
For one burdened by heavy ornaments does not perform activity again;
therefore, there should be golden ornaments made of thin skin. (48)
Or, bound with jewels and gold, it would not cause weariness;
the method of ornamentation for divine beings is taught according to their own desire. (49)
The ornament of human beings is that which is produced through diligent effort;
it may be woven, spread out, sewn together, or likewise knotted. (50)
Likewise, five kinds of garlands are prescribed that shine with long beauty; and there are many varieties of coverings originating from various cities. (51)
That object of knowledge is of three kinds: pure, red, and variegated.
This is the proclaimed method for the ornaments of the divine beings. (52)
*Pattana* means a region. *Śuddha* means white in color. *Rakta* means dyed with any one of safflower, indigo, or other dyes. *Vicitra* means multicolored. *Vibhakti* means division.
And for human beings, one should create a representation based on various regions, as well as through ornaments and costumes that reflect their diverse conditions. (53)
The classification of divine women born in their respective realms must be made:
[that] of the Vidyādharīs, Yakṣīs, Apsarases, and Nāga women. 54.
A diversity of dress is prescribed for the wives of the ṛṣis and the gods;
likewise for the women of the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and Sauras. (55)
Likewise, there were divine men and women with crests,
and those with topknots and crests adorned primarily with pearls.
The dress and equipment of the Vidyādharīs should be made pure;
likewise, the Yakṣiṇīs and Apsarases should be fashioned adorned with jewels.
The dress of all these Yakṣīs shall be identical, with the sole exception of their topknots;
the ornaments of the Nāga women should be made like those of the divine beings.
Their hoods consist solely of pearl-creepers;
"of them" (verse 59) refers to those female nāgas.
But the duty of the daughters of the sages is to wear their hair in a single braid. || 59 ||
Nor was their method of adornment or their dress suited to the forest; for the ornaments of perfected women consist primarily of pearls and emeralds. (60)
And for those very Gandharva women, their clothing and equipment should be made yellow,
and their ornaments should consist primarily of rubies.
He should be depicted with a lute in his hand and likewise dressed in saffron-colored garments;
the ornaments of the Rākṣasīs should be made of sapphires.
She should be depicted with white teeth and dressed in black garments;
the celestial women should be adorned with ornaments of lapis lazuli and pearls.
Their attire should be made of garments resembling the feathers of a parrot;
they should be adorned in some places with puṣyarāga gems and in others with lapis lazuli.
The attire of divine monkeys and women should consist of blue garments;
thus, the costumes based on divine ladies should be made to appear amorous.
Having reached another state, one who is pure should again perform [the rites] in that same manner;
however, those born in various regions should be made [to participate] among human women.
(120) Listen as I describe those combinations of dress and ornaments:
the hair of the young women of Avanti is adorned with *sālaka* flowers. 67.
The women of Gauḍa mostly wear their hair in a single braid with a crest-lock,
whereas the young women of the Ābhīras wear two braids.
A circumambulation of the head should be performed, as well as wearing clothing that is predominantly blue;
likewise, the women of the east and north should have their topknots tied up high.

In the rite of the region, it is prescribed that for those women, the covering [of the body] extends as far as the hair; likewise, for the women of the South, the work should be based on painting (ullekhya). 70.
Adorned with the *kumbhībandhaka* and likewise the *āvartalalāṭika*, such is the decoration for courtesans that cuts across their desires. (71)
According to the rules for region and caste, one should likewise arrange the dress, ornaments, shaving, and equipment for the remaining [deities] as well. (72)

Regarding the phrase *sālakakuntalam*: it is so described because its curls (*alakāḥ*) are in their proper place as locks of hair (*kuntalāḥ*). A garment that is mostly blue belongs only to the Ābhīras.
That which pervades the heart is "heart-pleasing" (*hṛdya*); thus, "attire" (*veṣaḥ*) refers to the arrangement of the hair and so forth. It dies completely (*ā samantāt mriyate*).
That by which beauty is nourished is an ornament, such as a crest-jewel or a serpent. Shaving is the arrangement of the hair and so forth.
Attire is the application of variegated garments. These—dress and the rest—are [employed] through deception.
(And one should employ the traditional authority [āgama] for the performance of drama in this manner behind the scenes): "For a costume not suited to the place will not produce beauty. (73)
When tied upon the chest of a woman wearing a girdle, it produces laughter;
likewise, when placed upon women whose lovers are away or who are stricken by calamity.
Her attire should indeed be soiled, and her head should bear a single braid; however, in the case of a woman’s separation from her lover, her dress here should be pure.
Neither excessively adorned with ornaments nor engaged in elaborate grooming—such is the dress of women, arising from the customs of their particular region and station. (76)
Furthermore, I shall describe the dress of men according to their true nature.
In that regard, the arrangement of the limbs must first be performed by those who employ dramatic action.
Thereafter, the costumes originating from various regions should be employed:
white, blue, yellow, and the fourth is indeed red. (78)
These are the syllables born of their own nature (*svabhāvajā*), by which the formation of the limbs [of the mantra] is performed;
furthermore, there are others known as *upavarṇas*, which are born of combination (*saṃyogajā*). (79)
"Place" refers to Avanti and so forth; "state" refers to passion, grief, and the like. "Therein" means among men alone.
This implies that the composition of descriptions—consisting of the transformation of the appearance of women—must be performed by male actors, not by female roles.
"Born of union" (*saṃyogajāḥ*) refers to those produced through the blending of two phonemes (*varṇa*); whereas "secondary descriptions" (*upavarṇāḥ*)...
The meaning is: by means of the mixing of many colors.
122) I shall fully explain those [colors] according to how they are to be employed by practitioners.
In the union of white and blue, it is known as the *kāraṇḍava*. || 80 ||
From the combination of white and yellow, the pale-white color is proclaimed;
from the combination of white and red, the lotus-colored (pink) is proclaimed. || 81 ||
From the combination of yellow and blue, that which is called green is born;
from the combination of blue and red, that which is called brown (kaṣāya) is born. || 82 ||
From the combination of red and yellow, the fair (gaura) complexion is said to arise;
these are the colors born of mixture, as well as other secondary (upavarṇa) hues.
Many [syllables] are proclaimed to be composed of three or four phonemes;
from among them, that which possesses strength shall constitute its portion. (84)
For the weak [pigment], one should cause two parts to be given, excluding the blue;
there shall be one part of blue, while the other four parts are for the coloring agent.
The powerful one among all the castes is proclaimed to be Nīla alone;
having thus understood the rule of colors based on various combinations, [one should proceed]. 86.

"One who is strong" refers to one who acts with dominance; "another color is double" provides an exception to this, stating "except for the blue color. In that regard, he shows the rule for the proportions: "one part of the blue," which means that among the colors, there is one part of the blue.
Then the wise one should perform the application of the limbs as appropriate; by means of this application, the form is covered, being divested of its own [ordinary] attire. (87)
But that which is engaged in the practice of dramatic art should be known as abiding in its natural state;
one's own true complexion is to be concealed by means of colors applied through the adoption of various costumes.
The form of that [deity] must be fashioned according to the nature upon which one is established, just as a living being abandons its own inherent nature for another bodily state. 89.
For one who has taken refuge in another body partakes of its very nature;
likewise, a person is concealed by dress and pigments. (90)
He assumes the nature of whichever being's dress he takes up—
whether it be a god, a dānava, a gandharva, a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, or a pannaga.

He explains the word *vartanā* through its synonyms as "covering" (*chādana*). "Abiding in its original nature" (*prakṛtisthitam*) means existing according to the distinctions of the natures of gods, humans, and so forth. He states the purpose of this abiding:
"Just as a living being [knows] its own nature. "Living being" (*jantu*) means the individual soul (*jīvātman*), and it...

The manifestation of pure, stainless, infinite consciousness and bliss, whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), abandons its own innate nature— which is inseparable from itself— and assumes another, distinct, bodily state arising from the body, suitable for the instruments of the physical frame; for that [state] is a different body, a specific modification of that very body.
The meaning is that they have resorted to [it] in its vicinity, on all sides, having attained it through an extremely close identification with its own nature.
For these are known as the perceptions of living beings, as well as those others which are the bonds of the individual soul (jīva).
The female states, mountains, rivers, oceans, and vehicles; || 92 ||
Likewise, various weapons should be understood as being designated by the term "living beings," as well as mountains, palaces, machines, shields, armor, and banners. (93)
Furthermore, various weapons and such are traditionally considered to be insentient;
or else, when endowed with a cause, they become embodied beings.

Having observed the dramatic conventions (nāṭyadharma), and having understood the rules regarding the social classes (varṇa), as well as their age and temperament, one should employ [the appropriate] dress, speech, and physical bearing. || 95 ||
One should fashion the arrangement of the limbs based on the region, caste, and age;
the gods are to be known as fair-complexioned, as are the yakṣas and the apsarases. (96)

This is what is meant: just as the Supreme Self, even while not abandoning the light of its own consciousness, displays a nature that appears as if colored by the mental fluctuations appropriate to the sheath of the body; so too the actor, without abandoning his own self-possession, [displays a different nature] due to the application of following the *sthāna*, *laya*, *tāla*, and so forth.

By means of changing his costume and so forth—which correspond to [the roles of] those situated within the body—he shows himself to the audience as if embraced by the nature appropriate to that [role]. He demonstrates that in the case of the spectators there is no conceit of being the actor; for in that context, there is the conceit of being Rāma. With this very intention, we have stated here and there that it is indeed a matter of cognition (*pratīti*).
This was explained at the beginning of the Chapter on Rasa (Rasādhyāya).

He explains the division of the "possessing life" (sajīva) [representation] as distinct from the "artificial" (āhārya) by means of the passage beginning with "gods, dānavas, gandharvas," and so forth.
Although mountains, palaces, and the like are included among the "lifeless" (nirjīva) because they are the subject matter under discussion, [they are treated here] in their specific states.

He states that they possess vitality even through the laws of dramatic performance (*nāṭyadharma*) by means of the passage beginning with "śaila" and so forth, as well as by the passage beginning with "kāraṇopetāḥ" and so forth.
He analyzes the arrangements of the limbs (*aṅgaracanāni*) by the phrase "of the complexions," meaning those such as fair (*gaura*) and the like.
Rudra, Arka, Druhiṇa, and Skanda are remembered as having the luster of refined gold; so too are Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Varuṇa, and the hosts of stars. (97)
The ocean, Himavat, and the Gaṅgā are indeed white, as is Bala;
one should know that Aṅgāraka is red, while Budha and Hutāśana are yellow. (98)
Nārāyaṇa and Nara, Śyāma and the serpent Vāsuki, as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Guhyakas, and Nagas. || 99 ||
In the six continents, the Piśācas are water-colored and the sky-colored, while men are black in color. (100)
They should be fashioned through the application of dramatic art, possessing the luster of refined gold;
however, the men of Jambūdvīpa’s region take on various complexions. (101)
Having excluded the Northern Kurus,
those men of Bhadrāśva, who possess a golden luster and are white in complexion, should likewise be depicted according to their color.
“Mountains” refers to the hills; “water” and “space” refer here to the deities presiding over them. “A region of Jambūdvīpa” refers to Bhārata. “And those too” refers to Uttarakuru.
In Ketumāla, men are dark-blue; in the remaining regions, they are said to be fair-complexioned.
Beings such as Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Pannagas are remembered to be of various colors.
Likewise, the Vidyādharas and the Pitṛs are equal to humans;
furthermore, learn of those various castes in the land of Bhārata. (104)
Kings may indeed be lotus-colored, fair, or even dark-complexioned; however, those mortals who are happy should be depicted as fair by the wise.
Those of evil deeds, those seized by planets, those afflicted by disease, those engaged in ascetic penance, those performing strenuous labors, those who are black, and those of low birth. || 106 ||
The sages should always be depicted with the luster of jujube fruits;
and the sages established in austerity should always be made dark-complexioned by the wise. (107)
"Furthermore, by the designation of their cause and by their own will, fathers are equal to men"—here, the particle *tu* is used in its own sense;

thus, "fathers are men" means they are identical. Regarding "those of evil deeds" (*kukarmiṇaḥ*), this refers to those whose actions (*karman*) are contemptible and censurable. "Exerted" (*āyasta*) means an action characterized by much physical suffering.

The meaning is "of those who. Low-born castes such as fishermen (dhīvara) and ḍombas, even though they possess the power of the jujube fruit (*badara*), are subject to an exception; this is stated by the words "those established in austerity are not dark" (*tapaḥ sthitā asitāḥ*). By this, however, there is no redundancy, as it implies that even among sages (*ṛṣi*), those devoted to austerity are not dark.

He states the pervasive definition by means of the designation "cause" (*kāraṇavyapadeśena*). An example of a cause is how an action involving an abundance of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes blackness. "By one's own will" (*ātmacchayā*) means according to the intention of the poet (*kavibuddhi*).
In that case, the caste should be determined according to the requirements of the region and the lineage. || 108 ||
Having understood the country, the occupation, the caste, and the dependence on the region of the earth, one should conduct the affairs of men according to their specific application.
[The people of] Kirāta, Barbara, Andhra, Draviḍa, Kāśī, and Kosala—
The Pulindas and those from the south are generally recorded as being dark-complexioned. || 110 ||
The Śakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas, and those who are Bāhlikas—those who generally dwell in the northern direction should be depicted as fair-complexioned. (111)
The Pāñcālas, Śaurasenas, Māhiṣas, Auḍras, Māgadhas, Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Śyāmas should be depicted according to their respective complexions. (112)
The Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas should indeed be made fair-complexioned;
likewise, the Vaiśyas and Śūdras should be made dark-complexioned according to their respective castes.
Having performed the movements of the face, limbs, and minor members according to the rule,
one should apply the rite of shaving the beard in accordance with the place, time, and age.

"Pure, variegated, dark, and likewise hairy"—this is stated in the *Bhārata*. "Pure" means entirely shaved with a razor. "Dark" refers to that which was previously subject to the practice of shaving, but for whom that practice has now been prohibited. "Variegated" means...
By means of the action of the razor and the action of production, the beard— composed of various arranged configurations and consisting of diverse internal states— becomes fourfold. (115)
But the duty of those bearing sectarian marks, as well as that of ministers and domestic priests, and of those men who are neutral or have taken up initiation, must be performed purely. || 116 ||
Whosoever are the divine persons—such as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others—as well as the princes of the earth and those who live in service to the king. || 117 ||
For those mortals who are full of passion and those who are intoxicated by youth,
their facial hair should be made variegated by actors who employ dramatic techniques.
One should employ a dark beard for those ascetics who have not fulfilled their vows, who are suffering, and who are struck by calamity. (119)
"Romaśam" means as it has arisen [naturally]. "Even for those possessing signs" refers to those such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*).
The half-verse beginning with "those men who stand in the middle and those who have resorted to initiation" is as follows:

The phrase "the duty of those bearing emblems [is] pure, as well as that of ministers and domestic priests" should be applied immediately after the preceding half-verse; however, due to a scribe's error, it is seen in a different location.
The term "neutral" (*madhyastha*) means neither superior nor inferior. "Intoxicated by youth" (*yauvanonmādinaḥ*)...
The sense is that this applies even to ministers and domestic priests.
129) And those among the sages, ascetics, and men who observe long-term vows—
And likewise, for those who have bound their hair in matted locks, a hairy beard is prescribed.
Thus, various kinds of facial hair should be employed by those who perform [the art].
Hereafter, I shall describe the diverse applications of costumes.
Attire is said to be of three kinds: pure, variegated, and soiled;
I shall describe their application correctly and in due order.

And likewise during the visit of a deity, at an auspicious occasion while remaining under a vow, during the conjunction of a lunar day and a constellation, and similarly at the performance of a marriage. || 123 ||
Whatever action is performed in accordance with the Dharma by women or men,
their dress shall be pure, as shall that of those men who are diligent in their efforts.
The diverse attire of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as that of harsh kings, has thus been described. || 125 ||
Of the aged Brahmins, the chief ministers, the family priests, the merchants, the chamberlains, and likewise the ascetics. || 126 ||
"Pure" generally refers to those wearing white garments and the like. "Exerting effort" (prāyatnikāḥ) means those who exist through effort, that is, those who are disciplined (vinītāḥ).
[This applies to] those men who reside in the settlements of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. (p. 130)
For them, a pure method of clothing should be provided, not one based on theatrical dress. || 127 ||
For those who are insane, for those who are intoxicated, for travelers, and likewise for those afflicted by calamity, a soiled dress is prescribed. (128)
One who knows the principles of drama should employ pure red and variegated garments as upper cloths for the two types of dress, the pure and the variegated.
A wise person should, however, act with impurity toward those who are impure—namely, among the Munis, Nirgranthas, Śākyas, Yatis, and Pāśupatas. (130)
One should adopt an outward appearance consistent with one's vows according to worldly custom;
specifically, one should employ rags, bark garments, and skins for those who are ascetics.
For the wandering mendicants of the Śākya sages, saffron-colored robes are prescribed;
however, among the Pāśupatas, garments of various colors and patterns may be worn.
And those men who are declared to be of low birth, as well as those who are appointed for entry into the inner apartments, [should be assigned] according to their fitness. 133.
"Cīra" refers to unspun, coarse tree bark; "valkala," however, is its opposite, such as the bark of the *bhūrja* tree or the hide of deer and other animals.
They too should be dressed in saffron-colored tunics according to the prescribed rule;
thus, the attire of men may vary according to their different conditions.
The attire of heroes is proclaimed to be martial indeed:
wearing diverse weapons and armor, with quivers fastened and bows in hand. (135)
A king must always maintain a diverse attire;
however, it should be purely simple during auspicious occasions such as the appearance of stars or portents.
In this way, this [costume] should be appropriate according to the region, caste, and age, whether for women or for men, and whether they are of high, low, or middle status. (137)
In this manner, the rules for costumes should be applied in the performance of a drama, having assumed various states according to the performer's role as a doer of good or evil. (138)
Likewise, one should also compose prologues based on dramas, which rely upon the gods and humans, and which depend upon their respective regions, castes, and ages. (139)
Those with [ornaments] on the sides, those on the head, and likewise those with crowns—this threefold crown should be known as belonging to the divine and the earthly. || 140 ||

(Regarding "nakṣatra"): This is the auspicious rite for the pacification of portents related to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), performed by a fortune-teller (*naimittika*) for the sake of the *śrāddha*.
For gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, pannagas, and rākṣasas, crowns of various designs with side-crests should be fashioned. 141.
Those who are the best among the divine should be made to wear crowns;
those of middle rank should wear turbans, and the lowest should wear simple head-wraps.
Crown ornaments should be placed upon the heads of kings by the wise, and likewise for the Vidyādharas, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas. (143)
The practitioners should fashion crowns of matted hair for the Rākṣasas,
Dānavas, and Daityas, for their hair and eyes are indeed tawny.
One should likewise fashion the faces of Hari and Śama with their respective crests;
furthermore, those who are the foremost among them should be depicted there with their crowns tilted to one side.
But for what reason were crowns created for use in divine and royal rites?
The cutting of hair is seen in the Vedic injunctions according to the sacred tradition.
Or, for one who has been consecrated in a sacrifice, the wearing of a crown is prescribed because of the desire to cover the head and because the hair is not long. (147)
Even from the worship of the gods and other such acts, there arises the hearing of stones. The form of *prakṛti* is the head;
the *pratiśiras* (counter-head) belongs to the commander-in-chief and also indeed to the crown prince. (p. 133)
One should join the half-crested [image], as well as those men who are high officials. || 48 ||
He should cause turbans with bound head-wraps to be made for the ministers, chamberlains, guild-leaders, and priests. (149)
The heads of Piśācas, those possessed by madness or spirits, practitioners who have not yet fulfilled their vows, and ascetics shall have long, hanging hair.
In the case of Śākyas, śrotriyas, Nirgranthas, Parivrājas, and those initiated for a sacrifice, the shaving of the head must be performed. || 151 ||
Likewise, the head of the remaining ascetics who follow their vows may be shaven, or curly, or even with long hair. (152)
For rogues, those who live by night, and for men whose minds are set on amorous passion, the hair should be curled. (153)
Even for children, [the head-dress] should be made adorned with three crests (*triśikhaṇḍa*).
Regarding the term "veṣṭana" (wrapping): it refers to those [head-dresses] upon which a cloth-band, tied for the purpose of wrapping and resembling a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), is fastened.
The three-parted tufts are the *triśikhaṇḍa*.
The head of the sages, moreover, should have matted hair bound into a crown. (154)
For servants, the hair should be trimmed into three tufts or shaved entirely;
for a jester (vidūṣaka), it should be bald or marked with a "crow's foot" (kākapada) design.
For the remaining [words], the head should be employed by the speakers according to their meaning, based on place and origin, and depending upon various different states. (156)
With ornaments, pigments, garments, and garlands according to the prescribed rule,
one should thus fashion various types of costumes through the power of the imagination.
But first, having established the natural disposition arising from the qualities of practice, and having reached such a state as belongs either to women or to men; (158)
All the divine beings should be depicted as depending on human forms;
furthermore, their lack of blinking and other such traits should not be employed by the artists. (159)
In this world, the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and the emotional states (bhāvas) are established by means of the dramatic determinants (dṛṣṭis);
for once an object has been established by the determinants alone, it is subsequently manifested by the constituent parts (aṅgas).
Thus, the arrangement of the components of the object of knowledge arises from various material causes;
I shall now describe the characteristics of that which is called "the living being" (sajīva).
(Regarding "crow's foot"): where there is a parting of the hair like the wing of a crow;
that which is the entrance for living beings is indeed designated as "sajīva."
It is likewise remembered as having four feet, two feet, and even no feet.
One should know bipeds as serpents, birds, and humans;
quadrupeds are to be understood as domestic and wild animals. 163.
Those [beings] who are equipped with various weapons should be employed by the wise in a drama during battles, skirmishes, and likewise during sieges. (164)
And the weapons must be fashioned according to the proportions of men;
I shall describe them according to the measurements found in the manuals.
The *bhiṇḍi* should be twelve *tālas* in length; then the *kunta* should be ten [tālas], and the *śataghnī*, the *śūla*, the *tomara*, or the *śakti* should be eight [tālas]. || 166 ||
Eight *tāla*s should be known as the measure of a bow; its length is two cubits (*dvihastaka*).

"Equipped with weapons" means they are suitable for combat. Thus, when the *nāga-astra* is discharged, it appears in the form of a serpent for the sake of demonstration, and likewise, with the *nṛsiṃha-astra*, it takes that [lion] form, and so forth. (The measurement of weapons.)
He shows [the hand gestures]: [the *bhiṇḍipāla* (sling], the *vajra* [... the *caturtāla*, and the *cakra*. The *cakra* is a shield for warding off weapons such as the sword in combat.
The arrow, the mace, and the thunderbolt are prescribed as being four tālas in length. || 167 ||
The sword-blade is forty finger-breadths (aṅgula) in measurement;
the discus is twelve finger-breadths, and the spear is desired to be half of that.
One should know that the *prāsavat* cloth is twenty finger-breadths in measure, and the staff (*daṇḍa*) is likewise twenty finger-breadths in measure;
indeed, the *kaṇaya* is also twenty finger-breadths according to the standard measurement. || 169 ||
The wise should fashion a shield (kheṭaka) thirty finger-breadths in length, with a width of sixteen finger-breadths, provided with a rim and equipped with small bells. 170.
The staff was broken, as was the wooden crossbar and the head-rest;
likewise, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the banner, and the water-pot were shattered. (171)
Whatever object in the world of men serves as a means for men, and whatever is an accessory—everything that is such is proclaimed in the context of drama. (172)
Whatever object it reaches, by that its characteristic should be inferred;
and I shall now fully describe the characteristics of the worn-out wooden staff.

"Whatever belongs to whatever"—that is to say, according to whichever treatise (*śāstra*) a particular subject matter falls under, or according to whichever person it pertains to, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of that object should be inferred (*ūhya*). Regarding the word "to be inferred," he states a distinction: a complete definition is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*), as when even while relying on the definition of a sword [the specific characteristics of a particular one must still be inferred].
(137) The banners have indeed been described by Viśvakarman according to their characteristics as belonging to Mahendra;
one should construct one of these from wood in a manner that is somewhat worn. 174.
Alternatively, it may be of tree origin, or even a sprout that is withered;
however, the bamboo is indeed the best, and I shall describe its characteristics.
Furthermore, a bamboo born on white ground and produced under the Puṣya asterism should indeed be carefully selected for the purpose of making a jarjara. || 176 ||
The measure of the fingers shall be one hundred and eight;
it should likewise be five joints, four knots, and the size of a palm.
One should not use a bamboo that has a large knot, nor one with branches, nor one infested by insects;
nor one whose joints are damaged by worms, nor one that is inferior to other bamboos.
Having worshipped the flute according to the rules with offerings of honey, clarified butter, and mustard seeds, preceded by garlands and incense, one should take up an old, worn-out flute.

It is also inferred that it may be constructed from materials such as iron; and that [construction], consisting of the application of dramatic performance, is to be carried out through reasoning and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇaiḥ*), the meaning is that according to the system of Viśvakarman, the characteristics of the great Indra-banner (*mahendradhvaja*) have been described with many subdivisions. "Nor inferior" (*na hīnaḥ*)—and so forth.
The meaning is that, even when other bamboos are rubbed together, that [sound] which is incomplete in its constituent parts is not desired.
Whatever ritual procedure and whatever sequence are prescribed for the Māhendra banner, they are remembered as being the same here.
That [instrument] of Jarjara should be made, resting upon a bamboo pole of the Puṣya species. || 180 ||
That bamboo which has long joints, thin leaves, and grains at the tips of its joints is celebrated as *puṣyaveṇu*. || 181 ||
This rule for the jarjara has been declared by me according to its measurement;
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the staff (daṇḍakāṣṭha). || 182 ||
Furthermore, the staff-wood may be made from the kapittha, bilva, or vaṃśa trees;
it should indeed be curved and endowed with the three-fold characteristics. || 183 ||
That staff-wood which is not infested by insects, nor afflicted by disease, and whose branches are sparse, should be used. (184)
But he who causes a wooden staff to be made that is devoid of these characteristics and is worn out will certainly incur great loss. || 185 ||

Now, for the purpose of dividing the head, a ghaṭī should be prepared with great care. He explains the *puṣyaveṇu*: "The bamboo should be characterized by long joints; such are the divisions of the head," as seen where it says "two heads, three arrows," and so forth, or wherever else [it is mentioned].
(139) Measured by one's own standard, it is indeed thirty-two finger-breadths. || 186 ||
The vessel should be made from the middle part of a bilva fruit, resting upon its head, and combined with the juice and the steamed paste of bilva. (187)
One should fashion a head-covering either with ashes or with husks;
then, having covered it with cloths smeared with bilva leaves and resting upon jars.
Having smeared a cloth with a paste of *bilva* fruit, one should join it to the jar;
one should not make it too thick, nor crooked, nor too thin, nor too long. (189)
When that [skin] has been dried by the sun, or even when it is thoroughly dried,
the wise perform the excision according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
Having divided it into equal halves with a very sharp instrument,
one should mark the corners on the forehead according to its own prescribed measurements.

The forehead should be made half a finger-breadth [in height], and it should be cut away for six fingers. Having concealed one's own head, another head is displayed. This same procedure applies to each foot and each hand. [Regarding the materials: the inner pith of the *bilva* tree, hair, bark of trees, and so forth. He explains how that [image] is to be fashioned:
"With sweat" means with ashes or husk-powder; "well-composed" means having the holes covered. "Not thick" is said for fear of excessive weight. "Not crooked" is because it would be fragile.
"To be cut" is for the purpose of creating openings between the parts.
Half of half an *aṅgula* should be cut away, and at the waist it should be two *aṅgulas*.
At the edge of the ear-lobe, an area of two fingers' breadth should be excised;
likewise, the ear-cavity should be three fingers in size and must indeed be excised.
Then, a well-proportioned *avaṭu* (notch) of twelve finger-breadths should be made;
for this is the rule always prescribed by me for cutting the *ghaṭī*.
Above that, crowns fashioned from many artistic designs should be made, covered with various jewels and adorned with many forms. || 195 ||
Likewise, one should provide various kinds of accessories here for the performance of drama, according to the specific nature of each character. || 196 ||
Whatever action or craft is prescribed in this world, which is filled with both the moving and the unmoving, that is remembered as an *upakaraṇa* (instrument).
Whatever object comes within its range, that very thing it pursues;
for there is no limit to men when they rely upon the requisites of drama. (198)
"Avatuḥ" refers to the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*). Whatever action, craft, application, or activity has been produced by this [ear], [it is perceived].
By him, the creation of that [world] was established as its authority and its defining characteristic.
That creation which was fashioned by the Great-Souled One, consisting primarily of wooden machinery, does not belong to us; why then should it cause distress in the practice of drama? (200)
Whatever substance exists in the world of living beings, characterized by various marks, its imitation in form shall constitute the equipment for drama. (201)
Palaces, houses, vehicles, and various weapons—
these cannot indeed be produced here according to the characteristics as they have been described.

One may be characterized by worldly phenomena (*lokadharmin*), while another is characterized by dramatic performance (*nāṭyadharmin*); however, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) belongs to the world, whereas manifestation (*vibhāva*) is indeed drama alone. (203)
Those who know the art must not make the theatrical apparatus out of iron, nor likewise out of steel, for it would cause excessive strain upon the teacher. (204)
Regarding wood, leather, garments, lac, bamboo, and leaves—[this was said] by the high-souled Viśvakarman. "Vibhāva" means that it is a mere mental conception (*bhāvanāmātra*).
One should have the implements for the drama here made of light materials. || 205 ||
Shields, armor, banners, mountains, palaces, temples, chariots, elephants, vehicles, celestial mansions, and houses; || 206 ||
First, having fashioned the ritual implements from bamboo leaves based on their intended purpose,
one should then cover them with cloths and bring them to a state of formal beauty.
Alternatively, if there should be a lack of cloth here,
the making of garments may be done with palm leaves or with kiliñja fibers, or even with smooth materials.
Likewise, weapons in a drama may be made from grass, bamboo, leaves, and so forth, as well as from waxen vessels, appearing in various forms. (209)
One should fashion figures resembling [the deity] using grass, bamboo, or vessels, according to each foot, each head, each hand, and each limb. || 210 ||
"Light implements" refers to those by means of which an action may be accomplished with ease.
"With palm-leaves" means with *tāla* leaves. "With vessels" refers to such things as gourds, bamboo slats, swords, and so forth.
Whatever form is similar to this, arising from the quality of resemblance,
one should have that entire [image] made of clay, yet fashioned in various forms.
Various serpents are to be fashioned from vessels, cloth, beeswax, lac, mica, and from flax, hemp, and bilva. (212)
One may also fashion various kinds of flowers and diverse fruits using resin,
cloth, beeswax, or lac.
With vessels, clothing, beeswax, and likewise with copper plates, as well as with indigo-dyed cloth and even with mica-plates; 214.
One should fashion the jewels with a colored leaf of mica, and likewise, one should have their setting made from copper and lead. || 215 ||
The various divine crowns that were previously described by me should be made radiant with cloud-like petals and adorned with jewels and snakes.
Wax and beeswax (sitkthaka)—
it is taught that their ritual action does not originate from the scriptures.
It should be performed with the thought that [the teacher] is the preceptor, employing the process of reasoning through inclusion and exclusion.
This application of mortal rites has been devised by me for the future;
for why else would there be such weakness among men? (218)
Even for mortals, manifestations consisting entirely of gold cannot be fashioned;
nor are crowns or ornaments desired when they are merely made of gold and jewels. (219)
In combat, wrestling, dancing, or in activities involving exposure to the rain, sweat and fainting arise for one who is exhausted by the state of heaviness. (220)
For one afflicted by perspiration, fainting, and exhaustion, the practice perishes;
moreover, there may at times be a loss of life due to excessive exertion. (221)
Therefore, ornaments should be fashioned from copper leaves, even if they are unrefined or merely colored,
as well as from bheṇḍa wood or beeswax.
Thus, by means of worldly convention and through the power of his own intellect,
the wise man should properly employ the accessories of the drama here.
(145) Nothing should be pierced, nor indeed cut, nor even struck;
on the stage, one should perform with weapons only as a mere symbolic representation. 224.
Alternatively, the discharge of weapons should be performed by the actors in the midst of the stage through yogic training, as if created by magic.
Thus, although various kinds of weapons and ornaments have not been mentioned by me, those which are to be taken from the world should also be employed.
This "artificial" (āhārya) representation has indeed been declared by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall explain the "general" (sāmānya) representation. || 227 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Representation through Costumes and Make-up," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
The *vidyā* (magical knowledge) called *sudhāmaka* consists of manual dexterity and the like; *māyā* consists of the binding of the eyes and so forth.
Concluding this chapter, [the author] indicates the remainder of what is to be said through gesture (*abhinaya*), stating:
"For this is indeed the *āhārya-abhinaya* (external representation). May there be auspiciousness!

In this chapter on the portrayal of externalized emotions (*āhāryābhinaya*), Abhinavagupta has accurately established this methodological procedure at the points where the text is knotted together, in due order.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on the Artistic Representation (*āhāryābhinaya*), in the *Abhinavabhārati*, the commentary on the *Nāṭyaveda*, composed by the venerable Great Māheśvara teacher Abhinavagupta.
Śrī.
The Twenty-second Chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra:
General Representation (Sāmānyābhinaya).
That which is known as general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) arises from speech, the limbs, and the inner being (*sattva*).
[From] Abhinavagupta’s *Abhinavabhāratī*, Chapter Twenty-two:
That which causes differentiation leads the self toward its own distinctness.
We praise Śiva, whose form is the very embodiment of pride through his universal gestures and postures.

Here, "another" refers to that which is coloring (uparañjaka) and another type of representation (abhinaya); "common" (*sama*) means existing therein, thus it is called *sāmānyābhinaya* (generalized representation). According to the ultimate sense, the elders who follow the tradition of Kohala state that generalized representation is sixfold. For instance, Kohala says:
"The wise know that this very [abhinaya] is sixfold in its general application: the remaining, the desired, the mixed, the curved, the manifest, and the state of being joined as one. Thus it is said.

In this context, "general" (sāmānya) refers to that which is common (sādhāraṇa). Therefore, that form which remains common to all modes of representation (abhinaya), which was not previously mentioned but must necessarily be stated, and which is taught in this chapter for the purpose of training both poets and actors— that is general representation (sāmānyābhinaya).

Thus, it is "common" (*sāmānya*) or "universal" (*sādhāraṇa*) among the *abhinayas*, because it is the object of *abhinaya*, or because of the etymological derivation of *abhinaya* as that which leads one toward one's own expressed meaning. For instance, the particularity of the *sāttvika* [sentiment], such as *hāva*, *bhāva*, and *helā*, which was not previously mentioned, is now stated; and its scope is as follows:

The bodily [expression] is described by the passage beginning with "consisting of six elements" (22.43), and the vocal [expression] is described by the passage beginning with "conversation and chatter" (22.52).

Now, one might ask: what is the distinction of this [type of expression] from the variegated expression (*citrābhinaya*), given that it is said to be "the very particularity of the bodily and other types of expression" (25.1)?

The distinction is stated: therein, there is variety due to the intermingling of speech, limbs, and mental disposition; here, however, [there is variety] through that which is individually determined and not explicitly mentioned.

This refers to the mention of another specific distinction. For it is said there that the word *citra* will be taught as "that which is not [otherwise] stated is called *citra*" (25.1). Likewise, here, however, the general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) is the practice of desire (*kāmopacāra*), for it is common to the entire class of living beings and brings all categories of creatures toward [the object].
It is called *abhinaya* because it is represented through the totality of vocal, physical, and internal characteristics, as well as by way of its general nature.

Since this representation of the nature of men and women—the application of desire—is performed according to the distinctions of their various states, this chapter is the "General Representation" (*sāmānyābhinaya*). Therefore...

Thus, this chapter, which constitutes the remainder of the preceding section and teaches the practice of desire (*kāmopacāra*), should be understood as the chapter titled "The Practices of the Courtesan" (*vaiśikopacāra*). Likewise, regarding the term *sāmānyam*: the action of those who are alike is *sāmānya*, and that is also its representation (*abhinayana*). Therefore, it is intended to convey a single unified representation by means of that.

A slight modification of the state of being (*bhāva*) is itself *hāva* when it reaches maturity, and *helā* when it reaches its highest degree. In the state of *prauḍhatā* (maturity), characterized by a disregard for passion (*madanāpekṣatva*), there is indeed *helā* (sportiveness). As youth gradually increases, when there is well-being of one's own self, senses, and mind, there is *hāva* (coquettish gesture); *helā* is a physical transformation (*śarīravikāra*). However, due to an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and so forth, when that [transformation] subsides, there is *pravilaya* (dissolution). Thus, from *helā*, it becomes joined with *bhāva* (emotion), and through *bhāva*, it becomes *hāva*.

Even the bodily transformations produced by youth, which do not depend on other causes, are not primarily "representations" (abhinaya) in the same way that qualities or dispositions residing in the face and limbs are; rather, they are perceived as such because they occur alongside slightly differentiated verbal and other representations and facial coloration.

The universal human goal is pervaded by the erotic sentiment residing in women and the heroic sentiment residing in men; moreover, these gestures and ornaments find no place elsewhere except in the form of an excellent woman, who is composed of *sattva*, for they cannot possibly exist in bodies characterized by *rajas* or *tamas*.

Even among Caṇḍālas, the perfection of beauty and charm is seen, yet not their gestures or ornaments; even in their case, you indicate their very excellence relative to their own class, or due to the loss of wealth and so forth. This has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Tauta: "And here, there is no [need for] ornaments..."

Regarding the statement that "the characteristic has the Great One (Mahat) as its substratum"— these [characteristics], being observed, are considered supreme because they are appropriate for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); yet they are devoid of a clear discernment of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, free from contact with the states of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), and entirely lacking in specific differentiation.

The common forms of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) are enacted through general gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*), yet they are not non-enactable like beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth; rather, these modifications of the body are indeed *anubhāvas*.

Therefore, it is precisely because of the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) that this occurs. The same applies to qualities such as grace (*śobhā*) and so on, which reside in the person.

These are merely general gestures (sāmānyābhinaya), conveying only this much: that "this person is of an energetic nature. Furthermore, whatever movement of women appropriate to the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is enacted, it is precisely therein that the ornaments of gesture (ceṣṭālaṅkāra) must necessarily be performed.

And because they are represented as following [the hero] through all states like a universal quality (*sāmānya*), the beauty and other attributes of the principal character are indeed "gestures of the universal" (*sāmānyābhinaya*). Likewise, these— speech, body, spirit, and costume— together with their respective subdivisions, having combined as far as possible, enter into [the representation], as in the case of *kilakiñcita*.

In the context of *vicchitti* (graceful elegance) and *vibhrama* (bewilderment), these are called *sāmānyābhinayas* (general gestures); and because they involve the union of speech (*vāc*), body (*aṅga*), and costume (*āhārya*), yet are characterized primarily by *sattva* (inner essence), they are termed *sāttvikas*.
In youth, the transformations arising from the face and body of women become excessive. || 4 ||
In the beginning, there are three born of the limbs (aṅgaja); ten others among them are innate (svābhāvika);
and furthermore, seven are effortless (ayatnaja), being augmented by rasa and bhāva.

Thus, by means of these very general gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*), the entire universe is pervaded through the medium of the principal women and men. These must be discussed in this chapter; therefore, he says: "But the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*)," where the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. Others have been mentioned in the chapter on emotions (*bhāvādhyāya*), but these must now be stated, as they were not mentioned there. For these—

The ornaments are merely confined to the body and do not consist of mental states (*cittavṛtti*). "Resorting to emotional states" (*bhāvasaṃśraya*) means that they merely represent the state of love (*ratibhāva*). For these [ornaments] are seen to be prominent in youth, unmanifest in childhood, and hidden in old age. As it has been said:

"Whatever these states of young women may be—even those such as *kuṭṭamita* and the rest—the lamp of passion makes them manifest, just as it reveals jars and other objects that are invisible in the night.
Thus, [these states] are born of the face and body; they are merely transformations of the physical form, and certainly not [the essence] as [some might claim].
