Just as tears and the like are observed within the region of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of throat-obstruction and so forth, so too are the limbs (*gātra*)—such as the chest and hips—of the *ceṣṭā* and *alaṅkāra* [gestures and ornaments] perceived; the face (*vaktra*), however, is mentioned again because of its preeminence. Among these, some modifications of the body (*dehavikāra*) are indeed of the nature of action (*kriyātmaka*).
Because they exist by the mere presence of the state of passion (*rati*) practiced in previous births, those very [emotions] arise when the body serves as the vessel;
thus they are called "born of the self" (*aṅgaja*), namely *hāva* and *helā*. Others, however, involve the entry of specific excitants (*vibhāva*) appropriate to the present birth.
In a body permeated by an emerging state of passion (*rati*), those [emotions] manifest;

they arise from their own inherent nature (*svābhāvika*) once that state of passion has become an object of the heart. Thus, for one woman, only a certain [man] arises through the power of her own nature, for another a different one, and for yet another both of them, and so forth; for this reason as well [it is established].
The natural [expressions] (*svābhāvikāḥ*)—namely, *bhāva*, *hāva*, and *helā*—occur in all cases among all excellent women who possess an abundance of sattva.
Likewise, there are the seven beginning with *śobhā*. Thus, these are the bodily [expressions], the natural ones, and those born of action.
Others, however, such as beauty (*śobhā*) and the like, have the nature of qualities (*guṇasvabhāva*); these are not produced by effort.

Those produced by effort are said to consist of action (*kriyātmaka*). For those who know the categories of reality maintain that effort arises from desire, and from that effort comes bodily action. Therefore, others are not produced by effort. This is what he says:
(155) Sentient being (*sattva*) consists of the body; from sentient being, emotional state (*bhāva*) arises;
from emotional state, gesture (*hāva*) arises; and from gesture, playful grace (*helā*) arises. (6)
Sport, gesture, and emotion arise from one another;
these exist within the body, established in its fundamental nature according to the variation of the constituent elements.
Through speech, physical gestures, facial expressions, disposition, and dramatic representation, one who brings to life the internal emotion of the poet is called a *bhāva*. (8)
"First, the three born of the body": among those ornaments, "first" means that they occur even earlier because they arise solely from the body as permeated by prior impressions (*pūrva-vāsanā*).
The phrase "strengthened by emotion" (*bhāvopabṛṃhitāḥ*) applies to both [the first two types]. "Innate" (*svābhāvikī*) means produced without effort through the state of one's own natural passion.

They become endowed with life. (With approval: "Furthermore" means that these [qualities] do not belong to sentient beings who exist merely as drawings or paintings on cloth. Regarding that, he first states the introductory basis for the three [categories], beginning with: "The sentient being would consist of the body. Thus, the sentient being is first conceived of as having the nature of a physical body.

The meaning is that it has attained the state of the supreme body (*uttama-śarīratā*). From that comes *bhāva* (feeling), from that *hāva* (gesture), and from that *helā* (coquetry). Thus, when the *sattva* (inner being) is exceedingly intense, [these qualities] reside in the body itself. But when the *sattva* is not so pierced [by aesthetic emotion], then there exists a requirement for another auxiliary cause arising from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior experience; this he demonstrates as follows:
"Playfulness (*helā*), gesture (*hāva*), and emotion (*bhāva*) arise from one another;

these exist within the differentiation of the *sattvas*, residing in the body according to their nature. Here, the first word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also" (*api*), while the other is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*); for [conjunction] is indicated in each individual case.

And the third *ca* (and) should also be read [there]. Thus, the meaning is this: even these [mental states], which abide in their own nature (*prakṛti*) and depend solely on the nature of the body, arise from one another.
For instance, when a young girl observes the playful gestures of another mature young woman, an emotional expression (*hāva*) arises in her.

If the emotion (*bhāva*) has been manifested previously, otherwise there would be merely the emergence of the emotion itself. Thus, when *hāva* is observed, there is either *bhāva* or *helā*. However, when the stage of *hāva* has already emerged previously and *helā* is seen later, then it is *helā* arising from *helā*. In this same way, one should state that *bhāva* arises from *hāva*, and *bhāva* arises from *bhāva*.
Thus, from hearing of the existence and other qualities belonging to another, [one perceives] such a state as having its being produced in that manner, distinct within its own sources.
One should not point to that entity here as being produced by a different state. (9)

In that context, *hāva*—rich with variations of the eyes and eyebrows, indicative of amorous form, and accompanied by a graceful movement of the neck—is to be understood as occurring while standing or rising. (10)
It should be understood that even from listening to poetry that is charming due to its subject matter, the arousal of *hela* and the other [emotions] occurs;
this is their mutual origination.

Now, one might object: "If these are inherent in the *prakṛtis*, then they are born of the limbs (*aṅgaja*) from that very source—so what is the need for dependence on anything else? To this, he says:

(Regarding the passage beginning with "vāgaṅga..."): The reading "vāgaṅgamukharāgeṇa" and so forth is indeed a verse from the *Bhāvādhyāya*, yet its meaning is not identical; rather, it has a different meaning altogether.
One should not consider it to have the same meaning as [the verse] by Śrī Śaṅkuka. Thus, [this concludes] the definition of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*).

That this is a property of the body is universally agreed upon. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: an emotion (*bhāva*) characterized by speech, gestures, facial expressions, and physical states is called the "emotion of the girl" precisely because it is a particularity of speech, gesture, and physical state. He says that there is no other distinction whatsoever; rather, it exists internally in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Cultivating and indicating the present emotion known as *rati* (love), he asks: "Is it for everyone? To which he replies: "No; rather, for the poet"—meaning for that connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) who perceives even the most subtle of meanings.
This is what is meant: while the two maidens, one superior and one inferior, are engaged in their respective behaviors, [the voice of] one speaks...

When one observes the movement of the eyes and other faculties, the paleness of the face produced by the exhaustion of playing and carrying [the child], the tears, and so forth, there arises in the heart a cognition that is particularly radiant— though it is indeed inferential in nature— it is as if produced by direct perception (*abhinaya*), for it determines the specific [object] with great clarity. This is truly a vast [cognition].

"Someone will be a heroine. Thus, that particular state of a specific form which arises from the presence of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of internal passion within speech and so forth—that particular modification of the body is *bhāva*. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "iva" (like), meaning it is equivalent to *abhinaya* (acting).
The meaning is that "state" (*bhāva*) is characterized by speech and so forth.

In that context, it is precisely a *tatpuruṣa* compound; for, by means of the characteristics of the [excellent] woman as the object (*pātra*), there arises a quality consisting of an extraordinary transformation—such as the eyes, chin, and neck being raised—and it is for this very reason [that it is so designated].
It indicates a form appropriate for love (*śṛṅgāra*), which touches the hearts of all people—both those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) and those without. *Hāva*:
for this [gesture] causes that maiden to "cause herself to be desired" (*hāvayati*) by offering her own mental state to another, giving it away.
Regarding the term *sthitasamutthita*: she is "standing" (*sthita*) and has "arisen" (*samutthita*) of her own accord (*svataḥ*).
That which is indeed *hāva* is itself called by the wise *helā*, arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) and consisting of graceful gestures (*lalita-abhinaya*). (11)

That *hāva*, however, which rests by repeatedly breaking through [the layers of restraint] and has as its sole purpose the outward expansion [of passion], may indeed be called *helā* (sportiveness); for this very reason, it is shown to be a close companion to the delicate *parikara* (coquettish gesture). In the state of *hāva*, one does not even consider oneself to be awakening love; rather, [it is merely a preliminary stage].
By the power of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it produces such modifications that, upon seeing them, one imagines [the object] to be so. However, when—
due to the awakening of the latent impression of pleasure— one conceives that pleasure as being fully awakened,
yet because of the absence of the support of appropriate excitants (*vibhāva*), it does not attain a clear manifestation due to its lack of an objective referent, then...
*Hilā* is a specific modification of the body produced by that [state]. In the *Dhātupāṭha*, it is listed as *hila* with the meaning "the cause of a state" (*bhāva*).
It refers to an action related to *bhāva* (or *hāva*), namely its expansion or the quality of being driven with speed.
In common parlance, one who moves with speed is said to *helati*. Thus he says, "The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is *rati*; from that, in the heart..."
The meaning is that *helā* (sportiveness) is that which exists; likewise, regarding the state of being experienced as the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*),
there is a possibility— a conceptualization— of its form being as if common [to all],
such that the conceptualization is indeed of a form similar to the tasting of the erotic sentiment by the audience.
Her very life-force consists of wonder alone; for, as long as the acquisition of objects appears to her, it does so because of the non-manifestation of specific excitants (*vibhāva*).
Thus, having transcended the stage of childhood—which was like a stone carved by a master sculptor—there arises the blossoming of youth; and for this very reason:

In this [state], graceful gestures do not attain the character of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), due to the intensity of the onset of emotional transformation (*vikāra*). Examples of these are given in sequence:
"The forceful breaking of locks of hair, the mass of the braid, and then the passion for training..."

The grooming of the teeth, the tying of the lower garment, the training of the eyebrows and the face, the playful glances of sidelong eyes, and the transfer of clever speech into words— this indescribable sequence of dalliance in women withers away moment by moment as childhood fades. (Viddhaśālabhañjikā 1)
A slightly charming smile; the power of the gaze, tremulous and sweet; the movement of speech, full of the flavor of graceful gestures and playful expression;
and the commencement of gait, adorned with budding grace.
What indeed is not charming in a deer-eyed woman who has reached her youth? (Subhāṣitāvalī, verse 158).
Playfulness, grace, charm, coquetry, and the affectation of anger;
Moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭamita, vibboka, and likewise lalita. || 12 ||
And "dalliance" (vihṛta)—these ten should be known as the innate natures of women.
Furthermore, I shall describe their specific characteristics individually. (13)
That she makes her limbs motionless like a doe at the sound of songs;
that she asks her friend again for news of her beloved even though it has already been heard; and that she sleeps within herself without waking—that, oh, I know to be the mark of a newlywed bride.
The mind-born god has set about sprinkling the creeper of love upon her heart.

For here, only the awakening of passion inherent within the state of being has been described; however, it should not be thought that "longing" (*abhilāṣa*) itself is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). Indeed, that [awakening] is the supreme festival for women, serving as the foundation for the temple of all future human goals, just as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is for a Brahmin.
The *Lokottarālaṅkāra* is renowned as a supreme place of unsurpassed bliss and the highest purity.

Although these [ornaments] belong to men as well, they are described specifically as pertaining to women because they constitute their very ornaments; for a man, however, the highest ornament is solely the account of his own valorous exertion (*utsāha*). And so it is said:

Among the various types of heroes (*nāyaka*), steadfastness (*dhīratva*) alone is stated as the defining characteristic. While qualities such as love (*śṛṅgāra*) and the like are subsumed under it, as in the case of the "steadfast and playful" (*dhīralalita*) hero and others.
Having thus explained the three [types] born of the limbs, he now points out the ten natural ones with the verse beginning "playful charm" (*līlā*) and "grace" (*vilāsa*).

When delight becomes manifest through its distinctiveness upon obtaining a distinguished excitant (vibhāva), the bodily transformations produced by its intensification— such as playful gestures (*līlā*) and so forth—
are not perceived due to their extreme subtlety; such is the view held by the Śākya teacher Rāhulaka and others.

To claim that gestures such as *helā* and *hāva* became ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) merely by being performed in the midst of *līlā* and so forth, and to rest content with this much—namely, that gesture in general is an ornament—is incorrect.
Līlā (sportive grace) is to be understood by those skilled in performance as the imitation of a beloved person through refined ornaments of speech and body, employed with sweetness and affection. 14.

That specific excellence which arises in standing, sitting, and walking, as well as in the actions of the hands, eyebrows, and eyes, when they are closely joined [with the emotion], is indeed *vilāsa* (grace). || 15 ||
The deliberate setting aside of garlands, coverings, ornaments, and ointments—indeed, even a slight such refinement produces a supreme beauty. (16)

Regarding this, he states the definitions of these ten [types of heroines] in sequence with the words "by speech, limbs, and ornaments. Through affection for her beloved, and by means of an excess of great respect toward him, she applies to herself speech that is sweet and delicate— not harsh, even if it were his own— and speech that is sweet yet distinguished, not merely so.

Because of the conceits of conceptualization (*kalpita*), for that very reason, through the form of imitation and manifestation, there is non-transformation; and through the internal appropriation of that [nature], there is great esteem (*bahumāna*) toward one's own self. These ten occur when the state of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) has been attained. However, the seven beginning with "beauty" (*śobhā*) are future [qualities] that exist only upon the attainment of the state of enjoyment. These...

In this matter, poets employ words such as *līlā* and others through a mixture of technical and worldly usage, as for example: "When the graceful, playful movements had ceased" (*Kumārasambhava* 1.33). In that case, one must accept either metaphorical application based on etymological fitness or worldly convention as the authority. Those learned in the systems (*tantra*) should read it thus: "when [the movements] had gone..."
Regarding the phrase "in those [gestures] beautiful through playful grace (*līlā*)," the disciples of Bhaṭṭendurāja maintain that this is incorrect;
for those [gestures] such as *līlā*, *vibhrama*, and so forth, which are yet to come, are practiced at that time as if they were being learned in accordance with their propriety.
Indeed, the time for the performance (*prayoga*) is when one is led away after having uttered [the words], whereas *līlā* and the rest belong to the stage of modesty (*vinaya*).
The agency of the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*) is here imagined.
Regarding the phrase "standing and sitting" (*sthānāsana*): standing is the state of being upright, and sitting is the state of being seated.

Even though [the gestures] were not learned through effort regarding standing and so forth, the graceful charm (*vilāsa*) consists in bringing about that very form by the power of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
"Adherent" (*śliṣṭa*) means not prominent (*anulbaṇa*). For example: "O girl, let the seat of the one who has gone abroad be [occupied] by a lover," and so forth.
Even though it is very slight, the greatness of the pride of good fortune produces a supreme beauty precisely through its smallness.
For it is as follows:
160) [it concerns] various meanings consisting of the application of speech, physical gestures, costumes, and inner disposition.
The reversal [of the natural state] produced by intoxication, passion, and joy is to be known as *vibhrama* (confusion). || 17 ||
The mingling of smiles, weeping, laughter, fear, joy, pride, sorrow, fatigue, and longing, occurring repeatedly out of delight, is to be known as *kilakiñcita*. (18)
In cases such as *kaca uparabbha-u sassara isiṇi-attha* and so forth;

however, that which was cited as an example—*sarasijamanuviddhaṃ śaivalenāpi ramyaṃ* (*Śākuntala* 1.20)—is incorrect. For here, the employment of the "negation of disregard" (*anādaranyāsa*) is not intended to produce pride in one's own excellence, but rather...
Enough of saying that it consists primarily of assuming an attire appropriate for ascetics.

"Of various kinds" refers to the distinction of yoga; thus, the arrangement of many objects—which possess numerous subdivisions through distinctions such as speech and so forth—in a manner other than their true nature, out of pride in one's own charm, is *vibhrama* (bewilderment), as previously described.

For example: speaking one way when something else ought to be said; taking with the foot what should be taken with the hand; placing a girdle around the neck, and so forth. Passion produced by liquor is the intense affection and joy directed toward one's beloved. Pride in one's own good fortune is as follows—
"Friend, bind it tightly, making it firm and secure; thus, O friend, will this auspiciousness remain unshakable. So she spoke.
"Friend, there is indeed such good fortune here, which cannot be moved even by the wind."
The term *saṃkara* refers to a mixture or blending arising from joy, pride, and so forth, through the intermingling of smiling, weeping, and laughing. For example, as in the passage beginning:
"maha...ṭimalalamakalati halahalanti sappadi-o vallavaccara iva i aṇekatti... and so on.
For here, pride, fatigue, sorrow, smiles, weeping, and laughter are described in sequence by means of regional (deśī) words;
[these occur] either during conversation with a beloved person or upon witnessing their playful dalliance and the like. (p. 161)
That which is produced by the cultivation of that state is called *moṭṭāyita*. || 19 ||

Kuṭṭamita is to be understood as that which arises from excessive joy and agitation due to the seizing of the hair, breasts, lips, and so forth; it is pleasure expressed through the guise of pain. (20)
The state known as *bibboka* should be understood as arising from pride and conceit upon attaining desired objects, and manifested through a display of disregard toward women. (21)
The graceful arrangement of hands, feet, and limbs, executed through the movements of the eyebrows, eyes, and lips, which arises from delicacy, is proclaimed as *lalita* (the graceful).

When it is said "of a beloved person," whatever playful gestures (*līlā*) and so forth arise in a woman upon seeing her lover, that is called *moṭṭāyita* because of the contortion of her limbs, reaching up to the crushing of the limbs of Love (*madana*), due to the power of the cultivation of that state of being.
As it has been said:
In such cases as *si-i-uṇathaṇasakkiyahattha-ūrū*, the phrase "by the seizing of the hair, breasts, and lips" implies "by the beloved. For example:
*deśikhaṇaṃmi ṇa-athaṇahi a-i-āpaḍi apuṇahe tihiṃ ajja*.
"What is the use of binding the feet with heavy shackles for the sake of suppressing wickedness? and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of desired things," this refers to garments, ornaments, and the like. "Acting with disregard" means that which is abundant in one who acts with disregard toward those very objects [is *bibboka*]. For example: "Even he who bears the name Candraghāsin—what indeed [is his power]?"
In such cases as "du āvilaṃ u-i-ā ko caṇḍa," and so forth.

Regarding "the arrangement of hands, feet, and limbs": *vilāsa* (graceful play) is that variety which arises in the actions of the hands and so forth simply by virtue of what must be done. In *lalita* (loveliness), however, there is merely the engagement in external activity; there is no thought of anything to be taken up or rejected, yet the movement of the delicate hands is not that of one who is wicked.
(To be seen? something [is required], yet there is a distinction regarding the ritual of Tārā and so forth.
As it is said on page 162:
"The placement of the hands, fingers, and limbs, joined with the eyebrows, eyes, and lips..."
This is known as *lalita* (the graceful), performed by women according to delicate procedures. || 23 ||
The failure to speak words that have been received and are full of affection—whether by way of a pretext or by one's own nature—is called *vihṛtam* (the evasive). || 24 ||
When women, out of modesty, refrain from speaking even words they have already acquired—whether by means of a pretext or by their very nature—this is declared to be *vihṛta*. || 25 ||
Beauty, loveliness, brilliance, as well as sweetness, fortitude, self-confidence, and magnanimity—these are qualities that arise without effort. (26)
The beauty of the limbs, augmented by the enjoyment of form, youth, and charm, is proclaimed as *śobhā* (splendor). (27)

"O you whose stream of beauty flows with the grace of a lotus-stalk, you who are exceedingly full... [you] who have completely destroyed all the afflictions of the world through the weight of your abundant compassion, O you who are like a fire that consumes [suffering] in an instant," and so forth.
Others, however, citing the *dhātu-pāṭha* entry "laḍa, to sport," maintain that it is indeed an excess of playful charm (*vilāsa*) [that is being described].
They consider this to be known as *lalita* (the playful).

Regarding the phrase "of sentences endowed with affection," the meaning is that they are suitable for utterance because the opportunity has been obtained—that is, due to the arrival of the proper occasion. "By nature" means either due to innocence, childhood, or being preoccupied with something else.

Regarding the phrase "by means of artifice" (*vyājāt*): the meaning is "by means of artifice and so forth, such as feigned innocence and the like, through an excellence of manifestation. Furthermore, for some women, such manifestation is indeed their very nature, as in the verses by poets: "...they act like a bee, they desire [him], and they even imitate death," and so on.
Now, regarding "those born without effort": [the qualities] such as beauty (*śobhā*) and loveliness (*kānti*). Their definitions follow in order.

By means of form, youth, and charm—these very same things, form and so forth, when being enjoyed by a man, take on another kind of radiance (*chāyā*). And that radiance possesses, in sequence, the states of being mild, moderate, or intense.
Likewise, *kānti* (loveliness) should be understood as beauty itself when passion (*manmatha*) is not yet fully developed;
*kānti* alone, when it is exceedingly expansive, is designated as *dīpti* (radiance). (28)
In all particular states, whether they be intense or graceful, the lack of excess in physical movement is designated as *mādhurya* (sweetness). || 29 ||
Freedom from agitation caused by fickleness, an absence of boastfulness regarding all matters, and a natural state of mental composure—this is designated as fortitude (dhairya). || 30 ||
Confidence is declared by the wise to be the absence of timidity in performance; nobility is said to be humility that accompanies one in all circumstances. (31)

From the constant cultivation of enjoyment, she possesses beauty; that is to say, loveliness and radiance. The meaning is: she for whom the cause is the enjoyment of desire, characterized by the phrase "love that is completely full" (*āpūrṇamanmatha*). However, another commentator, explaining [the term] as *apūrṇamanmatha* ("incomplete love"), [assigns] loveliness, radiance, and beauty respectively...
He speaks of its excellence (*sātiśayatva*). The teachers (*upādhyāyāḥ*) maintain that this is contrary to the initial statement.

Regarding the phrase "in the radiant" (*dīpteṣu*), it refers to anger and the like; the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "as if" (*iva*). Just as there is smoothness (*māsṛṇya*) in movements during graceful acts such as amorous play (*ratikrīḍā*), so too that which exists even in the radiant acts is *mādhurya* (sweetness).

Because it belongs to the category [of qualities] alongside beauty, youth, and so forth among all objects [of experience], this action—fortitude—is taught as distinct from physical forms. "Practice" (*prayoga*) means the sixty-four arts, such as the *kāmakalā* and others. As they say: "At other times, self-restraint (*śama*) is the ornament of a man, just as modesty is that of a woman."
"Valor [is appropriate] in the face of humiliation, as is boldness (*prāgalbhya*, *vaiyātya*) in sexual dalliances," as stated in *Śiśupālavadha* 2.44.
As for the interpretation by others that this refers to the subject of imitation (*anukartṛ*), that has already been refuted previously.
For even in all states such as indignation, jealousy, and anger, there is the non-utterance of harsh words and the like.

164) This is their "nobility" (*audārya*). Although these [transitory states] have the nature of mental fluctuations, some say that they are not included in the category of *bhāvas* because they lack the quality of being produced by external objects (*vibhāva*), and because they lack the capacity to evoke aesthetic moods (*rasa*) as *bhāvakas*.
And this is incorrect. For *śobhā* (grace), *kānti* (loveliness), and *dīpti* (radiance) are merely specific qualities residing in external form and beauty;

while *āvega* (agitation), *cāpalya* (restlessness), *trāsa* (fear), and *amarṣa* (indignation) are indeed mental states (*bhāva*). Since sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the like are not by nature modifications of the mind, what room is there for the suspicion that they are *bhāvas*? Thus, even that which is not a *bhāva* [can be considered] as another kind of *bhāva*.
If it is argued that because it appears as a qualifier of that [object], it is therefore of a positive (bhāva) nature,
let it be so; nevertheless, because it is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), because its form consists in the representation of a universal (*sāmānya-abhinaya*),
because it culminates in being grounded in an external body, and because its object is exclusively the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Because they encompass the entirety of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) as their object, these are mentioned separately from the group of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Furthermore, there is no intended restriction here that "these [transitory emotions] consist of only this many";
therefore, states such as innocence (*maugdhyamada*), transformation of emotion (*bhāvavikṛta*), and remorse (*paritāpana*) are also included.
The statement by Śākyācārya Rāhula and others that this is contradictory is sufficient; let there be no more.
These [faults] arise in delicate applications of a graceful nature.
For these two indeed become [the same] even when they are radiant, having abandoned their playful grace. || 32 ||
Beauty, grace, sweetness, steadfastness, profundity, as well as charm, magnanimity, and splendor—these are the varieties of the quality of *sattva* pertaining to manhood. (33)
Skill, heroism, enthusiasm, loathing for base matters, and rivalry with the most excellent qualities—from these, that which arises is known as *śobhā* (splendor). 34.
A steady-moving gaze, a gait as graceful as that of a bull, and speech preceded by a smile—this is celebrated as *vilāsa* (graceful charm). 35.
When, through practice, the integration of the instruments occurs even amidst great emotional transformations, that is remembered as *mādhurya* (sweetness). || 36 ||
Now, in order to establish that these constitute general gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*), he says: "These occur in the delicate.

When a performance characterized by grace (*lalita*) is being enacted, there is a "delicate" variety within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), such as the various types of union and separation (*vipralambha*). In all those cases, these [gestures] do not occur.

For this activity of the limbs is not empty [of meaning] and is fit for application; even regarding that variety of the manifestation of jealousy (*īrṣyā*) within the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), one must necessarily admit the occurrence of others through their sequence,
simultaneity, and so forth— thus it is common to the various divisions of the erotic.
The intended meaning is that because this is a performance (*abhinaya*), it is appropriately characterized as a "general performance" (*sāmānyābhinaya*).

Now, having introduced [the topic] regarding qualities pertaining to a person, he defines them starting with "grace" (*śobhā*), "charm" (*vilāsa*), and so forth. The connection is as follows: grace (*śobhā*) is that from which skillfulness (*dākṣya*) and other such qualities are inferred based on modifications of the body. A "bull-cow" (*govṛṣabha*) is an excellent cow.

"Even in great transformations" refers to the firm coordination of the organs—the actions of the hands, feet, and so forth—attained through practice in activities such as combat, wrestling, and physical exercise.
Steadfastness is defined as the immovability of one's resolve from that which is connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and which arises from what is auspicious or inauspicious. (37)
That power by virtue of which facial expressions are not perceived in states such as joy, anger, or fear—that is known as *gāmbhīrya* (depth). (38)
That which arises spontaneously from a nature free of transformation, consisting of gestures and movements in the form of the erotic sentiment, is declared to be *lalita* (the graceful). || 39 ||
Generosity, assistance, as well as pleasant speech,
and the absence of harshness where there is no physical distortion— this is *mādhurya* (sweetness). To claim that this belongs solely to the actor is incorrect,

because it contradicts the context [of the treatise] and because these qualities of the performer were discussed in the chapter on "Nature" (*prakṛti*) and the chapter on "The Varieties of Roles" (*bhūmikā-vikalpa*).

And because [this] will be explained [later], it has been stated that one who possesses merit and so forth as his fruit is "endowed" with them. Regarding the phrase "arising from the wholesome and the unwholesome":
these are those born of wholesome intentions and those born of unwholesome intentions. For even from the unwholesome...
A resolve turns away from what is unstable; just as Eḷa turned away from the four castes who were seizing all his possessions out of a desire for material gain and its fruits.
Others, however, considering this to be unbecoming of a hero, explain it otherwise regarding both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Regarding the term "arisen": by that, whatever is prescribed in the scriptures and is appropriate is undertaken. While that is being performed—whether it be auspicious, which brings about the easy attainment of wealth, or inauspicious, consisting of loss, expense, and so forth—nevertheless, any wavering from the resolve directed toward that object is merely a state of instability manifested as a physical transformation.

"Forms" (*ākāra*) are those by which the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) are manifested, such as facial expressions, passion, distorted views, and so forth. Even when these are absent, because the causal complex invariably produces its fruit, there may still be the occurrence of joy and the like;
yet, the very absence of facial expressions and the rest produced by those [fluctuations]—which is the very nature of a steady body—is what constitutes "depth" (*gāmbhīrya*).

Generosity (*audārya*) consists precisely in actions such as giving directed toward others, which take the form of a transformation of one's conduct. The inclusion of the word "one's own" (*sva*), however, is merely for the sake of common parlance; it does not imply that fear takes the form of disregard.
Whether toward one's own kin or even toward others, that is proclaimed as magnanimity. || 40 ||
That which is the non-endurance of insults, contempt, and the like employed by another, even at the risk of one's life, is declared to be *tejas* (spiritual splendor). (41)
O best of the twice-born, the performance born of the mind has been previously described by me;
now I shall explain the physical performance in its proper sequence.
The bodily [expression] consists of six elements: the sentence, the sprout of the cue, the branch, the dramatic performance, and the sprout of the withdrawal. (43)

He clarifies this very nobility (*audārya*): "Acceptance" (*abhyupapatti*) means the undertaking [of protection] by one who seeks to rescue and so forth; "by another" (*pareṇa*) means by an enemy, and not by a teacher, friend, or the like;
"even at the risk of life" (*prāṇātyaye 'pi*) means not merely by following worldly policy, nor by any means of conforming to place, time, and other circumstances.

The surrendering [of the kingdom] was preceded by endurance. And so it was for me alone: having borne a certain king upon my head, he entered within through my vulnerabilities, concealed his true form, and after inflicting incomparable torment, he finally cast me down.

"And since that sprout, being familiar with the nature of insentience, remains here in these stories as if by the decree of fate— I consider that supreme, irresistible brilliance [of yours] is merely being constrained.
Regarding this half-verse beginning with "The *sāttvika* has been mentioned previously," some state that its purpose is the dispelling of doubt.

For this reason, one might suspect why the horripilation and other [physical changes] associated with *sattva* (the quality of goodness) were not mentioned; to preclude that doubt, he says "previously," meaning they have already been defined in the chapter on *bhāvas*. Furthermore, this [verse] is not the word of the Sage (*ārṣa*), because [it would contradict the fact that] drama is established in *sattva*, as stated in the passage: "speech, limbs, and *sattva*."

Since the *sāttvika* general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*) was taught last, and because it was mentioned first [in the list], for that reason it will now be explained in reverse order— that is, in the proper sequence (*ānupūrvaśas*) as it follows logically. Immediately after *sattva*, the body’s general acting will be described.

Through a contrary application, there is the immediate succession of the physical [expression] as "speech, body, and spirit" (*vāgaṅgasattva*). Regarding the passage beginning with "the bodily" (*śārīram*), here the word *ca* has the sense of "because," and the word *api* has the sense of "therefore. In that regard, he states the enumeration: "consisting of six," etc.

The recitation in both Prakrit and Sanskrit, composed of metrical compositions endowed with various sentiments and meanings, and containing words with poetic flourishes (*cūrṇa*), as well as the dramatic representation of sentences, should be understood by the wise. (44)

That bodily expression (*śārīrābhinaya*) which was previously described with its many varieties of diversity consists of six types of intermediate general expressions (*avāntara-sāmānyābhinaya*); thus,

by virtue of possessing these six constituent parts through their connection to intermediate classes, and when combined with the internal (*sāttvika*) and verbal (*vācika*) expressions, it [constitutes the complete form].

The meaning of the word "tu" (but/however) is that when [the elements] have reached a state of succession and are combined, the general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) is accomplished. Regarding the term "vākya" (sentence): the physical representation (*śārīrābhinaya*) associated with a sentence is what is meant by "vākya. For the ancients maintain that those [elements] which bring about completion are not counted among the intermediate stages of the physical representation.

Regarding the term *śārīrasvara* (Nāṭyaśāstra 29.17): since speech is conventionally known as "bodily" (*śārīra*) by way of common usage, it is the very sentence itself—without depending on other modes of representation—that, when it possesses the qualities of good composition and diction, brings about the most vivid cognition of its own meaning; for that very reason, it becomes the means of experiencing rasa and bhāva.

"In that case, that very [speech] is the verbal-gestural representation (*vākyābhinaya*)," according to the *Kāvyakautuka* treatise. However, it must be considered here whether this refers to the general gestural representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) in the form of recitation (*pāṭhya*). If it is argued that it is so because of its entry into the body, then it would follow that it is independent of [the other factors], such as speed (*tvarita*) and so forth. Furthermore, there can be no speech in a poem that is to be represented if it is devoid of gestural representation.

The teacher has presented this as his own view— that there is nothing that exists [as a separate entity] and that there is no linguistic usage of "enactment" (*abhinaya*) regarding words— yet one should not be deluded into thinking that this is his personal position.

Regarding that, he states the definition of the dramatic representation of speech (*vākyābhinaya*): "That which is composed of metrical compositions endowed with various sentiments and meanings, using colloquial words (*cūrṇapada*),
and recited in both Prakrit and Sanskrit, should be known by the wise as the dramatic representation of speech" (22.44).

The meaning of a sentence consists of various specific nuances of rasa; those sentences endowed with such [nuances] may be composed in a poetic meter (*vṛtta*), or consist of prose (*cūrṇapada*), or again, be in the Sanskrit language.

That which is joined with or accompanied by these—namely, the bodily [expression] (*śārīra*) employed together with the sentence—is what is called "bodily representation of the sentence" (*vākyābhinaya*). This applies to the Prakrit language as well.

The compound *saṃskṛta-pāṭha* here is a *bahuvrīhi*; furthermore, this dramatic representation (*vākyābhinaya*) is fourfold, due to the distinction between *saṃskṛta* and *prākṛta*, and between prose and verse.
On this point, some say: "That meaning which always resides in the heart, for that very reason..."
That [sentence-meaning] constantly flashes forth entirely independent of the connection with reflection and so forth;
for when the sentence-meaning or the sentence itself is first indicated by the constituent parts of the substance (sattva), [it manifests].
Subsequently, the gestural representation of speech is designated as *sūcī*. || 45 ||
Just as Bhīmasena’s excessive anger toward the Kuru clan is [expressed] in a statement such as "with arms brandishing...

(*Veṇīsaṃhāra* 1.21), the bodily representation (*śārīro 'bhinaya*) consisting of the knitting of eyebrows and so forth occurs simultaneously with the recitation; however, this is incorrect, because [this is merely] a hint (*sūcā*).

Even when an action proceeds with reference to an object preceded by deliberation, why is the vocal expression (*vākya*) that is bound [to it] not also considered a bodily expression of speech (*śārīra-vākyābhinaya*), since it is accompanied by it? Nevertheless,
because of the connection with the fourfold types of vocal expression, we shall describe the many varieties of *sūcā* and the other [forms of gesture].
Let this suffice for now.

As it has been said: "Whether the sentence-meaning or the sentence itself is first indicated by the limbs of the body, that subsequent dramatic representation of the sentence is designated as *sūcī*. (22.45)

But when the particle *yad* occurs here in the sense of "in which case," then by those sattvic and physical [expressions] (*sāttvikāṅgika*) through which what is yet to be spoken is indicated, there indeed proceeds the indicative representation (*sūcābhinaya*), for the internal performance (*antar-abhinaya*) of those very things is set in motion. For the principle that "meanings are established by one's own intellect" or "the rule [of logic] should prevail" applies there in the case of the highest [characters].
Generally, preceded by intentional reflection, one thinks, "It is thus"; this period of intention is very long,
and it must be understood that for one who is possessed during that time,
there necessarily occurs a physical transformation produced by the entry into such a specific reality.

The gestural representation (*sūcābhinaya*) is likewise simultaneous. In that regard, there are two possible ways: either the subsequent utterance of words follows the very same sequence as the action projected by the intention while remaining stationary; for example, in [the verse] "In the kingdom where the enemy has been conquered, the entire burden has been placed upon a worthy minister" (*Ratnāvalī* 1.9), and so forth. For in that case...

The meaning of each subsequent intermediate sentence is indeed brought forth by the portions expressed in each preceding intermediate sentence; thus, the sequence there is exactly according to the sequence of intention.
However, where the intention is otherwise and the sequence is otherwise, that which distinguishes [the cases] is the absence of division.
The joining of the meaning of a sentence that requires connection [is as follows]: for example, in the *Māyāpuṣpaka*, Sugrīva says:

"Fortresses, land, ministers, servants, friends, wives, body, wealth, pride, and the joy of crushing enemies—what is the use of friendship with one who resembles an immortal? (Or rather, what is the excellence of such friendship?)"

Since all this [world] is devoid of those separated from their beloveds, we who are now powerless [to endure it] are unable— even with mountain fragments of stone that are easily obtained at will— to even construct a path for him.
(170) The gestural representation (*aṅgābhinaya*) residing in the heart is accomplished through skillful means by means of verbal expressions;
the gestural representation of a sprout (*aṅkurābhinaya*), however, is to be understood as produced by the *sūcī* [gesture] arising spontaneously. || 46 ||

For here, it is well known that for Rāma, his body, wife, land, wealth, servants, fortress, and the joy of crushing enemies are all "friends"; thus, this sequence of intended associations is appropriate,
having extended far away from the sequence of referring to proximate words [and being obtained here] by the force of the context.

Alternatively, one may enter [into the meaning] by the method of "let this stand for now, and this too after that," proceeding gradually; nevertheless, it should be understood according to the reverse order, starting with such well-known facts as "Rāma’s friend. Regarding that, it was stated in the first case that the sentence is indicated, for those who know [the subject] consider that sequence is indeed the sentence. One...
In passages such as "navavaca... śabdaḥ kramo yudhyata suhṛdbhiḥ," [the meaning is indicated]. Regarding the second position, it was stated that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is indicated.
However, another says: when one reflects upon it by oneself, then the sentence-meaning is indicated; when [one reflects] with others...

When another's speech is heard—such as in the passage beginning with "O friend, look! (*bho vayassa pekkha*)—and the description of the garden is completed, then the meaning expressed therein is indicated;
subsequently, there will be the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of that speech, such as "Friend, you have observed correctly," and so forth. In that context:

Regarding the term *sūcā* in the context of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), it is said that "the speech is indicated" (*sūcyate*). This is incorrect; for in that case, there is the representation of the sprout of cessation with respect to another's speech, whereas with respect to a future speech, the indication (*sūcā*) is something entirely different. It is this lack of familiarity with the definition of representation that commits the error here, as that which is non-representable is being treated as the object of representation.

What is the point of grasping the meaning of a sentence? Is this meaning something that cannot be accepted [by other means], such that the word "sentence" (*vākya*) would have to be employed again? Therefore, let it be granted that what was indicated here is indeed the meaning of a sentence uttered by another, and not the sentence itself.

This aforementioned fourfold speech— consisting of prose, verse, and the other two varieties— is appropriately sixteenfold when following the indicative representation (*sūcābhinaya*), being eightfold due to the distinctions in the indication of its meaning. It has just been demonstrated that there is no separate structural limb (*aṅga*) for the speech of another.
"The gestural representation (*aṅgābhinaya*) residing in the heart, accomplished through skillful means by means of verbal expressions,
is to be understood as the 'germinal' (*sūcī*) representation, which is produced from its inception like a sprout. Thus,
even when a sentence is directed toward another matter, that underlying object situated in the heart remains its primary focus.

That which is accomplished through bodily movements devoid of speech is *abhinaya* (gesticulation), which is performed by the head, face, shanks, thighs, hands, and feet in their respective order. (p. 171)
The path of seeing the branches is to be understood as the conviction regarding those branches. || 47 ||

That which is called the "Sprout" (*aṅkura*) is equal to a Sūcaka; it is bodily. For example, in the *Sāgarikā*, after saying, "Now I too, having gathered flowers, shall worship Kāmadeva," she demonstrates the gathering of flowers—which was contained within that speech—by means of a change in her limbs. And this "Sprout" is employed only by skillful performers.
It is to be accomplished and brought about by the audience, meditated upon by the mind,

produced through one's own intellectual imagination, and honored [by them]. Although it is the very words of the poet that serve as the basis here, nevertheless, such is the act of gathering flowers by Sāgarikā, which is infused with her good fortune, beauty, love, trepidation, and so forth.
"That ascetic does not possess such [a state] which is distinct from both," and so forth—
all of this is drawn precisely from the words [of the scriptures]; furthermore, although this is obtained from the words in such a clear manner,
it is said that it must be accomplished with skill, as it is accessible only through the excellence of profound reflection (*paryālocanātiśaya*).

Others, however, [hold that] the sprout is similar to the arising-phase of the seed-syllable (*sūcā*), because there is an absence of verbal expression regarding its prior existence; for this [point] has been stated by the word "nirvacana" (etymological explanation), as the meaning is not expressed through a compound.
"That which is performed by the head, face, shanks, thighs, hands, and feet, respectively,
is to be known as *śākhābhinaya*, the path of the demonstration of branches" (22.47). Thus,
*śākhābhinaya* is that which is employed through the entire operation of the *śākhās*, with *vartanā* as its primary element.
By means of a collection of *dvandva* compounds— formed through the singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) of terms such as "head, face, shanks, and thighs"—
and further by means of *dvandva* [compounds] such as "acting" (*nāṭyāyita*) and so forth, and [the terms] "place" (*sthāna*) and so forth;
[this refers to the moment] when a character who has already entered sees another character entering and observes his form.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "nāṭyāyitam" is as follows: even during the time of the entrance, the fixed singing (*dhruvāgāna*), the indication of that [entrance], the circumambulation, and so forth, there is no actual *nāṭya* (dramatic performance);

rather, it is the appropriate ritual gestures (*upacāra*) performed by the previously entered actor at those times which constitute "acting-like-nāṭya. This refers to [the performance] together with the actor who has already entered.

The meaning of the subsequent Āryā is as follows: after having performed a meeting, when one who has entered later finds himself standing silently while the vessel that entered first is engaged in circumambulating and so forth, and remains seated in that very spot, that too is "acting" (*nāṭyāyita*). This is the intended sense.

The venerable Śaṅkuka and others [hold this view], but that is incorrect. For the action of a character up until the point of mutual encounter must either be suitable for indicating the meaning of the speech uttered by another, or it must arise from mere propriety (*aucitya*) even in the absence of explicit words; in the former case, there is the "sprout of cessation" (*nivṛtty-aṅkura*).
In the subsequent [verse], "the sprout"—neither of these two has been treated as a dramatic representation (*nāṭyāyita*).
That which is rendered as a dramatic representation in a play through figurative expressions and by means of indicative gestures is called *nāṭyāyita*. (p. 172)
Due to the length of time, there is a meeting with the introductory sections (praveśakas). || 48 ||

For indeed, those skilled in performance remain in such a state, protecting the subject (*dharmī*) by thinking "he writes," just as one mimes the gathering of flowers. Furthermore, the nature of *sandhāna* (joining/continuity) in performance exists even in the case of speech, stage directions (*sūcā*), and so forth. Nor is it the case that performance is joined by performance.
How can this even be a figurative expression? Therefore, it must be explained in this way:

here, when even a dream is seen as a single reality, and while that very thing is being perceived, another person’s dream is described as having attained the state of waking—such that one says, "This dream was seen by me"—then [the distinction between waking and dreaming is lost].

The conventional usage of "dream" is made in relation to the waking state; since that [dream] is not ultimately real, its status as a dream is merely figurative in relation to it. Thus, the conventional usage of "acting like a dreamer" is observed for that [waking state]. In the same way, here too, while the drama remains a single, unified essence, because of the entry of unreal dramatic representation into that very [unity], [the convention applies] to the dramatic actors.

Among those things that have become social [conventions], that which is other than in relation to them—namely, drama (*nāṭya*)—possesses a real dramatic form; thus it is called "acting" (*nāṭyāyita*). And that is of two kinds: either residing solely in a dramatic form (*rūpaka*) or residing in some other action. Its definition is stated in succession by a pair of *āryā* verses. Regarding drama:

When a connection is made by means of characters who enter as if they were already within the drama—precisely because it has been stated "he enters from there"—that is *nāṭyāyita*. By what means? Through the indications provided by the door of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), which are treated as if they were the ultimate reality through their conventional usages. But is not both of these indeed drama?
Anticipating the objection, "Why does it not constitute a single solid mass?", he says:

because of the cause characterized by the extension of time, and because they exist at mutually distinct times, how could unity of mass be possible therein? This is the sense. The word *yāvat* means [to pervade] either a more extensive continuous series (*prabandha*) or a limited one—indeed, everything.

The meaning is "acted out" (*nāṭyāyita*). Likewise, whether it occurs by the principle of one dream within another dream, and yet another dream within that, or by the process of a single dense dream-continuity, in every way it is "acted out"—that is, it is a dramatic performance. In that regard, for this [dream] which extends over a great duration...
An illustration of "acting" (nāṭyāyita), which is like a dream containing many layers, is the entire performance titled *Vāsavadattā-nāṭyadhārā*, composed by the great poet Subandhu.
For in that work, Bindusāra—the subject matter to be enacted—is made the audience member within the life-story of Udayana; and he too [is Udayana].

Regarding the actions of Vāsavadattā: this matter becomes easily understood when one sees it in its own form as a *sūtra* (dramatic outline); however, for fear of excessive prolixity, it has not been fully displayed here. Nevertheless, one section is cited; for there, when Udayana is made the subject for the audience, the stage direction (*sūtradhāra-prayoga*) says: "By your virtuous deeds, he is victorious"—from that point, where does Udayana [come from]?
My well-composed treatise on dramaturgy declares (p.
"The enactment of stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as joy, sorrow, anger, and the like, which is performed [on stage], is called *abhinaya*."
That too, which is performed through the application of the aesthetic flavors (rasa) of the emotions (bhāva), should be known as dramatic representation (nāṭyāyita). || 49 ||
"Come, mother! What is the use of those guards, Kaṭaka and Piṅgala? I too am Udayana, who ought to be cherished by my children.
Yaugandharāyaṇa, bring the princess to me! Alas, Harṣarakṣita, you have lost your power!"

Right there, Bindusāra, having become a member of the assembly and considering [the matter] from the perspective of ultimate truth, sighs, "Blessed indeed are such outpourings of devotion! The female doorkeeper, to herself: "Ah!
Behold how the King is filled with sentiments that do not perceive the ultimate truth," and so forth.
An example of *nāṭyāyita* that is limited in scope and devoid of the *garbha* juncture is found in the *Sītā-svayaṃvara* within the *Garbha* act of the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*.
Thus, *nāṭyāyita*, which is subordinate to the dramatic forms (*nāṭyarūpaka*), has been explained.

However, that which is intent upon another action is now described. Here, when there is absorption in another sentiment (*rasa*), then the enactment of the *dhruvā* song—being brought into a state of equality with itself—is conceived as assuming a mutually unified form through a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*).
As, for example: "By the tears [falling] from the lotus petals... (*nalinīdala-aṇīsahasa-sukadehiṃ*)... [and so forth].
Thus she flies away, departs, breaks free, and vanishes; like a female swan in a lotus grove, she cannot be captured.
In such cases, the intention of the performer is indeed: "I shall demonstrate the *dhruvā* through gesture.

However, regarding the *prāsādikyadhruvā* being sung, it is because of the statement: "That which is not expressed by the poetry (or sentence), that the song shall embellish" (*a* 32). For in that context, the performance consists of an appropriate striking of the meaning of the *dhruvā*.

"He enacts the state of love. Being thus of the nature of a sprout, it occurs exactly as such through the force of reflecting upon the sequence of what precedes and follows; thus, even though not formally employed, the *dhruvā*—by chance (*kākatālīya*)—being applied in a subtle form, governs the drama as if it were the drama itself.
Thus, he demonstrates that *nāṭyāyita* is a physical expression (*śārīrābhinaya*) that brings about the state of acting (*nāṭyāyitatva*), stating:

"It is the expression performed during the *dhruvā* songs at the appropriate moment. Those who are "joined with" or "possessed by" the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and the stable aesthetic moods (*rasa*) through their own permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are those whose minds are solely intent on its accomplishment.

The performers perform that which is the dramatic representation (abhinaya) concerning the meaning of the *dhruvā* verses—this is what is done. How? It means that when the occasion arises, it occurs by way of chance (*kākatālīya-vaśāt*). As for the physical representation (*śārīra-abhinaya*), it is called "acting" (*nāṭyāyita*). Now, does this mean one must represent every single word? No; he says "by means of joy and so forth."

The meaning is: by means of the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*) and the vital essence (*sattva*) that indicate that [state]. "That too" means not only what was previously mentioned, but even this as well.

When another person joins a statement spoken by someone else through suggestive gesture (*sūcābhinaya*), how can that [gesture] become the "sprout of withdrawal" (*nivṛttyaṅkura*) for the sake of its connection? (50)
For these, however, the path should be endowed with the essence of the actual state of things (*yathābhāva-rasa*).
Where another person’s spoken word is joined by another through suggestive acting (*sūcābhinaya*), that which expresses the meaning connected thereto is the "Sprout of Cessation" (*nivṛtty-aṅkura*).

Anticipating the question of how a statement spoken by one person can be indicated through the performance of another by means of the sequence of limbs, minor limbs, and the internal state (*sattva*) which reveals mental activity, he states the reason:
"by telling its connection. Just as a sprout indicates the cessation of the seed and so forth, so too, when [the cause] has ceased...

In this passage, the "sprout of cessation" (*nivṛtty-aṅkura*) is mentioned. For instance, when the Vidūṣaka asks the Vatsarāja, "Does it bring pleasure to your eyes?", Sāgarikā replies, "Truly, I am situated between life and death. Thereupon the King says: "How can it be called 'pleasing' when, with difficulty, one passes between the pair of her thighs?"

He recites the verse beginning with *suciraṃ* (Ratnāvalī 2.10). As that is being heard in sequence, there is observed in Sāgarikā a movement of the limbs and sub-limbs of the *sattva* [sentiment], joined with the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) produced by the arising of doubt, longing, and passion as they truly are; this is the sprout of the *nivṛtti* [subsidence]. (The sprout of subsidence.)

And the *nāṭyāyita* is seen at every step in the *Vāsavadattā-nāṭya*. Since these [gestures] exist collectively through all modes of representation (*abhinaya*) and are generally present in every representable subject, they constitute "general representation" (*sāmānyābhinaya*); and it is for this very purpose that their nature has been described here in detail.
As was previously stated: "Its branches, its dance, and likewise its sprout—
this threefold entity is abhinaya..."

Thus, it has been established that there is no contradiction between this [system] and the *upāṅgābhinaya* (subsidiary limb expression); this should be understood from that very source. What is the use of repeating it here?
Having thus established the general *āṅgika* (bodily) expression, he now establishes the *vācaka* (verbal) expression: "But of these..."
The meaning is that "it would be the path" refers to the object. Even though the self is indeed devoid of an object when there is an absence of sentences—
therefore, those who consider these [beings] to be like sprouts or actors in a drama belonging to various branches of scripture, and who maintain that they are devoid of sentences— [it is not so].
(175) That which is indicated among the subjects of poetry consists of twelve types of dramatic representation (abhinaya). || 51 ||
Ālāpa, pralāpa, and likewise vilāpa;
then anulāpa, saṃlāpa, and similarly apalāpa. || 52 ||
Sandeśa, atideśa, and likewise another called nirdeśa;
upadeśa, apadeśa, and vyapadeśa are thus proclaimed. (53)
Speech that consists of addressing someone is known as *ālāpa*;
whereas speech that is devoid of meaning is proclaimed to be *pralāpa*. (54)

Those who restrict [the rule] "of all" (*sarveṣām*) and so forth to the scope of merely the first sprout of the indication of a sentence are not knowers of reality; for every dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), in the absence of subsistence upon the sentence and due to the lack of a cause for restriction, falls into inconsistency. Only...

Let the sentence indeed be split merely on the basis of whether [the action] belongs to that time or not that time; this has been explained at length in the *Upāṅgābhinaya*. Regarding the phrase "in poetic subjects," it refers to the twelve types among the varieties of the ten dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*) which consist of abhinaya (acting).

The meaning is that *bhāva* refers to the verbal representation (*vācikābhinaya*). He enumerates the twelve types with the words "and conversation" (*ālāpaśca*) and so forth, and defines them in their respective order with the words "but conversation is... (*ābhāṣaṇaṃ tu*) and so forth.
The meaning is that *ālāpa* is speech concerning the object of the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*), devoid of instruction and the like.
"You shine while worshipping the god whose banner is the sea-monster" (*Ratnāvalī* 1), or "May you be victorious," and so forth.

That speech which is devoid of meaning is called *pralāpa* (incoherent babble); the sense is that it consists of words connected to one another [only] by virtue of ignorance and the like. As Śakāra says in the *Daridracārudatta*: "I hear..."

I smell the fragrance of garlands; however, with my nose filled with darkness, I do not see the sound of ornaments very clearly. (I hear the fragrance of garlands; moreover, with my nose filled with darkness, I do not perceive the sound of ornaments clearly.)
That lamentation which arises from compassion is proclaimed as such;
a statement repeated many times is known as *anulāpa*. (55)
A dialogue joined by speech and reply is celebrated as *saṃlāpa*;
indeed, speaking otherwise than what was previously stated is recorded as *apalāpa* (denial). || 56 ||
"Speak these words"—this is called a *saṃdeśa* (message).
"That which was spoken by you has been spoken by me"—this is known as an *atideśa* (extended application). || 57 ||

That which arises from *karuṇa* (compassion/pity) is called *vilāpa* (lamentation). The mention of *karuṇa* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *duḥkha* (suffering); by this, *vipralambha* (separation) is also included. In that regard, speech connected with the *karuṇa-rasa* [in the context of] suffering is as follows; in the context of *vipralambha*, it is as follows: *(Mṛcchakaṭika, Act ?)* "Where are you? Give me an answer! [End of excerpt]

"The arrows of the fivefold Mind-born [god]... (*Ratnāvalī* 3.3), and so forth. It will be stated that lamentation (*vilāpa*), which is a particular state of love (*kāmāvasthā*) primarily consisting of this [sorrow], is the sixth state among them.
That which has been frequently uttered is called "repetition" (*anulāpa*). For the sake of restatement, that very same thing [is repeated].

The meaning is "being spoken again. For example, when the *sūtradhāra* says, "Even from another island" (*Ratnāvalī* 1.6), Yaugandharāyaṇa in the *nepathya* repeats, "So it is; even from another island. This is called *saṃlāpa*, which consists of a combination of speech and response.

What kind of examples are there? Concealment (*apalāpa*) is also the speaking otherwise of what was previously stated. For example, in the *Kṛtyārāvaṇa*, Śūrpaṇakhā—disguised in the form of Gautamī and desiring to make Lakṣmaṇa hear Rāma’s lamentation—first says: "Have you heard? Then Sītā...
(With agitation)—Ah! What is this? Then she said:
"O, let Sītā truly think that I am Gautamī; for thus did she say to me:
'Is this not heard by you?'—this is the message: 'Speak these words. [She speaks] by way of illustration."
The definition [of *sandeśa*] is to be inferred. Following that, *sandeśa* (a message) is the delivery of one's own words to another through the medium of another's mouth.

*Atideśa*, however, as stated by you, means "what was said by you is appropriate; what has been said by me is likewise"; its meaning is the application of the status of the established to the unestablished. In this context, regarding the domain of poetry (*sāhitya*), there is a distinction between *upadeśa* (instruction), *atideśa* (extended application), and *upamāna* (analogy).
The specific exposition regarding the logicians and Mīmāṃsakas which was composed by the commentators (p.
177) is designated as the "indication" (*nirdeśa*) in the form of "this very I speak."
In this context, "vyapadeśa" is said to be the telling [of something] by means of a pretext. || 58 ||
The instruction "Do this, having grasped this" is proclaimed as *upadeśa* (instruction). That which is a statement for another purpose is proclaimed as *apadeśa* (pretext). || 59 ||
These paths should be understood as those that employ all forms of dramatic representation;
furthermore, I shall describe their characteristics according to seven types. (60)
Direct (pratyakṣa), indirect (parokṣa), and likewise that which is produced by time (kālakṛta)—these are the three;
those residing in oneself (ātmastha) and those residing in another (parastha)—thus there are exactly seven types.

That [example], being delicate and captivating to the mind, is merely a futile wandering; since it serves no purpose here in the context at hand, it should indeed be disregarded. The definition is: "This very person am I" is an indication (*nirdeśa*).
"Speaking by means of another pretext" (*vyājāntareṇa kathanam*) means *vyapadeśa*; that is to say, by means of a specific pretext. For example:
In the *Mudrārākṣasa*, for the purpose of neutralizing Rākṣasa, the monk was first banished from the city;

there, Cāṇakya made a statement under a pretext: "This wicked man (Jīvasiddhi) has caused Parvateśvara to be killed by means of a poison-maiden employed by Rākṣasa; therefore, he is being banished. This...

"Kuru" means "do," while "gṛhāṇa" means "take"; thus, *apadeśa* signifies an injunction (*niyoga*). *Anyārthakathana* (speaking for another purpose) means that one speaks of something other than what one actually intends to say;

that is, speaking of another matter. For example, Sahadeva says to Bhīma: "This is the message sent by my elder brother regarding Suyodhana" (*Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Act 1). He concludes: "These, then, are the paths."
The meaning is "in all six types of physical [acting]. Likewise, they are called *abhinayas* because they are "enacted" (*abhinīyante*);

these are specific types of poetry such as dramas (*nāṭaka*). Since they exist in a general sense within those [dramas], the intended meaning is that they are therefore "general enactments" (*sāmānyābhinaya*).
when I say 'I do not speak' and 'I am speaking,' that speech would be both perceptible and imperceptible, as well as present. (62)
"I act, I go, I speak your word;
abiding in the self and present, he is indeed considered to be directly perceived. (63)
The speech "I shall do," "I shall go," or "I shall speak"—whether referring to oneself or another, and whether concerning the present or the future—is all merely so. (64)
All the hosts of enemies have been slain, conquered, and broken by me; that which was hidden within oneself and that which was beyond perception is remembered as the time of the event.
"He who says in the performance of a drama, 'They were killed by you' or 'They were conquered by you,' while being out of sight, situated elsewhere, and likewise referring to a time past; (66)"
When one says such words as "he speaks," "he acts," or "he goes," that [agent] would likewise be situated elsewhere, existing in the present, and directly perceived. (67)
Then, he states other varieties of this very [subject] beginning with "residing in oneself and residing in another," etc.
Here, he provides the direction for examples beginning with "I am doing," etc.
The statement "he goes" or "he acts," as it has been cited, would refer to something residing elsewhere, existing in the present, and indeed beyond the senses. (68)
The speech that says "they will do," "they will go," or "they will speak," concerns another person, a future time, and is indeed beyond direct perception. (69)
Whatever one says in the performance of drama while placing the hand inside [the mouth] is considered to be "located within oneself," "located in the heart," and indeed "out of sight. (70)
Due to the specific differences among others, oneself, and time, the divisions of these very seven types should be understood as manifold. (71)

Now, he demonstrates how even that which resides within oneself can be remote due to a difference in the scope of the audience, beginning with the words "having placed his hand inside," and so forth. In the case of *svagata*, *janāntika*, and *apavārita* [speech], although it resides within the speaker, it is not perceived by other characters due to the conventions of dramatic performance (*nāṭyadharma*); thus, even though it is within oneself, it is remote.
Even that which is worldly (*lokadharmya*) may be situated within oneself yet remain imperceptible (*parokṣa*), as in: "I indeed prattled while asleep or intoxicated.

As it has been said regarding even the highest objects, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] occurs due to mental distraction and so forth. [The author] states the possibility of other distinctions through their effects:
Through the distinctions of others, of oneself, and of time,
the divisions of this very sevenfold [classification] should be understood as manifold.
These applications should be understood as being joined with the performance of the Path;
when perfected within these, manifold dramatic representation (abhinaya) arises.

In this context, speech is first divided into twelve types; therein, those residing within oneself and those residing in another are each further divided into four kinds by way of being perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) or imperceptible (*parokṣa*).
These applications are to be understood as being employed in the dramatic representation of the path;
through these, various forms of abhinaya (acting) are perfected here. || 72 ||
However, that division of action which is equal across the head, hands, waist, breasts, shanks, and thighs is called *sāmānyābhinaya* (generalized gesture). || 73 ||

It should be enacted by those skilled in drama, who are endowed with aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and emotional states (bhāva), through graceful movements of the hands as well as soft gestures of the limbs. (74)

When multiplied by the three times, there are twelve varieties. Even regarding the past and the future, their status as objects of perception does not occur from the perspective of yogic perception and the like. Thus, when those twelve are multiplied by those same [twelve], there are one hundred and forty-four. As for what was stated regarding their threefold nature through the distinction between the refined (*saṃskṛta*) and the other:
By that multiplication, there are nine hundred and fifty-two varieties of the *vākyābhina*.

Because the *sūcā* possesses a twofold nature due to the distinction between the sentence and its meaning, there are one thousand eight hundred and four varieties of the *sūcā*. The varieties of the *aṅkura* are exactly equal to those of the *vākya*.
The distinctions of the *sūcā* (gestures) are to be multiplied by those [differences], and by those again the distinctions of the *śākhā* (branching movements);

furthermore, by those the distinctions of the two types of *nāṭyāyita* (stylized acting), and by those the distinctions of the *nivṛtti-aṅkura* (emergent movements). Thus, there come to be many hundreds of millions [of variations].
It is not, however, as stated by the venerable Śaṅkuka—that there are forty thousand [variations] and so forth.

Thus, this "generalized enactment" (*sāmānyābhinaya*), which is characterized by being distinguished yet enacted in a general manner, and which is joined with all enactments combined as the common ground of all enactments— this [is the basis] for that [unity] which serves as the foundation for unification and produces a state resembling a circle of fire (*alātacakra*).
(181) It is free from agitation and confusion, with bodily movements that are not overdone;
its nature is regulated by the measures of tempo, rhythm, and the beat. || 75 ||
When a dramatic performance consists of well-articulated phrasing and speech that is neither harsh nor cacophonous,
it should be known as internal (ābhyantara).

This very same [performance], when inverted, characterized by movements performed according to one's own whim, and consisting of unstructured song and instrumental music, is known as external drama (bāhya-nāṭya). || 77 ||
For that which is within the characteristics [of the teaching] is held to be internal;
whereas that which is outside the scripture is said to be external. (78)
Since by this both the performance and the action are characterized, therefore this indeed is the defining characteristic employed in this drama. (79)
In order to demonstrate the predominance of general gestural action (*sāmānyābhinayakriyā*), he says:

"not haughty, not agitated," and so forth. By the word "unperforated" (*anāviddha*), he indicates the generality pertaining to the physical (*aṅgika*) [aspect]. Showing that its absence constitutes a defect, he proceeds by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
He states the necessity of necessarily adopting the general gesture (*sāmānyābhinaya*) with the words "this very [gesture], when reversed," and so forth.
He explains "internal" (*ābhyantara*) himself by saying "because it is internal to the definition.

Now, one might object that since its definition is "endowed with vocal and physical gestures" (*vāgaṅgābhinayopeta*), it also possesses an external aspect; anticipating this doubt, he says "by this..."
The intended meaning is that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) consists precisely of the form of the general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*), because [the object] is characterized (*lakṣyate*) by it.
Regarding the term "employed" (*saṃprayojita*): first, the individual actions pertaining to the subject matter of drama (*nāṭya*) must be brought into a state of unification;
furthermore, the collection of actions that has attained that state of unification must also be brought into a state of unification. This is the point.

By means of the words "action" (*karma*) and "application" (*prayoga*), he expresses the term *nāṭya* through the locative case: "Without this [nāṭya], those who have not dwelt with a teacher and those who are excluded from the scriptures [cannot manifest it clearly]. (p. 182)
But they employ external means because they do not understand the ritual actions of the teacher.
The wise man should represent sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell, as well as the sense organs and their objects, through the various emotional states (bhāvas). || 81 ||
Having cast a sidelong glance and likewise tilted the head to the side,
the wise man should indicate sound by placing the index finger at the region of the ear.

The very nature of drama becomes directly experienced and determined as being vitalized by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). However, regarding the absence of proficiency [in this regard], he states "those who have not lived with a teacher," and so forth, because such proficiency is lacking in those such as the son of Bhaṭṭa who have not studied.

Now, he describes the general gesture (*sāmānyābhinaya*), which consists of the combined nature of representation, beginning with the words "sound, touch," and so forth. Regarding the term *indriya* (sense organ), there is the impossibility of its being qualified by terms such as "touch" [which refer to specific objects];
rather, it refers to the immersion in the apprehension of one's own object and the immersion in being graspable by one's own instrument for all the sense organs.

And for this very reason, the commonality of the enactment (*abhinaya*) with respect to these two types of meaning is demonstrated through the presentation of the objects (*viṣaya*). By the word "bhāvaiḥ" (by means of emotional states), the meaning is "by means of specific actions. He states these [actions] as: "having turned the gaze askance," and so forth.
By virtue of this respect, the entire burden reaches the region of the ear; as it has been said:
"For indeed, the functioning of the remaining senses has entered into these [ears] in its entirety, just like the eye" (Raghuvamśa 7.12).
By the use of the word "and" (ca), he states that the ear as well, being intent upon the apprehension of sound, becomes manifested by this [process];
the same applies to what follows.
Having slightly contracted the eyes and even raised the eyebrows,
as well as by touching the cheeks, one should indicate the act of touching.
Having placed the two flags (patākās) upon the head and slightly moving the face,
the wise performer should represent your form with a steady gaze.
Having slightly contracted the eyes and expanded the nostrils, one should indicate the scents of liquor and meat with a single exhalation. (85)
For these are the manifestations of the five sense-objects, belonging indeed to the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and likewise to the nose. (86)
For the sense objects become perceivers only when accompanied by the mind;
indeed, one without a mind does not know anything of the fivefold objects that have come [to the senses]. || 87 ||
The wise should understand that the state of the mind (*manas*) is threefold in dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).

He summarizes this with the words "of the five objects of the senses," and so forth. Since the objects of the senses are accompanied by the mind, just as sound is perceived in the ear through the act of grasping sound and the other [objects], so too is the mind.
Because it effects its presiding through the sequence of presiding over those [senses], this too constitutes a general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*).

As it has been said: "The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark (*liṅga*) of the mind.
