According to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the threefold state of the mind consists of that which arises from the conjunction of the mind with the self, characterized by desire, aversion, and neutrality (*mādhyasthya*).
That state of the mind is said to be threefold:
indeed, it is the desirable, the undesirable, and likewise the neutral. (88)
One should provide an indication of the desired [result] by the warming of the limbs, the bristling of the hair, and the blossoming of the face. (89)
When a desirable sound, form, touch, smell, or taste is encountered by the senses or the mind, one should manifest a cheerful countenance as a sign of appreciation.
By turning the head away, by pulling at the eyes and nose,
and by not allowing the gaze to be directed [toward the subject], one should indeed indicate that which is undesirable.
Neither with a mind of excessive joy nor with extreme loathing,
but with a perfectly neutral disposition, one should point out the intermediate direction.
In the Sāṃkhya view of Vindhyavāsin, however, it is the mind (*manas*) itself; whereas in the system of Īśvarakṛṣṇa, by the word "mind" (*manaḥ*), it is here the intellect (*buddhi*).

Expressions such as "by means of the body, [there is] delight" (*prahlādana*) and so forth should be illustrated as actions of grasping objects directed toward a desired object. For this reason also, its status as a general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) is to be understood.

He clarifies this very point with the words "when the sound is perceived" (*dṛṣṭe śabde*) and so forth. "A pleasant face" (*sumukhatva*) means a countenance endowed with serenity and other such qualities. "Drawings out" (*vikarṣaṇa*) and "contractions" (*saṅkocana*): by using the plural, he shows that there is no interruption of expansion in order to achieve the grasping [of the sound] in the middle.
"This belongs to him," "this is his," or "he does this"—
that which is a representation of something out of sight is known as the *madhyastha* (intermediary). || 93 ||
That object which is experienced by oneself is known as "situated in the self" (ātmastha);
whereas that which consists of the description of another's experience is designated as "situated in another" (parastha). || 94 ||
Generally, the accomplishment of all things is held to proceed from desire; and that [desire], endowed with the quality of will, is conceptualized in many ways. (95)

Now, he demonstrates the possibility of the previously mentioned method in this very context with the words "Therefore, this... and so forth. In the phrase "what was to be done has been done," there is both pastness and futurity. [If it were as you claim,] objects such as pleasure and the like would be inherent in the self, and thus all of them would reside within the self; for color and other qualities are inherent in something else [namely, the substance].
Anticipating the objection that [the object] must always be situated elsewhere, it is said: "That object which is experienced by the self (ātman).
Due to the proximity of the word *para* (other), the word *ātman* here refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the locus of the sense of "I.
That object which causes one to experience that self is "situated in the self" (*ātmastha*). Form and other such qualities are likewise [to be understood in this way].
If [the feelings] exist, how is it that pleasure and so forth belonging to others are not situated in the self? And if they are not so, how are they situated in the self?

Now, he establishes that the practice of desire (*kāmopacāra*) is a general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*), stating: "For the most part, of all states of being... "From desire" means from longing. Even if something occurs for one who lacks desire, that too—

And [this occurs] due to the predominance of past karma. The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāya*) in the phrase "preceded by karma" is for the sake of pervasion; the meaning is that its accomplishment arises from desire alone.
Now, what is this so-called "desire"? He says: "And that is desire," and it does not arise from mere desire alone.

He says that the "accomplishment of the effect" [occurs] when [the will] is perfected—that is, assisted—by its quality, namely the effort toward the effect, together with the activity of the effect and so forth; thus it is the performer of all effects. Now, one might object: "If the will is indeed only one, how can it produce multiple effects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is conceived in many ways," meaning that there are numerous [manifestations of] will.
As much as he recites, beginning with "one who desires the Dharma" and so forth:
186) "One who desires the Dharma, one who desires wealth, and likewise one who desires liberation."
But the union of a woman and a man is traditionally known as desire (kāma). || 96 ||
For indeed, for the entire world, desire is seen to be the primary means of warding off pleasure and pain; it provides happiness even in the midst of calamities.
That union of man and woman which brings about sexual enjoyment should be known as the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra); it is auspicious when produced through metaphorical treatment. || 98 ||

Dharma, desire (*kāma*), wealth (*artha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). Among these, desire is defined as longing; it occurs with respect to pleasure or the means to achieve it. In that regard, neither dharma nor wealth possesses the nature of pleasure in themselves, nor do they directly constitute the means to pleasure. For it is through dharma that the means to pleasure—such as access to the Apsarases and so forth—is acquired.

The same should be understood regarding the object [of desire]: although liberation, characterized by ultimate rest in supreme bliss and independent of external means, is indeed of the nature of happiness, nevertheless, because it is difficult to attain, the hearts of people are not deluded by it. But as for the union of man and woman—

Since it is the direct means of happiness, it alone is the object of desire; thus, by the word *kāma* used without qualification, that [happiness] itself is denoted. And by that, every object is colored [with desirability], as it has been said: "Even the mere name 'woman' is delightful" (*Kāmandakīyanītisāra* 4.52). Nevertheless, even when an object is touched by that [desire], it becomes transcendent for the world.
Through a resonance with the heart, a work attains the state of being heart-stirring without even effort. For example:

"O lover, do not treat as a 'khaṇḍitā' that woman who, like a love-messenger on a night darkened by the clouds of delusion, is full of passion, intoxicated with pride, and whose mind is turned toward you out of affection."

With this very intention, even the secret meaning has been composed by me within the secret [treatises] (primarily through the *mukhyā* function); for it is for this purpose alone that the employment of the *kaiśikī* style has been presented with care. Therefore, come... because the general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) of the practice of love (*kāmopacāra*) is more extensively pervasive, that very [representation] is [the focus].

Regarding the statement, "He demonstrates the union of woman and man," since even the mere desire therein for pleasure is produced through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), he says that one effects enjoyment characterized by desire.
This world almost always desires happiness above all else;
yet women are the root of happiness, and they, moreover, possess diverse characters. (99)
Of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and birds;
of piśācas, yakṣas, and vyālas; and of men, monkeys, and elephants. || 100 ||
Women are said to possess characteristics similar to those of deer, fish, camels, crocodiles, donkeys, pigs, horses, buffaloes, goats, wild oxen, and the like. 101.

Courtship (*upacāra*) is complete with activities appropriate for capturing each other's hearts. And here, if the character is of the highest type (*uttama-prakṛti*), then, according to the perspective stated in the chapter on *rasas*, it is called the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). This very point is reinforced by the statement: "This world almost always desires happiness at all times."

"Mostly" (*bhūyiṣṭham*) means more than what is already obtained; for this very reason, people are not satisfied anywhere except through the attainment of supreme bliss. "At all times" (*sarvadā*): even the absence of suffering is desired solely for the sake of happiness, for one desires the cessation of all suffering so that one may eat as much as one wishes and enjoy whatever is desired with happiness.

One might enjoy a beautiful woman; even a pearl necklace is discarded solely for the sake of attaining the pleasure produced by the touch of soft, cool breezes. For this very reason, those who know the secret of emptiness do not favor this liberation accepted by Kaṇāda, Sugata, and others, among the discerning.
In this regard, it has been shown that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of non-activity; so, enough with further elaboration.

It was stated that [this is] "done by way of metaphorical designation" (*upacāra*); therein, in order to understand that metaphorical designation, he shows the disposition (*āśaya*) of women, because appropriate metaphorical designation is preceded by the grasping of their disposition, [stating] "they have various characters" (*nānāśīlāḥ*). *Śīla* means *sattva* (nature/temperament).

Consciousness (*caitanya*), volition (*buddhipūrvaka*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and inclination (*hevāka*) are synonyms. By means of the passage beginning with "gods and demons" (*devadānava*), he defines those dispositions (*śīla*) according to their enumeration. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), he indicates that there are other dispositions as well.
With smooth limbs and graceful secondary features, steady and with slow, blinking eyes, free from disease and endowed with radiance, she is possessed of generosity, courage, and uprightness. (102)
One who perspires little, is moderate in passion, eats sparingly, is fond of sexual union, delights in perfumes and flowers, and is charming is known as a woman of divine nature (devaśīlā). || 103 ||
Delighting in unrighteousness and deceit, she is stubborn, prone to anger, and exceedingly harsh;
she is constantly fond of wine and meat, irascible, and excessively proud. (104)
Fickle, excessively greedy, harsh, and fond of quarreling;
envious by nature, unstable in affection, and having resorted to a demonic character. || 105 ||

Devoted to play, she has beautiful eyes; her nails and teeth are like well-blossomed flowers; she possesses lovely limbs, speaks with steadiness, has few children, and is fond of sexual pleasure. (106)

Delighting in song, instrumental music, and dance, she is joyful and well-groomed. "Samaratā" means neither too soft nor too sharp in voice; "svaṅgī" means one whose limbs are beautifully proportioned and well-set.
Gandharva beings are to be recognized by their smooth skin, hair, and eyes. || 107 ||
She has large and elongated limbs, wide red eyes, coarse hair, is addicted to sleeping during the day, and speaks in an excessively loud voice. (108)
Inflicting wounds with her claws and teeth, fond of anger, envy, and quarreling, and habitually roaming at night, she has adopted the nature of a rākṣasī. || 109 ||
She has a sharp nose-tip and teeth, a slender body, and copper-colored eyes;
she is the color of a blue lotus, prone to sleep, and exceedingly irascible.
A woman of the animal class is known to have unstable undertakings, heavy breathing, and excessive pride; she is devoted to perfumes, garlands, and liquor, and possesses the nature of a serpent. 111.
She is utterly distinct, possessing a sharp character, fond of rivers, devoted to wine, spirits, milk, and ghee, having many offspring, and loving fruits. (112)
She is constantly breathing, likewise fond of gardens and groves;
she is fickle, talkative, and swift, having resorted to the nature of a bird.
In which [vagina] the mouth is turned back, wide, and directed inward; she who moves about in a *niṣkuṭa*—that is, a domestic garden (*gṛhārāma*).
(Niṣkuṭa, p. 190)
With hands having deficient or extra fingers, wandering at night in the garden, habitually terrifying children, malicious, and speaking with affliction. || 114 ||
One who is of foul conduct, hairy-limbed, and loud-voiced, possessing the nature of a Piśāca, should be known as one fond of liquor, meat, and sacrificial offerings. 115.
She has limbs that perspire easily during sleep, she is fond of stable beds and seats, she is wise and intelligent, and she is fond of the scent of wine and meat. (116)
She experiences joy upon seeing those who have been long absent, and out of gratitude she does not sleep for long; such is remembered as the character of a Yakṣa woman. (117)

She who regards honor and dishonor as equal, whose skin is rough and whose voice is harsh, who speaks deceitful, false, and arrogant words, who is like a venomous serpent in nature, and who has reddish-brown eyes. 118.
She is always delighted by uprightness, skillful, endowed with the quality of patience, well-proportioned in limb, grateful, and fond of her gurus, gods, and brahmins. (119)

For she is devoted to the Dharma, sensual pleasure, and wealth, and is free from egoism; she is one who practices that conduct. "Of reprehensible conduct" means she is fond of sexual intercourse and the like. "Intelligent" [refers to her as follows]:
She was beloved by her friends, possessed of excellent character, and had taken recourse to a human form. || 120 ||
She has a compact and small body, is joyful, possesses reddish-brown hair, and is fond of deceit;
she is bold, fickle, sharp-tongued, and delights in trees, gardens, and forests.
She who always regards even the slightest service as great,
who is forceful and fond of pleasure, and who has resorted to the nature of a monkey— 122.
She has large jaws and a broad forehead, possesses a well-developed body,
has tawny eyes and hairy limbs, and is fond of perfumes, garlands, and intoxicants.
They are irascible, firm-minded, and fond of water, gardens, and forests;
they delight in sweet things and are proclaimed to have the nature of elephants. || 124 ||
She has a very small belly, a broken nose, and slender shanks;
she is like a cuckoo, with moving, wide eyes, fickle, and swift-moving. || 125 ||
One who is constantly fearful during the day, who delights in songs and instrumental music, and whose mind is unsettled in its dwelling, is proclaimed to have the nature of a deer. (126)
*Pratibhā* is the intellect characterized by the non-forgetting of everything without exception. *Prasahya* means having assailed the lover; that is the meaning. *Nivāsa* (p.
She has a long, stout, and elevated chest; she is restless and does not blink excessively;
she has many servants and many sons, possesses the nature of a fish, and is fond of water.
She has long lips, perspires profusely, and walks with a somewhat awkward gait;
she has a slender waist and is fond of flowers, fruits, salt, sour, and pungent flavors. (128)
With her waist and sides hanging down, speaking with a harsh and cruel voice, possessing an excessively high waist and neck, having the nature of a camel, she is fond of the wilderness. (129)
With a thick head, a curved neck, a gaping mouth, and a great roar, she should be known as having the nature of a crocodile; she is cruel and endowed with the qualities of a fish.
She has a thick tongue, lips, and teeth; her skin is rough and she speaks harshly;
she engages in amorous combat, is audacious, and delights in being scratched with nails and bitten with teeth. (131)
One who hates her co-wife, is clever, fickle, and quick-moving, is said to be diseased, to have many offspring, and to possess a harsh nature. (132)
She has a long back, belly, and face; her limbs are hairy and she is endowed with strength;
her forehead is very narrow, and she is fond of bulbs, roots, and fruits. (133)

Thus ends the section on the "Palace" and so forth. (Regarding *ratiyuddhakārī*: It is like a battle during sexual union. (Regarding *nakhā*: She who is characterized by the marks of nails and teeth; her face is fierce with fangs, and she has a short belly and hair. (p.
193) Her mouth is formidable with its tusks, and her abdomen and locks of hair are short.
One of base conduct who has many offspring takes on the nature of a pig. || 134 ||
She is steady, with well-proportioned sides, thighs, hips, back, head, and neck; she is fortunate, generous by nature, and possesses straight, thick hair. (135)
Lean, with a fickle mind, smooth-voiced yet swift-moving, and devoted to lust and anger—such is the woman who possesses the nature of a horse. (136)
With a thick back, eyes, and teeth; with slender sides and belly; firm;
covered with tawny body hair; fierce; hated by the world; yet fond of pleasure. (137)
With her face slightly upturned, fond of water-sports and forest groves,
possessing a broad forehead and beautiful hips, she has taken on the nature of a buffalo.
She is emaciated, with thin arms and chest, her eyes fixed and motionless; her hands and feet are drawn in, and she is covered with fine body hair. ||139||
A woman of goat-like nature is known to be fearful by character, agitated by water, having many offspring, fond of the forest, fickle, swift in movement, and lacking in constant strength.
He himself performs [the act] and considers it highly within himself. (Regarding "saṃkṣiptapāṇi"): *saṃkṣipta* means limited or measured.
With her limbs and eyes hanging down, she was intent on yawning;
she had a long and narrow face, and was adorned with very small hands and feet.
Loud-voiced, having little sleep, prone to anger, fond of good deeds, lacking in proper conduct, yet grateful—she is proclaimed to have the character of a dog. (142)
She has broad, full, and elevated hips, slender calves, and is beloved by her friends;
she has small hands and feet, is firm in her undertakings, and is devoted to the welfare of her subjects. (143)
Devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, truthful, pure, and fond of her gurus; steadfast, enduring hardship, and possessing the very nature of cows. (144)

Women are to be known as having various dispositions, each depending upon her own innate nature; having discerned them according to their respective natures, one should then attend to them accordingly. 145.
A gesture of courtesy, according to one's disposition, brings joy to women even if it is slight;
however, even a great one, if performed otherwise [inappropriately], will not produce satisfaction at all. (146)

Just as joy arises from obtaining what was prayed for, [the author] speaks of the utility of ethical conduct and knowledge, saying "and having understood [them], one should serve according to the capacity of beings. He states the purpose of service in accordance with the capacity of beings, saying "service according to the capacity of beings. And this being so, it is precisely this [that follows].
He states the distinction by saying, "even the Great One otherwise. "The Great One" means the Full One. "Otherwise" means not according to its true nature.
195) And the ritual application is prescribed for the sake of sexual union between a woman and a man. || 147 ||
For ascetic practice is for the sake of Dharma, and Dharma is desired for the sake of happiness;
women are the root of happiness, and enjoyment with them is desired. || 148 ||
The enjoyment of desire is declared in the dramatic theory (nāṭyadharma) to be twofold:
external and internal, pertaining respectively to women and men. || 149 ||
That [character] who is internal to kings should be employed in a *nāṭaka*; whereas that which is external or arrived from abroad should appear in a *prakaraṇa*. (150)
In this regard, I shall explain in due order the royal enjoyments, as well as the proper rules of conduct arising from the Kāma-tantra. 151.

"The nature of women is threefold, arising from various types of beings; why has this lack of proficiency regarding other human goals not been established?"—this [objection] is addressed by the passage beginning with "For the sake of dharma," which demonstrates the authority of the Vedas and so forth. Now, the application of this general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) to the present context is as follows:

He shows that the enjoyment of desires is of two kinds. "(In the dramatic convention)" means in the dramatic technique, that is, in the plot. "Internal" (*ābhyantara*) means occurring within the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). "In the *nāṭaka*" means also in the *nāṭikā*. "In successive order" refers to [what will be stated] by the Sage in the forthcoming text.

The threefold classification of women; the heroine’s attainment of desire in the service of the king; gestures; the perception of what is desired; the stages of love; the conduct of lovers in separation; the dispatching of a female messenger; the message; the consideration of means for union;
[the friend of the maiden]; and secret love-making.
It is indeed external, internal, and yet another that is both external and internal. (152)
Women of noble birth are to be known as internal; courtesans are remembered as external.
But that woman who has performed purification is remembered as both external and internal. (153)
In the service within the inner apartments, however, there may be women born of noble families or even maidens;
for in the royal service, the enjoyment of external women is not desired. (154)
He should be an intimate of the king and of the people outside;
for there is an association between kings and celestial women. (155)
That which is desired by a woman of noble birth should be understood to apply to maidens as well;
and even a courtesan here is exactly like a woman of noble birth. (156)
In this world, the arising of desire originates from various conditions; it occurs among women or men, and is of superior, inferior, or middling degree. (157)

The meaning is "in this sequence," beginning with "enjoyment in the inner apartments" (*antaḥpurabhoga*) and "residence" (*nivāsaka*). Enjoyment in the drama belongs specifically to the inner circle of kings, and not to kings alone. *Veśa* is the place of courtesans; those who belong there are *veśyās*. Regarding the term *kṛtaśaucā*: purity (*śauca*) has been performed.
She whose pure character is strictly confined [to one man] is a *punarbhavā* (a remarried woman), yet she is also a *veśyā* (courtesan);

the term *kanyā* refers to a courtesan who is also a maiden. Indeed, regarding the enjoyment of external women during royal service, he states an exception by saying "divine courtesan" (*divyaveśyā*) and so forth, as in the case of Urvaśī for Purūravas.
(197) From hearing, from seeing, from their forms, from the movements of their limbs and playful gestures,
and from their sweet conversations, desire arises. (158)
Upon seeing a distinguished man endowed with physical beauty, virtues, and the like, possessed of artistic skills and knowledge, and in the prime of youth, a woman becomes afflicted by passion. (159)
Then, one who is knowledgeable in this matter should observe the gestures indicative of desire among men and women who are longing for one another. (160)

Regarding the statement "the practice of desire," it is asked how desire arises therein; he replies with the word "from hearing" (*śravaṇāt*), which is to be supplied in every case. [Desire arises] from hearing of Sītā for Rāvaṇa, and from seeing Śakuntalā for Duṣyanta.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to a representation such as a painting; from that, [desire arises] for the Lord of Vatsa, even though his physical appearance has not been seen.
Desire arises from a gesture characterized by the play of a finger,
or it occurs through the restoration of lost passion, as in the case of King Udayana [the Lord of Vatsa] when the *abhisārikā-bandhitaka* (the "deceiver" or "trick") was composed by Viśākhadeva.
The non-recurrence of desire is declared to result from playful activities such as assuming the guise of Padmāvatī, Bhaṭṭa, or Śabarī; the same should be understood regarding sweet speech as well.
Sweetness consists both in its essential nature and by way of its meaning. By the use of the word "and" (ca), he indicates other causes as well.

Just as in the *Tāpasavatsarājacarita*, the arising of desire for Padmāvatī in the King of Vatsa is the cause [of his actions], and this is called "extreme devotion. Thus it is said: "Fixing his mind upon me, he has worn matted hair."
"She did not consider her own kin, nor her fresh youth;
thinking 'by following me,' she, full of affection, seems to wish to draw me back from my resolve. (4.8)
(198) The *lalitā*, the *calapakṣmā*, as well as the *mukulekṣaṇā*, and the *srastottarapuṭā*— these are the desirable gazes in this context. (161)
(With its corners turned and manifested by gestures consistent with grace, that gaze of women during a side-long look is called *lalitā*. 162.
In this [state], the color of the face becomes such that the cheeks are slightly reddened, variegated with drops of perspiration, and the hair stands on end while quivering. (163)
By means of intentional distortions of the limbs, side-long glances, as well as by the touch of ornaments and even by scratching the ears; 164.
By scratching with the tips of the thumbs, by showing the breasts and the navel, by pricking with the fingernails, and even by binding the hair; 165.
One should recognize a courtesan afflicted by passion through such signs as these; now I shall likewise describe the gestures of a woman of noble birth.
She seems to laugh with her eyes and gazes intently; she smiles secretly and speaks while looking down. (167)
A woman of noble family smiles first, speaks softly, conceals her signs of perspiration, bites her lower lip, and is startled. (168)
Thus, with such signs of passion, she who has not yet attained the festival of sexual union should display the ten states of love through various emotional expressions. || 169 ||
In the first stage there is longing; in the second, reflection occurs;
in the third, there is recollection; and in the fourth, the glorification of qualities. (170)
Agitation is declared in the fifth [stage], and lamentation is said to be in the sixth;
madness is to be known in the seventh, and likewise disease occurs in the eighth.
In the ninth [stage] there is indeed dullness, and in the tenth death occurs.

"The state of desire" (*kāmabhāva*) refers to the mental function called desire; the meaning is that the bodily distortions are the gestures produced by that [desire]. However, these distortions do not manifest when the festival of sexual union has been attained—that is, when enjoyment has already been achieved. When...
But desire (kāma) arises from that [separation] and so forth; the state of having attained enjoyment (*prāptasaṃbhogatā*) is simply the emergence of the states of desire.

Thus, even when there is separation (*vipralambha*) despite having attained enjoyment, these very states occur when the power of flowers, trees, and so forth is reached during the enjoyment of those filled with desire. And so it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Tauta:
The state of desire (*kāmāvasthā*) is not itself the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); rather, it is in some cases a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that sentiment.
This means that even when the enjoyment has already been attained, it serves as a constituent of the erotic sentiment;

for indeed, even in the case of those who have not yet attained enjoyment, the erotic sentiment is demonstrated in the Chapter on Rasas (*rasādhyāya*) through the examples of Sāgarikā and King Vatsarāja.
He explains that desire, which consists of longing, undergoes such stages in succession, beginning with the words "In the first, however, there is longing," and so forth. (p.
This is the rule for women and men; now learn their defining characteristics as well.
That which is initiated by determination, arising from intention and desire, and accomplished through the means of union—that is proclaimed as *abhilāṣa* (longing). || 173 ||
She repeatedly emerges and enters, and she assumes the very form of Love;
she stands within the range of vision, established in the foremost place of desire.
"By what means may he be attained, and how might he become mine?"—thus she should express her anxiety through the gestures communicated by the female messenger. (175)

In the second [act], however, there should be side-long glances with half-closed eyes, the touching of bracelets and waist-bands, and the contact of the hands with the knot of the garment and the navel. (176)
Certain *vyabhicārin* (transitory mental states) themselves are characterized here [in this context] as stages of love (*kāmāvasthā*) due to their connection with other defining features.

From "determination" (*vyavasāya*) follows the knowledge of the beloved person; from that comes desire preceded by a resolve for them; from that comes its "arising," which is its intensification. Thus, there is reflection upon the means of union and upon the object itself.
The second stage of the self is the "instrument" (*karaṇa*), because he will say: "By what means is it attained?

Thus, he says "it goes out and it enters," and so forth, referring to the activity of speech and the like, which is appropriate for the sound [of the mantra] accompanied by the first stage of reflection, as well as its association with other [stages]. This is the form of *madana*.
The meaning is that one should look at that specific feature—such as the eyes or other parts—by which the path of vision is prepared, or else one should be seen by means of it.

"By the states made known by the female messengers" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) meaning even by those imagined by oneself. "Ākekarām" refers to a sidelong glance that is both flickering and steady.
(201) Repeated sighing, the contemplation of mental desires,
and aversion toward other activities— these are declared to be the signs of recollection (anusmṛti). || 177 ||

Neither on a seat nor on a bed does one find composure, being distracted by one's own task due to being preoccupied with that [object]. Because of this state of being overcome by such thoughts, one should apply oneself to the third [meditation] in this manner.
"Through the grace of his limbs and minor members, and through his speech, gestures, smiles, and glances, there is no other like him"—this would be the praise of his qualities (guṇakīrtana). (179)

In the fourth [act], however, there is the employment of dramatic representation through the praising of virtues, sighing, the wiping away of tears and sweat, and the confidential conversations regarding the messenger and the state of separation.
She finds no satisfaction in sitting or lying down, nor does she remain still;
she is constantly restless, having taken her place in a state of agitation. (181)
One should express that very state through the exhaustion of anxious sighs, by the simulation of a burning heart,
and by the simulation of extreme agitation.

"Staying here, sitting here, and having arrived here by me"—the term *vihasta* means "incapable. The compound [refers to] the messenger's lack of separation [from the beloved]. The state known as agitation (*udvega*) is a particular condition; the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of agitation has been shown under the heading of despondency (*nirveda*). Weeping, sighing, and so forth belong to the preceding stage.
He shows that she becomes one who descends from the north with the words "distressed" (udvignā);
thus, one should employ lamentation through various kinds of wailing. || 183 ||
Exceedingly agitated by longing and lack of fortitude, she wanders here and there, lamenting and resorting to places for her wailing. (184)
For even when engaged in discourse concerning that [object], a man feels aversion toward other things in every situation; this is proclaimed as *unmāda* (insanity). 185.
Standing with unblinking eyes, sighing deeply, and falling into meditation; weeping during the time for recreation—this would be dancing in a state of madness. (186)
After conciliation, gifts, shared enjoyment of wealth, and even desirable commands have all been rejected, illness subsequently arises. (187)

"She becomes one who laments while yet alive" means that she does so even in every state, even in the presence of her elders; by this, he makes clear the nature of her madness. "At times of recreation" means she weeps during times suitable for play.
"Dancing" implies that this is not the kind of dancing described for those who are insane, such as with pieces of cloth, shards, or broken bowls; rather, it is the intended meaning.

When desire, which consists of the fluctuations of the mind, reaches such an extreme as madness, even the body undergoes a transformation; thus he says: "Afterwards, [there is] disease caused by all [desires] having been rejected. (p. 203) "Rejected" means...
The heart becomes bewildered, a sharp pain arises somewhere in the head, and one finds no steadiness; thus one should employ the eighth [day]. 188.
When questioned, she says nothing; she neither hears nor sees.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Woe!", she remains silent, having lost her memory through a state of stupor. (189)
In the representation of stupor (*jaḍatā*), there should be an involuntary utterance of "huṃ," as well as slackened limbs and a face overcome by labored breathing. (190)
If, despite all the remedies employed, union does not occur, then death arises for her who is set ablaze by the fire of desire. || 191 ||
Thus, having carefully examined the system of desire (kāmatantra), these positions should be employed;
however, one should avoid those that do not lead to the attainment of the desired object, with the exception of the final one.
In this same way, a person should employ these various forms of desire through diverse emotional states arising from deception. || 193 ||

"By those that have become fruitless. The reason for her fainting is that "her heart does not remain steady. "Alas, what misery!"—this means that apart from this [lamentation], she speaks nothing else, remaining silent. "By remedies" means by means of ways to bring about union. "Naidhanam" means death. "Of various forms" refers to the [different] states.
This is the meaning. (p.
204) Thus, for women or even for men who desire in this manner...
A wise person should employ the dramatic representation by means of the application of common qualities. || 194 ||
By the distress of anxious sighs, by the simulation of a burning heart, by following after her, and likewise by gazing at the path; || 195 ||
Also from gazing at the sky, as well as from speaking with a dejected tone; from touching and crushing, as well as from taking refuge in that which provides a basis for harm. || 196 ||
With these [means], which arise from various bases and originate from deception, one should employ all the objects of desire to the greatest extent possible. || 197 ||
Burning with the fire of desire, he resorts to garlands, ornaments, perfumes, houses, and groves as cooling remedies. (198)
Burning with desire, afflicted by many conditions, and tormented in various ways,
he should, out of passion, send a female messenger who can reveal his own state.
And he should deliver a message for the messenger that is centered on love.

With the intention that, because men are easier means [for union], a meeting can be accomplished even at an intermediate stage— whereas this is not so for women— the stages of passion (kāmāvasthā) are taught with reference to women and then extended by analogy to men.
That which was stated by the words "garlands, ornaments, perfumes," and so forth, should be applied as appropriate for remaining in that state. (p. 205) Secret desire.
She should explain her situation with discipline, saying, "This is my current condition. (200)
Then, having understood the state of her feelings, he should consider the means for sexual union;
this procedure should be performed by those who know the rules when the desire is secret. (201)
I shall again explain in truth the procedure for royal service, which pertains to those within the inner circle and arises from the science of love (kāmatantra). 202.
Whatever states, whether productive of happiness or suffering, arise from various moral conducts that a king performs, those very same things the world follows.
Qualities that carry out the commands of kings for the sake of women are not difficult to find; however, it is desire arising from courtesy that truly brings about pleasure. (204)
The meaning is that [the king] is being withheld from other heroines out of great respect for the queens and out of fear of those who are dear to him.
Now, one might ask: "What is impossible for kings that they would undergo the exertion of sending messengers and so forth? To this he says: "No."

"Difficult for kings to obtain," and so forth. "Means" (*upāyāḥ*) refers to qualities that carry out commands; the sense is that they are derived from "approaching" (*upa*), meaning "by way of example" or "through enticement. The genitive case in "means of kings" (*rājñām upāyāḥ*) is a genitive of relationship; therefore, there is a prohibition regarding [their use] for the sake of military force. The phrase "out of courtesy" (*dākṣiṇyāt*) applies to both [types of heroines], as well as to former mistresses.

"Courtesy" refers to the courtesy shown by a desirable woman; the meaning is that her love is directed toward the king. To the question "Why is it concealed?", he says: "by great respect," using the genitive case in the sense of the object.
For queens who have received consecration must necessarily be treated with great distinction by the king.
(206) A secret desire of the king toward his retinue [should be conveyed]. (205)
Although kings possess many methods for the pursuit of pleasure, that which is practiced in secret is indeed what brings true delight. (206)
That which consists of attachment to what is forbidden, that from which one is turned away, and the rarity of finding a noble woman—that is the supreme delight of desire. (207)
For the people of the royal harem, enjoyment during the day is prescribed;
and whatever arrangement for their dwelling there may be, that is declared to take place at night. (208)

They are to be honored as such. "In many ways" means by way of being married, kept as a concubine, and so forth. Regarding "being intent upon women," those who know the nature of passion say that desire is easily offended;
for if an object of longing has already been attained, what further longing could there be? Therefore, [the mind] is directed toward what has been attained.

This desire, increasing through a continuous succession—whereby what was obtained seems as if stolen away, and what has passed seems as if it were obtained again—spreads the highest pleasure. For here, cessation is not the goal, as it is in the case of scratching an itch;
rather, the goal is pleasure consisting of enjoyment. Thus, because it is the cause of *rati* (pleasure), the meaning is that *kāma* is *rati*.

Now, he describes the clearly intended [sexual union] as "the enjoyment by kings among the women of the harem during the day. Enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) consists of mutual gazing, amorous quarrels, musical performances, and so forth, as it has been said: "The day was spent gazing at the moon of her face. Here, "women of the harem" refers to married wives, remarried women, and secluded courtesans.
The secret love of a maiden or a female servant has already been described. Now he speaks of the conduct regarding the bedchamber of one who has many previous wives:
"In turn, for the sake of fruit, or with a new wife, or even at the time of childbirth..."

In sequence, for the sake of the fruit, at the onset of a new pregnancy, or during childbirth; likewise, in times of suffering and in times of joy—these six are known as the [proper] occasions for visiting. (209)
Kings should approach women in their proper dwelling, whether during their fertile period or not; they should likewise approach those who are disliked as well as those who are beloved. (210)
"In suffering and indeed in joy, these six are known as the periods of residence" (Nāṭyaśāstra 22.209).
Thus, the sequence follows the intended order; her "turn" may be for one day, two days, and so forth.
He states the exception to that rule with the words "for the sake of fruit," meaning during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). "Nine" refers to when nine [periods] have passed since the birth.

She is distressed by long separation; she should be comforted, for she is grieving due to the calamity of her relative’s death. "Delight" (*pramoda*) refers to festivals such as those celebrating her son's birth, for such festivals are indeed worthy of honor.
"Dwelling" (*vāsa*) means staying overnight in that place; the amorous attentions appropriate for the night are for the sake of the fruit [of union].

For this reason, in order to demonstrate that [the king] must avoid all forms of partiality and to establish that even those who are disliked or unfortunate must be attended to in due order by a king who acts according to dharma, he says:
"By kings, in a suitable dwelling, or even during the women's fertile period..."
"Furthermore, one should approach those who are either disliked or desired.
For even though the period of menstruation (*ārtava*) is long, it becomes limited in terms of its fruitfulness. As it has been said:
"The fertile period (*ṛtu*) consists of sixteen days; among these, the first four and the tenth day are to be avoided."
The thirteenth day and odd-numbered days are censurable for the birth of a girl;
the sixth, eighth, and tenth days are superior for both castes; and an even-numbered night is for the birth of a son. Thus it is said.
In that regard, there is the woman prepared for a tryst (*vāsakasajjā*), or the one longing in separation (*utkaṇṭhitā*),
or the one who has her husband under her control (*svādhīnabhartṛkā*), or the one separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*). (211)
The abandoned woman, the deceived woman, likewise the woman whose husband is away, and the woman going to meet her lover—these eight heroines are to be known. (212)
She who, longing for sexual enjoyment, joyfully adorns herself in her appointed dwelling is indeed the *vāsakasajjikā*. (213)
She whose beloved does not come due to being occupied with various affairs is afflicted by the suffering of his non-arrival; she is indeed one who longs in separation. 214.

Even in that case where the hero is bound by the excesses of love at her side, there too one must avoid certain specific constellations. Furthermore, for kings, a son is the primary fruit, as it is said:
"For householders, offspring is the goal" (Raghuvamśa 1.7). On this point, however, the elders say: "The cattle... [or "the beasts"]... say:

O dear son, one may approach at will a woman who has recently given birth, one who is six months pregnant, one who has had a fever for a single day, or a beloved wife who has just emerged from the dye-vat. (Nāṭyaśāstra 59)

"Be one who desires! (This is that which is prohibited in the Smṛti and in medical treatises. Here, [the author] shows the different types of heroines characterized by the presence or absence of the state of being "ready for the tryst" (*vāsakasajjā*), beginning with the words "at the appropriate time for the tryst" (*ucite vāsake*). "Appropriate" means arrived according to the method previously described.

She who is longing (*lālasā*), full of desire (*sābhilāṣā*), possessing her own longing (*svābhilāṣā*), and having attained the quality of intense joy (*sāndrāmodaguṇaprāptā*), becomes one whose husband is under her control (*svādhīnabhartṛkā*). || 215 ||
When a lover does not return after departing due to jealousy or a quarrel, she, having fallen under the sway of resentment, becomes a woman separated by a quarrel (kalahāntaritā). || 216 ||
She whose beloved has not come to the appointed dwelling due to some distraction, and who is afflicted by the pain of his non-arrival, is celebrated as the *khaṇḍitā*. || 217 ||
She whose lover has sent a messenger or even given a rendezvous but has not arrived here for some reason, she indeed becomes deceived. (218)
When a husband has gone abroad for various affairs, his wife whose husband is away should keep her hair and the ends of her locks grown long. 219.
But she who, casting aside shame, being embraced by intoxication and passion,
goes to meet her beloved, she shall be known as an *abhisārikā*.

The quality of fragrance is joy (*harṣa*) and pride in one’s own good fortune. "From attachment" (*vyāsaṅgāt*) means from the object of another woman. Her locks of hair (*alakāḥ*) and the mass of her braided hair (*kabarībhāraḥ*) have grown long and become pendulous. Others [explain it as] she whose [hair] has grown into a single braid.

They describe the emergence of hair on the forehead and the crown of the head as being due to the performance of [ascetic] rites; "intoxication" refers to that caused by wine. By the use of the word "and" (ca), he indicates the predominance of the god of love alone over these two.
An "abhisāra" is a companion; through his activity, she goes beyond her lover—that is, she acts upon him or describes him.

Therefore, because it transcends the nature of the elements (*dhātu-rūpa*), there is the lengthening [of the vowel] in the word *sṛṣṭeḥ*. In these states, the heroine who is the basis of the drama is easily discernible.
And I shall explain for them the various methods of the science of love in many ways.
Through sighs of anxiety and weariness, through the simulation of a burning heart, through conversations with her friends, and by observing her own physical state; || 222 ||
By means of exhaustion, dejection, and the shedding of tears, by the onset of anger, by being devoid of ornaments, by being unkempt, and by weeping out of sorrow. (223)
One who has been rejected, one who has been deceived, one separated by a quarrel, and likewise one whose lover is away— these women should employ these emotional states.
But she whose husband is under her own control should be depicted with variegated and radiant attire, her face illuminated with joy, and possessing exalted beauty.

States such as "being angry" or "being pacified," however, are not mentioned here among the varieties of heroines (*nāyikā*), because they do not exist in the absence of a dwelling place (*vāsaka*). "Based on drama" (*nāṭkāśrayāḥ*) means having drama (*nāṭya*) as their subject matter.
In that context, the life of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) exists within *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment).

He first demonstrates the basis for the distinctions among heroines cultivated through the absence of a dwelling place by means of the verse beginning with "by anxiety, sighs, and perspiration. Since this is a representation within the general practice of love-service—which is common to all and resonates with the hearts of everyone—it is also a "general representation" (sāmānyābhinaya). [The phrase] "these emotional states" (bhāvān etān) refers to this.
Those states which are appropriate to the expressed emotions (*anubhāva*), the latent emotions (*vyabhicārin*),
and the permanent emotions (*sthāyin*)— even though the collection of expressed emotions is not explicitly mentioned here— it demonstrates them all,

up to the point where the woman adorned for her tryst (*vāsakasajjā*) and the woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*) are equal to the woman who has her husband under her control (*svādhīnabhartṛkā*) at their respective occasions.
They are not mentioned separately [in the verse]:
"By the users of courtesans, women of good family, and female servants... (p. 211).
By means of these specific dispositions, the act of approaching [the beloved] should be performed. || 226 ||
Modest, with gentle gestures, and surrounded by her attendants, the courtesan, her limbs adorned with various ornaments, should proceed slowly. (227)
A woman of noble family should walk with her limbs drawn together, timid, with her face cast down, and veiled by a head-covering. (228)
With speech faltering from intoxication, eyes wide and rolling,
and her movements and gait agitated, the female messenger should proceed with haughtiness.
When she has gone there and sees her beloved asleep,
she should then awaken him with this following procedure.
A woman of noble birth should awaken [her husband] with ornaments; a courtesan with cool perfumes; and a servant girl with garments and fans. (231)

Now he describes the nature of the *abhisāraṇa* (the going to meet), beginning with the words "of the courtesan" (*veśyāyāḥ*) and so forth. "By means of particular states of being" (*bhāvaviśeṣaiḥ*) means by means of particular objects (*vastuviśeṣaiḥ*). "Conversation" (*saṃlāpaḥ*) is the exchange of speech between the female messenger (*dūtī*) and the female companion (*sakhī*).
(Regarding the word "ornament" [*alaṅkāreṇa*]: the term "ornament" refers specifically to such items as anklets and the like.)
(212) This rule concerning the locus of love has not been stated as applying exclusively to women of noble family,
because a drama must be experienced by [characters] in all their various conditions. (232)
When she is engaged in new amorous desires or is angry at the time of union,
he should bring about the rendezvous through pretexts and various stratagems.
Filled with joy, he should enjoy various ornaments, garments, perfumes, and garlands, as well as food and drink prepared and served by his beloved. 234.

Now, one might object: "Since the conduct of kings involving courtesans and the like is crowded with concealment and the resulting misfortunes, what is the purpose of showing this here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For a drama (*nāṭaka*)—that is to say, a theatrical performance (*nāṭya*)—is that in which every state (*sarvāvasthā*) is to be experienced (*anubhāvya*), meaning it must be led toward a state of being perceived as if it were directly present."

In the *Daśarūpaka* (Chapter 18), it is stated that even sexual union with a courtesan occurs at the beginning of a *prakaraṇa*. If, then, every mode [of love] is to be demonstrated in a *nāṭaka*, then since the "manifest mode" (*prakaṭaprakāra*) has been described in the context of a tryst (*vāsaka*), the "deceptive mode" (*vyājaprakāra*) must likewise be mentioned; with this intention, he says: "of her who has newly engaged in love. Regarding "newly":
When a courtesan who has begun to frequent a man’s company,

or a remarried woman (*punarbhu*), or a maiden to be wed by the *gāndharva* rite intends to have union with him, she does not openly accept his advances, even when he employs various pretexts; for such is the nature of the "appointed day" (*vāsaka*) and its deceptive artifice.

Furthermore, the hero becomes instantly apprehensive of other heroines. Even if she is one who has been confined (*avaruddhā*), one whose lover has been unfaithful (*khaṇḍitā*), or one separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*), she is made to accept the chamber under some pretext.
In that regard, he describes the hero's formal courtesy (*upacāra*) as a means for his cleverness (*vidagdhatā*) in winning over the heroine's heart:
"Adorned with various ornaments," and so forth; (p.
213) a human being does not exist in that way.
One under the sway of passion who does not obtain a beloved woman becomes twice as joyful when he is united with his dear one. || 235 ||
Endowed with the qualities of expanding the sweetness of grace, gestures, speech, and playfulness,
[he was moved] by their mutual glances of love.
But a union brought about by desire should indeed be performed. || 236 ||
Then, when passion has been aroused by the various attentions, the heroine should prepare her chamber for the arrival of the hero. (237)
One might object: "If a young woman has been obtained, then one's desire for her should cease; so what is this excessive display of courtesy?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is not so. *Madana* means born of desire (*kāma*), thus it is desire itself. He cites the root *mad*, meaning "to exhilarate" or "to soften"; therefore, in union, desire is redoubled, and consequently, there is this display of courtesy.

Regarding where [these] are appropriate, he says: "the states of *vilāsa*," and so forth. *Vilāsa* has been explained as [pertaining to] women in the passage beginning with "of standing, sitting, and walking" (22.15), such as "the steady-moving glance of a woman" (22.35). For men, however, these are primarily their emotional dispositions (*bhāva*) and gestures (*ceṣṭita*). *Iṅgita* refers to those [gestures] that indicate love.
The ritual procedure has been explained [in the passage] beginning with "by means of a desired modification of the limbs" (p. 214) and ending with "she should become startled.
Then, having taken perfumes, garlands, as well as aromatic powders and garments—
One should take up a mirror at will, or again and again, as a play.
In the practice of dressing, there should not be an excessive taking up of ornaments;
rather, those consisting primarily of girdles and anklets, which are resonant with sound, are praised.
There is no wearing of fine garments on the stage, nor bathing, nor anointing with unguents;
likewise, there is no application of collyrium, no body-paste, and no binding of the hair.
Neither uncovered, nor wearing but a single garment, nor when her lower lip is devoid of red dye— no woman, whether of high or middling rank, should ever perform [this] at any time.
This entire rule always applies to those of inferior [status].

The "play of speech" (*vākyalīlā*) has been described in relation to the limbs, the attainments (*sādhya*), and so forth; likewise, sweetness (*mādhurya*) exists in all particular states, as stated in [the verses] beginning with "and for men, through the practice of the organs" (22.36). By means of the quality of expansion (*vistāra*) of these [elements]:
The origin of this [word] is properly derived from the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) made in the description of a poet (*kavi*). *Cūrṇa* means powdered scent (*paṭavāsa*);

*vāsa* means clothing (*vastra*). It is said "not excessively" because it would cause distress. Furthermore, for the poor, who see their sleeping quarters devoid of lamps due to being invisible at night, its quality of sounding [on impact] serves as a cause [for their recognition].
Since, in this cause, by means of a praiseworthy sound suitable for the play of sexual union,
one might encounter another motive, one should not act even because of that. (242)
In the drama, female servants and others, as well as women or even men, must perform the act of taking ornaments and likewise the act of taking flowers. (243)
Having applied her ornaments, she should await the arrival of her beloved;
she should assume a playful, adorned attire that is not inconsistent with her character. (244)
The heroine should prepare the chamber according to the prescribed rite upon the arrival of the hero;
then, while awaiting him, she should give the signal by the sound of a *nālikā*.
This is correct. By the statement beginning with "not taking up garments on the stage," he provides a prohibition as a corollary.

However, for the sake of establishing the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of clothing, this [prohibition] should be applied even on the stage as being useful for that metaphorical treatment; for such is the possibility according to the *Kopa-sambhavanā*.
Thus, although there is a general statement regarding "not taking up garments," because of the specific method [of the *uttamā* heroine], [the rule applies].
"And of the middling [woman]," this is understood. "And of the low [woman], this occurs even with respect to her limb.

Having thus stated the prohibition regarding the low [women] and then again the injunction, he intends the very practice under discussion, beginning with "the taking of ornaments," and so forth. He shows his regard for this previously mentioned practice.
"One should prepare the chamber according to rule" means one should perform the customary services appropriate for the chamber.
216) But having heard the sound of the water-clock, she becomes anxious at the prospect of the hero's arrival.
Dejected and trembling, she should go to the very gateway. || 246 ||
Holding the archway with her left hand and the door-panel with her right,
she should stand leaning against the archway and wait for the hero.
Resorting to the archway, the woman might feel doubt, anxiety, and even fear;
not seeing her lover, she would become despondent for a moment. (248)
Sighing deeply and shedding tears from his eyes, and making his heart heavy, he should release his body upon the seat. (249)
She should also deliberate regarding the arrival of the hero through various means of inquiry arising from both auspicious and inauspicious circumstances. (250)
Is my beloved perhaps occupied with duties for his guru, or with friends, or with counsel regarding state affairs, or even attended upon by his beloved wife? (251)
Now, one might ask: "If the lover has not arrived when the appointed time for the rendezvous has ended, what should she do? To this, he says: "Waiting... [and so on].

He further says, "She should announce the sound of the *nālikā*," implying that such a period of time has already passed; thinking, "Why has he not arrived?"—lest he fail to come—he prescribes this rule even for the case where he has not yet arrived, saying: "But having heard the sound of the *nālikā*... and so forth.
One should also point out portents arising from both auspicious and inauspicious causes,
by means of signs residing within oneself, such as throbbing and pulsation. (252)
In auspicious matters, the omen on the left side of a woman is favorable;
however, in all undesirable matters, the omen on the right side shall be so.
If the left eye, the forehead, the eyebrows, the nose, and likewise the lips,
as well as the thighs, arms, and breasts should throb, there will be a meeting.
If these undergo a change, one should declare it to be an ill omen;
upon seeing such an ill omen, one should then fall into a moment of confusion.
In the absence of a leader, the hand should be placed upon the cheek;
furthermore, one should display disdain for ornaments and act out weeping. (256)
Now, if that omen should be auspicious regarding the arrival of the hero, the heroine should indicate his proximity by means of perceiving the scent. (257)
Regarding what was stated as "by those various means of deliberation," that is the illustration therein. He states the future means with the words "by a heavy task," and so forth.

The group of consequent emotions (*anubhāva*), however, arises from transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as envy, exhaustion, and reflection on matters, according to their respective application.
It should be applied. An *utpāta* is a sudden, inauspicious vibration of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Having seen it, she should rise up and, being delighted, go forth to meet [the guest] according to the prescribed rule.
Then, with eyes blossoming with great joy, she should gaze upon her beloved.
Placing her hand upon her friend’s shoulder and assuming a wide stance,
she should then show her lover his mark— a fresh wound.
If he has indeed committed an offense through various such actions, then the hero should be reproached with words that express censure. (260)
The utterance of words by women arises from pride, contempt, and delusion, as well as from concealment and advances; it is brought about by jealousy. (261)
In confidence, affection, and passion; likewise in doubt, intimacy, and satisfaction; as well as in rivalry, courtesy, censure, and amorous playfulness. (262)
And that [movement] resides in another. "Trembling" (*sphurita*), "moving" (*calana*), and "throbbing" (*spandita*)—these are stated with distinction as being located in one's own body.

Regarding "the eye" and so forth, it should be understood that "left" means the left [eye]; likewise, "the arms" refers to a change in state when there is throbbing on the right side. "She would go out to meet him" should be construed with the nominative case as referring to the heroine (*nāyikā*).

Thus, by this much, the general mode of performance (*sāmānyābhinaya*), consisting of a mixture of speech, physical gestures, and internal disposition (*sattva*), has been shown up to the point of attaining the beloved through the *vāsakasajjā* (the woman who adorns herself for her lover). Now, the [behaviors] of the *khaṇḍitā* (the woman whose lover has been unfaithful) and others are to be demonstrated:

"If he should have offended," and so forth, through various means such as indignation (*māna*), dissimulation (*avahittha*), the tearing of garments (*vastrabhaṅga*), weeping (*abhiṣyanda*), and the like.

Regarding the expression of anger due to speaking otherwise than what is appropriate, he states the refutation of that [charge] beginning with "visrambha" (confidence), etc., concerning a certain matter to be determined, which is characterized by confidence.
In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma; in secret speech;
in jest, curiosity, agitation, and likewise in times of calamity; || 263 ||
Whether the anger between a man and a woman was caused by one or the other, or whether it was mutual,
even if he is normally not to be spoken to, he should nevertheless be addressed as a beloved for these reasons.
Wherever there is affection, there arises jealousy born of passion;
understand now as they are being described its four origins. || 265 ||
Dejection, offense, unpleasantness, and resentment—of these, I shall now describe the characteristics in their proper order. (266)

Affection (*sneha*) is the concern shown by one who observes another’s physical infirmity and so forth during inquiries after their welfare; the passion (*anurāga*) characterized by its influence is the doubt as to whether an offense has been committed, whether it is real or not; endearment (*praṇaya*) is the request;

satisfaction (*paritoṣa*) is the prosperity of offspring and so forth; and the persistence of arts (*kalāsthiti*, i.e., proficiency in crafts and the like) is [manifested] through the aspect of guile (*nikṛti*).

When rivalry or competition must be instigated by the lover on behalf of her circle of friends or companions, she should observe courtesy regarding the subject of the dispute over their interests; she should display wonder at feats such as magic illusions;
and she must certainly manifest delight in matters conducive to virtue, wealth, and pleasure, such as religious vows, household duties, the *kaumudī* festival, and joyful celebrations.

Regarding that which ought to be done but is unpleasant, there is "remembrance" (*smaraṇa*); or, by way of reproach, there is "inquiry" (*smaraṇa*) as to what he might say. When a hero asks something with great earnestness, that is "curiosity" (*kutūhala*). When everyone laughs, that is "laughter" (*hāsya*). A portent such as fire and the like is "distress" (*saṃbhrama*).

Vasubandhu [states that] misfortune such as separation and so forth would indeed result from not speaking to them in this way; otherwise, there would be a total lack of affection. Regarding the phrase "caused by anger," the meaning is "simultaneously.
Having stated "one who has offended," he begins to demonstrate that offense with the words "wherein affection... and so on.

There are four sources and causes [of displeasure]: dejection (*vaimanasya*), offense (*vyalīka*), unpleasantness (*vipriya*), and resentment (*manyu*). He defines them in sequence with the verse beginning "with a gait languid from sleep and fatigue" (*nidrākhedālasagatim*) and so forth, [referring to] sleep during sexual union (*surate*).
Seeing her beloved in such a state—with a gait sluggish from the exhaustion of sleep, bearing visible marks, and covered in fresh wounds—a woman will experience dejection of mind. (267)

One should act out [the scene] as follows: with eyes narrowed in envy toward sleep, her limbs trembling with rage, she should express herself with words such as "Excellent! and "Very well!", saying, "It is beautiful. (268)
Even though she is restrained in many ways, if she is seen looking at that very person, a feeling of resentment arises in the woman there due to rivalry and envy. (269)
Placing the left hand upon the chest and likewise shaking the right hand,
while supporting oneself on the feet, one should perform the gesture for feigned anger.
"As long as you live, I shall live; I am your slave, and you are dear to me.
Whoever speaks thus and then acts otherwise, an offense against that [deity] is incurred. || 271 ||
Through messengers, letters, and replies, as well as by means of anger, laughter, and weeping, one should employ gestures of displeasure, along with shaking the head. (272)

(“Asūyitā” means: by that looking [at her] with envy. (“Bahudhā” means: the connection is that she is seen in that very woman from whom she is being warded off. (“Saṃgharṣa” means: *saṃgharṣa* is a friction (*gharṣaṃ*) performed thoroughly (*samyaṅ*). (“Having spoken thus,” etc.)
But when one who boasts of his own good fortune approaches from the presence of a rival with [signs of] his identity revealed, from that, resentment arises. (273)
Then, by turning her bracelets and loosening her girdle with a lifting motion,
she should express her indignation with eyes full of tears and filled with apprehension.
Seeing her beloved standing there, apprehensive, guilty, and deeply ashamed,
[she addressed him] with words born of jealousy.
For he should indeed be wearied by means of reproaches. || 275 ||
One should not speak harshly, nor should one indulge in excessive laughter or jesting;
[one should speak] with words mixed with tears.
[He is known] by means of those [teachings] associated with the presentation of the Self. || 276 ||

The failure to fulfill what has been promised is disagreeable. The breach, censure, or refusal of those replies intended for conciliation—which were conveyed through messengers, letters, and the like—is [the offense]. (Regarding the verse beginning with *valaya*... At that very moment, due to her resentment, her limbs become thin; thus, there is a loosening of the bracelets.

"The turning over of the garment and the lifting up of the girdle. However, some sensitive critics say: "Due to her indignation, she experiences a state of nonchalance characterized by a lack of regard even in the midst of her circle of friends; and it is this [indignation] that causes the turning over of the bracelet."
By the rotation of the eyes and so forth, the raising of the girdle,
and by placing the hands upon the chest through the separation of the tips of the middle fingers and thumbs.
And also by means of continuous gazes with eyes rolled upward. || 277 ||

Through the turning of the hands at the waist, through their separation, as well as by the joining of the palms, and also by the whirling of the head, the striking down, the falling, and the embracing; || 278 ||

Whether through a glance of feigned indifference, the bending of fingers, or graceful threats—with these specific emotional expressions, one should perform the dramatic representation during acts of conciliation. (279)
"You shine; you are seen well. Go, why do you delay?
Do not touch me! Go to where she who dwells in your heart—your beloved—is. (280)
Having said, "Go," and having turned away, she should,
by means of some pretext, turn back again and once more instill joy with a word.
"And the raising by a machine. By the phrase "from the shifting of the tips of the middle fingers and the thumbs," it recalls the root operation situated therein. (Regarding "the waist":
it refers to) the separation of the hand located at the side of the waist—the hand whose *añjali* is being turned—by means of the two *patākā* hands, through the action of *avahittha*.
By that gaze characterized by depth, a wide stance is implied; for its application therein has been stated [at 12.164]. (p.
Furthermore, having considered the offense, one should appease the woman by seizing her by the hand, the garment, or the hair with force. 282.
When a woman has grasped [the victim] by the hand, the garment, or the end of the hair,
she should slowly effect the release while approaching her beloved.
Then, when she has grasped him by the hair, or again by the hand or the garment, as she approaches saying "Huṃ! Let go!", the lover should speak with sluggishness due to her touch.
A woman standing on the tips of her toes, slightly exaggerated in her coquettish movements,
should slowly loosen her hair with the "horse-step" (aśvakrānta) gesture.
When her hair-tuft was not being released, she, with slight beads of perspiration appearing and her limbs languid from his touch, should be told: "Hum hum! Let go! Move away! (286)
With the angry words "Go!", she should go and then return; for some reason, she should say, "I will not go. (287)
One should employ the syllable *huṃ* with a shaking hand;
it should be used during the act of shaking, as well as in oaths and under false pretexts.

He says, "Having said 'Go,'" because the state of being indifferent arises; for he delays because the subsequent [instruction] has cessation as its primary focus. Regarding the word "offense" (*aparādha*): when an offense is slight, [the punishment is] on the head, in the middle [of the forehead], on the palm of the hand, or on the decorated garment. Regarding the word "pretext" (*vyāja*): such as "a vow of fasting was undertaken by me," and so forth.
One should cover one's eyes and embrace from behind;
furthermore, when a woman's garment has been snatched away, one should shield her from the light of the lamp. (289)
One should continue to press him until he has come underfoot;
then, once he has reached the feet, one should look toward the messenger girl.
Then the heroine, having raised the hero and embraced him,
being delighted by the enjoyment of love, should proceed toward the bed.
One should employ this with a gentle method of singing when it is associated with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and serves as a cause for sexual enjoyment. || 292 ||
And when the poetry concerns a person situated in the sky or relies upon speech, then this performance must indeed be carried out by a woman. (293)
Even in that poetic composition related to the inner apartments which occurs in a drama and is joined with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), this same rule shall apply. || 294 ||

[Objection: But surely, the removal of garments, lying down, and so forth are prohibited on the stage; what is the use of mentioning that? [Response: True, but its utility lies in the presentation of *lāsya* (dance), whereas here it is mentioned because of the context of the application of amorous gestures (*kāmopacāra*).
To this he says: "By means of this method of singing. Nor is there a total lack of utility for this in drama (*nāṭya*); for instance, as follows:

In the case of the reciter (*bhāṇaka*) and others: when a principal character who has not yet entered the stage is mentally visualized (*bhāvita*) by the actor already on stage as an "ether-person" (*ākāśapuruṣa*), he should then say, "This and this are being seen by me.
Likewise, when something situated elsewhere is explained, it is not employed as if it were directly perceived (*pratyakṣatvena*).
He demonstrates this by showing the connection with the inner apartments:
225) "One who understands the theatrical convention (*nāṭyadharma*) must not perform the act of lying down on the stage."
For some specific purpose, the branding of the body is prescribed. || 295 ||
Alternatively, he may sleep alone or even together with her, as required by the circumstances;
likewise, there may be kissing, embracing, and whatever else is secret. (296)
One should not perform the biting of teeth, the scratching with nails, the loosening of the waist-knot, or the pressing between the breasts in the midst of the arena. || 297 ||
One should not cause such things as eating, playing in water, or anything that causes shame to take place on the stage. (297)
Since a drama depicts a father, a son, a daughter-in-law, and a mother-in-law, all of these should be avoided with great effort. (299)
An expert in the art should compose a drama using words that are exceptionally refined, pleasant to hear, sweet, and not too harsh, and which are joined with beneficial instruction. (300)

[Objection: "In that case, would it not follow that everything [is permissible] here? [Response: Anticipating the objection that "lying down is seen in cases such as with Utpalaceṭā," he says, "Or rather, she might lie down. The intended meaning is that the purpose here is not the prohibition of lying down, but rather the prohibition of kissing and so forth. [Regarding the verse beginning with] "Father and son" and so on: consequently, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) would be destroyed, for that [flavor]...
We state, moreover, that there is a "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) consisting of the mutual interpenetration of common elements;
even within this general category of gesture (*abhinaya*), there is also the gestural expression through speech (*vācika*).
(Thus should the performance of actions within the inner apartments be conducted by the wise); furthermore, at the gathering of women, words concerning love should be spoken. (301)
Learn here those words which are used toward beloved ones:
"dear one," "beloved," "well-behaved one," "protector," "master," and "life. (302)
For there are indeed words such as "Nandana" (the Delighter) used for one who is beloved;
however, [others refer to] one who is ill-behaved, of evil conduct, deceitful, perverse, or boastful. (303)
One who is shameless and cruel is said to be beloved only in his anger;
whereas he who does nothing unpleasant and speaks nothing improper [is truly dear]. (304)
Likewise, he who is upright in his conduct is called "dear" (priya), provided that no mark arising from another woman is seen upon him. (305)
Whether regarding his lower body or his person, he is called "beloved" (kānta) because even when a woman is enraged, he does not offer a retort. (306)
He who does not speak harshly is called disciplined;
he is one who seeks the welfare of others, capable of protecting them, free from pride, and devoid of envy.
With this intention, he said: "Words regarding beloved things. (p. 227) He who is undeluded in all undertakings is designated as the "Lord" (nātha).
Through conciliation, gifts, and the enjoyment of wealth, as well as through fondling and protection. || 308 ||
He who attends upon a woman is called her master; he skillfully performs the act of lying with her according to her desired intentions. (309)
He who performs [this] in the enjoyment (saṃbhoga) is known as "Life" (jīvita).
He is of noble birth, steadfast, skillful, dexterous, and eloquent in speech. (310)
That son of Nanda is praised among his friends;
these arrangements of speech are considered to be those that bring delight to Rati. || 311 ||
Likewise, listen to these words of displeasure as I speak them:
"He is cruel, intolerant, arrogant, insolent, and boastful. (312)
He whose mind is unstable is considered to be of immoral conduct;
he who, having reflected, would carry out even beating or binding [of others]. (313)
Likewise, he who is harsh in speech and of evil conduct is stretched out;
whereas he who is sweet in speech but does not act accordingly is also [so treated]. (314)
That rogue is rebuked by women for even a slight matter;
that is, with words desired by women, and not with those appropriate for himself. (Regarding "ratiprītīti": when there is sexual pleasure...
In whatever matter one is restrained, that very thing he performs.
And he who is fixed in perverted views is designated as "left-handed" (vāma);
he is marked by wounds from sexual intercourse and is boastful of his success with women. (316)
One who is excessively proud, as well as stubborn and boastful, is thus described;
he who, even when being restrained, approaches a woman with even greater persistence. || 317 ||
He who commits an offense against a woman and desires to pursue her impetuously is known as one who possesses both a mark and a transgression, and is thus considered shameless. (318)
And one who possesses a mind lacking clarity is called "cruel.
These are the arrangements of speech spoken as pleasant and unpleasant. (319)
Many other [performers] as well should be employed in the drama, supported by female dancers;
this, however, is the rule for a delicate arrangement of song.

That which arises from the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), which causes exhaustion through the enjoyment of sexual union, and that which is the "space-person" (ākāśapuruṣa) based on the speech of another; 321.

That joy and satisfaction which occurs in sexual union, and even anger, as well as satisfaction toward one's children and so forth—both of these are included [in the definition]. "Suddenly" means without having first propitiated [the deity]. "Others too" means that this is merely an illustration; such is the meaning.
He summarizes what was previously stated: "This is the rule for song" refers to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) in [the context of] the Sky-Man (*ākāśapuruṣa*) and so forth.
229) Thus, the erotic sentiment alone should be the subject matter; even there, this same sequence should apply.
Or rather, in a drama, the action involves a connection with human beings. (322)
Even there, this same sequence should apply when combined with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa);
in this manner, the performance should be employed when situated within the inner apartments (antaḥpura). || 323 ||
I shall now explain, in due order, the ritual for divine women:
their attire is eternally radiant, and their minds are eternally joyful. (324)
For the gods, time is eternally pleasant, providing a basis for their play;
there is neither envy, nor anger, nor malice, nor the need for propitiation.
Among divine men and women as well, those emotions which belong to humans, whatever their limbs may be, and whatever their gestures, are likewise observed in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). || 326 ||
All that which is to be done by divine beings in their union with humans must be performed [in this way], whenever the enjoyment of human beings occurs with divine women. (327)

The phrase "in this manner" means that whether the speech is uttered with affection or with anger, this same sequence of delivery applies there as well. "Connected with a person" means associated with a perceptible individual. Regarding the statement that kings have sexual union with celestial courtesans, he describes the general mode of representation there with the words beginning "always," and so forth. In this regard—

In the two verses, the connection should be established by supplying "even though" (*yadyapi*) to the phrase "those entities" (*ye bhāvāḥ*), and by supplying "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) to the subsequent section.
At that time, all those states of being that depend upon humans must be brought about; likewise, this occurs for divine beings due to the lapse of their curse or out of a desire for offspring. (328)
An association with humans, centered on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), should be enacted; even though she is invisible, she should entice them with flowers, ornaments, and words. 329.
Having granted another vision, she may vanish in an instant,
