even while providing garments, ornaments, garlands, and the like, as well as sending written messages.
When the hero is driven to madness by such attentions,
the passion arising from that intoxication becomes the source of sexual delight.
But that which has attained its own nature is not something that exists in an ultimate sense;
in this way, indeed, the royal etiquette based on internal reliance should be observed. (332)

The sense is that pride in life is indeed a delusion. Regarding the phrase "having driven him to madness," he states the reason as "because of causing madness"; let this be clearly observed in the *Vikramorvaśī*. May there be auspiciousness.
"Now I shall also explain the external figurative representation (upacāra) according to the Vaiśika school.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "General Representation" (sāmānyābhinaya), in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata;
this general representation is integrated within the sections on the joints (granthisthāna).
This was composed by Abhinavagupta, who is ever mindful of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter on General Representation in the Abhinavabhārati, a commentary on the Nāṭya-veda composed by the great devotee of Maheśvara, Abhinavagupta.
The Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter Twenty-three.
(Vaiśika:
He is called Vaiśika because he distinguishes all the arts;
or, he is proclaimed as Vaiśika because he is proficient in the conduct of the brothel (veśa). || 1 ||
For he who is endowed with all arts, skilled in every craft, and proficient in capturing the hearts of women—he shall be a man of the courtesans. (2)

Salutations to that Supreme Lord, who is the abode of liberation; he whom even the mind of a courtesan—though powerless to attain him alone, yet manifesting a state of exclusive devotion while filled with manifold emotions—takes as its goal. Abhinavabhāratī, Chapter Twenty-three.

In the preceding chapter, it was concluded that the *vaiśika* (the specific) is merely a subset of the *sāmānyābhinaya* (general representation). With the statement, "Now, in the *vaiśika*, I shall explain even the external application," the connection is established that the *vaiśika* must be discussed. Commencing that [section], he first provides the etymological definition (*nirukta*) with the words "one should distinguish" (*viśeṣayet*). This is the act of distinguishing (*viśeṣaṇa*).

"He knows by that, and thus he causes [them] to pass beyond"—such is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), for those who know it, the Vaiśeṣikas (or *Vaiśikas*), hold that this is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
He is a lover of courtesans (*veśyākāmuka*), and because of his skill in distinguishing all desires, he is called a *vaiśika*.
Now, he provides an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) appropriate to grammar: "or one who is adept in the service of the *veśa*. *Veśa* means a courtesan.
The meaning is that "occurrence" (*bhava*) refers to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). He analyzes the very sense of "occurrence" by means of the word *sādhī*.
Therefore, he says that such a person is a "knower of the distinctions among the arts" (*kalāsu viśeṣajña*), for he is indeed "endowed with all the arts.
His qualities, however, should be known as arising from his own body;
they are, in brief, thirty-three, consisting of both those acquired and those innate. || 3 ||
He was accomplished in the sciences and the arts, handsome and pleasing to behold; he was valiant and steadfast, endowed with youth, a graceful appearance, and noble birth.
Fragrant, sweet, generous, patient, not boastful, free from apprehension, speaking kindly, clever, auspicious, and pure. (5)
Skilled in the practice of love, dexterous, knowing the proper place and time, free from harsh speech, smiling, eloquent, capable, and sweet-spoken.

One who is fond of women, generous in sharing, full of faith, firm in memory, not over-familiar with those who should be approached, and possessed of self-respect— such indeed is the professional courtesan's lover (vaiśika).
He should have a companion who is devoted, pure, skillful, upright, and possessed of right conduct,
who speaks with eloquence, and who shares those same qualities.
She is endowed with the qualities of discernment (*vijñāna*), firmness, and the marks of her lineage.

Her acquired qualities include knowledge of the sciences and the like; her innate qualities include physical beauty and charm. Furthermore, being distrustful even toward women who are accessible, he does not approach them impulsively, but rather seeks out their true disposition. He should be thus.

"Citrābhidhāyin" means one who is skilled in *vakrokti* (indirect or figurative speech). "Tasya" refers to the *vaiśika* (the man-about-town). "Kathī" refers to one who is skilled in recounting or listening to stories such as those in the *Bṛhatkathā*. "Liṅginī" means a female painter. "Prātiveśyā" [refers to] a neighbor woman.
A neighbor, a female friend, a maidservant, a young maiden, and a woman skilled in crafts. || 9 ||
She was a nurse, a heretic, and likewise a professional dancer;
she was skilled at incitement, eloquent in sweet speech, clever, and knew the proper timing.

A messenger (dūtī) who is charming and keeps her mantras secret should be appointed for these qualities; she, in turn, must provide encouragement by demonstrating various reasons [for the practice]. (11)
It is the speaking exactly as it was said and likewise the manifestation of the true state;
it is neither dull, nor merely endowed with form, nor meaningful, nor distressed. (12)

One who dwells in a nearby residence; a female heretic (*pāṣaṇḍinī*); one observing a vow (*vratinī*); a woman of the stage (*raṅgopajīvinī*), namely a washerwoman (*rajaka-strī*) or a female bard (*cāraṇa-strī*).

"Skilled in incitement" (*protsāhane kuśalā*) and so forth are adjectives qualifying all of them. Thus, there are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*): "incitement" (*protsāhana*) is that which incites together with [the heroine]. The heroine incites, and the hero is incited by her.
The meaning is that she brings [the message] face-to-face.

He states another function of hers: "as stated" means that this [messenger] must perform two tasks: the delivery of the message and the examination of the feelings of the beloved woman. [The messenger is called] *jaḍa* (insentient).
He says that one is unable to perform those tasks that must be done and are to be accomplished by immediate wit:

"One who is endowed with beauty or wealth may secure his own interest; however, a sick person, merely by being seen, produces disgust, and since he is indifferent to pleasure, the sick man is not a messenger of desire."
A wise man should never employ a male messenger or a female messenger who has made excessive boasts regarding his or her lineage, enjoyments, and wealth. (13)
The messenger should announce his desire and describe the purpose;
however, there should be no union with one who is unwilling or who is angry. (14)
Indeed, no improper means should be employed by a female messenger, for she must rely upon men;
[these occasions include] a festival, wandering at night, a garden, or the house of a friend. (15)
In the houses of nurses, or likewise at the invitation of a female friend, under the pretext of illness, or by staying in an empty house; 16.
Men should arrange a meeting with women at their first encounter;
having thus arranged the meeting with skillful means and according to the prescribed rule, [they should proceed]. (17)
One should discern whether she is attached or detached by means of her gestures and outward forms.
Having created various reasons for encouragement, it is said that these are the "motivations";

he states them as beginning with "family enjoyment" (*kulabhoga*) and so forth. "Festival" (*utsava*) refers to a festival primarily consisting of nocturnal excursions held right within one's own home.
"First union" means a Gāndharva marriage or the union with a prostitute or a remarried woman. (p.
236) A woman who is the locus of passion through her extraordinary natural qualities... [18]
Constantly afflicted by love, she performs her amorous pastimes in secret;
in the midst of her friends, she speaks of his virtues and bestows her own wealth upon him. (19)
Her friends honor her, she always hates her enemies, and she becomes exceedingly joyful during the comings and goings of her companions. (20)
She is pleased by his words and gazes at him with affection;
when he sleeps, she sleeps behind him, and when kissed, she kisses him back. (21)
She rises before him and likewise endures his hardships;
she is joyful in his festival and sorrowful in his misfortune. (22)
A woman endowed with such qualities is considered to be "attached" (anuraktā).
As for the signs of one who is "disaffected" (viraktā): when kissed, she does not kiss the navel. (23)

"By nature" (*svabhāva*): the connection is that she is "attached," characterized by those excellences in sexual union (*surata*) such as the capacity to endure nails and teeth. "Friends [regard] the enemy"—the word "of the hero" (*nāyakasya*) is to be supplied. "Lying down afterwards and rising first."
"Without him, what happiness is there here?
thus she speaks of an undesirable matter, and even when addressed with pleasant words, she becomes angry.
He hates his friends and likewise associates with people who are his enemies. || 24 ||
She even lies on her bed with her face turned away from him as he lies there first; and even when a very great service has been rendered, she does not attain satisfaction.
She who cannot endure affliction and likewise becomes angry without cause—one of such a nature as this should be designated as "dispassionate. (26)
The means of capturing the heart, her active exertion, the manifestation of purpose, and furthermore, the presentation of gifts—these constitute [the stages]. (27)
An unsolicited mention, as well as appearing ill even during a festival—these indicate the hero's misfortune. She tells an unpleasant story;
[this refers to what was done] even before on the mountain. By those means by which her heart is captured—of her who is thus impassioned.

"Activity of effort" (*vyāpāraceṣṭita*) refers to the intent toward the act of capturing his heart; this is the "effort" (*ceṣṭita*) in the science of love (*kāmatantra*). "Displaying wealth" (*arthapradarśana*) means [saying], "I possess this. "Offering" (*upanyāsa*) means [saying], "I shall give you wealth. "Offering" (*upanyāsa*) by way of another person means [saying], "There is a certain woman who is in love with him."
Explanation: (*Vyādhitā*) refers to the state of one who possesses various mental afflictions (*ādhi*). For that reason, there is non-attendance;
that is to say, withdrawing from his presence under the pretext of observing various intentions.
Then there is abandonment through artifice, as well as the introduction of a latent emotion from what is proximate. || 28 ||
From poverty, from disease, from suffering, from harshness, and likewise from the unpleasantness of hearing [evil], from going into exile, from excessive greed, and from transgression. (29)
Furthermore, due to excessive intimacy or likewise due to causing displeasure—
for these reasons, either a woman or a man becomes disenchanted.
Women's actions directed toward passion should be performed with an apprehension of their inner disposition, so that the woman finds satisfaction and is subsequently obtained by men.
One should win over a greedy woman by the gift of wealth, a learned woman by knowledge of the arts, a clever woman by charm, and a proud woman by devoted service.
(And by taking up ornaments, he may become eloquent with amorous passion. He should approach her who hates men with beloved topics of conversation and appropriate advances. || 33 ||
(“Abandonment under a pretext”): This is the suggestion of an internal state (*bhāvopakṣepa*), expressed through another person’s mouth as “he is attached elsewhere.
He states that even for one who is passionate, these are causes for detachment, beginning with “due to poverty,” and so forth;
and that which is harsh speech, such as the mention of the death of a child and other matters unfit to be heard.

Therefore, since this is so, one should protect her passion; thus she is "one who grasps the inner intent. "Is obtained" means, in short, "is served. "By men" implies by those who are skillful—this is the sense. To explain how she finds satisfaction, he says "the greedy," and so forth. "The wise" refers to those who know the arts (*kalā*).
By means of charm and boldness;
239) by means of playthings for the child, and by means of consolation for the timid woman.
She who was noble-minded was made arrogant by the service of the lowly, and she who was refined was made conceited by displays of artistic skill. || 34 ||
For all women indeed, three types of nature are recorded: superior, middling, and inferior; however, for courtesans, these are innate by their very nature. (35)
She who speaks kindly and never unkindly even to one who stands in opposition to her, who does not harbor long-lasting resentment, and who is likewise proficient in the arts; || 36 ||
She who is desired by men distinguished by their virtue, beauty, and noble lineage—skillful in the arts of love, clever, and endowed with radiant form. (37)
She restrains her anger for a specific reason, speaks without envy, and knows the particular timing required for action; she who possesses such beauty is remembered as the most excellent.
She who is desired by men and likewise desires them, being skilled in the arts of love yet envious of her rivals. (39)
"By means of service to the lowly" refers to such acts as touching their feet and so forth. "By means of displays of craft" means by means of things that cause wonder.
With the intention that it is impossible to enumerate the varieties of each step individually, he says "of all of them," meaning of the superior, middling, and inferior types respectively.

A woman who is afflicted by jealousy, lacking self-control, whose anger has diminished yet who is excessively proud, and who is gracious for only a moment— she is considered a woman of middling quality. (40)
She who is prone to anger for no reason, who is of wicked character and excessively proud, fickle and harsh, is considered the lowest woman due to her long-standing resentment. (41)

It is traditionally held that there are four distinct stages of youth for all women, which they attain through the qualities of their attire, appearance, gestures, and virtues while embodying the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). 42.

That first stage of youth should be known as characterized by full thighs, cheeks, hips, lower lips, and breasts; it is firm, delightful for sexual pleasure, and filled with the impulse of erotic passion. (43)
Her body has its limbs fully developed, her breasts are full, and her waist is slender;
this second stage of youth is the very essence of desire. 44.
This third stage, youth, is endowed with all splendors, generates the causes of delight, is rich in the qualities of passion, and its beauty is nourished by desire. (45)

(Regarding the phrase "of all [women]"): first, youth lasts until twenty; thus, there is a division at thirty, forty, and fifty. Others, however, state the division as sixteen, twenty-five, thirty-five, and forty-five.
When youth has passed away, as it does in the second or even the third stage,
this fourth stage is indeed the enemy of love. (46)
With cheeks, hips, lips, and breasts that have not yet faded, and with beauty only slightly diminished, this fourth stage of youth indeed does not breathe heavily toward passion. 47.

A woman who cannot endure excessive hardship, who neither becomes angry nor rejoices excessively because of men, and who is attached to pleasures and virtues, should be known as being in the prime of her youth. 48.
In the second stage of youth, he displays some pride, some anger, and indeed some envy; yet, even when provoked to anger, he remains silent.

A woman who is skilled in the enjoyment of sexual union, free from malice toward her partner, rich in the qualities of passion, and possesses unrestrained and proud gestures, is to be known as the third type. (50)
In the fourth [period], however, a woman who possesses no envy and is capable of grasping the mind through her supernormal powers desires a man who is never separated from her. (51)
Regarding these, he states the distinction of the modes of conduct (*upacāra*): "not excessively" means that she does not tolerate excessive exertion in activities such as chewing food.
"Rich in the qualities of passion" means she is skilled in the application of the methods of the science of love (*kāmatantra*). "Not separated" means by all three [types] of mental states (*bhāva*).
These four varieties of youth are to be understood in dramatic works;
furthermore, I shall explain them again according to the Kāmaśāstra for men. (52)
The four superior types, the middling, the inferior, and the *pravṛttaka*—these five types of men are to be known in the context of sexual union with women. (53)

One who endures both suffering and afflictions equally, who is skilled in appeasing both affection and anger, who seeks his purpose without following his own whims, and who is dexterous and clever—he is to be understood as a bodhisattva. (54)
He who does nothing to displease his wife, who harbors no thought of aversion toward her, whose heart’s desires she knows, and who is mindful and steadfast—he indeed is the superior [husband]. (55)
The superior man is sweet-natured and generous; he does not succumb to passion, nor does he fall under the sway of lust. Even when slighted by a woman, that excellent man remains detached.
He who, being impartial toward all objects, does not grasp at their existence as a noble one [does], but becomes dispassionate upon seeing some fault, would be a person of middle capacity. (57)

With the intention that the distinction between types of persons should be understood for the sake of conventional usage (*upacāra*), he says "the four, beginning with the *uttama*," and so forth. He defines the five in sequence, starting with "one who shares in suffering" (*samaduḥkha*). "One whose heart's desire is unknown" means one who is profound;
that is to say, one who is senior (*jyeṣṭha*). Now, [one might ask: what of another's...?
For at the proper time, a donor does not give way to excessive anger even if he is treated with contempt;
yet this middling type becomes detached upon seeing even a mere slight offense. (58)
Though insulted by his wife, he, out of shamelessness, approaches her with an unchanged countenance,
even when she has transferred her affection to another.
And there is the transformation of the state through the application of unctuous substances. || 59 ||
He who, even when being restrained by friends, becomes more firmly attached to a fresh offense committed in his presence, should be known as the lowest of men. (60)
Disregarding fear and resentment, of a foolish nature, prone to laughter, stubbornly holding to his own views, and shameless in matters of love. (61)
In the playful conflicts of amorous passion, he is not harsh; such a man is a plaything for women, according to those who know [the art].
But when it has set forth, it is indeed difficult to discern. || 62 ||

He says "sneha... [meaning] that she might transfer [her affection] due to the force of necessity; she is one whose state of mind—that is, her intention—is turned toward another by means of another's affection (sneha), that is, love (preman).
Women should be known to have diverse characters, with hearts and desires that are hidden;
having discerned their true nature, one should approach them accordingly. (63)

Having understood her states of arousal and non-arousal, a man should then attend to the woman with various appropriate means, having carefully observed the principles of the science of love (kāmatantra).
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, as well as punishment, and even indifference—these should be employed regarding the domain of women. (65)
"I am yours, and you indeed are mine; I am your slave and you are dear to me.
That which is performed by offering oneself is celebrated as *sāma*. (66)
Wealth should be given from time to time according to one's means;
that which is given for a specific occasion is known as *pradāna*. || 67 ||

Now, one might ask: "What is the use of this knowledge of the dispositions (*bhāva*) of women? To this he replies: "Of various characters" (*nānāśīlāḥ*). "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to purpose or intention; it is their heart that harbors hidden intentions. "According to their nature" (*yathāsattvam*) means according to their disposition (*āśaya*).

"Presence and absence of disposition" (*bhāvābhāvau*) refers to passion (*anurāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*). Regarding women, "bondage" (*bandhana*) means acceptance (*svīkāra*); that [he understands].
The meaning is that when that [object] is to be accomplished, the five means beginning with *sam* (conciliation) and ending with *upekṣā* (indifference) are employed.

He explains them in sequence, starting with "I am yours," and so forth. The "presentation of oneself" (*ātmana upakṣepaḥ*) is the manifestation of one's own disposition; [the time for this is] at the appropriate moment during the day, [thinking] "it must be given."
In this world, the discovery of faults in one's beloved, along with the means [to address them],
as well as confinement and beating, is designated as "punishment" (daṇḍa). (68)
One should win over a neutral woman with conciliation, a greedy one with the gift of wealth, and one whose affection is bound to another by means of sowing dissension. || 69 ||
When a wicked conduct has been initiated, arising from another's disposition, punishment must be inflicted through mild beating and binding. (70)
(The hero or man should speak thus: "And he should strike that heroine;
the wise man should strike that woman with a rope or with a split bamboo cane. || 71 ||
But when the application of conciliation and the other means has been exhausted in due order,
the wise person should remain indifferent toward that [result] which has not been achieved through meditative absorption.

The meaning is that when there is no fixed rule, she sustains herself through gifts given on account of specific occasions, such as those arising from joy or distress. The distinction is this: her faults are presented in such a way that they might be perceived by him as being true; thus he says "with a stratagem" (*sopāyam*). This refers to her own [application] of the four means (*upāya*).

He states his own position regarding the object [of desire] with the words "one who is indifferent" (*madhyasthām*); the meaning is: one who feels some affection. "Should bring her" (*ānayet*) means he should take her as his own.

"Should offer her" (*pratipādayet*) means he should cause her to come face-to-face with himself. "Evil conduct" (*duṣṭācāra*) refers to such things as fleeing from one's country or residing in the house of another man, and so forth; and even in that regard, among women—

"He should be indifferent" refers to mild beatings and binding; he states the object of indifference with the words "of conciliation and so forth," for even by means of punishment, one should remain indifferent toward that [offender].
Whether he is hateful, beloved, or indifferent to women, he is to be discerned by the color of his face, his eyes, and his gestures and movements. (73)
For the sake of wealth, a courtesan always accepts a man whether he is dear to her or not, with the sole exception of divine women and the wives of kings. (74)
They call the hateful "dear," and likewise the dear "dearer"; they call the ill-behaved "well-behaved," and the virtue-less "rich in virtues. (75)
And seeing whom she laughs with eyes whose pupils are wide open, her joyful facial expression is perceived through the manifestations of her inner emotion. (76)

Having understood both presence and absence [of desire], and having set aside those [unsuccessful] approaches, one should diligently attend to the woman while observing the principles of the science of love (kāmatantra).

It has been said: "The wise man should disregard whatever [feeling] she abandons. To the question "What does one perceive?", he says "by the color of her face," and so forth. With the intention that the mind of a courtesan is difficult to discern and must therefore be examined with effort, he says "but for the sake of wealth. Does this apply to all of them?

He says that this rule does not apply to courtesans, stating: "except for the wives of divine beings and kings. Now, one might ask: "Does the statement mean that one should observe the heart of a courtesan? He replies: "But they say she is dear even when she is hated. Here, the particle *tu* (but) has the sense of *api* (even). Now, one might ask: "Are their hearts truly devoid of their own interests? He replies: "No, because of the power of their artifice (*upacāra*)."
The meaning is "out of desire for wealth"; or else,
because of the weakness of our power and likewise because of deception.
From them, desire is produced, just as fire arises from wood. || 78 ||
This conduct of women, as described and based on the *vaiśika* [treatise], should be properly applied according to the requirements in a dramatic context and in a play (*nāṭaka*). (79)
O best of the twice-born, this service to a courtesan should be performed by those who know it;
hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the [eight] prakṛtis.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

[Regarding] "by means of service" (?): now, having raised the doubt—"If they are of such a nature, why are they desired by people?"—he repeats this very point, saying: "and because of the power of their refinements. For...

Because he censures the courtesies appropriate for winning her heart and deceives her in the midst of them, desire becomes eager for him; thus it is said that he is one who is obsessed with desire. The phrase "fire from wood" implies, on the contrary, that he is difficult to cure.

He applies to the present subject the chapter that was undertaken under the heading of the "man seeking a woman" (*vaiśikapuruṣa*), beginning with the words "of women. The mention of "the drama" (*nāṭaka*) is because divine courtesans exist therein, and because [such characters] belong to the roles of the banner-hero (*patākānāyaka*) and so forth. May there be auspiciousness! This is the twenty-third chapter, concerning the man seeking a woman.
Thus has the sequence of words for the auspicious knots been composed by Abhinavagupta.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on the Vaiśikas, in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭya-veda* composed by the illustrious Great Maheśvara teacher Abhinavagupta.
The Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter Twenty-four.
(On the Conduct of Men and Women) In brief, however, the nature of both men and women is proclaimed to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
The Twenty-Fourth Chapter of the Abhinavabhāratī:
I bow to that Prakṛti of Śambhu, through the manifestation of whose three powers (śakti) a person is conceptualized in three ways and upon whom [the world] is metaphorically attributed.

In this context, the practice of desire has been shown previously, and it was stated that desire is caused by women and men. Although the natures of both women and men are diverse, they are impossible to calculate individually; therefore, all of them can be subsumed within three fundamental types.

The three *prakṛtis* (types of characters) must be described. Accordingly, it says "in brief. Furthermore, since the conduct of love culminates in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and that conduct resides specifically in the hero (*nāyaka*), the various types of heroes must be described. Moreover, the poet must describe everything regarding that hero: what is the name of his harem or his retinue, whether he is internal or external, and how large that retinue is.

And it must be understood by the actor: thus, having described the distinctions among the primary hero and his retinue, this chapter is commenced for the purpose of [explaining] the application of these distinctions, such as the "primary nature" (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
Possessing mastery over her senses and endowed with wisdom, she was skilled in various arts;
she was the supreme Lakṣmī of the southern quarter and the consoler of those who were afraid.

Endowed with the meaning of various scriptures, characterized by profundity and magnanimity, and possessed of the qualities of steadfastness and generosity—this should be known as the highest nature. (3)
Skilled in worldly conventions, proficient in the sciences of the arts,
and endowed with discernment and sweetness— such is remembered as the middling nature.
They were harsh-spoken, ill-behaved, base-natured, and dull-witted; they were prone to anger, murderous, treacherous toward friends, and conceited in their own worthlessness.
They are slanderers, arrogant in speech, ungrateful, and likewise lazy;
they distinguish between those worthy and unworthy of respect, are lustful for women, and fond of quarreling.
Since women and eunuchs lack [active] desire (*kāma*), their conduct consists of affectionate behavior (*snehavyavahāra*);
this constitutes the thematic connection of the chapter. Regarding that, he first describes their natural behavior (*prakṛtivyavahāra*) with the words "In brief, however" (*samāsatas tu*).
The word "however" (*tu*) indicates a distinction: previously, their nature was shown in detail, whereas now it is presented concisely.

(Regarding "worldly convention"): Worldly convention is common usage; and in that regard, one inevitably falls [into error]. Those who forget a benefit received are ungrateful; they are those who do not distinguish between the honorable and the dishonorable—this is the summary.
Slanderers, performers of evil deeds, and stealers of others' property—
endowed with these faults, men become base in this world. (7)
Thus, the threefold nature of men according to their conduct has been declared;
now, furthermore, I shall explain the nature of women in due order. (8)
Gentle in nature, steady, speaking with smiles, and free from harshness; she was skilled in following the words of her elders, modest, and endowed with humility.
Endowed with natural qualities such as beauty of form, noble birth, and sweetness, and possessed of profundity and fortitude—she is to be known as the best of women. (10)
Endowed with all these very qualities, though not to an excessive degree,
and permeated by minor defects, such is known as the middling nature.

The word "again" (*punaśca*) means that although it was stated previously, it is nevertheless [stated here]. For in that [previous] instance, the threefold nature of the *prakṛti* was explained with the intention of referring to the pursuit of sensual desires;

here, however, the distinction is seen in that it pertains to the domain of all worldly transactions (*sarvavyavahāra*). Furthermore, [in the previous case], the status of being "superior" (*uttama*) and so forth was based on a difference in objects (*viṣaya*).

Because they arise from *sattva*, foods that are savory, unctuous, and so forth are said to be dear to one characterized by *sattva*. For in that case, *sattva* pertains specifically to the domain of food; thus, a sage who observes a vow of eating pungent food along with smoke is not *sāttvika*, nor is a thief who eats ghee, molasses, milk, and rice.

"Being *sāttvika*": she is skillful in speech, modest toward her elders, and [speaks with words] that are neither excessively superior nor deficient in excellence, and which are not incomplete—that is, not fragmentary—nor confused.
That which is proclaimed as the lowest nature of men should, in brief, be understood as the very same for women who are base. (12)
The neuter should be known as mixed and indeed inferior;
likewise, those such as servants and the like should be known as mixed castes, O twice-born ones. (13)
The Śakāra, the Viṭa, and whoever else of this kind there may be—these mixed characters are to be understood by the wise as the lowest in the drama. (14)
These natures are to be known through men, women, and eunuchs;
I shall now fully explain their procedure based upon their character.
In this [drama], exactly four types of heroes (nāyaka) are proclaimed, characterized by various attributes according to their middle or superior natures. (16)

The heroes are proclaimed to be of four types: the haughty-resolute (dhīroddhata), the playful-resolute (dhīralalita), the noble-resolute (dhīrodātta), and likewise the tranquil-resolute (dhīrapraśānta). || 17 ||
Gods are to be known as *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty), while kings are *dhīralalita* (bold and playful).
The commander-in-chief and the minister are proclaimed to be *dhīrodātta* (bold and noble). (18)

Thus, some are of mixed nature and some are indeed of inferior nature; and since the female attendants are of mixed character, they act in accordance with the master's disposition. The *viṭa* (libertine) and even the *śakāra* likewise perform the actions of the superior and middle classes because they have experienced such wealth, and are thus "mixed. But in reality, however—
The servant, the *viṭa*, and the *śakāra* are indeed inferior.

Having described the classification of characters (*prakṛtibheda*), he states the classification of the hero (*nāyakabheda*) with the words "here there are four. Regarding matters of sexual union (*surata*), one who subverts peace (*sandhi*) with conflict (*vigraha*) or conflict with peace is a *vidūṣaka*. As for deception (*vipralambha*)...
They are called *vidūṣakas* because they corrupt through the giving of diversion and cause [others] to forget.
252) Brahmins and merchants are to be known as *dhīrapraśāntas*.
Furthermore, among these, four should be known as the *vidūṣakas*. || 19 ||

One who bears the sectarian mark (liṅgin), a twice-born man, one who lives by the king, and a disciple—these, respectively, one should employ for the gods, the sovereign, the ministers, and the brahmins. (20)
These friends in times of separation are skillful in pleasant conversation;
for one who is afflicted by calamity or suffering deserves to attain prosperity.
Thus the wise call that Puruṣa the Pradhāna and the Leader, wherein the misfortunes and successes of many beings repeatedly occur. (22)
Where those two exist together with nourishment, there the hero (nāyaka) shall not be; [these types of women are:
the celestial woman (divyā), the king’s wife, the woman of good family (kulastrī), and likewise the courtesan (gaṇikā).
These heroines are to be known by their various temperaments and characteristics;
they may be firm (dhīrā), graceful (lalitā), noble (udāttā), or modest (nibhṛtā). || 24 ||

"Respectively" (*yathākramam*) means that the propriety here is sequential; the application is as follows: a *liṅgin* is [the attendant] of a *ṛṣi*; a *dvija* is [the attendant] of a god; a *vīra* is [the attendant] of a general; a *rājajīvī* is [the attendant] of a king; and a *śiṣya* is [the attendant] of a *brāhmaṇa*. He describes their function: "The friend in separation" refers to the *vidūṣaka*.
Now, regarding the plot concerning the birth of a single person, he asks who the hero is and says: "the one addicted to vice" (*vyasanī*). Or, "having encountered suffering.
This one was not already fallen into vice; rather, having been happy, he has now encountered suffering.

But surely, according to this definition alone, even multiple characters would [be the hero], as in the *Rāmāyaṇa* where Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa are also [heroes] like Rāma; thus he says: "where there are many...
Indeed, divine royal women are endowed with excellent qualities;
a woman born of noble lineage should be both dignified and modest.
The graceful and the exalted [styles] are employed by courtesans and artisans;
however, for all the constituent elements [of dramatic expression], they are traditionally held to be twofold according to their application. (26)
There is both the external and the internal; I shall describe their characteristics.
Among them, that which constitutes the royal service is indeed the internal.
Then, that for whom there is the external practice of verbal etiquette is so described;
furthermore, regarding the royal etiquette, that which pertains to the inner apartments of kings [is explained].
I shall now declare the classification of women according to their functional roles;
indeed, I shall describe the royal service pertaining to the inner apartments.
Likewise, the Great Goddesses, the goddesses, and the mistresses were also established, as well as the enjoyers, the artisans, the actresses, and the dancers. (30)

And the female attendants (anucārikās) are to be known, as well as the female servants (paricārikās), likewise the female messengers (saṃcārikās), and those who carry out errands (preṣaṇakārikās). || 31 ||
The high-ranking female attendants, the doorkeepers, the maidens, the elderly women,
and the royal officials— all these people of the inner apartments were free from illness.

Having described the classification of the hero (*nāyaka*), he states the classification of the heroine (*nāyikā*) with the words "and divine" (*divyā ca*). Next, he describes the classification of the retinue (*parivāra*) with the words "the royal service" (*rājopacāra*) and so forth. The group of women consists of seventeen members, beginning with the chief queen (*mahādevī*) and ending with the attendant (*āyuktikā*);
the group of eunuchs and others is the eighteenth. For this very reason, he will state later: "this is of eighteen kinds."

In this regard, she who has been consecrated as a queen, who is endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, possessed of good qualities, in the prime of youth, moderate in temperament, and likewise free from anger— (33) ||| p. 254 ||
Free from envy, she knew the king's character; she shared equally in his joy and sorrow, and constantly sought her husband's welfare through rites of peace and auspicious blessings. (34)
Peaceful, devoted to her husband, steadfast, and intent on the welfare of the inner apartments—one endowed with these qualities is designated as a "Great Queen" (Mahādevī). || 35 ||
Possessing these very same qualities but devoid of those refinements, they are arrogant, exceedingly beautiful, and intent upon mutual enjoyment. (36)
Those women who possess a pure, eternal, and radiant form, who are free from envy toward their rivals, and who are enriched with youth, beauty, and virtue, are called "goddesses. (37)
Furthermore, those daughters who may belong to a general, ministers, or servants, and who are free from any equal status [in their husbands], [should be avoided]. (38)
Those women who are endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities, who are beneficial to the king, and who have received honor for their own merits, are known as *svāminīs*. (39)

"Antaḥpura" (inner apartment) has been mentioned; its meaning is the retinue belonging to that [king]. By the term "Mahādevī," singularity is intended. He states the characteristics of the Mahādevīs in sequence, beginning with "here, she who is consecrated on the head" (*mūrdhābhiṣiktā*).
She is "consecrated" because she occupies the primary position upon the heads of all [the attendants]. She "stands in middle age."

The neutral one (*madhyasthā*). (Regarding "in the harem" [antaḥpureti]): for the group both within and outside the harem, it is the accomplishment of skill beneficial to the harem. Regarding "the queens" (*devyaḥ*): the Great Queen (*mahādevī*), however, is not particularly suited to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*);
with the intention that she does not approach too closely, poets refer to Vāsavadattā and others by the designation "Queen" (*devī*).
They conduct themselves [in such a way]:
endowed with beauty and youth, harsh yet possessed of graceful charms.
They are skilled in the enjoyment of sexual pleasure and are envious of those who practice counter-measures. || 40 ||
They were skillful, always knowing their husband's mind, radiant with perfumes and garlands;
they followed the king's will and were free from envy, pride, and arrogance. (41)
Those who are diligent, free from negligence, having abandoned laziness, not cruel, and who discern between those worthy of honor and those not, are known as the "Established" (sthāpitā). || 42 ||
Those who have received honor due to their noble lineage and good character, who are gentle, not overly bold, impartial, composed, and patient, are known as *bhoginīs*. (43)
They were experts in various specialized arts, skilled in diverse crafts,
knowledgeable in the classification of perfumes and flowers, and discerning in the distinction between what is worthy of being depicted and what is not.
They were experts in the arrangement of beds and seats, clever, sweet-spoken, dexterous, gentle, articulate, eloquent, and discreet craftsmen. (45)
Those who know the release and dissolution of the planets, who discern the various sentiments and emotions, who are clever, skilled in drama, and expert in reasoning and refutation; || 46 ||

(The phrase "by her own qualities" is the same [as before]). She was endowed with qualities—that is, joined with artistic skills, good character, and youth. Yet she was harsh due to the pride of her good fortune.

Those women endowed with beauty and youth are known as actresses; they are rich in playful gestures (*helā*) and specific emotional states (*bhāva*), as well as in inner being (*sattva*) and dramatic representation (*abhinaya*). (47)
She was endowed with sweetness of voice and likewise skilled in musical instruments;
she possessed all major and minor limbs and was versed in the sixty-four arts.
They were clever, endowed with humility, and free from the faults of women;
they were always bold, as well as devoid of laziness and having conquered fatigue. (49)
She was skilled in the application of various arts, proficient in dance and song, and endowed with beauty, virtue, generosity, fortitude, good fortune, and moral character. (50)
And her throat was melodious, sweet, tender, resonant, and variegated;
she stood among the assembled women who were endowed with beauty, youth, and splendor. (51)
She who has no equal in her qualities is known as the *nartakī*; she is she who does not abandon the king during any situation or in the performance of services. (52)

The attendants should be understood as follows: the clever *dakṣā*, the dancer (*nāṭyajñā*), the bed-guardian (*śayyāpālī*), the parasol-bearer (*chatradhārī*), and likewise the fan-bearer (*vyajanadhāriṇī*).
The female masseuse, the preparer of perfumes, likewise the female decorator, as well as the female jewelry-setter and the female garland-maker; || 54 ||
Those who are of such a kind should be known as attendants;
they move through various courtyards and likewise wander through the groves. (55)
The goddesses who sport in the temples, the attendants of the palaces, the yāminīs, and likewise those women who possess such characteristics. (56)

Those described by experts in drama as "intermediaries" (saṃcārikās) are to be understood as occurring in the sending of messages not involving desire, and in matters arising from secrets or hidden things. (57)
Those women who are appointed by kings [to these tasks] should be known as attendants;
they are employed in the protection of the entire inner apartment through praise and benedictions.
Those who rejoice in prosperity should be known as the most eminent; they arise from various practices connected with peace and war. (59)
Those who announce matters are known as *pratihārīs*;
they have not experienced the enjoyment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), nor are they agitated or arrogant. (60)
Maidens and young girls are known to be modest and bashful;
they are ignorant of the ways of former kings, yet they have been honored by those former kings.
Those who are well known as "the elders" because they followed former kings;
the word *atha* (now) has the sense of *api ca* (and also). Those *yāmakinyas* who remain awake at every watch (*pratidahara*).
Likewise, those appointed over the treasuries and those appointed over the armories [were also slain]. || 62 ||
Likewise, there was one who supervised fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs, and another who was concerned with perfumes, ornaments, garments, and garlands. (63)
In that way, those who are attached to many [men] should be known as improper; thus have the women who move within the inner apartments been described in brief. (64)
O twice-born ones, I shall indeed describe them according to their specific distinctions:
they are reddish, devoted, and arise from various sides. (65)
Those appointed to official duties and various tasks who are neither arrogant nor confused, neither greedy nor cruel; (66)
They were self-controlled, patient, serene, having conquered anger and subdued their senses; they were free from desire, devoid of greed, and entirely liberated from the faults of women.
She should be employed in moving within the inner apartments of the king's palace; likewise, artisans, chamberlains, and eunuchs [should attend to her]. (68)

"Distinction" (viśeṣaṇam) means that I shall state the distinction of the *āyuktikās* from others. "Desirable" (*ākāmya*) means she is not fit to be desired by another, nor is she capable of being desired; for indeed, everyone praises her in matters of application (*āyojanas*).
A shaven attendant woman should be employed for the task of sending messages among women, as well as for the protection of young girls and infants. (69)
One should appoint those who follow the conduct of kings to positions of authority within the inner apartments, as they are capable of conveying all matters of news to the palace.
Those who are disciplined, of little strength, truly impotent, possessing the nature of women, and not at fault by birth—they are indeed known as *varṣavara*s. (71)
Brahmins who are skilled, elderly, and free from the defects of desire should always be employed by kings for the rites of the goddesses.
Thus, this eighteenfold inner harem has been described by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the external [harem] arising from men.
The king, the commander-in-chief, the domestic priest, as well as the ministers, the counselors, the judges, and the officials in charge of the princes; || 74 ||
Now he speaks of the external retinue, beginning with "the king. Here, the term "king" refers to the crown prince (*yuvarāja*). Regarding the phrase "the minister":
one should understand that there are many other honorable persons who belong to the king. (p. 260)
I shall describe their specific distinctions according to their characteristics; listen.
Strong, endowed with intelligence, truthful, and having conquered his senses;
skillful, bold, steadfast, valiant, wise, and pure. (76)
Far-sighted, possessed of great energy, grateful, sweet-spoken, and gentle;
observing the vows of the world-protectors, he was expert in the path of action. (77)

He should be industrious and vigilant, devoted to the elders, learned in the treatises on statecraft, skilled in discerning the intentions and gestures of others, brave, and endowed with protective measures. || 78 ||
He was one who deliberated through reasoning and refutation, an employer of various crafts, skilled in the meaning of the treatises on ethics, and likewise full of affection. (79)
A king should be knowledgeable in the Dharma and free from vices through these qualities;
[his ministers] should be of noble birth, endowed with intelligence, and learned in various treatises. (80)
The people of that land are affectionate, cannot be led astray by others, and are never heedless;
they are free from greed, humble, pure, and likewise righteous.
Indeed, domestic priests and ministers should be endowed with these qualities:
they must be intelligent, proficient in political ethics, free from laziness, and pleasant in speech. (82)

The word *amā* signifies "together"; thus, "those who exist together," "those who move together," or "ministers" (*amātyāḥ*)—these are one meaning. "Possessing affection" means that the subjects are naturally attached to him; for affection [arises] toward the subjects...

He should be one who knows the methods for detecting the vulnerabilities of others, understands the specific requirements of the timing for military expeditions, is skilled in the meaning of the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra), is loyal, and is of noble birth. || 83 ||
Those who know the truth of legal procedure, who are intelligent and highly learned, should always be appointed by kings as experts in both place and time. (84)
Impartial, righteous, and steadfast, they distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
patient, self-controlled, and having conquered anger, they look with equanimity upon all things. (85)
Such twice-born men should be appointed as judges upon the seat of dharma—those who are upright, vigilant, free from laziness, and have conquered fatigue. (86)
Kauṭilya says that [the ministers] possess all virtues: they are free from vices, unattached to women, liquor, hunting, gambling, and the like;
they understand the meaning of the *Arthaśāstra* through its unity of purpose and intent;
they are "unassailable by others," meaning they are incorruptible; and they possess knowledge of the *Arthaśāstra* and its application.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to skill in that basis; that is to say, it is the knowledge of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the term *prāḍvivāka*: one who asks for a determination regarding a subject of dispute is called a *prāḍvivāka*. Those by whom the distinction (*viveka*) among those who mostly engage in disputes is expressed are the *prāḍvivākas*. The form *prāk* is derived from the root *pracch* (to ask) with the suffix *kvip*; when the long vowel is applied, the form becomes *prāk*. This is [the derivation] of the prefix *pra-* combined with the root *vac* (to speak).
In the case of the suffix *ghañ* [applied to the root *vac*], it becomes *vivāka*. Here, "naya" refers to the treatise on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), because it is the cause of policy (*naya*).
Those who are affectionate, patient, disciplined, impartial, and likewise skillful—
They were knowers of logic and knowers of discipline, and were skilled in the processes of reasoning and refutation. || 87 ||
Likewise, those appointed as princes should be endowed with the meaning of all the scriptures;
one should desire for them the qualities described in the doctrine of Bṛhaspati.
That which is to be known, that which is to be presented, and the deliberation of the members of the court—thus has this decision of the judge been declared by me to you. (89)

Thus, the Vinaya is the legal treatise (dharmaśāstra) here; they are appointed for the protection of the princes, the sons of kings. And this has been stated as their essential nature in brief; however, in detail, it should be sought from those who specialize therein.

He shows that one should ascertain [this] from the treatises by the phrase "from the doctrine of Bṛhaspati," meaning from the works of Bārhaspatya, Auśanasa, and others. Regarding the phrase "of these," it refers to those beginning with the king’s army commander and ending with the prince’s appointed officials; whatever is to be known by them, or what is to be offered or accomplished.
The connection is that one should also observe the [opinions] of Bārhaspatya and others.

Now, as to how many judges there should be, he says "and of the members of the court" (*sabhyānām*). The meaning is that one should know [the truth] precisely from their opinion. It is the king’s duty to protect his subjects from the "law of the fish" (*mātsyanyāya*).
The "Mātsyanyāya" (the law of the fish) is prevented by the determination of legal disputes; and in that regard, the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) alone is the primary authority.

Thus, it is well known in the world that the presiding judge occupies the position of the king. By designating the matter in terms of the principal figure, he concludes: "Thus has this decision of the presiding judge been declared by me to you. It is for the benefit of the king.
This concludes the determination of the external and internal retinues.
Hereafter, I shall further explain the various modes of dramatic representation.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*, titled "The Conduct of Men and Women.
The author introduces the next chapter with the words "henceforth" (*ata ūrdhvam*). This intention is repeated again and again:
although there is a variety of acting within general dramatic representation, the specific nature of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) has nevertheless been demonstrated.
For it has already been shown that the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), its transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), and so forth, possess primacy.

However, in the case of *citrābhinaya* (pictorial representation), what is called "harmonization" (*samānīkaraṇa*)—consisting of a blending and cultivation of the various modes of representation—is directed toward external objects suitable for the [expression of] sentiments and the like. By means of this:
The variegated dramatic gesture (citrābhinaya) is indeed a specific instance of the general dramatic gesture; may there be auspiciousness!
The twenty-fourth chapter, containing a brief analysis,
has been composed by me, Abhinavagupta, who is solely devoted to the service of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on the conduct of men and women, in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭyaveda* composed by the illustrious Great Śaiva teacher Abhinavagupta.
The Nāṭyaśāstra,
Chapter Twenty-five:
Citrābhinaya (Representation by Means of Gestures).

That particular variety of gestures of the limbs and so forth which, in various instances, is not explicitly mentioned [in the rules] but is nevertheless expressed, is known as the "Variegated" (citra) or "Diverse" (citrābhinaya). || 1 ||

Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter: Victorious is Śiva, who takes the form of the Supreme Person— the protagonist in the drama of saṃsāra— and who is skilled in the composition and application of the various modes of dramatic representation through speech, limbs, spirit, and gesture.

It has been stated that the variegated acting (*citrābhinaya*) is the remainder of general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*). In the chapter on general acting alone, there was a unification of the specific objects of acting, which are primarily of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Here, however, the subject matter consists of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, which are useful for that [general acting]. Furthermore, the very same acting that was previously defined is precisely what is treated here.

When another action cannot be obtained, one who represents a meaning contrary to that [action] is called *citra* (the "extraordinary"). The connection [of this topic] is that it will be defined in the chapter on *vairādhya* (contrariety). This is what he states: "Of the representation of limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth.
By "limbs" (*aṅga*), he means the *karaṇas* and *aṅgahāras*; their status as representation (*abhinayatva*) has not yet been stated. Therefore, he will say:

"The performance of those [beings] such as the peacock, the crane, and the swan, which are naturally terrestrial, should be [accomplished] through *recakas* and *aṅgahāras*. ... (Nāṭyaśāstra 25.68, 69, etc.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it will be stated that the *vibhāva* and so forth are also the performance (*abhinaya*) of the *vibhāva*.

*Abhinaya* (acting/gesture) is so called because one is represented (*abhinīyate*) by means of it; its specific varieties will be described later starting with "the highest of the high" (*uttamottama*).

Furthermore, that which is represented is also called *abhinaya*. For that which has been described as acting by another [author] is here also stated to be acting in the sense of another form of acting, such as through the pressing of the *alapa* and *padmaka* gestures.

Regarding the phrase "the grasping of all meanings" (25.13, second half): the connection is that the term *aṅgābhinaya* functions as a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and it refers to the specific distinction that is being stated. "In some cases" means not everywhere.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward and positioned them in the svastika gesture at the sides, with the head tilted upward and gazing upwards; || 2 ||
He perceived the dawn, the sky, the night, the twilight, and likewise the day;
the seasons, the clouds, the forest edges, and vast bodies of water.
One should perform the representation of the quarters, the planets together with the stars, and whatever else may be stable, accompanied by various glances.
Again with these same hands and that same head,
one should then indicate those situated on the ground by looking downward.
One should indicate the moonlight, pleasure, wind, taste, and smell by means of the very perception of touch and likewise by its sudden intensification.

In this regard, because there is no difference [between them], that specific detail is sometimes not mentioned and sometimes indeed mentioned, such as in the passage beginning with "the performance of the *svastika* and *vicyuti*" (9.22). That very same superior specific detail is itself the *citra-abhinaya* (variegated representation), since it brings about a state of equilibrium; therefore, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), it is called *citrābhinaya* in various places.

Since dawn and so forth are common to all people, he says, "having placed the two hands palm upwards," in order to demonstrate the variety of the performance (*abhinaya*) concerning those objects through the application of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). By means of the movement known as *svastika-vicyuti*, that which is to be performed includes the directions,
the clouds, the sky, the forest, the oceans, the seasons, the surface of the earth, and vast expanses.

It has been stated [in verse 9.136]: "In the *saṃyukta* hand-position, there is the *svastika*. Here, specific details such as the upward-facing position, the head being turned to the side, the lifting of the head, and the upward direction of the gaze are described. This should be applied accordingly in the subsequent sections.
Regarding "various gazes" (*nānādṛṣṭi*): at times it is the "astonished" gaze, and at times the "diminished" gaze, and so on in sequence, [ending with] the upward [gaze].
He states that what is contrary to oneself should be represented as being situated below, saying "by looking downward.
Regarding the statement that things are "situated in their own place," he asks how objects such as the moon in the sky are to be represented;
he replies: "precisely by the perception of touch."
By covering himself with a cloth, he may ward off the sun, as well as dust, smoke, and wind; likewise, by desiring shade, he may protect himself from the heat of the earth and the burning sun. (7)
With an upward and squinting gaze, one should indicate the sun at midday;
likewise, with expressions of wonder, one should point out the sun at its rising and setting.
Those [sentiments] which are associated with gentle objects and produce a state of happiness should be enacted through bodily touches that cause horripilation.
The wise man should also represent those forms that are fierce through lack of contact, through agitation, and through contortions of the face.
A wise person should represent matters endowed with profundity and nobility through limbs that are full of majesty, pride, and graceful poise.
Having slightly contracted the eyes and raised the eyebrows, likewise by touching the cheeks—(22.83)—he whose shoulders shake upward like an owl;
"rajas" means dust; the sun that has gone to the mountains of sunrise and sunset, the eastern and western mountains.
"Smaya" (wonder) is the "abhinaya" (representation), meaning those for which the purpose is representation by way of wonder;
thus, it means one should demonstrate them through gestures of wonder. He states the definition that encompasses all [of these]:
"those which are joined with gentle meanings. This clarifies that their very purpose is gentleness.

Of that state in which happiness is predominant, the accomplishment was made for those [beings] from whom that state of predominant happiness proceeds—[a state] as gentle and pleasant as Soma. By means of "contractions" (*vikuṇṭhanaiḥ*), that is, by means of "compressions.
The expression "endowed with the profound and the sublime" (*gabhīrodāttasaṃyuktān*) is a designation emphasizing the abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna*). Therefore, regarding that object...

[This section concerns] profundity and loftiness. Herein, at the beginning, there is an expansion of the branches: starting from the self-designation as "Gandharva," following the sequence of profound and noble [themes], there is the performance of the necklace appropriate for a king... [and] the swan situated in the region of the sacred thread (*upavīta*). The first [hand gesture] has the thumb bent and curved like a bow; the rest [is as follows].
One should indicate laughter by placing the hand in the region of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
When the two hands are moved apart in the *svastika* gesture, it indicates necklaces, garlands, and strings of pearls. (12)
By the rotation of the index finger and the turning of the gaze, there occurs the grasping of all objects through the pressure of the *alapa* and *padmaka* [mudrās]. || 13 ||
That which is to be heard should be indicated through the application of hearing, and that which is to be seen through the acts of looking;
one should point out whether it resides within oneself, in another, or in between.
Lightning, meteors, the roar of clouds, sparks, and flames should be represented by the performers through trembling limbs and the blinking of eyes. (15)

For when the [fingers] are separated and turned upward within the interval, it is the burden of the body; the removal of the ornament from the chest is likewise the grasping of everything by that very same movement—thus is the action of the *sūcīmukha* described. By means of the rotation of the index finger, he describes a specific mode of movement through such circumambulation.
Regarding the performance of all objects through vision, he also mentions another type of performance, namely *alapadmakapīḍā* and so forth.

By the term *alapadmaka*, its fingers are meant; *pīḍā* is their contact with the palm, and a plurality is intended therein. Thus, the meaning is as follows: those [fingers] which are *āvartinī*s (revolving) in the palm—this is what is called *alapallava*.
It has been stated that, in its sequence, the little finger (*kanīyaḥ*) should be joined with the palm of the hand;

this constitutes the *sarvārthābhinaya* (the gesture representing all objects). Furthermore, this form was not previously mentioned for the *alapadma* [mudrā]. Now, when the word "all" (*sarva*) is employed in its entirety—as in the expression "the entire word" (*sarvaḥ śabdaḥ*) and so forth—then:

He states the specific auxiliary [condition] by saying, "it should be audible through the application of hearing" (25.14). Having turned the gaze sideways and with the head slightly bent to the side, this constitutes the "application of hearing.

All modes of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) whose objects are sounds accompanied by that [application], as well as those representations previously mentioned for objects such as lightning and the like, [are included here].

As it has been said: "For example, like a needle, fingers spread apart, lightning, a wheel, and a flash of lightning" (9.66). He states their specific characteristics with the word "terrified": [it refers to] the gesturing of the limbs and eyes out of fear of a real object.
Having made the hands in the *udveṣṭita-parāvṛtti* gesture and bowing the head,
one should perform [the rite] with a sidelong glance when there is no contact or when it is undesirable.
One should ward off wind, heat, and darkness by covering the face,
and one should also keep away dust, water droplets, gnats, and bees.
Having formed them into the shape of a svastika with their palms closed like lotus buds and facing downwards,
one should visualize lions, bears, monkeys, tigers, and other beasts of prey.
The *svastika* and *tripatāka* gestures are prescribed for bowing at the feet of one's gurus;
the *khaṭaka* and *svastika* are likewise recorded for holding the goad.

The term *nimeṣa* means contraction. He also describes the gestures (*abhinaya*) suggested by lightning and other phenomena with the words "twisted and turned around. When twisted all around and turned, the fingers—having been released one by one starting from the little finger—form a fist in the front part, but in the rear part...

"Averse" means free from greed. In this context, it is established that [the gaze] belongs to one who has attained [this state] through a "crooked" look (*jihyadṛṣṭi*). A "crooked look" (*jihmā dṛṣṭi*) is defined as: "One that is contracted by being drawn [downward], with the eyelids slightly closed, gazing slowly and askance, and hidden with a concealed pupil" (8-73). This is the acting (*abhinaya*) for lions and tigers, according to the *Ūrṇanābha* [tradition] (9-121).
The ritual action has been stated. Regarding that, he states the specific detail: "having formed them in the shape of a svastika.

Since the phrase "like the buds of a lotus" was mentioned previously without a subsequent specification, and because the lotus bud is the subject under discussion, the fingers of the hands are contracted;
this is the *ūrṇanābha* [gesture]. Others say that the aforementioned action belongs specifically to the lotus bud itself.

It demonstrates the unmentioned function of the *tripatāka* [hand gesture]: "The *svastika* and *tripatāka* [gestures] are for the salutation of the feet of the gurus. The function of the *khaṭakāmukha* [gesture] has been stated:
"The tasks of churning, drawing arrows, gathering flowers, and goading" (compare 9.63). In that regard:
Regarding the specific function of the goad, he says: "The *khaṭaka* and *svastika* [positions] are also for the grasping of the goad."
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eightfold; or it may be nine or even ten—such is the counting that occurs by means of the fingers. (20)
Those known as ten, those known as a hundred, and likewise those known as a thousand, should be employed by performers with their hands acting as banners. (21)
That which occurs here beyond the enumeration known as the "ten" must be accomplished through the meaning of the sentence itself and by means of indirect representation (*parokṣābhinaya*).
The parasol, banner, and flag are to be indicated by means of holding a staff;
furthermore, various weapons are to be indicated based on their specific modes of grasping. (23)

Now, demonstrating the gestures of numbers used in all conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*), he shows the previously unstated functions of the very same hands mentioned before. This is what is meant: with the index finger in the shape of a needle-point (*sūcīmukha*) and the other fingers in the *tripatāka* position, [the number] eight is formed by four upward-pointing fingers.

Through the opening of the bud-like hands, there is the enumeration beginning with one up to five; however, from six onwards, it proceeds by twos—just as in the case of a needle-pointed bud, [the count] goes up to six, and so on until the enumeration reaches ten. Beyond that, there is the representation of plurality.
He says "evam" (thus) and so forth, beginning with "daśa" (ten). Those which have "ten" as their designation here are the numbers twenty and so on; for "viṃśati" is [derived from] "viṃśat.
Therefore, he says that the representation here is by means of two flags (*patākā*), using the term "designated as ten" (*daśākhyā*).
The word "designation" (*ākhyā*) denotes a limit. It signifies that as many states (*bhāva*) extend [therein] until ten. Thus, they are limited by ten.

"Whatever the number" means the counting that extends up to ten; beyond that, it should be indicated in brief or by mere plurality. Here, the word *vākyārtha* (sentence-meaning) indicates "briefly," for it is the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*) that are condensed therein. And this applies to the representation of things that are not present to the senses (*parokṣābhinaye*).
In the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), however, the counting is by means of the designation of each individual item. Regarding the phrase "grasping the long staff" (9-62):

although the action of the *khaṭakāmukha* hand has been stated in general terms, he says "umbrellas, banners, and flags" in order to show its specific application; the meaning is that these are included within the very manner of holding the staff.
By the word "ca" (and), he indicates another gesture here as well; and in the case of the word "atha," it is as follows: [one should place the hand] above the head with the palm facing downward.
For when Vitarka is recollected in meditation, one should have a single-pointed mind, look downward, keep the head slightly bent, and form the pincer gesture with the left hand.
Having raised the head and made the two swan-wings move circumambulatorily, they should be performed by the practitioners as being elevated and shaped like offspring.
Having raised the head and likewise directed the swan-face upward, one should appease that pride which is designated as "long-lived" (dīrghasattva). || 26 ||
Raising the left hand in a curved position at the level of the head,
one should employ it when [the subject] has departed, when [an action] is completed, when [something] is destroyed, and when speaking with exhaustion.
With all his senses in good health and a serene countenance, one should designate the autumn by the various sights of the earth. (28)
Furthermore, the winter season should be enacted by men of middle and lower status through the contraction of their limbs and by attending to the intense heat of the sun and fire. (29)

In the case of the banner and the parasol, there are five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for the upward-pointing flag; in the needle-fingered banner, there are the fist, the peak, the *kapittha* fruit, the deer-head, and so forth, according to their application in weapons. In the yoga-meditation, it is "small" (*stoka*). (9-114) In some cases, people are amazed by the sight of an unprecedented abundance of rice; in others...
"Because of not seeing what is desired by the sick," and so forth; "the first occurrence of calamity," such as the various types of views and the like;
"in that [calamity], the state resulting from its causes," which is the attainment of another condition; "from that cause"—this is the grammatical connection.
Regarding the word "rūkṣasya": it refers to that which causes agitation, just as the monsoon rains at night do not rain in their initial portion.
"Wherein the monsoon clouds [are present]" (p.
by the trembling of the head, teeth, and lips, and by the contraction of the limbs.
And by moans accompanied by hissing sounds, a low person indicates cold. || 30 ||
Having reached another state, even the most excellent ones may at times perform the representation of cold due to the occurrence of some divine calamity. (31)
Likewise, by smelling the fragrance of flowers blooming in their season,
and from the touch of dry wind, the wise man should perceive the quality of cold.
The spring season is to be enacted through various kinds of enjoyments that produce delight, and by displaying diverse flowers. (33)
A wise person should represent the summer through the wiping away of sweat, the heat of the ground, the presence of seeds, and the touch of hot wind.
One should indicate the rainy season by means of groves of Kadamba and Nīpa trees, grassy meadows filled with Indragopaka insects, and clouds accompanied by winds pleasant to the touch. (35)

*Nirghāta* is a crashing sound like a thunderclap in the sky, a noise distinct from mere rumbling; it is a sign, specifically one of the six types such as *puṣpa-puṣpa*. Regarding the phrase "that which is appropriate for that time," although it should be stated as "the ornaments, decorations, and so forth [of the object] in which [time]," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here by depending on the mere relationship, as in the expression "the action" (*karma*).
In some cases there is a following of form, and so forth; for example, in one place sunlight, in another the moonlight.
The representation of entities through their determinants (*vibhāva*) is, for instance, the use of the needle-mouthed face, fingers, and so on, for anger directed toward another.
Then, one should predict a rainy night by means of deep sounds like the roar of a mass of clouds, the falling of torrents, and the thunderous crashes of lightning. (36)
If a person's mark, dress, action, or even physical form is indicative of it, then that season is to be identified by it, because it reveals both desired and undesired objects. (37)
One should indeed represent these seasons according to their purpose, following the nature of their flavors:
those that are pleasant as endowed with happiness, and those whose meaning is sorrowful as joined with suffering. (38)

Whoever is permeated by a certain state of being, whether it be one that bestows happiness or its opposite, perceives everything as consisting of that very state due to the latent impressions (saṃskāra) instilled by it. (39)

One should perform the representation of the emotions (bhāva) through the illustration of the determinants (vibhāva), and likewise, the accomplishment of the emotions is brought about through the consequents (anubhāva). (40)
The effect brought about by *vibhāva* is conveyed by the *anubhāva*;

through that medium, anger (*krodha*) is clearly indicated. By this, the specific intention regarding what was stated in the same chapter is shown. For it was said there: "In the same way, anger [is manifested] toward an enemy in one's own country" (22-).

(Adhyāya). Thus, the connection is as follows: one should perform the enacted representation (*abhinaya*) set in motion by the accomplishment of the emotional states (*bhāva*) through the "swan's wing" (*haṃsapakṣa*), which consists of the single word named "affection" (*sneha*). .......... &o; this is the enacted representation [performed] by means of facial contortions and so forth appropriate for grief. Now, raising the objection, "How can an excitant (*vibhāva*) be an enacted representation?", he says:
"The effect is brought forth by the determinants (vibhāva). This means that the determinant is the instrument (*karaṇa*), that is to say, the indicator (*gamaka*).
For it is by means of the determinant that the effect is brought forth; indeed, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), even when deviating from the effect, necessarily indicates it.
One's own experience is the state (bhāva), while the perception of another is the non-state (vibhāva). || 41 ||

Whether he be a teacher, a friend, a companion, an affectionate one, a relative, or even a kinsman—whoever is approached and made known [as such] is traditionally known as the *vibhāva* (the excitant). 42.

But that worship which is performed with devotion through hurried rising, offerings of water for the feet and guest-reception, seats, and so forth, is proclaimed as *anubhāva* (manifestation). || 43 ||
In this way, [the relationship] should be understood for other cases as well, by demonstrating various effects.
Now, one might ask: "How can an emotion (*bhāva*) be the indicator (*gamaka*) of an ensuant (*anubhāva*)? To this he says: "by means of the ensuant" (*anubhāvena*).
The truth in this matter is that it is an indicator because of the experience of its co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with another experience [of the emotion]. As it has been said:

"One should perform the representation (*abhinaya*) of the consequents (*anubhāva*) as they proceed from the establishment of the states (*bhāva*). Now, for those who are prone to forgetfulness, he demonstrates the nature of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the states (*bhāva*), and the consequents (*anubhāva*) by pointing them out individually, beginning with:
"The state (*bhāva*) is the experience within oneself," and so forth. That experience which rests within the self...

The meaning is that "existence" (*bhāva*) is that which has the nature of the cognition of pleasure and pain. By the inclusion of the term "self" (*ātman*), it is implied that the experience of jars and other such objects is not existence. Others read the suffix *ṇic* [in the root *anubhū*]; in that case, the meaning is: "that by which the self is experienced. Since no such object exists, a sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*) is understood. Therefore...
Whatever possesses the nature of an attained reality must necessarily be experienced in the form of pleasure and so forth; that alone is said to be "bhāva" (the state of being).
However, all cognition of objects distinct from that [experience] is "vibhāva" (the determinant cause), because it generates pleasure and the like. Thus he says:
The *vibhāva* is "the sight of another. He illustrates this with the passage beginning "the teacher and the friend," and so forth.

When the teacher is seen, at the very outset there is enthusiasm for the acquisition of discipline; in this regard, the state of being an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) should be applied to the friend and others as appropriate, such as joy.

A "friend" (*mitra*) is one who, by virtue of some business, shares a common reputation; a "companion" (*sakhi*) is one known from playing together in the dust; and a "playmate" (*sahapāṃsukrīḍana*) is one familiar from childhood play.

By the phrase "is made known," he shows that the object of perception itself possesses existence. By the phrase "having been reached," he states the cause by indicating the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the teacher and others when the mental modification (*citta-vṛtti*) arises. As for the phrase "of whomsoever," it refers to the rising up or going forth to meet the teacher and others out of respect, performed with great effort.
The meaning is that the two indicators [of the emotion] are expressed through words such as "embracing" and "gathering" according to what is appropriate for the state [of the emotion].
He shows that this is merely an illustration by saying, "and so it is with others as well.
Whether it be the absence of emotion (vibhāva) or the presence of emotion (bhāva), it should be understood by the wise according to the requirements of the context. || 44 ||
Furthermore, whatever message from the master is delivered here by the messenger should be understood as "anubhāva" (the expressive power), as it is manifested through the counter-message. || 45 ||
Thus, emotion (bhāva), its cessation (vibhāva), and the consequent emotion (anubhāva) have been described;
these are to be enacted by men or even by women. (46)
In the representation of natural disposition (*svabhāva-abhinaya*), the stance for men should be the Vaiṣṇava;
for women, the stance should naturally be either the Āyata or the Avahittha. (47)
