Indeed, the remaining [expressions] also arise by virtue of the specific purpose, through various enactments of different states and through diverse applications. (48)
The sense is that this refers to the sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and so forth; or rather, by a single mention, the manifesting emotion (anubhāva) is indicated.

The word "api" serves as a disjunctive particle (vikalpa), while it also conjoins (samuccinoti) the nature of both the permanent (sthāyin) and transitory (vyabhicārin) emotions. "By the force of the matter" means by the force of the purpose.

But surely it can be said that this [object] is invariably the *vibhāva* (excitant cause) for this mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), since we observe that the same thing serves as a *vibhāva* elsewhere when associated with a different purpose. It is not only perception that makes the directly observed experience known as a mental modification; rather, it is so even through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

To show that [the object] is also unknown through words and so forth, he says: "But even that which is a counter-message. This is also an illustration for inference; for in deep darkness, [an emotion] is inferred from the stammering and heavy speech of a virtuous person, and indeed, the comprehension of grief arises even from tears.

He concludes this with the words "In this way," and so forth. Regarding the statement "by men or by women," he indicates their place without causing distraction, and demonstrates their movement through the passage beginning with "the natural acting" (*svabhāvābhinaya*). The phrase "the remaining ones" means other places as well. As it has been said:
The activity of men should be endowed with firm and graceful limbs, while the activity of women should be performed with soft and playful gestures of the limbs. (49)
The graceful movements of the hands, feet, and limbs of women are prescribed [as *lalita*], whereas those of men performed by practitioners are known as *sudhīra* and *uddhata*.
Just as there is the manifestation of the emotions of women according to their sentiments and dispositions, so too is there the distinct representation of the emotional states of men and women. (51)
I shall explain in due order the appropriate experience of these states:
through the embracing of the limbs and with a smiling glance.
Likewise, by the act of embracing, a man should display joy, with his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears. (53)
The dancer should manifest joy through affectionate words accompanied by smiles;
meanwhile, [the lover] should have his eyes wide and bloodshot, and his lower lip bitten.
Having performed the actions of a man endowed with the graceful play of fortitude, the performers should then enact the behavior of women in a different manner. (25.49)

"With bodily movements characterized primarily by gentleness and grace"—thus he states the reason for its being established as such in that context with the words "the movement of hands, feet, and limbs. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a reason. "By means of the embracing of the limbs" means that they mutually embrace only their own respective bodies. "But one should represent anger through [transitory] emotions" refers to the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory mental states).
It should be understood as "attainment.
276) And the man, his limbs trembling with sighs, should express his anger.
With eyes filled with tears, due to the trembling of his chin and lips. || 55 ||
By shaking the head, by knitting the brows, by silence, by the movement of a finger, and by the avoidance of garlands and ornaments. || 56 ||
When a woman stands in a long-stretched posture, she may be angry; this is indicated by frequent sighs and gasps, and by her downward gaze and brooding thoughts. (57)
Furthermore, one should indicate the suffering of men by means of words concerning the sky, as well as by weeping, sighing, and striking the head. (58)
One should cause suffering to women through the impact of falling from heights;
whether that suffering arises from joy, from affliction, or indeed from jealousy. (59)
That which was previously described as "weeping" should be applied to women and low-born persons, along with gestures of agitation and haste, and by means of brandishing weapons. (60)
One should feign fear in men by means of the agitation of courage, strength, and so forth, through eyes with trembling pupils and limbs that throb and tremble. (61)

For while the general representation of the *rasas* was shown by way of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic), here it is shown among the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*). "Suffering" refers to grief (*śoka*). Regarding the phrase "with blows from the hands upon the ground":
*hastatāḍana* means striking with the hands; thus, [the gesture] is performed with the hands in such a manner of striking against the ground, and likewise [the gesture] of the space (*ākāśa*).
The meaning is that even though it is empty, it proceeds as a support;
and because his heart is terrified, he gazes toward his sides.
And likewise from searching for her husband and from crying out loudly. || 62 ||
A woman should also fear the embrace of her lover; she should employ those intoxications previously described toward low men. (63)
By means of soft, stumbling steps due to constant support from the sky, as well as by rolling of the eyes and languid speech; || 64 ||
A woman should manifest intoxication through the trembling of her limbs;
by this method, the applications arising from specific causes should be performed. 65.
Whether they arise from the male or the female, all emotional states (bhāvas) pertaining to dramatic representation must be performed with great effort by women in a graceful manner.
One should perform heroic actions endowed with firmness and sweetness;
one should employ these with the fingers in the *tripatāka* gesture, which are bent.
Parrots and mynas, as well as those birds that are minute, and peacocks, cranes, swans, and others, even those that are large by their very nature. (68)

With their movements described as "clinging," "discoursing in artistic grace," "moving slowly with shifting steps," "with expanded *aṅgahāras*," and "with the modes of gait defined in the fourth chapter [of the *Nāṭyaśāstra*]," they performed appropriate actions of the head, neck, and so forth— such as the hurried gestures of women and low-born men out of fear.
Their performance should be carried out through exhalations (*recaka*) and bodily gestures (*aṅgahāra*).
[The subjects include] donkeys, camels, mules, lions, tigers, cows, buffaloes, and so forth. (69)
These—beings, piśācas, yakṣas, and dānavas along with the rākṣasas—should be represented by the performers through their movements, gaits, and bodily gestures. (70)
They are to be indicated by means of *aṅgahāras*, even by the proclamation of their names;
those who are not directly perceptible are to be indicated by means of *aṅgahāras*. (71)

The gods, however, should be represented visibly through gestures of fear and agitation, along with expressions of wonder, as well as by their characteristic marks, acts of prostration, inner dispositions, and physical movements.
For in dramatic performance, those things that are not directly perceptible must be conveyed by those skilled in the art through the power of meaning;
thus, with the right hand raised and slightly curved, one should touch the head. (73)
For this salutation is prescribed for a man who is not present in person, whether he is known as Khaṭakāvardhamāna or Kapota. (74)
One should salute the deities, the gurus, and women;
as well as those celestial dwellers who are worthy of worship and those who appear in person.

For the highest [type of spectators], however, there is wonder at the sight of Rākṣasas and the like. And here, the [emotions] residing in the *bhāvas* and so forth are expressed by words such as *anubhāva*... [and] by the *bhāvas*... (as on p.
One should engage them—great people, circles of female companions, as well as parasites and rogues—with authoritative means, displays of power, and profound meanings. (76)
A person should represent mountains by means of a circular hand gesture combined with height,
and likewise tall trees by means of elevation.
One should employ the *samūhasāgara* formation against an army that is very extensive and spread out, using both arms extended and raised high.
With both hands in the *patākā* (banner) gesture raised, one should indicate heroism, fortitude, pride, arrogance, generosity, and loftiness. (79)
One should display the *tvarāla* [mudrā] by means of the position at the forehead;
the two hands, however, are drawn away from the chest region in the form of a deer’s head (*mṛgaśīrṣaka*).
The *vistīrṇa* (extended) and *pradruta* (flowing) movements, along with the upward toss (*utkṣepa*), should be employed when the space is open;
the hands, with palms facing downward and then upward, are slightly extended.
Having performed this, one should represent the time [of their return] as being at the entrance of a cave, a house, or a mountain cavern;
they may be portrayed as being at will possessed by curses or planetary spirits, or with minds afflicted by fever.
The wise should perform the gestures (ceṣṭita) of these [deities] with hands corresponding to their respective limbs and so forth.

Regarding the gestures of Rudra’s fierce performance (raudrābhinaya) as he speaks, just as Rudra’s emblems are known— specifically his trident being properly understood in its circular form— the term "patāka" alone is used here by virtue of the context.

A distinction must be understood [here]. Regarding the phrase "by means of the limbs and so forth" (*aṅgādyaiḥ*), the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompasses the *adṛṣṭi* (the gaze) and the *sāttvika* (involuntary physical expressions).
"By similar ones" (*sadṛśaiḥ*) refers to forms such as swinging hands and the like. "By moving ones" (*vilolanaiḥ*) means by those that are flickering; this is the intended sense.
One should perform the ritual gesture of the swing by means of the swaying of the swing. || 83 ||
When the swing, Aṅgavatī, becomes manifest as a physical object through the agitation of its limbs and the grasping of the ropes, [it is successful]. (84)
For those who have entered upon their seats, swinging (ḍolana) should be performed there;
I shall now speak here of the words of the void and those directed toward the self. 85.
The *apavāritaka* (aside) and the *janāntika* (whispering), as well as that which is spoken from a distance and the communication of the bodiless (unseen). 86.
A sentence that is indirect or interrupted is called "speech like space" (ākāśavacana);
in that case, one should engage in conversation using sentences composed by the respondent.
That speech which, arising from the nature of poetry and joined with various causes, resides within the heart, is considered to be "internal" (ātmagata). (88)

That [speech] accompanied by *vitarka* (deliberation) is generally to be employed in dramas and the like. Now, in connection with the topic of vocal expression (*vācika*), he promises to describe various modes of performance, beginning with "words from the air" (*ākāśavacanāni*). He says "bodiless" (*aśarīram*) because it refers to a conversation with a character who is situated at a distance and has not yet entered the stage.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the announcement": by means of what is spoken by another, there is a connection with a character who has entered but is hidden or separated [from the audience].

Anticipating the objection—"But how can a statement concerning someone not present on stage be uttered?"—he says: "In that case, by those things performed as subsequent," meaning one should employ those sentences performed as subsequent [replies], such as "Do not speak thus," and so forth. This refers to what was stated previously.

The point is that agency belongs only to the character who has actually entered [the stage]; the statement of another's words is merely a shadow of a report, as if one who has entered [the role] were to speak thus.
That which is joined with a concealed intention is known as apavāritaka. || 89 ||
That which is not heard by those standing nearby due to the exigency of the action is *janāntika*;
that which is held in the heart with mental construction (*savikalpa*) is *bhāvastha*, and that which is directed toward oneself alone is *ātmagata*. (90)
Thus, these words containing hidden meanings in this drama should be employed by the speakers as *janāntika* (aside) into the ear. 91.
However, that matter which was previously discussed should be told again for a specific reason; it should be spoken in the ear so that it does not become a mere repetition. (92)
One should recite without deviation the *ākāśabhāṣita*, *janāntika*, *ātmagata*, and *pāṭhya* speeches—those which are direct or indirect, self-originated or originated by others. (93)
Having placed the hand out of sight, performers should employ the *janāntika* (aside) and likewise the *apavāritaka* (secretly). || 94 ||
The meaning of a sentence spoken in a dream, however, cannot indeed be enacted through the movements of the hands;
rather, that meaning of the sentence should be enacted by means of the very words uttered while asleep. (95)
"Secret intention" (*nigūḍhabhāva*) refers to that which is concealed so that only one person may hear it; this is *apavārita*.

"In private" (*janāntika*) and "in seclusion" (*ekāntika*) are also [used] when only one person's [intention] is concealed; however, the distinction lies in the fact that [the latter two] refer to the concealment of [the speaker's] own state.

Others, however, say: "Both" refers specifically to the *janāntika* (aside). For it is said in the presence—meaning in close proximity—to as many people as must be addressed by it. On the other hand, that is called *avatāritaka* where, after deliberation (*tūha*), one does not speak with reference to another; yet the intention of the speech remains precisely this: "May the other hear."

That *apavāritaka* (aside) is joined with a concealed feeling or intention (*bhāva*) and is invariable; this means that everything previously mentioned, such as the time and so forth, should be followed here.

In a recitation characterized by dreams, the performance should be done with slow modulation of voice, making the meaning of the words clear yet indistinct through repetition, and based on the recollection of what occurred previously.

At the time of death, one should produce a faltering, plaintive cry accompanied by hiccupping and labored breathing, with speech echoing the sound of a bell whose tolling consists of loose and heavy syllables of compassion.

One should describe someone afflicted with hiccups or asthma as being like one dead when fainting occurs; likewise, even in cases of extreme intoxication or during a dream-like state, the performance should be conducted in that same manner.
One should employ for the elderly a recitation with faltering and stumbling syllables, as well as one with unfinished syllables; but for children, it should have a sweet, warbling sound.
Having assumed various states in the representation of death, which is highly celebrated [in this context], it should be performed with hands and feet cast about, yet restrained and drooping. (100)
And for one overwhelmed by disease, death should be represented with the limbs in a collapsed position;
likewise, for one afflicted by hiccups and labored breathing, the movement of the limbs should be portrayed as dependent on others.

"Indeed not" means that there is no gesturing with the hands in that case. Having stated "spoken while asleep," he describes those [speeches] by way of their characteristics, beginning with "with a slow movement of voice," and so forth. Those which were performed or employed through the recollection of what preceded, yet are slack—falling away from their proper place—and heavy, clumsy in their own functions.

The syllables associated with the tip, the edge, the middle, and the root of the tongue, as well as that primary speech which imitates a ringing bell— characterized by the variations of faltering voice arising therefrom,
such as high and low pitches, and acute and grave accents— with these [qualities] it is marked.
The connection is that one should utter a faltering voice at the time of death. "With a sweet sound" means with a melodious tone.

Thus, there is speech pertaining to the following: what is spoken from the air (*ākāśābhāṣita*), what is directed to oneself (*ātmagata*), what is whispered aside (*apavārita*), what is spoken in the presence of others (*janāntika*), what is spoken into the ear (*karṇokta*), what is spoken as if in a dream (*svapnāyitokta*), what is spoken during death, fainting, or intoxication, and what is spoken by the elderly or children. These constitute the categories of speech.

Having explained the various dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*), he says "attained through manifold states" (*nānābhāvopagata*) in order to describe what pertains to that [acting] by way of incidental discussion. Poison (p.

Even when poison has been drunk, death must be depicted with the limbs, hands, and feet thrown about, joined with the onset of the poison's force, and accompanied by the twitching of the body's movements. 102.
In the first stage of fever, emaciation is to be represented; in the second, trembling; likewise, burning sensation in the third; and in the fourth, there shall be a parching of the throat. 103.
If the Moon is in the fifth house, there is swelling; in the sixth, the neck is broken;
in the seventh, there is stupor; and in the eighth, death shall occur. (104)
In that regard, during the first stage [of emaciation], there should be the representation of a thin face and cheeks;
one should act out a state of leanness and speak very few words. (105)
One should likewise represent trembling of all the limbs, scratching of the body parts,
the tossing of hands and limbs, and even a burning sensation.
One should represent *vilallikā* in this manner: by means of rolling the eyes and blinking, by belching, vomiting, and tossing about, and by speaking indistinct syllables. (107)
Through the application of belching and vomiting, by various kinds of tossing the head, one should act out frothing at the mouth, as well as unconsciousness and the closing of the eyes. 108.
"One who has drunk poison" (*viṣapīta*) means one by whom poison has been consumed. In this context, it also serves as an illustration for the person who has been bitten.

The connection is as follows: during the first impulse (*vega*) of the poison, there is a circulation through the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), beginning with the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and ending with the vital essence (*ojas*); the performance of emaciation (*kṛśatva*) at that stage is what must be enacted here. The "itching" (*kāmilā*) and vomiting (*chardi*) occur.
The touch of her shoulder and cheek was like an internal burning at its onset; then there was the bending of the head and the glance from the corner of the eye.
Thus, one should act out a state of dullness due to the total delusion of all the sense faculties.

Due to the closing of the eyes, or from the increase of disease, or from being bitten by a serpent—in this manner, indeed, deaths should be enacted by the wise according to the rules of dramatic performance. || 110 ||
Furthermore, in cases of agitation, anger, or those arising from grief and distress, there is no fault here in the repetition of words that are otherwise appropriate. (111)
"Excellent! Alas! Me! And 'Hā hā!'—why do you say this to me? 'Do not say it'!
One should cause such actions to be performed two or three times.
When a poem is performed that is deficient in its constituent parts or is distorted, the wise should not apply the technical definitions of dramatic representation therein. (113)

One should not apply to those of middle status that disposition which belongs to the highest; nor should one apply to those of low status that disposition which belongs to those of middle status. (114)

The meaning is that there is an excess of water (*vāryudreka*) due to contact with the touch of the shoulders and cheeks. "Breaking of the head" refers to the dislocation of the neck joints; the phrase "not repeated among them" implies "not a fault.
He illustrates this with the verse beginning "O, how wonderful! (*sādhv aho*), and so forth. In that example, the repetition of words is seen in "excellent, excellent" (*sādhu-sādhu*), and so on.
"Meaningful repetition," such as "Aha! Well done! O auspicious one! and so forth; "deficient in some minor limb," and so forth.

Because it is primarily characterized by laughter (*prahasana*), it should be performed without being deficient in any minor limb (*pratyaṅga*) or element of refinement (*saṃskārāṃśa*). Precisely because of its distorted nature, it is dominated by humor; therein, even the acting (*abhinaya*) is unconventional (*alākṣaṇika*).
Even so, it is for the sake of laughter alone, however that may be.
Through the various aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) arising from one's own actions, drama attains its passion (*rāga*) among the superior, the middling, and the inferior. (115)
These specific modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya) should be performed, joined with the internal state of being (sattva-bhāva);
however, those others which are worldly should all be executed according to worldly custom.
Just as a garland-maker weaves a garland from various kinds of flowers,
so should one employ the primary and secondary limbs, the sentiments, and the emotions in the performance of drama.
Whatever movement and whatever gait are prescribed for one who has entered the stage,
provided with the proper equipment,
that very same [movement and gait] he should perform, remaining focused on his character.
Until he has withdrawn from the stage. || 118 ||
Now he states the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) which benefits all, beginning with the words "the state (*bhāva*) of the highest ones," and so forth.
"It goes toward passion" means that it becomes something that delights everyone.
Its status as a supplement to the general dramatic representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) follows from the meaning already stated, by way of a concluding summary through that very [expression].

He demonstrates that these are the specific varieties of *citrābhinaya* (variegated acting). By the phrase "endowed with the nature of *sattva*," he recalls that acting is distinct from the [mere] state of being (*sattva*), and so forth. By the word "of various kinds" (*nānāvidhaiḥ*), both the synthesis of the various types of acting and their variegation (*citratva*) are shown. [This occurs] step by step.
With the intent that "what has been accumulated through the power of effort must be preserved with exertion," he recites the verse beginning:

"Whichever is one's sport, the fixed course... (25.118). One whose being is liberated (*vimuktasattva*) is one who has abandoned support and is "fully stilled" (*pratinirvṛta*); by this term "stilling," cessation will be explained. Thus, "withdrawn" (*vṛtta*), he turns away from sense objects, people, and so forth. By that—
(286) Thus have these modes of dramatic representation been declared by me in due order. As for others that are worldly, they should always be adopted by the wise from the world itself. || 119 ||
The world, the Veda, and likewise the inner self—these are remembered as the threefold authority. Drama is for the most part established upon the subjects of the Veda and the inner self. 120.

But drama, which is endowed with the Vedas and the inner self, and possessed of the rules of grammar and prosody, becomes perfected through worldly consensus; for drama is thus of the very nature of the world. (121)
The meaning is that [the actor] should exit once he has finished with the stage and so forth. One might ask: "Is this the only mode of dramatic representation?
To which he replies: "But there are others, namely, worldly ones. Anticipating the objection, "What authority is there here for the world?
he says: "The world, the Veda, and likewise the inner self (adhyātma). This refers to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) established in the world—namely, perception, inference, and scripture.

These are spoken of by the term "world" (*loka*). As for "Veda," it refers to traditional scripture (*āgama*) that is well-known in the world according to its own specific form, such as the *Dhanurveda* among the sciences of logic (*nyāya*), the *Gāndharvaveda* in the context of musical notes and rhythms, and so forth. Regarding "the self" (*adhyātma*), this refers to one's own direct experience (*svasaṃvedana*). Drama (*nāṭya*) [is established] upon those objects of knowledge that are cognized through both the Vedas and the self.

Regarding the phrase "it is well-known," he states the reason: "but it is endowed with Veda and the inner self. The particle *tu* (but) indicates the reason. The word *samanvitam* (endowed) is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). This means that the consistency of words is established by the scripture known as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), while the consistency of meter is established by one's own direct experience (*svasaṃvedana*), for its aesthetic quality (*śravyatā*) is perceived by those who know it.
In cases where self-cognition is established, [the status of] things such as melodies (*rāga*) and linguistic expressions (*bhāṣā*) is brought forth, just as in the case of songs.
This is merely an illustration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the Veda and other scriptures. Then, in order to establish the world as a means of valid cognition, he says:
"That which is established in the world. This means that whatever is established in the world is established; it does not mean that it is unestablished for anyone. For indeed...

No one capable of reasoning would deny what is well-known in the world; for if even one who is utterly deluded were to deny it, the consequence would be that he would become like a piece of wood or a stone. Thus, for that very reason—that is, from that same cause—it is said that *nāṭya* consists of the world, having the nature of a recitation of the world.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a treatise to establish a definitive rule regarding the internal dispositions and activities of the world, both the stationary and the moving. (122)
The dispositions of beings possess diverse characters, yet drama is established upon character;
therefore, those who speak of drama must understand that it is indeed measured by the world. 123.
Having correctly understood these rules of dramatic representation,
the person who applies them on the stage is a practitioner of the performance of the principles of drama.
For he indeed receives the highest honor in the world. || 124 ||

Now, one might object: "If something is established by worldly consensus, it is already known through scripture alone; why then is it stated again by the world? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it is not possible for the world... (verse 122). *Śīla* means inherent nature (*svabhāva*). He concludes the context with: "Therefore, the world indeed must be understood as a means of valid cognition. These...

Regarding the phrase "the rules" (*vidhīn*): by stating that one must "thoroughly understand those rules concerning the forms of performance (*abhinaya*) that are to be carried out, from the general gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*) up to the end of this chapter," he indicates the existence of *citra-abhinaya* (varied or dramatic gesture), even though it is established as a subject of practice in the treatises of Kohala and others.
Therefore, we shall demonstrate illustrative examples so that there may be no interruption in the flow of the tradition:
near the primary [position], Skanda [is formed] from the wings of the swan, or from the sight of the Śakti;
with Khaṭaka hands facing each other on both sides, there is the representation of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
With a pair of tongs consisting of playful glances,
one should fashion Kāmadeva from Durgā as one would from Rudra, and Sarasvatī with skillful means.
...with the skull-bowl likewise [he worships] Śrī;
and with the tusk, the goddess Gaurī and Vārāhī—thus [are] the Mothers.
One should demonstrate [the lineage] through the characteristics residing in the Brāhma and other [varnas] as appropriate;
she whose fingers are like needles, who is a daughter of the Mountain (Himavat), and who is elevated in conduct, is a Nayonnatā.
With that same [hand] turned upward and downward, one forms the *tripatākā-mukha*;
likewise, with the fourth [hand], one forms two serpent heads.
Moving the *ḍola* hand higher and higher with a lateral swaying motion,
one performs the *arāla-tripatāka* gesture and the shaking of two *patāka* hands.
The *abdhi* (four) and *puṣpapuṭa* (two) hand gestures are used for ascetics;
they consist of three fingers extended upwards and turned outwards, with the tips pointing outward and inward respectively.

With the hand placed above the elbow in the *tripatāka* gesture, there should be women on the side with the *ardhakaṭaka* gesture; the world-protectors should be accompanied by their respective emblems.
With bodies stiffened and hands released, one should know that the Jina, the Vidyādharas,
and the subjects have been destroyed by fire, or else the Rākṣasas have perished from the needle-mouthed [demon].

One should know that by means of the two *tripatākā* hands placed on the head, one indicates kings and monkeys; and by means of the two *patākā* hands in the form of snake-heads, positioned in the *svastika* gesture.
Furthermore, Dharma is represented by white and other colors; the seasons are the jewels;
O Lord, the enemy is measured by the *kāṅgula*; and a woman is indicated by the knotted ring finger.
The *sārasa* [hand] is formed by bending the elbows with two trembling *patākā* hands;
the *vṛścika* [hand] is formed by extending both arms for the sake of representing birds on the ground.
In the Śṛṅgī [mudrā], the middle finger and the thumb are raised above the top of the Patākā [hand] from the uplifted position;
the foot is bent, and the two hands are alternately lowered and raised.
(289) Thus, these modes of representation— arising from speech, costume, and the limbs—
must be employed by one skilled in performance who desires success in the drama. 125.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Varied Representation," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
With two hands, he holds a *garuḍa* below both sides of the base of his staff;
with his arms bent at the elbows like banners, he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, manifesting a wrathful form.
The index finger separated at the mouth is used for the representation of speech;
likewise, one should hold it aloft over the crest-lock, the head, or the secondary limbs to signify the grief of a woman.
From the chest and sides, it moves upward into the air with the *patāka* and *svastika* gestures;
likewise, with both hands in the *prabhāta* position, the fingers are whirled about with speed.
If the two [omens] face away, it indicates night; or [it is indicated] by banners, the *svastika*, and so forth.
Due to the covering of the mouth, there is baldness and the like; due to locusts, dust, and smoke-colored [omens], there is distress.
One should place the *patāka* mudrā on the chest for friends; the *arāla* for one’s children and so forth;
the *abhi-mūrdha* for hunchbacks, dwarfs, and children.

When the banner is at the top, it is "fragmented" (khaṇḍa); when the svastika has fallen away, it is "with a treasure" (nidhimat) when the left elbow is contracted, as in the case of Bhūdhara and others.
Their heads should be turned upward, for their distinctions are not seen [otherwise].

She was like a female elephant, with her two cheeks moving gracefully and smeared with ichor;
she was adorned with lotuses, umbrellas, buds, svastikas, and a scorpion.

the Muṣṭi, the Malla, and the Śalya [are formed] with the Khaṭaka in the middle of the chest.
With the *saṃdaṃśa* gesture, the mind is raised from the navel and established in the chest;
with the *pallava* gesture, touching one's own head, there is salutation to the sky-farers (*khecaras*).
With two flags turned away from the face and a svastika displaced from the mouth, there are two door-panels;
from this pair of hands, one beholds a herd of elephants.
In the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, under the Kaniṣṭhā [digit], instruction should be given by a clever person;

In words such as *śūlapāṇi* ("spear-in-hand"), some [hold that] the quality (*guṇa*) is based on the member-word (*varti-pada*), while others manifest it as being based on the qualified object (*viśeṣya*); still others hold it to be based on both.
When the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is unimpeded,
there may be bathing with two banners upon the head, or [the figures] facing each other on a cart.
The elbows should be bent with the hands in the *tripatāka* (three-peaked) position;
this is used for indicating blacksmiths and the like, while the *khaṭaka* (sword) hand is used for the flight of elephants.
In Gaṇeśa, the face is like a bud; then, from the dispersal [of light], rays emerge.
From the head and the two sides... [there are] two triple-patākas, and the matted locks.
The Great Goddess [is worshipped] with two peaks joined one above the other;
or alternatively, the lines may be drawn with a fistful of four grains, such as rice and so forth.

By means of the *khaṭaka* [mudrā], those who are thus mute [become eloquent]; by the sequence of the empty and upturned [palms], through the skillful application of downward-slipping and the closing [of the eyes].
On the left peak, below, with the *patāka* [hand] on the right;
when the two *khaṭaka* hands meet, they are for the Sun and his charioteer, positioned behind and in front.
The *pramāṇa* and *mānaparimā* [gestures] are performed with fingers extended like needles;
the *elākrīḍā* is considered the *pulindābhinaya* (the mimetic representation of a Pulinda) through the application of the bow gesture (*dhanuryoga*).
In the *yāmā* [mudrā] and others, there are the *khaṭaka* and *ārāla*; in the *kapīlinī*, one stands with feet even (*samapāda*).
However, in the *svabāhu* [mudrā], both hands are in the *khaṭaka* position, and the foot is cast to the side (*pārśvakṣepa*).
In the Mahābhairavanātha [mudrā], the hands are placed on the shoulders and knees;
for one who has not yet reached the higher stages, the foot is positioned as described at the conclusion of the ritual action.
The wise know that the mental construction of it through one's own intellect is the "variegated representation" (citrābhinayana).

This has been shown by me, Abhinavagupta, for the sake of the wise, so that their comprehension may be firmly established regarding the subjects as they have been written down. Even the speech of Vācaspati would falter here; how much more so, then, that of those like us?

Thus, having understood [the art] through the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by means of representation (*abhinaya*), he who applies it on the stage in the assembly applies the representations according to their true nature in drama and attains equal [success]; this is how it should be construed.
This application (*prayoga*), which consists of the mutual coordination of the various elements and takes the form of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), is supplementary to the representation itself.

And since there is no accomplishment whatsoever without these, he shows all the general types of leading heroes (*nāyaka*) by means of the verse beginning with *evam*, which—under the guise of a conclusion—demonstrates them as being characterized by the quality of *sattva* through the acceptance of the term "hero" (*aṅgin*). Thus it is established; may there be auspiciousness!
This chapter on various dramatic gestures (abhinaya), its essence having been expounded,
has been composed by Abhinavagupta, who is graced by the grace of Śiva.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Representation of the Variegated," in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭya-veda* composed by the venerable Great Māheśvara teacher Abhinavagupta.

Chapter Twenty-six: The Classification of Temperaments.

When that exists, this conceptualization of the natural state departs from his heart in three ways, becoming something to be cherished;
he is one for whom passion is a majesty within the abode of the venerable.
May he always be full of passion for that as well.

The enactment (*abhinaya*) characterized by unification (*samānīkaraṇa*) has been introduced in relation to the general [definition]. In that regard, just as the mutual unification of the various modes of enactment (*abhinaya*) is to be taught, so too is the unification of the enactor (*abhinetr*) and the enacted (*abhineya*). Thus, by means of the enacted, the enactment is unified by the enactor. This is what is meant by "that very thing" (*tadetad*).
The unification of the performer and the performed, which takes the form of a general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*),
is designated here as the chapter on *prakṛti*. To indicate its purpose, with the intention of demonstrating the logical connection (*saṅgati*),
it was established at the conclusion of the chapter on *vṛtta* that one who "employs" (*prayuṅkte*) is a "performer" (*prayoktṛ*) and one who "knows the performance" (*prayogajña*).

For only he who knows the nature of the instigator and the instigated understands the application [of the term]. In that context, the action (*kṛti*) is to be imitated by the instigated and is to be proclaimed [as such].
They had many arms and many faces, as well as distorted countenances;
they possessed the faces of beasts and wild animals, and the faces of donkeys, camels, horses, and elephants.
These and many others of various forms exist;
these should be fashioned by the teacher from clay, wood, lac, or leather.
One should enter the performance arena in one's natural form,
having concealed one's own appearance with paints and ornaments.
Whatever form belongs to anyone by nature, that very form should be employed in the performance of drama, in accordance with age and dress. (6)
For just as one, having abandoned the nature of being alive, assumes another bodily state,
so does one resort to another state of existence by taking refuge in that other state.
Thus the wise one, remembering with his mind that "I am He," the Supreme Being,
should conduct himself through the speech, gestures, and activities of those [devotees].

These are the synonyms. In that regard, the agent (prayoktṛ) may be similar to the object of application (prayojya), or dissimilar, or of both natures. Among these, "similar" means corresponding; "of both natures" means corresponding to the form of both. By this, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is characterized as belonging to those two alone. Correspondence (*ānurūpya*) arises from similarity.

Although a threefold classification is possible everywhere in some way due to the combination of both [sexes] according to their respective forms, nevertheless, for an intellect like ours— which conforms to the consensus of all the world— there is a corresponding usage in that regard: between a male agent and a male object, or between a female [agent] and a female [object].

There is, however, a dissimilarity between the woman and the man. She [the woman] has a lion-like face, ten faces, and so forth, whereas the men [the husbands] possess similarity with others. He says "anurūpa" (conformable), etc., in order to demonstrate that threefold nature of the *prakṛtis* (characters). Regarding the term "pātrāṇām" (of the characters): by the statement "that from which rasa is held," the concealment of the actor's own intellect is indicated.
Indicating the intellect of the actor—
that which is a delicate performance producing delight for kings;
Having attained the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), one should apply it toward those women. || 9 ||

Those [mantras] fashioned for the fierce and violent combat of battle, and those which appear to be the fury of warriors—these should not be employed against women; they should be employed against men.
It was performed without ostentation and without confusion, with bodily movements that were not exaggerated;
its syllables were regulated by the measures of tempo, rhythm, and the subtle divisions of time.
One should employ such a dance as this, performed by women, wherein the phrasing of the words is well-articulated, neither harsh nor confused. (12)
In this manner, those skilled in dramatic performance should establish the stage-setting;
for women possess the nature belonging to women, and men possess that belonging to men.
That [recollection] is known as being appropriate according to age and condition;
however, when a man assumes a feminine state through his form, [he experiences it]. (14)

He explains the state of being free from fault (*nirduṣṭatā*): it is called *prakṛti* because it is produced in an eminent manner (*prakarṣeṇa kriyate*) and is apprehended as the object of direct perception, conceptualization, and reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
Since this [nature] exists through the future differentiation of its threefold *prakṛti*, it would clearly manifest the drama (*nāṭya*) in an intense manner.

The purpose of knowledge has been stated. To the question "How could it illuminate the universal? he provides the reason by means of a qualification: "by its own nature," and so forth. For the nature of the person to be employed [in drama] must be enacted. In that regard, when a man of delicate nature is to be employed, gracefulness and refinement are achieved for women without effort; thus, he...

In that case, the one who employs [the words] is the one who is "joined" (yukta), or rather, her own nature is what conforms to the form [of the expression]. However, when the person being addressed is arrogant, it is the man himself who is properly joined as the employer;

for when the nature of the person to be addressed is already conformable, the mere recitation [of the words] may somehow be accomplished with effort. Therefore, the respondent must remain attentive in that situation.
O wise one, that innate disposition (*prakṛti*) should be known as corresponding to one's form during practice;
according to her own will, a woman may adopt the masculine stage (*pauruṣī bhūmi*) in a manner suited to herself. (15)
The elderly and the childish should not be employed in the mutual gestures;
for in the performance of the recitation, men should indeed be employed in the Sanskrit.
The voices of women are naturally sweet, whereas those of men are powerful;
even if a man should know the rules of singing along with their technical characteristics. (17)
That song which is devoid of the quality of sweetness (mādhurya) does not produce beauty, wherein the sweetness of men's throats [is surpassed] by the qualities of the women's recitation. 18.
These two ornaments, produced by the reversal of natural order, should be understood as occurring generally in the palaces of gods, kings, generals, and eminent men. (19)

Anticipating the objection that it is indeed appropriate for a nature to correspond [to its effects], he says "nānā" (verse 2): by means of various states— such as the qualities of playfulness, grace, and arrogance—
and by actions.

Since it is endowed with qualities such as being gentle or exalted, and with activities such as going to gardens or donning armor for battle, it is therefore appropriate that *prakṛti* (nature) indeed possesses various forms. He clarifies the essential nature of that *prakṛti* through its synonyms by the term *bhūmikā*. *Bhūmi* means a supporting ground or a state; as it is said in the *Dhyānapaṭa*:

One directs one's intellect toward the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva in forms such as the ten-armed and five-faced [Śiva], yet one should not attend to the specific location or time of that [image]; nor should the material substance made of vermilion, yellow arsenic, and so forth, be regarded as anything more than a mere support for that [divinity]. Thus it is.

Rāma and the others are merely the substratum (avaṣṭambha-sthāna). Nor is that substance made of vermilion, yellow arsenic, and so forth, which serves as the mere substratum. Thus, Rāma and the others are merely the substratum; and this has been explained in detail at the beginning of the Chapter on Rasa (Rasādhyāya).

Therefore, *bhūmikā* means "ground" (*bhūmi*) [in the sense of a stage]. The suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of "itself. Because a formless primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is impossible, and because [the state] is to be accomplished by that [nature], he first states its essential nature with the words "many-armed," and so forth. They have deformed faces; among them, those such as the unclad ones have animal faces, as follows:
Performances composed by women come to possess the nature of men;
thus, in heaven, the art of drama was established among Rambhā, Urvaśī, and others. (20)
In the same way, in this world of men, within the inner apartments of kings,
the teachers must diligently instruct the womenfolk.
Wise men should not personally assume the roles of the various characters in a drama;
rather, the performance should be diligently applied to women, with the roles based on male characters.
Since grace inherent in one's very nature exists in women, therefore, O dear one, their limbs are naturally sweet and easily possessed of beauty. (23)
That which is graceful and elegant is considered the supreme ornament;
furthermore, the performance based on drama should be understood as being of two kinds. (24)

Those with cow-faces, horse-faces, lion-faces, and the faces of beasts of prey—just as those with lion-faces [are described] by the words "in the kingdom of donkeys" and so forth—it follows that they should be made in their respective forms with their entire bodies; this is the necessary implication.
Here he states the reason: "by means of their natural form. That is, by means of a form appropriate to the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is to be celebrated.

"By means of form" (*rūpeṇa*) refers to one's own form (*ātmarūpa*), and by the word "also" (*api*), it includes the form of an actor (*naṭarūpa*), as well as forms fashioned from clay, wood, and so forth, such as [statues with] arms and faces. To demonstrate the primacy of the yoga of support (*avaṣṭambhayoga*), he recalls the reason stated in the twenty-first chapter: "just as the individual soul (*jīva*)," [meaning its inherent nature].
(Verse 7) "Miti" | The connection is: one should emulate the supreme state, such as that of Rāma and others, by means of dress and other attributes.

By the phrase "I am he," he declares that one's own self must not be abandoned. Otherwise, following [the path of] dissolution (*laya*) and so forth would be impossible. Now, raising the question of where the *prakṛti* conforming to that form resides, he says:
"Delicate application" (*sukumāra-prayoga*) is an elliptical expression referring to kings; "delight" (*āmoda*) is the fullness of the determinants (*vibhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "among those women": here, the female performers are intended as the objects of the action by virtue of being the ones upon whom the application is directed. "He should apply it" refers to the master of dramatic performance (*nāṭyācārya*).
(297) The *sukumāra*, the *tathāviddha*, and that which is the locus of the flavors (*rasa*) of various emotions (*bhāva*):
the *nāṭaka*, the *prakaraṇa*, the *bhāṇa*, the *vīthī*, and the *aṅka*. (25)
These objects of knowledge are delicate and resorted to by human beings;
this application of delicacy brings delight to kings. (26)
Having attained the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), one should employ that [dance] for women;
as for those warriors who are fierce in battle, impetuous, and full of violent agitation—[for them, it is otherwise]. 27.

Those [arts] should not be performed by women; rather, they should be performed by men, consisting of combat involving piercing and cutting, as well as the execution of limb-movements according to the prescribed rules. (28)

Now, one might object: "Is there not, then, a corresponding *prakṛti* (nature) regarding the hero (*puruṣa*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Created by those exultant in battle and pierced" (verse 10). The word "applications" (*prayogāḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject.
They are "created"—that is, pervaded—by those who are exultant in battle and by those who are pierced; for this very reason, they are characterized primarily by fury (*saṃrambha*).

[The styles] beginning with *ārabhaṭī*. He states that the meaning of "the roles of woman and man" (*strīpuruṣabhūmikā*) is pervasive by saying "not prominent" (*anudbhaṭa*, verse 19). To define the corresponding nature (*prakṛti*), he says "for a woman" (*striyā hi*). He defines [the nature] as both conforming to and not conforming to the performer by saying "pertaining to man and woman" (*puruṣastrīgata*). Where...

Just as Sāṃkṛtyāyinī exists by assuming the state of a man, so too [gender] does not apply everywhere; this is the meaning. By saying "the woman is employed by the man," he shows that it is applicable everywhere, using the word "at will" (*chandataḥ*).
Regarding the terms "old man" and "child": since these are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*), they imply their respective correlates; thus, "old man" [implies a young man].

A youth should not be employed in the role of an elder, nor should a fool be employed in the role of one who is deformed; this is an illustration. The meaning is that wherever a particular purpose is not applicable, one should not be employed there. Regarding "the application of recitation" (*pāṭhyaprayoga*): it refers to that which is dominated by the recitation of Sanskrit.
"In one where the performance of *sukumāra* (delicate) Prakrit recitation predominates" means in a performance where song (*gīta*) predominates.
He states the reason for this: "For the most part, nature [is such]" (*prāyaḥ prakṛtiḥ*). Regarding the verse "The powerful ones" (verse 17):
they possess deep voices suitable for filling the stage. Now, one might object: do not men also experience emotions (*bhāvayanti*)?
Anticipating the objection as to how it can be said that [this] is the nature of women, he says: "Even though the man...
(verse 17).
It is full of illusion and sorcery, illuminated by the costumes and attire of men.
It was frequented mostly by men, with few women, and was moreover boisterous. || 29 ||
The dramatic performance known as Āviddha is characterized by the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī styles;
likewise, there are the Ḍima, the Samavakāra, the Vyāyoga, and the Ihāmṛga. (30)
These should be known as "pierced" (āviddha) by practitioners;
their application should be performed by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas. (31)
And those men who are haughty, yet endowed with heroism and valor— for them,
that appropriate effort must always be performed with vigilance.

Anticipating the objection that the reverse is also observed, he says "at least the ornaments" (verse 19). This means that [the reverse] occurs only occasionally. In this regard, he shows that the method which imitates the practice of women and men is the most prevalent one, by saying "generally" (verse 19). This [method] is characterized by women as being employed through the nature of men.
[The examples] have been composed and are to be employed. Here he shows the restatement [of the rule] with the words "in the case of Rambhā, Urvaśī, and so forth.

He states the reason for this: "it is to be taught" (*upadeṣṭavyam*). The meaning is that it is capable of being taught. The word "by oneself" (*svayam*) refers to men; here, "application" (*nyāsa*) means usage (*prayoga*).
Now, one might object that even a man, relying on the perception of aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*), might harbor such a doubt; therefore, he states another reason with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
Furthermore, an object associated with a person appears exceedingly charming. Thus he says:
"That is the ornament" (verse 24). This refers to what was stated previously by the words beginning with "not prominent" (*anudbhaṭa*) and "exultant in battle" (*yuddhoddhata*).

By dividing the two types of performance according to their respective forms, he demonstrates through the passage beginning with "nāṭakam" that the *tadrūpaka* (the form corresponding to the drama) is appropriate when accompanied by performance (*saprayoga*). Through these seven verses beginning with "śauryavīryasamanvitāḥ," it is stated that for the most part, the nature of women is suited to song (*geya*), whereas for men, the rule is recitation (*pāṭhya*).

In this regard, having raised the objection as to what purpose there could be for the practice of *guṇanikā* (repetition) initiated by the master of dramatic arts (*nāṭyācārya*) when the matter is already established, he says: "The refinement through music" (*saṃgītaparikleśa*). Sweetness is natural.
For without skill, there can be no excellence whatsoever in the essence of aesthetic flavor;
thus, the constant labor involved in music is truly a virtue for women.
That sweetness and firmness which women attain through the practice of drama,
and that manifold beauty which they acquire through dramatic charms— by these means she becomes skilled in the arts of love and especially desirable. (34)
Singing, dancing, instrumental music, the performance of ritual expansions, and the training of disciples are remembered as the six qualities of an Ācārya. || 35 ||

Roughness and the presence of obstacles arise from practicing the arts repeatedly. Now, for the purpose of encouraging the practice of drama (*nāṭya*), he says: "A woman [should be employed] with dramatic charms.
It has been stated that the wise should not personally undertake the assignment of roles (*bhūmikā-nyāsa*) in a drama; regarding that:

In response to the doubt—"Does a master of dramatic performance (nāṭyācārya) know [this], by which he is called 'wise'?"—he says "song, dance," and so forth. The meaning is: one who knows the musical notes (svara), one skilled in the fourfold instrumental music (caturvidhātodya) including the performance of *agrahāra* (vocal ornamentation), one who knows rhythm (tāla), and one who understands how to benefit the world. The meaning is that [such a person] does not obtain [the status of a sage]. Following that, there is the section on *ūha* (inference/reasoning) and so forth.
They are called "qualities" (guṇas) because they bring about that which is most excellent; thus they are described with distinction. *Ūha* is the conceptualization of what has not been stated;
*apoha* is the following of what has not been stated. *Pratibhā* is the manifestation in the form of a prior intuition;
*smṛti* is the non-forgetting of what has been taught; *medhā* is the immediate grasping of what has been taught.

The meaning is that the training of disciples and the effort to proclaim their virtues do not flourish unless the instruction is suited to the disposition of the disciples. Regarding "attachment" (*rāga*): it refers to a practice characterized by an absence of concern for personal gain and a commitment that exceeds mere competition in the arts.
He who knows these five is proclaimed as an *ācārya*: namely, *ūha* (reasoning), *apoha* (elimination), *mati* (intellect), *smṛti* (memory), and likewise *medhā* (retentive power). (36)
Intelligence, memory, praise of virtues, passion, emulation, and enthusiasm—these six alone are known as the qualities of a disciple. (37)
Thus should the differentiation of various levels be performed by those skilled in application.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the accomplishments as well. (38)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of Temperaments," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
[The section on] Rivalry. Concluding this and introducing the next chapter, he says "Thus" (evam). And regarding "from here onwards" (ata ūrdhvam):

although there are two types of accomplishments (siddhi), they are said to be "of the accomplishments" (siddhīnām) because of their multiplicity due to internal subdivisions. May there be auspiciousness!
In this chapter on the conceptualization of primordial nature (*prakṛti-vikalpa*),
Abhinavagupta— acting as a bee at the lotus feet of the Three-eyed Lord (*Viṣamalocana*)— has composed this examination of difficult passages.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, on the Varieties of Temperament (*prakṛti-vikalpa*), in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Bhāratīyanāṭya-veda*, composed by the illustrious Great Śaiva Master (*Mahāmāheśvarācārya*) Abhinavagupta.
Śrī Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter Twenty-Seven.

(The Indicator of Success): I shall now declare the characteristics of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) based on drama, because this entire performance has been presented for the sake of attaining success. (1)
Success should be known to be of two kinds, arising from speech, mind, and body;
it is both divine and human, originating from various states of being. || 2 ||
Abhinavabhāratī— Chapter Twenty-Seven:

I bow to Him who bears half of the Daughter of the Mountain, who brings about perfection through His own wisdom within the stainless stage of *sattva*, which is divided by the distinctions between the divine and the human.

In this regard, it has been stated that for one who desires success (*siddhi*), whatever [gesture] is to be employed in whatever [context] according to the performance— this applies to all gestures (*abhinaya*) up until their successful accomplishment. This was taught in the seventh chapter on the gestures of the minor limbs (*upāṅga-abhinaya*), following the sequence of the general gestures.

Thus, it has been shown that even the general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*), which consists of the unification through the coordination of [individual] gestures (*abhinaya*), has as its fruit only success. In the chapter on various types of acting, it is said: "Indeed, these acts of acting—which arise from speech, costume, and the limbs—must be performed by one who knows the practical application (*prayoga*) in a drama, if he desires success."
In the verse from that very same [work], *Nāṭyaśāstra* 6.10, "rasas and bhāvas...," the attainment (*siddhi*) was indicated; now,
there must be a desire to know what this so-called "attainment" is,
and with that intention, it has been shown at the end of the chapter in the subsequent passage.
Human accomplishment has ten components, while divine accomplishment is traditionally held to be twofold:
that produced by relying on various sentient beings, and that born of speech, gesture, and body. (3)
Smitāpahāsinī, Hāsā, Sādhu, Aho, Kaṣṭa, and Prabaddhanādā— thus is the accomplishment consisting of speech (vāṅmayī siddhi) to be known.
Physical perfection is desired through horripilation, bristling of the body hair, rising from one's seat, as well as by the gift of garments and the gesture of snapping the fingers. || 5 ||
When a slight residue of rasa is joined with dancing, it is called *hāsya* (the comic);
this should always be received by the spectators with a smile.
Whatever is slightly humorous, as well as speech that is likewise [humorous], should always be understood by the spectators through its underlying meaning. (7)

"Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the *siddhis* as well. In this context, what is called *siddhi* is the accomplishment of a purpose that was previously unattainable; and this pertains both to the actors and to the audience.
Anticipating the question of which of these two should be discussed, he says:

"I shall now declare the characteristics of the *siddhis* (accomplishments) as they relate to drama. The particle "tu" (but/now) indicates a distinction. Although the characteristics of the *siddhis* ought to be stated both as they relate to the audience and as they relate to the drama, I shall speak only of those relating to the actor (*naṭa*), and not the other. Here, "drama" (*nāṭaka*) refers to...
The etymology of "naṭa" is indeed "one who dances. Anticipating the question, "Why then is the other [meaning] not mentioned? he says:
303) "That which is produced by the destruction of the *vidūṣaka* and that which is produced by artistic skill (*śilpa*)."
But that should always be grasped by the spectators with great laughter.
Likewise, pride should be understood as arising from the nature of men;
it is that which is associated with the state of dharma and arises from excellence.
In that regard, the word "sādhu" (well done) should indeed be employed by practitioners when there is a state of being overcome with wonder, and for the purpose of expressing great joy. (10)
In the *karuṇa* [rasa] as well, a difficult [intonation] produced by the treatise should be employed;
likewise, a continuous sound (*prabaddhanādā*) is always used for matters of wonder (*vismaya*). (11)
In the presence of words containing reproach,
one should win them over with great respect, accompanied by horripilation and eyes wide with curiosity.
"For this entire ritual application has been demonstrated for the sake of accomplishment" (27.1).

Thus, the phrase "the ritual application which is for the sake of the accomplishment of the assembly members" finds its rest in the qualifying portion [of the compound]. This is like the statement from the *Daṇḍin-preṣa*: "Those wearing red turbans proceed," as in the case of the distinction of injunctions (*vidhi-vivakṣā*).

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as a performance is purposeful through its accomplishment (siddhi) when it is for the sake of the audience, so too, since the origin of drama was intended for that very purpose, the Vedic practice—such as the injunction that "this [Veda] should not be recited among the Śūdra castes"—is not applicable here, because the performance is shown to have been directed toward that end; thus, that accomplishment has already been demonstrated previously.
The supreme accomplishment that follows as an inseparable consequence of employing that [means] is demonstrated by this chapter.
This is what is meant: first, for the sake of the audience...
Whatever action takes place in a blazing region—consisting of cutting, piercing, and combat;
involving flight or exultation; and arising from battle or wrestling. (13)
With shoulders and head trembling, with tears, and even while rising up—
this [state] must be treated by skilled observers according to the prescribed method.
Thus should this human accomplishment (siddhi) be achieved by those who know it;
furthermore, I shall now explain the divine accomplishment according to its true nature.
That which is endowed with excellence of being and likewise possessed of essence—
such divine accomplishment (daivī siddhi) should be brought about by the spectators through their application.
There is no sound, no agitation, and no appearance of portents;
and the completeness of the performance—this is remembered as divine success (daivī siddhi). || 17 ||

Success (*siddhi*) is characterized by the attainment of a desired fruit (*saṃhitaphalāpti*). That it is of the nature of rice and so forth, as in the passage "attaining [it] among rice and other grains," has already been established in that context. Furthermore, because it is intended for human beings, it is called "human" (*mānuṣī*); yet even there, he is not conjoined with it in the same way [as described below].
The female celibate student (brahmacāriṇī) whose nature consists in the manifestation of her own supreme bliss free from objects attains the state of the Supreme Brahman;
for the object of the Gītā and so forth— being submerged through its role as an embellishment within the drama— is equal to the object [of ordinary experience] for the actor and others.

Because Rāma and the others have been sublated, because they are insubstantial, and because they are rendered objects [of experience] precisely through the absence of spatial and temporal constraints— and since their impossibility has been established here—
that very element of accomplishment constitutes the state of being the fundamental nature of all aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) for the pacification of destiny (*daiva-śānti*).
(305) This success, both divine and human, has been declared by me.
Hereafter, I shall explain the calamities arising from fate. || 18 ||
The wise should understand that afflictions are of three kinds: those arising from fate, from oneself, and from others;
occasionally, a fourth type, arising from portents, may occur among these. (19)
The collapse of pavilions caused by wind, fire, rain, elephants, or serpents, as well as the entry of insects, snakes, ants, or wild beasts, are all brought about by fate. (20)
Next, I shall fully describe the symptoms of those joined with the supreme [poison]:
discoloration, lack of movement, confusion, and loss of memory. (21)
"Furthermore, irrelevant speech, poetic flaws,
and physical agitation— these self-originated defects are to be recognized by those skilled in performance.
(22) For those who maintain that "rasa arises from the *sthāyibhāva* upon encountering its respective cause," this [definition] is indeed appropriate.
This is because there is a clear compliance [with the rules], and because the secret meaning of the scripture is intended for something else. As it was said by Bhaṭṭanāyaka:
"When the primary part has attained success, the subsidiary elements of its performance follow as a consequence."
In the same way, these [other genres] such as the *geya* and so forth are useful for him in three ways.
And that [ladder] consists of a series of steps leading toward the touch of liberation;
since it is the means by which one is liberated, how could the sages call it "secret" in any other sense?
For they would indeed reveal it in the treatise for the purpose of establishing the measurement of the *tāla*. Thus [it is said].
p.

306) Whether out of stinginess or hatred, or because of siding with that [side], or likewise because of a difference in purpose—these harms arising from others should always be recognized by the wise. (23)
Excessive laughing, weeping, bursting [of objects], and the overturning of water-jars, as well as the scattering of cow-dung, clods of earth, and ants, arise from the presence of enemies. (24)
There are also sudden calamities caused by signs appearing when one enters while intoxicated or not intoxicated;
furthermore, I shall describe those various calamities that arise from oneself. || 25 ||
Unusualness, lack of mastery over one's movements, loss of memory, speaking incoherently, as well as poetic utterances, distressed cries, and agitation; || 26 ||
Excessive laughter, weeping, distorted sounds, the cries of ants, insects, and animals;
the falling of crowns and ornaments; and the defects of poetry arising from the *puṣkara* [musical instrument]—these are [inauspicious]. || 27 ||

However, as for that manifest portion of divine accomplishment characterized by the attainment of human goals, that too has already been demonstrated by [the passage beginning] "Dharma is for those engaged in dharma; desire is for those who indulge in desire" (Nāṭyaśāstra 1.109).
Therefore, it need not be stated that accomplishment depends upon the audience.

Regarding its definition, it is said: "It is correctly and pre-eminently manifested. As for the actor, that accomplishment characterized by the successful completion of the correct performance is the "accomplishment of performance" (*prayogasiddhi*), which is essential; for without the successful completion of performance, there is no drama itself—how could it exist? And this successful completion of performance...
The perfection of the general representation itself is attained; however, in the ultimate sense,

it is called "human" because it was previously produced by humans, whether through the power of the cognition of the manifestation of the fundamental nature arising from the varying degrees of another's encouragement, or through the majesty of one's own innate intuition (*pratibhāna*).

The banner [is raised] due to an excellence of accomplishment (siddhyatiśaya). But if there is no excellence anywhere, then how is it so? He says: the word "iti" is to be supplied. With the intention that drama, which has this or that rasa as its primary element, gives rise to rasa at various times, he says "place and time" (deśakālau). The reading is in the *nepathya* (backstage); that which is to be performed...

Because he knows [it], it is called "yoga"; thus its inclusion is within that which is to be accomplished by the vessel (*pātra*). For the vessel is indeed that which has entered into the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). When [the factors] are fully assembled...
Regarding the adornment of purity, however, the variegated arrangement of garlands, ornaments, and garments is designated as "abundance" (samṛddhi). || 102 ||
O best of the twice-born, when all these ornaments are combined and become one, that is the characteristic of the *siddhis* as described by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the classification of musical instruments (*ātodya*).
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Accomplishment," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

By this, he speaks of the nature of general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*). Indeed, that very subject has been explained through five chapters. It was stated [previously] that it is like the origin of drama, ending with the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite). And he will say later: "the ornament" (*alaṅkāra*).
The meaning is that it possesses an extreme degree of splendor and fullness.
With the words "from here onwards" (104) and so forth, he indicates what remains to be said. May there be auspiciousness!
He who was known by the name Sukhalābha, purified by learning and also bearing the other name Nṛsiṃhagupta,
was joined with the sciences of the body by him.
He accomplished the practice that brings about great purpose.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Accomplishment (*siddhyadhyāya*), in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭyaveda*, composed by the venerable Kashmiri Great Maheshvara teacher, Abhinavaguptācārya.
