Chapter Thirty-three (ṇ).
Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of the *prakṛtis* (heroines) and, in accordance with reality, those of all four types of *nāyakas* (heroes).
In brief, the nature of women and men is proclaimed to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling. (2)
In drama, these four alone are proclaimed as the heroes, characterized by various attributes within a middle class of nature. (3)

The heroes (nāyakas) based on drama are the bold-and-arrogant (dhīroddhata), the playful (lalita), and the calm-and-resolute (dhīrapraśānta). Gods are to be known as bold-and-arrogant, while kings are playful-and-resolute.
The sages, as well as the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) and so forth, are proclaimed to be the "noble and exalted" (dhīrodātta);
while guests and merchants are said to be the "calm and composed" (dhīrapraśānta). || 5 ||
Furthermore, it should be known that there are four types of these [companions], namely the Vidūṣakas;
they are always to be understood as being like the Nāyaka in poetic compositions. (6)
Furthermore, I shall describe the four types of heroines:
the Brahmin woman, the king’s wife, the woman of noble family, and likewise the courtesan.
These heroines are to be known by their various temperaments and characteristics:
the steadfast (dhīrā), the graceful (lalitā), the noble (udāttā), and likewise the modest (nibhṛtā). || 8 ||
For these celestial women born from the limbs [of the gods] are indeed said to be endowed with virtues;
however, a woman born of noble lineage should be both exalted and modest.

The courtesan and the artisan are said to possess the *udātta* (noble) and *lalita* (graceful) styles; furthermore, it should be understood that for the *madhyā* (intermediate) woman, the qualities are mixed and common (*prākṛta*). || 10 ||
The neuter (napuṃsaka) should also be known as mixed and indeed base;
likewise the Śakāra, the servant (ceṭa), and whatever other men are base. (11)
O best of the twice-born, these should also be understood as mixed types in drama;
they are to be known by nature as male, female, or neuter.
I shall now describe the classification of these very [types] according to the characteristics of their conduct;
for all natures (prakṛtis), however, two types are traditionally taught. (13)
In that regard, whoever belongs to the internal royal service should be known as being inside; whoever belongs to the external royal service should be known as being outside. || 14 ||
Therefore, regarding the royal services, I shall again explain the inner quarters, the classification of women, and likewise the conduct [of service]. (15)
The Great Queen, likewise the Goddess, the Mistress, the Residing One, the Sister, the Artisan, the Dramatic Actress, and the Dancer. || 16 ||
Likewise the attendant, the one so engaged, the female servant, the one who moves about, and the one who carries out errands. || 17 ||
The chief female doorkeeper, the maidens, the elderly women, and the appointed attendants—this is the inner circle of the kings. (18)
In that regard, the wise should recognize [a woman] who is adorned with noble family and good conduct, who is of equal age and status, and who is free from anger. (19)
Free from envy toward the king’s person, always equal in joy and sorrow, she constantly desired peace, well-being, and prosperity for her husband. (20)
Devoted to her husband, endowed with forbearance, and intent on the welfare of the inner apartments—one possessed of these qualities is proclaimed a Mahādevī. (21)
(323) Endowed with these very same qualities, yet devoid of great respect, the princess was honored [by others] and intent upon the cessation of sexual enjoyment. (22)
She who is eternally youthful, possessing the qualities of her lineage, yet envious toward her rival, and intoxicated by the virtues of youth and so forth—she is called the Goddess. (23)
The [deities] designated as Svāni and so forth preside over the army commander, the ministers, the staff-bearers, those devoted to them, and the lords of sons. 24.
Endowed with the qualities of virtue and beauty, she is beloved by the king;
born from a family of noble masters, she is indeed remembered as the *svāminī*. (25)
Endowed with beauty and youth, she was both harsh and graceful; skilled in the enjoyment of pleasure, she was envious of her rivals. (26)
She should be skillful, excellent, radiant, adorned with perfumes, garlands, and ointments; she should act according to the king's will and be entirely free from envy. || 27 ||
She is ever-present, vigilant, and exceedingly eloquent; indeed, she is not harsh. Known as Mālyā, she is an expert in the selection of garlands and is celebrated as Sthāyinī. || 28 ||
She who is virtuous, receives honor, is gentle, impartial, composed, and patient is known as the "enjoyer" (bhoginī). || 29 ||
They were experts in various specialized arts, skilled in diverse crafts,
knowledgeable in the preparation of perfumes and flowers, and proficient in both painting and sculpture.
She was skilled in the knowledge of beds, seats, and vehicles; she was clever, sweet-voiced, dexterous, full of discernment, and a performer of [virtuous] deeds.

She should be known as one who possesses the tempos (laya) mentioned first, is endowed with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva), understands the primary and secondary emotional states, and likewise follows the instructions of her teacher. || 32 ||
She was skilled in the four modes of dramatic representation, adept at reasoning and refutation,
proficient in instrumental music, and possessed the pride of being a dancer. (33)
She who follows the king in his movements while remaining in a state of virtuous being should be known as a true attendant of the king. (34)
She was appointed to the treasury and likewise to the armory; she was occupied with medicinal herbs, fruits, and roots, as well as with the preparation of remedies. || 35 ||
She was skilled in the application of perfumes, ornaments, and garments, as well as in narrative tales and wealth;
likewise in the use of parasols, beds, and seats, and in the work of fanning; she was proficient in massaging, the art of perfuming, and personal adornment.
Likewise, O King, she who is to be known by name as a *paricārikā* is she who attends to the fastening of ornaments and the arrangement of garlands. (38)
She knew the arrangement of various courtyards, as well as the movement through the wind-paths; she sported in the temples of the deities and wandered through the palaces. (39)
Those who are appointed to the watches and likewise have various roles are to be known by those skilled in drama as *saṃcārikās* (female messengers) according to conventional usage.
That which is employed by the wise through expedients connected with desire, arising from both the secret and the non-secret, should be known as *praghanakārikā*.
That affection which is expressed through blessings, auspicious rites,
and the like, and which one constantly celebrates, should be known as the greatest.
Those who report various matters arising in connection with peace and war are known as *pratīhārīs*. (43)
They have not yet attained the union of sexual pleasure, they are modest and not ostentatious;
being conversant with the customs of former kings, they are honored among all kings.
Those who knew the conduct of former kings were designated as "the elders. || 45 ||

Those for whom the application of the definition of *niyoga* is entirely successful, and who are beyond verbal expression both in their applications and likewise in their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (46)

For they are unassuming, unperturbed, free from envy, devoted to knowledge and other virtues, patient, self-controlled, of excellent character, having conquered anger, and having mastered their senses. (47)
Free from desire, modest, and devoid of feminine anger,
she should be employed in her duties, being honored and free from pride.
That which is a neuter name is the third nature;
she too should be employed in the movement within the inner apartments and in the stable residence.
The bath-graduates (snātakas), the chamberlains (kañcukīyas), as well as those eunuchs (varṣavaras);
there should be two [of each], along with the Śakāra and the courtyard guards (kakṣyārakṣaka). || 50 ||
But those men who are not male, being devoid of feminine traits—
these were appointed as attendants in the inner apartments for their specific duties.
One should perform the placement within the site while engaged in the practice of sitting;
in matters concerning journeys, one should employ chamberlains.
Likewise, he should also appoint the eunuchs (*varṣavara*), who,
being exempt from personal attendance, are instead employed for the purpose of issuing commands.
One should employ attendants for the duties of honor regarding women; one should station those who have been trained in the observation of all activities within the theater.
And for one's own desired undertaking, those aged nine years are prescribed as the best. || 55 ||
The Śākya people have perished; they are devoid of the qualities of men and women.
They should be known by name as "shaven-headed," being destitute of both desire and discernment. (56)
Those Brahmins who are free from the performance of desires and are skilled in theoretical and practical knowledge are known as Kañcukīyas. || 57 ||
Thus, this eighteenfold inner apartment has been described by me;
hereafter, I shall explain the movement of external persons.
Likewise, the ministers, counselors, and those appointed to administrative duties. || 59 ||
These and many other similar stars belong to the king;
I shall describe their divisions and their individual characteristics one by one.
Virtuous, endowed with success, truthful in speech, and having conquered his senses;
he was skillful, bold, possessed of mindfulness, courageous, and of matchless luster.
Far-sighted, possessed of great energy, grateful, and pleasant of speech;
observing the vows of the world-protectors, he was heroic, steadfast, and endowed with patience. (62)
He is industrious and vigilant, skilled in serving his elders and in counsel;
he understands the prevalence of various dangers, knows the secrets [of the state], and is discerning. (63)

He understands the characteristics of others' dispositions, is adorned with the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya), knows the true meaning of various scriptures, and is an expert in the application of various arts and crafts. || 64 ||

The king should be knowledgeable of the proper place, the intellect, and the decline [of his enemies], skilled in perceiving the vulnerabilities of others, grateful, well-disposed, and endowed with virtuous qualities. (65)
He is well-versed in song and instrumental music, free from laziness, and speaks kindly;
he knows how to discover the vulnerabilities of others and understands the specific requirements of time for military expeditions. (66)

For he who knows the true meaning of the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), is loyal, of noble birth, and possesses knowledge of the country and the time, is endowed with all the qualities of a commander-in-chief. (67)
He was endowed with the wisdom of the six political expedients and was proficient in the Vedas and the rules of statecraft;
likewise, the members of his assembly were devoted, pure, and righteous. (68)
Indeed, ministers and counselors become possessed of virtues; they are wise, discerning, and know the true principles of legal and practical affairs. (69)
Indeed, those who are learned, virtuous, and discerning regarding what ought and ought not to be done, come to possess these qualities in various forms. (70)
By the command of Bṛhaspati, it is to be understood by those skilled in ritual action that this [text] is the manifestor of the qualities of the members of the assembly during their duties.
It is said that drama always arises from the highest qualities; how then can the qualities of a king be enacted by dramas with limited resources? (72)
To this it is replied: when the dramatic conventions were set forth in the world, at that very moment this drama, complete in every respect, was created by me. (73)
Accompanied by the cutting of colors and other such techniques, and adorned with ornaments,
no one else could ever be a true actor unless he possessed both depth and a sense of humor.
Suppose there were some single man here who possessed the seven continents as his domain;
even by him, the task must be performed here according to the principles of reality. (75)
The preceptor Brahmā was peaceful, honored for his excellence and his physical attributes; and because he shone forth from that rain, [the world flourished].
As is the actor, so is the king; as is the king, so is the actor.
Because the realization of the dramatic emotion arises from both, their excellence of limbs in play is equal.
Just as an actor becomes beautiful through the instruction of a master, so too should a king always be eloquent by nature. (78)
(328) For that indeed is the supreme conduct of kings;
thus, a drama should be performed, endowed with appropriate dress, speech, and action. (79)
Whatever form belongs to anyone by nature, that very form should be adopted by one desiring to employ [the ritual] according to the rules for age and place. (80)
In this manner, the gathering of men should be conducted with royal protocol;
hereafter, I shall explain the various characteristics of men.
The light of various moral virtues—superior, inferior, and middling—is to be understood therein; the practitioner is likewise to be known individually according to their respective natures. (82)

They were accomplished in various arts, possessed of wisdom, and had conquered their senses; they were experts in the composition of verses, specialists in particular sciences, and discerning in all matters of dharma. || 83 ||

Those who are knowledgeable in the scriptures, history, and the ways of the world, who are firmly established in moral conduct and behavior, and who undertake actions preceded by careful deliberation, are traditionally regarded as the highest by nature. (84)
Those who understand the divisions of worldly conventions, who desire to speak of the arts and sciences, and who possess the qualities of wine and meat by nature, are known as the middling. || 85 ||
They are speakers of subtle words, of evil conduct, devoid of courage, and of little intelligence; they are wrathful, murderers, ungrateful, and fickle in their views. || 86 ||
They are addicted to futile undertakings, trivial speakers of whatever comes to mind, petty-minded, backbiters, devoted to evil, lustful for women, and fond of quarreling. (87)
And thieves are ignorant of the specific varieties of garlands;
being possessed of these faults, they are considered by nature to be base. (88)
Thus, the wise should understand that nature is threefold according to one's conduct;
hereafter, I shall explain the virtues and faults of those who employ it. (89)
329) Therein, we shall describe the qualities of the *sūtradhāra*. First of all, he must possess knowledge of the characteristics [of performance].
For upon him depends the refinement of speech, as well as the knowledge of the rules for the timing of song and the vocal registers (*svara*). Furthermore, [he must know] the musical instruments.

And he possesses knowledge of reality. He is skilled in the four types of musical instruments, established in the practice of the sciences, knowledgeable in the performance of various artistic crafts, and a knower of the true meaning of the treatises on ethics. (90)

Skilled in the service of courtesans, expert in the preparation of meat dishes, knowledgeable in the movements of various social classes, and proficient in the expression of aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and emotional states (bhāva). || 91 ||
Skilled in the performance of drama, endowed with various arts and crafts, knowing the principles of prosody and ritual procedures, and proficient in all the sciences.

One who knows the true nature of the planets and constellations, who understands the conventions of regional dialects, and [who knows] of the earth, the continents, the regions, the mountains, and of people; 93.
He is authoritative, knows their conduct, and is well-versed in the royal lineage;
he is a listener to the meanings and duties of the scriptures, and having heard them, he is one who discerns their true significance. || 94 ||
One who has mastered [the text], is capable of application, and is likewise a traveler in the teaching—such a person, possessing these qualities, is ordained as an Ācārya and a Sūtradhāra. (95)
And learn from me as I speak of his innate qualities:
he is mindful, wise, heroic, noble, courageous, and a seer.
He is free from disease, sweet-natured, patient, self-controlled, and well-born;
he is liberated from the faults of intoxication, truthful in speech, and likewise upright.
He should be free from greed, capable of receiving instruction, and endowed with natural virtues;
he should also possess the qualities of a stage director and be fully conversant with the dramatic sentiments.
The middling one, who is of ordinary nature, should be recognized by those who know [the art] as the *pāripārśvika* (attendant).
They are radiant, handsome, and their actions and instruments are clearly visible. || 99 ||
Intelligent, knowledgeable in the rules, skilled in their own tasks, and steadfast—
all the performers are endowed with the qualities of a stage director. (100)
A *viṭa* (libertine) should be skilled in the arts of courtesans, sweet-spoken, clever, a poet, capable of reasoning and counter-reasoning, eloquent, and dexterous. (101)
Wearing bright garments and ornaments, he becomes angry without cause and is easily appeased; this low-born Śakāra, who speaks the Māgadhī dialect, is full of many transformations.
Dwarfed, buck-toothed, hunchbacked, twice-born, and imaginative;
bald and with tawny eyes—he is to be appointed as the Vidūṣaka. (103)
Fond of strife, engaging in much talk, and practicing separation;
such indeed are the servants known as those who distinguish between what is fit for a garland and what is not. 104.
Thus they are to be known by these qualities arising from effort, as well as others;
hereafter, I shall further describe the nature of women.
They speak with moderation, are clever, modest, and not harsh;
they know how to cultivate virtues and character, and they delight in the instructions of their teachers. (106)
Endowed with profundity and vigor, they are known as the supreme by nature;
possessing various characters, they are skilled in performance and experts in the application of drama. || 107 ||
Through his application, he was always devoted to serving the teacher, by means of the various states of being and non-being, as well as through his goodness and discipline. (108)
They were endowed with sweetness, possessed of the sixty-four arts, skilled in performing services, and free from the faults of women. (109)
Speaking kindly, engaging in pleasant conversation, being well-disposed, and having overcome fatigue—these are indeed the qualities that belong to a courtesan. (110)
She was endowed with beauty, virtue, youth, a golden complexion, sweetness, and courage;
she was radiant as fire and possessed of great sweetness, gentleness, auspiciousness, and protection. || 111 ||
The vessel and its form, tāla... [and so forth].
Thus, those who know [the subject] should fashion the heroine endowed with such qualities. (112)
Among the women assembled there, though they were endowed with youth and beauty,
not even one dancer was seen who was possessed of [such] virtues, even among thousands.
Laughing with a pure smile, liberated, and possessing a graceful gait;
having manifested playfulness, the masculine emotion (*bhāva*) of a man has departed.
Just as it corresponds to one's age, so too should that [expression] be produced by him. (114)
If one who is old in years but remains a fool in his state performs the role of a fool in a drama, that is not considered [proper] acting; it should not be done, for it is not so defined. 115.
Furthermore, whatever feminine disposition a man assumes, she should be known as a "vessel of excellence" (supātra) in form; such is her nature in performance. || 116 ||
By that very [mantra], a woman should perform the *pauruṣī* [rite] well-accomplished through its application;
at the conclusion, she should perform it for the elderly and the ignorant with the *mānavīṣṭā* [mantras].
But that which is most delicate is presided over by women of virtuous conduct;
such is the nature of the objectives for both divine and human beings. (118)
Dancing is not proclaimed as being performed by the *prakṛtis* in heaven, nor likewise in the world of men, even in the palaces of kings. (119)
Even when teaching those with physical impairments, his application [of mind] remains focused;
he becomes one who provides musical accompaniment for the people. || 120 ||
The merits and defects inherent in dramatic performances arise from these [rules].
A wise man should not employ a stage arrangement consisting solely of women for female characters. (121)
A *bhūmikā* (stage) accompanied by actions of a uniform state is intended as a *nyāsa* (placement);
likewise, a *bhūmikā* accompanied by actions of various states is [intended as] *prakṛti*.
In drama, one should illuminate the *bhiṣa* [sentiment] by relying on the natural disposition and the technical execution;
likewise, there are those with many arms, many faces, and distorted countenances. (123)
Those with the faces of beasts and wild animals, as well as those with the faces of donkeys, camels, and dogs—these and many others who possess various forms [arise]. 124.
They should be made with clay, wood, lacquer, or leather, having their movements artificially produced; one should enter the stage with a natural action.
Having completely concealed one's own true form with cosmetics and ornaments, whatever form belongs to anyone by nature remains exactly that. (126)
In the performance of drama, one should employ [the appropriate style] according to age and appearance,
just as one embraces the inherent nature of a seed and the physical body.
He who performs the state of another which is based upon his own body—thus the wise one firmly [realizes] in his mind, "I am that supreme state. (128)
One should engage in the graceful movements and gestures of the courtesans;
this practice is delicate and arises from the quality of passion (rajas). || 129 ||
Having attained the preeminent erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), one should apply it to those women who are exultant in battle, impetuous with speed, and eager for union. 130.
These [arts] should not be employed by women; they should be applied toward men in a manner that is unostentatious, composed, and without violent movements of the limbs. 131.
Endowed with a collection of light syllables, fixed in its metrical measure, with well-divided phrases and expressions, it is neither harsh nor boastful. (132)
If such a drama should occur, one should employ women [in roles] that are characterized by martial exuberance, impetuosity, agitation, and fear. (133)

These [roles] should not be performed by women, but rather by men who are experts in drama; thus should the assignment of roles (*bhūmikā*) be carried out by those who understand the application of dramatic performance. (134)
Hereafter, I shall explain the classification of the Bharatas:
the Bharata-āśraya, the Nārī, the Vidūṣaka, the Taurika, the Ānandī, the Nandī, the Sūtradhāra, the Nāṭyajña, and the Nāyaka. (135)
The crown-maker, the jeweler, the decorator, the garland-maker, the painter, and the cobbler—these, along with the artisan and the actor, are to be known by their respective names. (136)
Because a single extraction, like that of a leader, is joined with multiple stages, Bharata maintains that drama is properly constituted by the grasping of the vessel and its accessories. (137)
The worlds are fashioned upon the foundation of desire and are joined with the activity of all fundamental natures;
likewise, a woman everywhere creates various foundations. 138.
One who possesses ready wit, provides entertainment, and reveals the inner secrets of the court, whose head is adorned with a circlet—such a person is to be known as a *vidūṣaka*. || 139 ||
That man who plays all musical instruments, being skilled in the performance of instrumental music and engaged in the mastery of the *tūra*, is to be known as a *taurika*.

This term "naṭa" (actor) has the meaning of the verbal root *nṛt* (to dance); because he enacts (*nāṭayati*) the worldly events that have occurred, endowed with aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), emotions (*bhāva*), and inner states (*sattva*), he is therefore called a "naṭa. || 141 ||
Since one indeed praises the entire world with sweet words consisting of praise and salutations, and through most auspicious conducts, for that reason one should become a speaker. 142.
